Today the daughter is 1 part and the mother is 5 parts. 1 plus 5 equals 6.
Find one part. 48 divided by 6 equals 8.
Check: 8 and 40 now, 14 and 46 in 6 years. 14 plus 46 equals 60.
The daughter is 8 years old now.

G4A_AGES_037.q: The ages of two cousins multiply to give 84. The older cousin is 5 years older than the younger one. What do their two ages add up to?
hints: List the pairs of numbers that multiply to give 84. Then look for the pair with the right gap.
Some pairs are 2 and 42, 3 and 28, 4 and 21. Keep going and find the gap between the two numbers in each pair.
A similar one: two ages multiply to 40 and are 3 apart. The pairs are 1 and 40, 2 and 20, 4 and 10, 5 and 8. Only 5 and 8 are 3 apart, and they add up to 13.
steps: List the pairs that multiply to 84: 1 and 84, 2 and 42, 3 and 28, 4 and 21, 6 and 14, 7 and 12.
Find the gap in each pair: 83, 40, 25, 17, 8 and 5.
Only 7 and 12 are 5 apart. 7 times 12 equals 84.
Add the two ages. 7 plus 12 equals 19.
Their ages add up to 19 years.

G4A_AGES_038.q: Kabir's age in months is the same number as his grandfather's age in years. Their ages add up to 78 years. How old is Kabir?
hints: Change both ages to the same unit. Think about how many months make one year.
If Kabir is 1 year old he is 12 months old, so his grandfather would be 12 years old. The grandfather's age is always how many times Kabir's age?

A similar one: a girl's age in months equals her aunt's age in years, and together they are 39 years. The aunt is 12 times as old, so there are 13 parts. One part is 3, so the girl is 3 and the aunt is 36.
steps: A year has 12 months, so Kabir's age in months is 12 times his age in years. His grandfather is 12 times as old as Kabir.
Kabir is 1 part and his grandfather is 12 parts. 1 plus 12 equals 13.
Find one part. 78 divided by 13 equals 6.
Check: Kabir is 6 years, which is 72 months, and his grandfather is 72 years. 6 plus 72 equals 78.
Kabir is 6 years old.

G4A_AGES_039.q: Tara's age and her uncle's age are in the ratio 2 is to 5. Six years ago, their ages were in the ratio 1 is to 4. How old is her uncle now?
hints: Ages in the ratio 2 is to 5 could be 2 and 5, 4 and 10, 6 and 15, and so on. Test these pairs against the clue about six years ago.
Both people must be older than 6. Try 8 and 20: six years ago they were 2 and 14. Is 14 exactly 4 times 2? If not, try the next pair.

A similar one: ages in the ratio 1 is to 3 now, and 1 is to 5 four years ago. Try 6 and 18: four years ago they were 2 and 14, which is 1 is to 7. Try 8 and 24: four years ago they were 4 and 20, which is 1 is to 5. So the ages are 8 and 24.
steps: List pairs in the ratio 2 is to 5 with both ages above 6: 8 and 20, 10 and 25, 12 and 30, 14 and 35, 16 and 40.
Take 6 years off each: 2 and 14, 4 and 19, 6 and 24, 8 and 29, 10 and 34.
Look for the pair where the second is 4 times the first. Only 6 and 24 fit.
That pair comes from 12 and 30, so her uncle is 30 years old now.

G4A_ALGEBRA_001.q: Meera had p rupees. She bought 3 pencils that cost q rupees each. Which expression shows the money she has left, in rupees?
options: 3 times, open bracket, p minus q, close bracket
hints: Money left is the money she had minus the money she spent. Write the money spent as an expression first.
One pencil costs q rupees. Write the cost of 3 pencils using q, then take it away from p.
A similar one: Arun had m rupees and bought 5 erasers at n rupees each. The erasers cost 5 n rupees, so he has m minus 5 n rupees left.
steps: One pencil costs q rupees, so 3 pencils cost 3 times q, which is 3 q rupees.
Money left equals money she had minus money she spent.
So the money left is p minus 3 q rupees.

G4A_ALGEBRA_002.q: In a cricket match a team scored r runs in the first innings. In the second innings it scored 40 runs fewer. Which expression shows the total runs in both innings?
hints: Write an expression for each innings, then add the two expressions together.
The first innings is r. The second innings is 40 fewer than r. Write that with a minus sign.
A similar one: a shop sold k kites on Monday and 15 more on Tuesday. Tuesday is k plus 15, so the total is k plus k plus 15, which is 2 k plus 15.
steps: First innings: r runs.
Second innings: 40 fewer, so r minus 40 runs.
Add the two innings: r plus r minus 40. The two r terms make 2 r.
The total is 2 r minus 40.

G4A_ALGEBRA_003.q: Simplify: 7 A plus 3 b minus 2 A plus b.
hints: Only like terms can be put together. Collect the terms with A, and separately the terms with b.
The A terms are 7 A and minus 2 A. The b terms are 3 b and b. Remember that b on its own means 1 b.
A similar one: 4 x plus 2 y plus 3 x minus y. The x terms give 7 x and the y terms give 2 y minus y equals y. The result is 7 x plus y.
steps: Collect the A terms: 7 A minus 2 A equals 5 A.
Collect the b terms: 3 b plus b equals 4 b, because b means 1 b.
The A terms and b terms are unlike, so they stay separate.
The simplified expression is 5 A plus 4 b.

G4A_ALGEBRA_004.q: The odd numbers in order are 1, 3, 5, 7, and so on. Which expression gives the nth odd number?
hints: A good rule must fit every position, not just the first. Test each expression with n equals 1, n equals 2 and n equals 3.
The 1st odd number is 1, the 2nd is 3 and the 3rd is 5. Compare them with the even numbers 2, 4, 6 in the same positions.
A similar one: the numbers 5, 10, 15, and so on, are given by 5 n. The numbers 4, 9, 14, and so on, are each one less, so they are given by 5 n minus 1.
steps: The even numbers 2, 4, 6, 8, and so on, are 2 times their position, so the nth even number is 2 n.
Each odd number 1, 3, 5, 7, and so on, is one less than the even number in the same position.
Check with n equals 4: 2 times 4 is 8, and one less is 7, the 4th odd number.
The nth odd number is 2 n minus 1.

G4A_ALGEBRA_005.q: An isosceles triangle has two equal sides of 2 A plus 3 centimetres each. Its third side is A minus 2 centimetres. What is the perimeter of the triangle?
hints: The perimeter is the sum of all three sides. An isosceles triangle has two sides that are the same, so one expression is added twice.
Write the three sides in a row: 2 A plus 3, 2 A plus 3, and A minus 2. Collect the A terms first, then the plain numbers.

A similar one: equal sides of x plus 4 centimetres each and a third side of x minus 1 centimetres. The x terms give 3 x and the numbers give 4 plus 4 minus 1 equals 7. The perimeter is 3 x plus 7 centimetres.
steps: Add the three sides: 2 A plus 3, plus 2 A plus 3, plus A minus 2.
Collect the A terms: 2 A plus 2 A plus A equals 5 A.
Collect the numbers: 3 plus 3 minus 2 equals 4.
The perimeter is 5 A plus 4 centimetres.

G4A_ALGEBRA_006.q: A rectangular garden is p metres long and q metres wide. One long side is along a wall, so a fence is put only on the other three sides. What is the length of the fence?
hints: Picture the four sides of the rectangle: two long sides and two short sides. Decide which sides get a fence.
The wall takes the place of one long side of p metres. The fence covers the other long side and both short sides.
A similar one with numbers: a pen is 9 metres long and 4 metres wide with one long side against a wall. The fence is 9 plus 4 plus 4, which is 17 metres.
steps: A rectangle has two long sides of p metres and two short sides of q metres.
One long side is the wall, so the fence covers one long side and two short sides.
Add them: p plus q plus q.
The length of the fence is p plus 2 q metres.

G4A_ALGEBRA_007.q: If A equals 6 and b equals 4, what is the value of 3 A minus 2 b plus A b?
hints: Put the numbers in place of the letters. Two letters written side by side, or a number next to a letter, mean multiply.
Work out each part on its own: 3 A means 3 times 6, 2 b means 2 times 4, and A b means 6 times 4.
A similar one: if A equals 2 and b equals 5, then 4 A minus b plus A b is 8 minus 5 plus 10, which is 13.
steps: 3 A means 3 times A. 3 times 6 equals 18.
2 b means 2 times b. 2 times 4 equals 8.
A b means A times b. 6 times 4 equals 24.
Put the parts together. 18 minus 8 plus 24 equals 34.
The value is 34.

G4A_ALGEBRA_008.q: The nth odd number is 2 n minus 1 and the nth even number is 2 n. How much more is the 30th odd number than the 12th even number?
hints: Use each rule to find the actual number first. Then subtract the smaller from the greater.
For the 30th odd number put n equals 30 into 2 n minus 1. For the 12th even number put n equals 12 into 2 n.
A similar one: the 10th odd number is 2 times 10, minus 1, which is 19. The 6th even number is 12. The difference is 19 minus 12, which is 7.
steps: The 30th odd number: put n equals 30 into 2 n minus 1. 2 times 30, minus 1, equals 59.
The 12th even number: put n equals 12 into 2 n. 2 times 12 equals 24.
Subtract. 59 minus 24 equals 35.
The 30th odd number is 35 more.

G4A_ALGEBRA_009.q: Anu is x years old. Her father's age is 4 years more than three times Anu's age. What will be the sum of their ages after 5 years?
hints: Write each person's age now as an expression. After some years, every person is older by that many years.
Three times Anu's age is 3 x, so her father is 3 x plus 4 now. In 5 years, both of them will be 5 years older.
A similar one: Ravi is y years old and his mother is 20 more than twice his age, which is 2 y plus 20. After 3 years they are y plus 3 and 2 y plus 23, and the sum is 3 y plus 26.
steps: Father's age now: three times x and 4 more, which is 3 x plus 4.
After 5 years Anu is x plus 5 and her father is 3 x plus 4 plus 5, which is 3 x plus 9.
Add: x plus 5 plus 3 x plus 9. The x terms make 4 x and the numbers make 14.
The sum of their ages will be 4 x plus 14.

G4A_ALGEBRA_010.q: Three numbers come one after another. The smallest of them is n. What is the sum of the three numbers?
hints: Numbers that come one after another go up by 1 each time. Write all three numbers using n before adding.
The smallest is n. The next is n plus 1. Write the third number, then add the three expressions.
A similar one: two numbers one after another, the smaller being k, are k and k plus 1. Their sum is 2 k plus 1. Check with 7 and 8: the sum is 15.
steps: The three numbers are n, n plus 1 and n plus 2.
Add them: n plus n plus 1 plus n plus 2.
The n terms make 3 n and the numbers make 1 plus 2 equals 3.
The sum is 3 n plus 3.

G4A_ALGEBRA_011.q: A taxi charges 50 rupees for the first kilometre and 12 rupees for every kilometre after that. Which expression gives the fare, in rupees, for a ride of d kilometres, d is more than 1?
hints: Split the ride into two parts: the first kilometre, and all the kilometres after it. Count carefully how many kilometres come after the first.
After the first kilometre there are d minus 1 kilometres left. Each of those costs 12 rupees. Add the 50 rupees for the first kilometre.

A similar one: an auto charges 30 rupees for the first kilometre and 10 rupees for each one after. For k kilometres the fare is 30 plus 10 times, open bracket, k minus 1, close bracket, equals 30 plus 10 k minus 10, which is 10 k plus 20.
steps: The first kilometre costs 50 rupees.
The remaining kilometres number d minus 1, and each costs 12 rupees, so they cost 12 times, open bracket, d minus 1, close bracket, equals 12 d minus 12.
Add the two parts: 50 plus 12 d minus 12.
The fare is 12 d plus 38.

G4A_ALGEBRA_012.q: Riya has 3 boxes with m mangoes in each and 5 loose mangoes. Sameer has 2 boxes with m mangoes in each and 4 loose mangoes. Riya gives one full box to Sameer. How many more mangoes does Sameer have than Riya now?
hints: Write an expression for each child's mangoes after the box has moved. Then subtract Riya's expression from Sameer's.
After giving a box, Riya has 2 boxes and 5 loose mangoes. Sameer now has 3 boxes and 4 loose mangoes.
A similar one: Asha has 4 bags of k marbles and 2 loose, Bela has 3 bags of k and 6 loose. Asha gives Bela a bag. Now Asha has 3 k plus 2 and Bela has 4 k plus 6, so Bela has k plus 4 more.
steps: After giving one box, Riya has 2 boxes and 5 loose mangoes: 2 m plus 5.
Sameer now has 3 boxes and 4 loose mangoes: 3 m plus 4.
Subtract Riya's from Sameer's. The boxes give 3 m minus 2 m equals m, and the loose mangoes give 4 minus 5, which takes 1 away.
Sameer has m minus 1 more mangoes.

G4A_ALGEBRA_013.q: The letter n stands for an even number. Which expression gives the 5th odd number that comes after n?
hints: Try the idea with a small even number of your own and list the odd numbers that follow it.
The first odd number after the even number n is n plus 1. Write the next ones from there.
Similar problem: the 3rd odd number after the even number 20. The odd numbers after 20 are 21, 23, 25, so the 3rd is 25, which is 20 plus 5.
steps: n is even, so the very next number, n plus 1, is the first odd number after it.
Odd numbers go up in twos: n plus 1, n plus 3, n plus 5, n plus 7, n plus 9.
Check with n equals 10: the odd numbers after 10 are 11, 13, 15, 17, 19, and 19 is 10 plus 9.
The 5th odd number after n is n plus 9.

G4A_ALGEBRA_014.q: A piece of wire is bent to make a square with each side 3 A plus 6 centimetres long. The same wire is then straightened and bent to make a triangle with three equal sides. How long is each side of the triangle?
hints: The wire does not get longer or shorter. Think about what stays the same for both shapes.
First find the whole length of the wire: a square has 4 equal sides of 3 A plus 6 centimetres.

Similar problem: a wire makes a square of side 3 b plus 3 centimetres. Its length is 4 times, open bracket, 3 b plus 3, close bracket, equals 12 b plus 12 centimetres. Bent into a triangle with equal sides, each side is, open bracket, 12 b plus 12, close bracket, divided by 3, equals 4 b plus 4 centimetres.
steps: The wire is as long as the perimeter of the square: 4 times, open bracket, 3 A plus 6, close bracket, equals 12 A plus 24 centimetres.
The triangle uses the same wire, so its three equal sides add up to 12 A plus 24 centimetres.
Share it equally among 3 sides: 12 A divided by 3 equals 4 A and 24 divided by 3 equals 8.
Each side of the triangle is 4 A plus 8 centimetres.

G4A_ALGEBRA_015.q: If 2 x plus y equals 10, what is the value of 6 x plus 3 y minus 4?
hints: You do not need to know x or y on their own. Look for the given expression hiding inside the new one.
Compare 6 x plus 3 y with 2 x plus y. How many times bigger is each part?
Similar problem: if A plus 2 b equals 7, find 4 A plus 8 b plus 1. Each part is 4 times bigger, so 4 A plus 8 b equals 4 times 7, which is 28, and 28 plus 1 equals 29.
steps: 6 x is 3 times 2 x, and 3 y is 3 times y, so 6 x plus 3 y is 3 times, open bracket, 2 x plus y, close bracket.
2 x plus y is 10, so 6 x plus 3 y is 3 times 10, which is 30.
Now take away 4. 30 minus 4 equals 26.
The value of 6 x plus 3 y minus 4 is 26.

G4A_ALGEBRA_016.q: The letter p stands for an odd number. Which of these is always a multiple of 4?
hints: The word always matters. One test is not enough, so try more than one odd number in each expression.
Try p equals 1 and then p equals 3 in each expression and see which ones stay multiples of 4 both times.
Similar problem: q is an even number; is q plus 2 always a multiple of 4? With q equals 2 it is 4, but with q equals 4 it is 6, so it is not always a multiple of 4.
steps: Test p equals 1: p plus 3 equals 4, 2 p equals 2, 4 p plus 2 equals 6 and 2 p plus 2 equals 4. Only p plus 3 and 2 p plus 2 are still possible.
Test p equals 3: p plus 3 equals 6, which is not a multiple of 4, but 2 p plus 2 equals 8, which is.
Why it always happens: 2 p plus 2 is 2 times, open bracket, p plus 1, close bracket. Because p is odd, p plus 1 is even, and 2 times an even number is a multiple of 4.
The expression that is always a multiple of 4 is 2 p plus 2.

G4A_ALGEBRA_017.q: Three years ago, Meena was twice as old as Ravi was then. Ravi is x years old now, and x is more than 3. How old is Meena now, in years?
hints: There are two moments in this story: three years ago and now. Keep track of which moment each age belongs to.
Start with Ravi: if he is x years old now, write his age three years ago.

Similar problem: two years ago Asha was three times as old as Bala was then, and Bala is y now. Two years ago Bala was y minus 2 and Asha was 3 times, open bracket, y minus 2, close bracket, equals 3 y minus 6. Now Asha is 3 y minus 6 plus 2, which is 3 y minus 4.
steps: Three years ago Ravi was x minus 3 years old.
Then Meena was twice that: 2 times, open bracket, x minus 3, close bracket, equals 2 x minus 6 years old.
That was three years ago, so add 3 to reach her age now: 2 x minus 6 plus 3.
Meena is 2 x minus 3 years old now.

G4A_ALGEBRA_018.q: Rina makes a row of squares with matchsticks. The first square needs 4 matchsticks. Each new square shares one side with the square before it, so it needs only 3 more matchsticks. How many matchsticks does she need for a row of n squares?
hints: Try small rows first and count, then look for a rule that fits every row.
Count the matchsticks for 1 square, 2 squares and 3 squares: 4, 7, 10. How many squares are new in a row of n squares?

Similar problem: a row of triangles where the first needs 3 sticks and each new one needs 2 more. For n triangles there are n minus 1 new ones, so the sticks are 3 plus 2 times, open bracket, n minus 1, close bracket, equals 2 n plus 1.
steps: The first square uses 4 matchsticks.
In a row of n squares, the other n minus 1 squares are new ones, and each needs 3 matchsticks: 3 times, open bracket, n minus 1, close bracket, equals 3 n minus 3.
Add them: 4 plus 3 n minus 3 equals 3 n plus 1.
Check with 3 squares: 3 times 3, plus 1, equals 10, which matches 4, 7, 10.
She needs 3 n plus 1 matchsticks.

G4A_ALGEBRA_019.q: Anu has 5 k plus 3 rupees and Bala has 3 k plus 11 rupees, where k is a whole number. For how many values of k from 1 to 10 does Anu have more money than Bala?
hints: Make a small table of both amounts for different values of k and compare them row by row.
Start with k equals 1: Anu has 8 rupees and Bala has 14 rupees. Keep going and watch the gap between them.
Similar problem: Rita has 4 k plus 1 and Sam has 2 k plus 7, for k from 1 to 8. They are equal at k equals 3, 13 each. Rita has more for k equals 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, which is 5 values.
steps: Each time k goes up by 1, Anu gains 5 rupees and Bala gains only 3, so Anu catches up by 2 each time.
At k equals 1 Anu has 8 and Bala has 14, a gap of 6. The gap closes at k equals 4, when both have 23.
Equal is not more, so k equals 4 does not count. Anu has more for k equals 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 and 10.
Anu has more money for 6 values of k.

G4A_ALGEBRA_020.q: A rectangular card is 2 A plus 5 centimetres long and A plus 1 centimetres wide. A small square with each side A centimetres is cut out from one corner of the card. What is the perimeter of the card that is left?
hints: Imagine walking around the edge of the card after the corner is cut. Think about which edges disappear and which new edges appear.
Cutting the corner removes two pieces of edge, each A centimetres long. Now count the new edges the cut makes and how long they are.

Similar problem: a card 10 centimetres by 6 centimetres has a 2 centimetre square cut from one corner. Two 2 centimetre pieces of edge go and two new 2 centimetre edges appear, so the perimeter stays 2 times, open bracket, 10 plus 6, close bracket, equals 32 centimetres.
steps: Perimeter of the whole card: 2 times, open bracket, 2 A plus 5 plus A plus 1, close bracket, equals 2 times, open bracket, 3 A plus 6, close bracket, which is 6 A plus 12 centimetres.
Cutting the corner square takes away two pieces of the outside edge, each A centimetres long.
The cut makes two new edges on the inside of the corner, each A centimetres long, so the distance around does not change.
The perimeter of the card that is left is 6 A plus 12 centimetres.

G4A_ALGEBRA_021.q: The nth term of a number pattern is 4 n minus 1, so the pattern begins 3, 7, 11, 15, and so on. Which of these numbers is a term of the pattern?
hints: Work backwards: undo what the rule does to n and see whether you land on a whole number.
The rule multiplies n by 4 and then subtracts 1. To undo it, first add 1, then see whether 4 divides the result exactly.
Similar problem: is 35 a term of 3 n minus 1? Add 1 to get 36, and 36 divided by 3 equals 12, a whole number, so 35 is the 12th term.
steps: A term is 1 less than a multiple of 4, so adding 1 to a term must give a multiple of 4.
44 plus 1 equals 45, 45 plus 1 equals 46 and 46 plus 1 equals 47. None of these is a multiple of 4.
47 plus 1 equals 48, and 48 divided by 4 equals 12, a whole number.
So 47 is a term of the pattern: it is the 12th term.

G4A_ALGEBRA_022.q: Sana has s rupees and Tara has 20 rupees more than Sana. Tara gives 15 rupees to Sana. Who has more money now, and how much more?
hints: When one person gives money to another, both amounts change. Write both new amounts before comparing.
Tara starts with s plus 20 rupees. Write what each girl has after 15 rupees moves from Tara to Sana.
Similar problem: Raj has 12 rupees more than Dev, who has d rupees. Raj gives Dev 8 rupees. Raj now has d plus 4 and Dev has d plus 8, so Dev has 4 rupees more.
steps: At the start Sana has s rupees and Tara has s plus 20 rupees.
After giving 15 rupees, Tara has s plus 20 minus 15 equals s plus 5 rupees.
After getting 15 rupees, Sana has s plus 15 rupees.
s plus 15 is 10 more than s plus 5, so Sana has 10 rupees more.

G4A_ALGEBRA_023.q: Five whole numbers come one after another, like 6, 7, 8, 9, 10. The middle number is m. Which expression is the sum of the smallest and the greatest of the five numbers?
hints: Write all five numbers using m, starting from the middle and stepping outwards on both sides.
The numbers just before and after m are m minus 1 and m plus 1. Go one more step each way to find the smallest and the greatest.
Similar problem: three numbers in a row with middle number k are k minus 1, k and k plus 1. The smallest plus the greatest is k minus 1 plus k plus 1, which is 2 k.
steps: The five numbers are m minus 2, m minus 1, m, m plus 1 and m plus 2.
The smallest is m minus 2 and the greatest is m plus 2.
Add them: m minus 2 plus m plus 2. The minus 2 and the plus 2 cancel each other.
Check with 6, 7, 8, 9, 10: 6 plus 10 equals 16, and 2 times 8 equals 16.
The sum of the smallest and the greatest is 2 m.

G4A_ALGEBRA_024.q: The perimeter of a rectangle is 10 A plus 6 centimetres. Its length is 3 A plus 2 centimetres. What is its breadth?
hints: The perimeter is made of two lengths and two breadths. Work backwards from the perimeter.
Half of the perimeter is one length plus one breadth. Find half of 10 A plus 6, first.

Similar problem: perimeter 8 b plus 10 centimetres and length 3 b plus 4 centimetres. Half the perimeter is 4 b plus 5. Take away the length: 4 b plus 5 minus 3 b minus 4 equals b plus 1, so the breadth is b plus 1 centimetres.
steps: One length and one breadth together make half the perimeter: half of 10 A plus 6 is 5 A plus 3.
Take the length away from this: 5 A plus 3 minus, open bracket, 3 A plus 2, close bracket.
5 A minus 3 A equals 2 A and 3 minus 2 equals 1.
The breadth is 2 A plus 1 centimetres.

G4A_ALGEBRA_025.q: A two-digit number has tens digit t and ones digit u. A second number is made by swapping the two digits. Which expression is the sum of the two numbers?
hints: A digit in the tens place is worth ten times the digit. Write each number using place value before adding.
The first number is worth 10 t plus u. Write the swapped number in the same way.
Similar problem: the number with tens digit 4 and ones digit 3 is 43, and swapped it is 34. In the sum, the tens are 4 plus 3 equals 7 and the ones are 3 plus 4 equals 7, so the sum is 77.
steps: The first number is worth 10 t plus u.
After the swap, u is in the tens place and t is in the ones place, so the second number is worth 10 u plus t.
Add them: 10 t plus t equals 11 t and u plus 10 u equals 11 u.
Check with 43 and 34: 43 plus 34 equals 77, and 11 times 4, plus 11 times 3, equals 77.
The sum of the two numbers is 11 t plus 11 u.

G4A_ALGEBRA_026.q: The value of 3 x plus 2 is 20. What is the value of 3 times, open bracket, x plus 2, close bracket?
hints: The two expressions look alike, but the bracket changes what is multiplied by 3. Open the bracket first.
3 times, open bracket, x plus 2, close bracket, means 3 times x and also 3 times 2. Write it without the bracket and compare it with 3 x plus 2.
Similar problem: 2 y plus 1 is 15. Then 2 times, open bracket, y plus 1, close bracket, equals 2 y plus 2, which is 1 more than 2 y plus 1, so it is 16.
steps: Open the bracket: 3 times, open bracket, x plus 2, close bracket, equals 3 x plus 6.
3 x plus 6 is 4 more than 3 x plus 2.
3 x plus 2 is 20, so add 4. 20 plus 4 equals 24.
Check: 3 x equals 18, so x equals 6, and 3 times, open bracket, 6 plus 2, close bracket, equals 24. 3 times 8 equals 24.
The value of 3 times, open bracket, x plus 2, close bracket, is 24.

G4A_ALGEBRA_027.q: A carpenter cuts a long wooden pole into n pieces. Each cut takes him 3 minutes. How many minutes does all the cutting take?
hints: Count the cuts, not the pieces. Try it with a small number of pieces.
To get 2 pieces you need 1 cut, and to get 3 pieces you need 2 cuts. How many cuts give n pieces?
Similar problem: cutting a ribbon into 5 pieces needs 4 cuts. If each cut takes 2 seconds, the cutting takes 4 times 2 equals 8 seconds.
steps: One cut makes 2 pieces and two cuts make 3 pieces, so the number of cuts is always 1 less than the number of pieces.
For n pieces he makes n minus 1 cuts.
Each cut takes 3 minutes: 3 times, open bracket, n minus 1, close bracket, equals 3 n minus 3.
All the cutting takes 3 n minus 3 minutes.

G4A_ANGLES_001.q: Three angles lie side by side on a straight line. Two of them are 48 degrees and 67 degrees. What is the third angle?
hints: Angles that lie side by side on a straight line add up to a straight angle. Remember how many degrees that is.
A straight angle is 180 degrees. Add the two angles you know, then see what is left.
A similar one: two angles of 50 degrees and 70 degrees on a straight line make 120 degrees together, so the third angle is 180 degrees minus 120 degrees, which is 60 degrees.
steps: Angles on a straight line add up to 180 degrees.
Add the two known angles. 48 plus 67 equals 115.
Take this away from 180 degrees. 180 minus 115 equals 65.
The third angle is 65 degrees.

G4A_ANGLES_002.q: A round pizza is cut from the centre into 8 equal slices. Ria eats 3 slices. What angle at the centre do the remaining slices make together?
hints: The angles all the way around a point add up to 360 degrees. Equal slices share this equally.
Find the angle of one slice by sharing 360 degrees among 8 slices. Then count the slices that are left.
A similar one: a cake cut into 6 equal slices has 360 degrees divided by 6, which is 60 degrees, in each slice. If 2 are eaten, the 4 left make 4 times 60 degrees, which is 240 degrees.
steps: The angle at the centre of one slice. 360 divided by 8 equals 45.
Slices left. 8 minus 3 equals 5.
Angle made by the slices left. 5 times 45 equals 225.
The remaining slices make an angle of 225 degrees.

G4A_ANGLES_003.q: Through how many degrees does the hour hand of a clock turn between 3 p m and 7 30 p m on the same day?
hints: The hour hand goes once around the clock, 360 degrees, in 12 hours. Find how far it turns in one hour.
In one hour the hour hand turns 360 degrees divided by 12, which is 30 degrees. How many hours are there from 3 p m to 7 30 p m?
A similar one: from 1 p m to 3 30 p m is 2 and a half hours. The hour hand turns 30 degrees plus 30 degrees for the two hours and 15 degrees for the half hour, which is 75 degrees.
steps: The hour hand turns 30 degrees every hour. 360 divided by 12 equals 30.
From 3 p m to 7 30 p m is 4 and a half hours.
Four hours give 120 degrees, and half an hour gives half of 30 degrees, which is 15 degrees. 4 times 30, plus 15, equals 135.
The hour hand turns through 135 degrees.

G4A_ANGLES_004.q: Arjun is facing East. He makes a three-quarter turn anticlockwise. Which direction is he facing now?
hints: A quarter turn is 90 degrees and takes you from one main direction to the next. Anticlockwise is the opposite way to the hands of a clock.
Starting from East, one quarter turn anticlockwise brings Arjun to North. Make two more quarter turns the same way.
A similar one: facing North, a half turn anticlockwise goes North to West to South. So that person ends up facing South.
steps: Going anticlockwise, the directions come in the order East, North, West, South.
First quarter turn: East to North. Second quarter turn: North to West.
Third quarter turn: West to South.
Arjun is now facing South.

G4A_ANGLES_005.q: A ladder leans against an upright wall on level ground. The ladder makes an angle of 58 degrees with the ground. What angle does the ladder make with the wall?
hints: The ladder, the wall and the ground make a triangle. An upright wall meets level ground at a right angle.
One angle of the triangle is 90 degrees, so the other two angles together make 90 degrees. One of them is 58 degrees.
A similar one: a ladder that makes 65 degrees with the ground makes 90 degrees minus 65 degrees, which is 25 degrees, with the wall.
steps: The wall and the ground meet at 90 degrees. The three angles of the triangle add up to 180 degrees.
So the two angles at the ends of the ladder add up to 90 degrees. 180 minus 90 equals 90.
Take away the angle with the ground. 90 minus 58 equals 32.
The ladder makes an angle of 32 degrees with the wall.

G4A_ANGLES_006.q: At 6:00 the hands of a clock make an angle of 180 degrees. By how many degrees has the angle between the hands become smaller at 6 30?
hints: Both hands move. In half an hour the minute hand goes halfway around, and the hour hand moves a little too.
At 6 30 the minute hand points at 6. The hour hand is not at 6 any more: it is halfway between 6 and 7. How many degrees is half of one hour space?

A similar one: at 3:00 the angle is 90 degrees. At 3 30 the minute hand is at 6 and the hour hand is halfway between 3 and 4, so the angle is 90 degrees minus 15 degrees, which is 75 degrees. The angle became smaller by 15 degrees.
steps: At 6 30 the minute hand points exactly at 6.
The hour hand has moved halfway from 6 to 7. One hour space is 30 degrees, so half of it is 15 degrees. 30 divided by 2 equals 15.
So the angle between the hands at 6 30 is 15 degrees.
Compare with the angle at 6:00. 180 minus 15 equals 165.
The angle has become smaller by 165 degrees.

G4A_ANGLES_007.q: The lamp of a lighthouse turns at a steady speed and makes one full turn every 40 seconds. Through how many degrees does it turn in 15 seconds?
hints: One full turn is 360 degrees. Find how many degrees the lamp turns in one second, then in the number of seconds asked.
Share 360 degrees equally among 40 seconds to get the turn in one second.
A similar one: a wheel makes a full turn in 20 seconds, so it turns 360 degrees divided by 20, which is 18 degrees, each second. In 5 seconds it turns 5 times 18 degrees, which is 90 degrees.
steps: A full turn is 360 degrees. Find the turn in one second. 360 divided by 40 equals 9.
Multiply by 15 seconds. 15 times 9 equals 135.
The lamp turns through 135 degrees.

G4A_ANGLES_008.q: The supplement of an angle is 3 times its complement. What is the angle?
hints: The complement of an angle is what must be added to make 90 degrees. The supplement is what must be added to make 180 degrees. You can test each choice.
The supplement is always 90 degrees more than the complement. If the supplement is 3 times the complement, then that extra 90 degrees is 2 times the complement.

A similar one: the supplement of an angle is 7 times its complement. Try 75 degrees: its supplement is 105 degrees and its complement is 15 degrees, and 105, which is 7 times 15. So that angle is 75 degrees.
steps: The supplement is 90 degrees more than the complement, because 180 degrees is 90 degrees more than 90 degrees.
The supplement is 3 times the complement, so the extra 90 degrees is 2 times the complement. 90 divided by 2 equals 45.
The complement is 45 degrees, so find the angle. 90 minus 45 equals 45.
Check: the supplement is 135 degrees, which is 3 times 45 degrees. The angle is 45 degrees.

G4A_ANGLES_009.q: Two straight lines cross each other. One of the angles formed is 4 times the angle beside it. What is the largest angle formed?
hints: When two straight lines cross, two angles that are beside each other lie on a straight line, so they add up to 180 degrees.
Think of the smaller angle as 1 part and the angle beside it as 4 parts. Together the 5 parts make 180 degrees.
A similar one: if one angle is twice the angle beside it, then 3 parts make 180 degrees. One part is 60 degrees, so the angles are 60 degrees and 120 degrees, and the largest is 120 degrees.
steps: Two angles beside each other on a straight line add up to 180 degrees.
The angles are 1 part and 4 parts, which is 5 parts in all. 180 divided by 5 equals 36.
The larger angle is 4 parts. 4 times 36 equals 144.
The largest angle formed is 144 degrees.

G4A_ANGLES_010.q: Five angles meet at a point and fill the whole turn around it. One of them is 80 degrees and the other four are equal. How big is each of the four equal angles?
hints: Angles that fill the whole turn around a point add up to 360 degrees. Take away the angle you know, then share the rest.
Take 80 degrees away from 360 degrees. What is left is shared equally among the four equal angles.
A similar one: four angles fill the turn around a point. One is 60 degrees and the other three are equal. They share 360 degrees minus 60 degrees, which is 300 degrees, so each is 100 degrees.
steps: Angles around a point add up to 360 degrees. Take away the known angle. 360 minus 80 equals 280.
Share the rest equally among the four angles. 280 divided by 4 equals 70.
Each of the four equal angles is 70 degrees.

G4A_ANGLES_011.q: What is the smaller angle between the hour hand and the minute hand of a clock at 2 40?
hints: At 2 40 the hour hand is not pointing exactly at the 2. It has been moving all the time since 2 o'clock.
The minute hand is on the 8. The hour hand moves 30 degrees in a whole hour, so work out how far it moves in 40 minutes, which is two thirds of an hour.

Similar problem: at 4 20 the minute hand is on the 4, which is 120 degrees from the 12. The hour hand has moved one third of 30 degrees, which is 10 degrees, past the 4, so it is 130 degrees from the 12. The angle between the hands is 130 minus 120, which is 10 degrees.
steps: The minute hand is on the 8. Each number on the clock is 30 degrees from the next. 8 times 30 equals 240.
The hour hand moves 30 degrees in 60 minutes, so in 40 minutes it moves 20 degrees. 30 times 40 over 60 equals 20.
So the hour hand is 20 degrees past the 2. 2 times 30, plus 20, equals 80.
Subtract to find the angle between the hands. 240 minus 80 equals 160.
So the smaller angle between the hands is 160 degrees.

G4A_ANGLES_012.q: From 2 10 to 2 50 on the same afternoon, both hands of a clock keep turning. How many more degrees does the minute hand turn than the hour hand in this time?
hints: Both hands move during this time, one fast and one slowly. Find how far each one turns, then compare.
From 2 10 to 2 50 is 40 minutes. The minute hand turns 6 degrees every minute. The hour hand turns 30 degrees in a whole hour.

Similar problem: from 5:00 to 5 30. The minute hand turns half a full turn, 180 degrees. The hour hand turns half of 30 degrees, which is 15 degrees. The minute hand turns 180 minus 15, which is 165 degrees, more.
steps: Find the time that passes. 50 minus 10 equals 40.
The minute hand turns 6 degrees each minute. 40 times 6 equals 240.
The hour hand turns 30 degrees in 60 minutes, so 1 degree every 2 minutes. 40 divided by 2 equals 20.
Find how much more the minute hand turns. 240 minus 20 equals 220.
So the minute hand turns 220 degrees more than the hour hand.

G4A_ANGLES_013.q: At 12 noon the hour hand of a clock points straight up at the 12. Later the same afternoon, the hour hand has turned through exactly 75 degrees from that position. What time is it?
hints: Work backwards from the angle. Think about how many degrees the hour hand turns in one hour, and be careful when you change a part of an hour into minutes.
The hour hand turns 30 degrees every hour. Find how many 30s there are in 75, and what is left over.

Similar problem: the hour hand has turned 105 degrees since noon. Three hours take 90 degrees, and 15 degrees are left. Since 15 degrees is half of 30 degrees, that is half an hour, or 30 minutes. The time is 3 30 p m.
steps: The hour hand turns 30 degrees in one hour.
Two hours take 60 degrees of the turn. Find what is left. 75 minus 60 equals 15.
15 degrees is half of 30 degrees, so it takes half an hour. 60 divided by 2 equals 30.
So 2 hours and 30 minutes have passed since noon.
So the time is 2 30 p m.

G4A_ANGLES_014.q: At 12 20, Sana says: "The minute hand is on the 4 and the hour hand is on the 12, so the angle between the hands is 120 degrees." By how many degrees is Sana's answer different from the true angle between the hands?
hints: Check each part of what Sana says. Is each hand exactly where she says it is at 12 20?
The minute hand is exactly on the 4. Now think about the hour hand: 20 minutes is one third of an hour, and the hour hand moves 30 degrees in an hour.

Similar problem: at 12 30 someone says the angle is 180 degrees. But the hour hand has moved half of 30 degrees, which is 15 degrees, past the 12. The true angle is 180 minus 15, which is 165 degrees, so that answer is 15 degrees too big.
steps: The minute hand is on the 4, so it is 120 degrees from the 12. 4 times 30 equals 120.
In 20 minutes the hour hand has moved one third of 30 degrees past the 12. 30 divided by 3 equals 10.
The true angle between the hands is smaller than Sana's. 120 minus 10 equals 110.
Compare Sana's answer with the true angle. 120 minus 110 equals 10.
So Sana's answer is different from the true angle by 10 degrees.

G4A_ANGLES_015.q: Farhan is facing North-East. He turns 90 degrees clockwise, then 225 degrees anticlockwise, and then 135 degrees clockwise. Which direction is he facing now?
hints: Follow the turns one at a time and keep track of the direction after each turn. Watch which way each turn goes.
The eight compass directions are 45 degrees apart. A turn of 90 degrees clockwise from North-East moves two directions on: find where that is first.

Similar problem: Asha faces North, turns 90 degrees clockwise and then 135 degrees anticlockwise. After the first turn she faces East. Going back 135 degrees is three steps of 45 degrees: North-East, North, North-West. She faces North-West.
steps: From North-East, a 90 degree clockwise turn moves two steps of 45 degrees: he faces South-East.
225 degrees is five steps of 45 degrees. 225 divided by 45 equals 5.
Five steps anticlockwise from South-East go East, North-East, North, North-West, West: he faces West.
135 degrees is three steps of 45 degrees. 135 divided by 45 equals 3.
Three steps clockwise from West go North-West, North, North-East.
So Farhan is facing North-East, the direction he started in.

G4A_ANGLES_016.q: Ravi turns 135 degrees clockwise and then 90 degrees anticlockwise. Now he is facing South. Which direction was he facing before he turned?
hints: You know where Ravi ends, not where he starts. To go back in time, undo each turn by turning the opposite way.
Start from South. The last thing Ravi did was turn 90 degrees anticlockwise, so undo it first by turning 90 degrees clockwise.
Similar problem: after turning 90 degrees clockwise, Asha faces West. To undo this, turn 90 degrees anticlockwise from West, which gives South. So Asha was facing South at the start.
steps: Start from where Ravi ends: South.
Undo the last turn. It was 90 degrees anticlockwise, so turn 90 degrees clockwise from South: West.
Undo the first turn. It was 135 degrees clockwise, so turn 135 degrees anticlockwise from West: South-West, South, South-East.
Check forwards: from South-East, 135 degrees clockwise is West, and then 90 degrees anticlockwise is South.
So Ravi was facing South-East before he turned.

G4A_ANGLES_017.q: A toy robot is facing North. Each time Kavya presses a button, the robot turns 45 degrees clockwise. Which direction is the robot facing after Kavya has pressed the button 13 times?
hints: The robot keeps going round and round. Look for the number of presses that brings it back to where it started.
A full turn is 360 degrees. Find how many presses of 45 degrees make a full turn, and then how many presses are left over after that.

Similar problem: a robot facing North turns 90 degrees clockwise at each press. Four presses make a full turn. After 10 presses, 8 presses make two full turns and 2 are left, so it faces East and then South. It ends facing South.
steps: Find how many presses make one full turn. 360 divided by 45 equals 8.
After 8 presses the robot is facing North again.
Find how many presses are left. 13 minus 8 equals 5.
Five more presses from North go North-East, East, South-East, South, South-West.
So the robot is facing South-West.

G4A_ANGLES_018.q: Three angles meet at a point and together fill the whole turn around the point, with no gaps and no overlaps. The second angle is twice the first, and the third angle is three times the first. What kind of angle is the largest of the three?
hints: First decide what the three angles add up to. Read carefully: do they lie on a straight line, inside a triangle, or all the way round a point?
Call the first angle one part. Then the three angles are 1 part, 2 parts and 3 parts. Find how many parts there are in the whole turn.

Similar problem: two angles fill the whole turn around a point, and one is 3 times the other. There are 4 parts in 360 degrees, so one part is 90 degrees. The angles are 90 degrees and 270 degrees, and the larger one is a reflex angle.
steps: Angles that fill the whole turn around a point add up to 360 degrees.
The angles are 1 part, 2 parts and 3 parts, which is 6 parts. 360 divided by 6 equals 60.
The largest angle is 3 parts. 3 times 60 equals 180.
An angle of 180 degrees makes a straight line.
So the largest angle is a straight angle.

G4A_ANGLES_019.q: Two straight lines cross each other and make four angles around the crossing point. Three of these angles add up to 250 degrees. What is the size of the smallest of the four angles?
hints: The four angles go all the way round the point. Find the angle that was left out, then use what you know about the angles made when two straight lines cross.
Take 250 degrees away from the whole turn to find the fourth angle. The angle beside it lies with it on a straight line.

Similar problem: three of the four angles add up to 300 degrees. The fourth is 360 minus 300, which is 60 degrees. The angle beside it is 180 minus 60, which is 120 degrees. The four angles are 60 degrees, 120 degrees, 60 degrees, 120 degrees, so the largest is 120 degrees.
steps: The four angles add up to a whole turn, so find the fourth angle. 360 minus 250 equals 110.
The angle beside it makes a straight line with it. 180 minus 110 equals 70.
Angles opposite each other are equal, so the four angles are 110 degrees, 70 degrees, 110 degrees and 70 degrees.
Check the three that were added. 70 plus 110 plus 70 equals 250.
So the smallest of the four angles is 70 degrees.

G4A_ANGLES_020.q: An angle is 30 degrees more than its complement. What is the supplement of this angle?
hints: There are two different ideas here, complement and supplement. Find the angle first using its complement, and then answer what is asked.
The angle and its complement add up to 90 degrees, and the angle is 30 degrees bigger. Take the extra 30 degrees away from 90 degrees and share what is left equally.

Similar problem: an angle is 10 degrees more than its complement. Taking 10 from 90 leaves 80, so the complement is 40 degrees and the angle is 50 degrees. The supplement of the angle is 180 minus 50, which is 130 degrees.
steps: The angle and its complement add up to 90 degrees. Take away the extra 30 degrees and halve. 90 minus 30, then divided by 2, equals 30.
The complement is 30 degrees, so the angle is 30 degrees more. 30 plus 30 equals 60.
The supplement is what the angle needs to make 180 degrees. 180 minus 60 equals 120.
So the supplement of the angle is 120 degrees.

G4A_ANGLES_021.q: Angle P and angle Q are complementary, so they add up to 90 degrees. Angle Q and angle R are supplementary, so they add up to 180 degrees. Which of these is true whatever the size of angle P?
options: Angle R is equal to angle P
Angle P and angle R are supplementary
Angle R is 90 degrees more than angle P
Angle R is twice angle Q
hints: No sizes are given, so the statement must hold for every possible angle P. Try one size for angle P, and then try a different size to make sure.
Let angle P be 20 degrees. Find angle Q from the first clue and angle R from the second clue. Then do the same again with angle P as 40 degrees.

Similar problem: angle X and angle Y add up to 180 degrees, and angle Y and angle Z also add up to 180 degrees. If X is 50 degrees, Y is 130 degrees and Z is 50 degrees. If X is 70 degrees, Y is 110 degrees and Z is 70 degrees. Whatever X is, Z is equal to X.
steps: Try angle P equals 20 degrees. Then angle Q is 70 degrees and angle R is 110 degrees. 90 minus 20 equals 70, and 180 minus 70 equals 110.
Try angle P equals 40 degrees. Then angle Q is 50 degrees and angle R is 130 degrees. 90 minus 40 equals 50, and 180 minus 50 equals 130.
Both times angle R is 90 degrees more than angle P. 110 minus 20 equals 90, and 130 minus 40 equals 90.
This always happens: going from 90 degrees to 180 degrees adds 90 degrees to the total, and angle Q is the same in both.
So angle R is 90 degrees more than angle P.

G4A_ANGLES_022.q: Angle A O B is 70 degrees. A ray O C is drawn from the same point O so that angle B O C is 30 degrees. Riya says angle A O C must be 100 degrees. Which of these is true about angle A O C?
options: It could be any angle from 40 degrees to 100 degrees
It could be 100 degrees or 40 degrees
hints: There is no picture, so imagine it. The ray O C can be drawn on either side of the ray O B.
First picture O C on the far side of O B, away from O A. Then picture O C on the near side of O B, between O A and O B. Find angle A O C each time.

Similar problem: angle X O Y is 50 degrees and angle Y O Z is 20 degrees. If O Z is outside angle X O Y, angle X O Z is 50 plus 20, which is 70 degrees. If O Z is inside angle X O Y, angle X O Z is 50 minus 20, which is 30 degrees. So angle X O Z could be 70 degrees or 30 degrees.
steps: The ray O C makes 30 degrees with O B, and it can lie on either side of O B.
If O C is on the side away from O A, the two angles add. 70 plus 30 equals 100.
If O C is between O A and O B, the smaller angle is taken away. 70 minus 30 equals 40.
These are the only two places where O C can be.
So angle A O C could be 100 degrees or 40 degrees.

G4A_CIRCLE_001.q: The diameter of a circular plate is 18 centimetres. What is its radius?
hints: Think about how the radius and the diameter of a circle are related.
The radius is half of the diameter. Find half of 18.
Example: A circle has diameter 10 centimetres. Its radius is 10 divided by 2, which is 5 centimetres.
steps: The radius goes from the centre to the circle. The diameter goes right across through the centre, so it is two radii.
Halve the diameter. 18 divided by 2 equals 9.
The radius is 9 centimetres.

G4A_CIRCLE_002.q: Kiran wants to draw a circle of diameter 12 centimetres with a compass. How far apart should the needle point and the pencil tip be?
hints: The needle of a compass sits at the centre and the pencil draws the circle. Think about which length that is.
The opening of the compass is the radius. Find the radius of a circle whose diameter is 12 centimetres.
Example: For a circle of diameter 20 centimetres, the compass is opened to the radius, 20 divided by 2 equals 10 centimetres.
steps: The needle is at the centre and the pencil is on the circle, so the opening of the compass is the radius.
The radius is half the diameter. 12 divided by 2 equals 6.
The needle point and pencil tip should be 6 centimetres apart.

G4A_CIRCLE_003.q: A circle has a radius of 8 centimetres. How long is the longest chord that can be drawn in this circle?
hints: A chord joins two points on a circle. Think about which chord is the longest of all.
The longest chord passes through the centre, so it is the diameter. Find the diameter when the radius is 8 centimetres.
Example: In a circle of radius 5 centimetres, the longest chord is the diameter, 2 times 5 equals 10 centimetres.
steps: The longest chord of a circle is the one through the centre, which is the diameter.
The diameter is twice the radius. 2 times 8 equals 16.
The longest chord is 16 centimetres.

G4A_CIRCLE_004.q: A circle has a radius of 6 centimetres. Point P is 4 centimetres away from the centre of the circle. Where is point P?
options: At the centre of the circle
hints: Every point on a circle is exactly one radius away from the centre. Compare the point's distance with the radius.
Is 4 centimetres less than, equal to, or more than the radius of 6 centimetres?
Example: A circle has radius 5 centimetres and a point is 9 centimetres from the centre. Since 9 is more than 5, that point is outside the circle.
steps: Points on the circle are exactly 6 centimetres from the centre.
Point P is 4 centimetres from the centre, and 4 is less than 6.
A point closer to the centre than the radius lies inside the circle, so P is inside the circle.

G4A_CIRCLE_005.q: O is the centre of a circle. A and B are two different points on the circle. If O A equals 7 centimetres, how long is O B?
hints: Think about what kind of line joins the centre of a circle to a point on the circle.
O A and O B both go from the centre to the circle, so both are radii. What do you know about all the radii of one circle?
Example: In a circle with centre C, if C P equals 4 centimetres and Q is also on the circle, then C Q is also a radius, so C Q equals 4 centimetres.
steps: O A joins the centre to a point on the circle, so O A is a radius.
O B also joins the centre to a point on the circle, so O B is a radius too.
All radii of a circle are equal, so O B equals 7 centimetres.

G4A_CIRCLE_006.q: Four equal circles, each of radius 3 centimetres, are drawn in a straight row so that each circle touches the next one. What is the distance from the centre of the first circle to the centre of the last circle?
hints: When two equal circles touch, think about how far apart their centres are.
The centres of two touching circles are one radius plus one radius apart. Find that distance for radius 3 centimetres.

Example: Three circles of radius 2 centimetres touch in a row. Neighbouring centres are 4 centimetres apart, and there are 2 gaps from first to last, so the distance is 2 times 4, which is 8 centimetres.
steps: Centres of neighbouring circles are two radii apart. 3 plus 3 equals 6.
From the first centre to the fourth centre there are 3 gaps.
Multiply. 3 times 6 equals 18.
The distance between the first and last centres is 18 centimetres.

G4A_CIRCLE_007.q: Six round bangles, each of radius 4 centimetres, are placed in a straight row on a table so that each bangle touches the next. How long is the row from end to end?
hints: Each bangle takes up its full width in the row. Think about which length of a circle is its width.
The width of one bangle is its diameter. Find the diameter when the radius is 4 centimetres.
Example: Five coins of radius 1 centimetre in a row. Each coin is 2 centimetres wide, so the row is 5 times 2, which is 10 centimetres long.
steps: Each bangle is one diameter wide. 2 times 4 equals 8.
There are 6 bangles in the row. 6 times 8 equals 48.
The row is 48 centimetres long.

G4A_CIRCLE_008.q: A circle is drawn inside a square of side 10 centimetres so that it just touches all four sides of the square. What is the radius of the circle?
hints: Picture the circle fitting snugly in the square. Think about which length of the circle stretches from one side of the square to the opposite side.
The circle reaches from one side to the opposite side, so its diameter equals the side of the square, 10 centimetres.
Example: A circle just fits in a square of side 8 centimetres. Its diameter is 8 centimetres, so its radius is 4 centimetres.
steps: The circle touches opposite sides of the square, so its diameter equals the side of the square.
The diameter is 10 centimetres.
The radius is half the diameter. 10 divided by 2 equals 5.
The radius of the circle is 5 centimetres.

G4A_CIRCLE_009.q: A circle of radius 6 centimetres fits exactly inside a square, touching all four sides. What is the perimeter of the square?
hints: First find the side of the square from the circle, then find the distance around the square.
The side of the square equals the diameter of the circle. Find the diameter when the radius is 6 centimetres.
Example: A circle of radius 2 centimetres fits exactly in a square. The side is 4 centimetres, so the perimeter is 4 times 4, which is 16 centimetres.
steps: The side of the square equals the diameter. 2 times 6 equals 12.
A square has 4 equal sides. 4 times 12 equals 48.
The perimeter of the square is 48 centimetres.

G4A_CIRCLE_010.q: Two coins lie flat on a table and touch each other. The radius of one coin is 5 centimetres and the radius of the other is 3 centimetres. How far apart are their centres?
hints: Imagine a straight line from one centre to the other. It passes through the point where the coins touch.
The line goes from the first centre to the touching point, one radius, then on to the second centre, the other radius.
Example: Circles of radius 4 centimetres and 2 centimetres touch side by side. Their centres are 4 plus 2, which is 6 centimetres apart.
steps: The line joining the centres passes through the point where the coins touch.
It is made of the radius of one coin and the radius of the other.
Add the two radii. 5 plus 3 equals 8.
The centres are 8 centimetres apart.

G4A_CIRCLE_011.q: Two circles are drawn with the same centre. The radius of the big circle is 9 centimetres and the radius of the small circle is 5 centimetres. How wide is the ring between the two circles?
hints: Walk in a straight line from the centre outwards. You cross the small circle first and then the big circle.
The width of the ring is how much farther the big circle is from the centre than the small circle.
Example: Circles with the same centre have radii 10 centimetres and 7 centimetres. The ring between them is 10 minus 7, which is 3 centimetres wide.
steps: Going out from the centre, the small circle is 5 centimetres away and the big circle is 9 centimetres away.
The ring is the gap between them. 9 minus 5 equals 4.
The ring is 4 centimetres wide.

G4A_CIRCLE_012.q: The diameter of a circle is 12 centimetres longer than its radius. What is the radius of the circle?
hints: A diameter is made of two radii. Think about what is left when you take one radius away from the diameter.
Diameter equals radius plus radius. If the diameter is also radius plus 12 centimetres, what must the second radius be?
Example: A diameter is 5 centimetres longer than its radius. Since the diameter is radius plus radius, the extra part is one radius, so the radius is 5 centimetres.
steps: The diameter is two radii: radius plus radius.
We are told the diameter is radius plus 12 centimetres.
Comparing the two, the second radius must be the extra 12 centimetres.
Check: the diameter is 24 centimetres, and it is 12 centimetres longer than the radius. 24 minus 12 equals 12.
The radius is 12 centimetres.

G4A_CIRCLE_013.q: A circle has a radius of 6 centimetres. Which of these lengths can not be the length of a chord of this circle?
hints: A chord joins two points on the circle. Think about how long the longest possible chord is.
The longest chord is the diameter. Find the diameter when the radius is 6 centimetres.
Example: In a circle of radius 5 centimetres the longest chord is 10 centimetres, so a chord of 11 centimetres is not possible, but chords of 3 centimetres or 10 centimetres are.
steps: The longest chord is the diameter. 2 times 6 equals 12.
So a chord can be any length up to 12 centimetres, but never longer.
4 centimetres, 9 centimetres and 12 centimetres are all possible. The length that cannot be a chord is 13 centimetres.

G4A_CIRCLE_014.q: A rectangular tray is 20 centimetres long and 8 centimetres wide. Round biscuits of radius 2 centimetres are laid flat on it in straight rows, touching each other but not overlapping. What is the greatest number of biscuits that fit on the tray?
hints: Each round biscuit needs a square space as wide as the biscuit. Find how many fit along the length and along the width.
The width of one biscuit is its diameter. Find the diameter when the radius is 2 centimetres.
Example: A tray 12 centimetres by 6 centimetres holds circles of radius 3 centimetres. Each is 6 centimetres wide, so 2 fit along the length and 1 along the width: 2 times 1 equals 2 circles.
steps: Each biscuit is one diameter wide. 2 times 2 equals 4.
Biscuits along the length. 20 divided by 4 equals 5.
Rows along the width. 8 divided by 4 equals 2.
Multiply. 5 times 2 equals 10.
The tray holds 10 biscuits.

G4A_CIRCLE_015.q: A piece of wire is bent to make a circle of radius 7 centimetres. The same wire is straightened and bent again to make a square. What is the side of the square? Use pi as 22 over 7.
hints: The length of the wire does not change. It is the distance around the circle, and then the distance around the square.
Find the circumference of the circle: 2 times 22 over 7 times 7.
Example: A wire makes a circle of radius 14 centimetres. Its length is 2 times 22 over 7 times 14, which is 88 centimetres. Bent into a square, each side is 88 divided by 4, which is 22 centimetres.
steps: The length of the wire is the circumference of the circle. 2 times 22 over 7 times 7 equals 44.
The same 44 centimetres of wire goes around the square.
A square has 4 equal sides. 44 divided by 4 equals 11.
The side of the square is 11 centimetres.

G4A_CIRCLE_016.q: The radius of a big circle is equal to the diameter of a small circle. The radius of the small circle is 3 centimetres. What is the diameter of the big circle?
hints: Go one step at a time: small radius, small diameter, big radius, big diameter.
Find the diameter of the small circle first: twice 3 centimetres.
Example: A small circle has radius 2 centimetres, so its diameter is 4 centimetres. A big circle with radius 4 centimetres has diameter 8 centimetres.
steps: Diameter of the small circle. 2 times 3 equals 6.
This is the radius of the big circle, so the big radius is 6 centimetres.
Diameter of the big circle. 2 times 6 equals 12.
The diameter of the big circle is 12 centimetres.

G4A_CIRCLE_017.q: Three equal circles with centres A, B and C each have a radius of 4 centimetres. Each circle touches the other two. What is the perimeter of triangle A B C?
hints: Each side of the triangle joins the centres of two touching circles. Find the length of one side first.
When two circles touch, the distance between their centres is one radius plus the other radius: 4 plus 4.
Example: Three circles of radius 5 centimetres touch each other. Each side of the triangle of centres is 10 centimetres, so its perimeter is 3 times 10, which is 30 centimetres.
steps: Each side joins two centres of touching circles. 4 plus 4 equals 8.
The triangle has 3 such sides. 3 times 8 equals 24.
The perimeter of triangle A B C is 24 centimetres.

G4A_CIRCLE_018.q: Ten equal circles are drawn inside a rectangle in 2 rows of 5. Each circle touches the circles next to it, and the outer circles touch the sides of the rectangle. The perimeter of the rectangle is 84 centimetres. What is the radius of each circle?
hints: Write the length and the width of the rectangle as a number of diameters, then use the perimeter.
The length is 5 diameters and the width is 2 diameters. How many diameters make up half of the perimeter?

Example: Six circles in 2 rows of 3 fill a rectangle of perimeter 40 centimetres. Length plus width equals 3 plus 2, which is 5 diameters, or 20 centimetres, so a diameter is 4 centimetres and the radius is 2 centimetres.
steps: The length is 5 diameters and the width is 2 diameters.
Length plus width is half the perimeter. 84 divided by 2 equals 42.
Length plus width is 7 diameters. 42 divided by 7 equals 6.
The radius is half the diameter. 6 divided by 2 equals 3.
The radius of each circle is 3 centimetres.

G4A_CIRCLE_019.q: A small circle of radius 3 centimetres lies inside a big circle of radius 10 centimetres and touches it at exactly one point. How far apart are the centres of the two circles?
hints: Draw a line from the big centre to the touching point. The small circle's centre lies on this line.
From the big centre to the touching point is 10 centimetres. From the small centre to the same point is 3 centimetres.
Example: A circle of radius 2 centimetres touches a circle of radius 8 centimetres from inside. The centres are 8 minus 2, which is 6 centimetres apart.
steps: The big centre, the small centre and the touching point lie on one straight line.
The big centre is 10 centimetres from the touching point, and the small centre is 3 centimetres from it.
The distance between the centres is the difference. 10 minus 3 equals 7.
The centres are 7 centimetres apart.

G4A_CIRCLE_020.q: Three circles of radii 2 centimetres, 3 centimetres and 4 centimetres are drawn in a row with their centres on one straight line. The middle circle, of radius 3 centimetres, touches the other two. What is the distance from the centre of the first circle to the centre of the last circle?
hints: Travel along the line from the first centre to the last centre and note which parts of each circle you cross.
You cross one radius of the first circle, then the whole middle circle, then one radius of the last circle.
Example: Circles of radii 1 centimetre, 2 centimetres and 5 centimetres in a row. From first centre to last centre: 1 plus, 2 plus 2, plus 5 equals 10 centimetres.
steps: From the first centre to its edge is one radius, 2 centimetres.
Crossing the whole middle circle is its diameter. 2 times 3 equals 6.
From the edge of the last circle to its centre is one radius, 4 centimetres.
Add the three parts. 2 plus 6 plus 4 equals 12.
The distance between the first and last centres is 12 centimetres.

G4A_CIRCLE_021.q: The circumference of a circle is 88 centimetres. The circle fits exactly inside a square, touching all four sides. What is the side of the square? Use pi as 22 over 7.
hints: Work backwards from the circumference to the radius, then think about how the circle sits in the square.
Circumference equals 2 times 22 over 7 times radius. So 44 over 7 times the radius is 88.
Example: A circle has circumference 44 centimetres. Then 44 over 7 times the radius is 44, so the radius is 7 centimetres. The square around it has side equal to the diameter, 14 centimetres.
steps: The circumference is 2 times 22 over 7 times the radius. 44 over 7 times 14 equals 88.
So the radius is 14 centimetres.
The side of the square equals the diameter. 2 times 14 equals 28.
The side of the square is 28 centimetres.

G4A_CIRCLE_022.q: A circle of radius 7 centimetres is cut out of a square sheet of paper of side 14 centimetres. What is the area of the paper that is left? Use pi as 22 over 7.
hints: The paper left is the square with the circle taken away. Find two areas.
Find the area of the square first: 14 times 14.
Example: A circle of area 154 square centimetres is cut from a square sheet of side 20 centimetres. The square is 400 square centimetres, so 400 minus 154 equals 246 square centimetres is left.
steps: Area of the square. 14 times 14 equals 196.
Area of the circle. 22 over 7 times 7 times 7 equals 154.
Take the circle away from the square. 196 minus 154 equals 42.
The area of paper left is 42 square centimetres.

G4A_CIRCLE_023.q: Five points are marked on a circle. Every pair of points is joined by a straight line. How many chords are drawn?
hints: Each chord joins two of the points. Count the pairs in an orderly way so that none is counted twice.
Call the points P, Q, R, S, T. Start by counting the chords from P to each of the other four points.
Example: With 4 points on a circle, the first point joins 3 others, the next joins 2 new ones, and the next joins 1 new one: 3 plus 2 plus 1 equals 6 chords.
steps: From the first point, 4 chords go to the other points.
From the second point, 3 new chords can be drawn, then 2 from the third and 1 from the fourth.
Add them. 4 plus 3 plus 2 plus 1 equals 10.
10 chords are drawn.

G4A_CIRCLE_024.q: Two square trays each have a side of 24 centimetres. The first tray is exactly filled by 9 equal round plates in 3 rows of 3. The second tray is exactly filled by 16 equal round plates in 4 rows of 4. In each tray the plates touch each other and the sides. How much longer is the radius of a plate in the first tray than in the second tray?
hints: In each tray, the plates in one row share the 24 centimetre side equally. Find each plate's diameter, then its radius.
In the first tray, 3 plates fit across 24 centimetres. Find the diameter of one plate: 24 divided by 3.

Example: A 20 centimetre square tray holds 2 plates across, so each is 10 centimetres wide with radius 5 centimetres. If it holds 5 plates across, each is 4 centimetres wide with radius 2 centimetres. The radii differ by 5 minus 2, which is 3 centimetres.
steps: First tray: 3 plates across. 24 divided by 3 equals 8.
So the radius of a plate in the first tray is 4 centimetres.
Second tray: 4 plates across. 24 divided by 4 equals 6.
So the radius of a plate in the second tray is 3 centimetres.
Compare the radii. 4 minus 3 equals 1.
The radius in the first tray is longer by 1 centimetre.

G4A_CIRCLE_025.q: A wire 132 centimetres long is cut into 3 equal pieces. Each piece is bent to make a circle. What is the radius of each circle? Use pi as 22 over 7.
hints: Each piece of wire becomes the distance around one circle. Find the length of one piece first.
Divide 132 centimetres by 3 to find the length of one piece.
Example: A wire 176 centimetres long is cut into 2 equal pieces of 88 centimetres. For a circle, 44 over 7 times the radius is 88, so the radius is 14 centimetres.
steps: Length of one piece. 132 divided by 3 equals 44.
This is the circumference of one circle: 2 times 22 over 7 times the radius is 44.
A radius of 7 centimetres fits. 2 times 22 over 7 times 7 equals 44.
The radius of each circle is 7 centimetres.

G4A_CIRCLE_026.q: Twelve equal circles are drawn inside a rectangle in 3 rows of 4. Each circle touches the circles next to it, and the circles on the outside touch the sides of the rectangle. The area of the rectangle is 432 square centimetres. What is the radius of each circle?
hints: Each circle sits snugly inside its own little square, and the twelve little squares fill the rectangle exactly. Work backwards from the area.
Share the area of the rectangle equally among the 12 little squares. Then find the side of one little square, and think about how that side is related to the circle inside it.

Similar problem: 6 equal circles in 2 rows of 3 fill a rectangle of area 96 square centimetres. Each little square has area 96 divided by 6, which is 16 square centimetres, so its side is 4 centimetres. That side is the diameter of a circle, so the radius is 2 centimetres.
steps: The rectangle is made of 12 equal little squares, one around each circle. 432 divided by 12 equals 36.
A square of area 36 square centimetres has a side of 6 centimetres. 6 times 6 equals 36.
The side of the little square is the diameter of the circle inside it.
The radius is half the diameter. 6 divided by 2 equals 3.
So the radius of each circle is 3 centimetres.

G4A_CIRCLE_027.q: A round pond has a radius of 7 metres. A path 7 metres wide runs all the way around the pond. What is the area of the path? Use pi as 22 over 7.
hints: The path is a ring. A ring is what is left when a small circle is taken out of a bigger circle with the same centre.
Find the radius of the big circle made by the pond and the path together. It reaches from the centre of the pond to the outer edge of the path.

Similar problem: a pond of radius 14 metres with a path 7 metres wide. The big circle has radius 21 metres and area 22 over 7 times 21 times 21, which is 1386 square metres. The pond has area 22 over 7 times 14 times 14, which is 616 square metres. The path is 1386 minus 616, which is 770 square metres.
steps: The pond and path together make a big circle. Find its radius. 7 plus 7 equals 14.
Find the area of the big circle. 22 over 7 times 14 times 14 equals 616.
Find the area of the pond. 22 over 7 times 7 times 7 equals 154.
Take the pond out of the big circle. 616 minus 154 equals 462.
So the area of the path is 462 square metres.

G4A_CIRCLE_028.q: When the radius of a circle is made twice as long, its circumference becomes 88 centimetres longer than before. What was the radius of the circle at the start? Use pi as 22 over 7.
hints: Think about what happens to the circumference when the radius is doubled. You can also test each choice: find the circumference before and after, and see how much it grows.
Try a radius of 7 centimetres. The circumference is 44 centimetres. With a radius of 14 centimetres it is 88 centimetres. Find how much it has grown, and compare with what the question says.

Similar problem: doubling the radius makes the circumference 132 centimetres longer. Doubling the radius doubles the circumference, so the extra part equals the old circumference, 132 centimetres. Since 2 times 22 over 7 times 21 equals 132, the radius at the start was 21 centimetres.
steps: When the radius is doubled, the circumference is doubled too.
So the extra length is exactly as long as the old circumference: the old circumference is 88 centimetres.
Find the radius of a circle with circumference 88 centimetres. 2 times 22 over 7 times 14 equals 88.
Check: the new radius is 28 centimetres, and the circumference has grown by 88 centimetres. 2 times 22 over 7 times 28 equals 176 and 176 minus 88 equals 88.
So the radius at the start was 14 centimetres.

G4A_CIRCLE_029.q: Seven points are marked on a circle. Each point is joined by a straight chord to every other point, except the two points right next to it. How many chords are drawn?
hints: Work out how many chords leave one point. Then think carefully before you multiply: every chord has two ends.
From one point there are 6 other points. Two of them are its neighbours, so find how many chords start at this point.

Similar problem: five points on a circle, each joined to every point except its two neighbours. Each point sends out 2 chords, and 5 times 2 equals 10. But every chord has been counted from both of its ends, so there are 10 divided by 2, which is 5 chords.
steps: From each point, take away the point itself and its two neighbours. 7 minus 3 equals 4.
Seven points each send out 4 chords. 7 times 4 equals 28.
Each chord joins two points, so it has been counted twice.
Halve the total. 28 divided by 2 equals 14.
So 14 chords are drawn.

G4A_CIRCLE_030.q: Eight points are marked on a circle, equally spaced all the way round. Every pair of points is joined by a chord. How many of these chords are not diameters of the circle?
hints: Count all the chords first, in an orderly way. Then decide which chords pass through the centre, and be careful not to count any of those twice.
The first point is joined to 7 others, the second to 6 new ones, and so on. A chord is a diameter only when it joins a point to the point exactly opposite.

Similar problem: six equally spaced points. The chords number 5 plus 4 plus 3 plus 2 plus 1, which is 15. The six points make 3 opposite pairs, so 3 chords are diameters. That leaves 15 minus 3, which is 12 chords that are not diameters.
steps: Count all the chords. 7 plus 6 plus 5 plus 4 plus 3 plus 2 plus 1 equals 28.
A chord is a diameter when it joins two opposite points.
Eight points make 4 opposite pairs, so there are 4 diameters. 8 divided by 2 equals 4.
Take the diameters away from all the chords. 28 minus 4 equals 24.
So 24 of the chords are not diameters.

G4A_CIRCLE_031.q: A small circle is drawn inside a big circle. The small circle touches the big circle at exactly one point, and it also passes through the centre of the big circle. The diameter of the big circle is 24 centimetres. How far apart are the centres of the two circles?
hints: Imagine a straight line from the point where the circles touch to the centre of the big circle. Think about what this line is for each of the two circles.
That line is a radius of the big circle. It also goes right across the small circle, from one side to the other through its centre.

Similar problem: the big circle has diameter 40 centimetres. Its radius is 20 centimetres, and this is the diameter of the small circle. The small circle's centre is halfway along, 10 centimetres from the big centre. So the centres are 10 centimetres apart.
steps: Find the radius of the big circle. 24 divided by 2 equals 12.
The line from the touching point to the big centre is 12 centimetres long, and it is a diameter of the small circle.
The centre of the small circle is halfway along this line. 12 divided by 2 equals 6.
So the small centre is 6 centimetres from the big centre.
So the centres of the two circles are 6 centimetres apart.

G4A_CIRCLE_032.q: Three coins of different sizes lie flat on a table, and each coin touches the other two. The distances between their centres are 7 centimetres, 8 centimetres and 9 centimetres. What is the radius of the largest coin?
hints: When two coins touch, the distance between their centres is one radius plus the other radius. Think about what you get if you add all three distances.
Add 7, 8 and 9. In that total every radius has been counted twice. Halve it to find the three radii added together.

Similar problem: the distances are 5 centimetres, 6 centimetres and 7 centimetres. They add up to 18 centimetres, so the three radii add up to 9 centimetres. The two smaller coins are 5 centimetres apart, so the largest coin has radius 9 minus 5, which is 4 centimetres.
steps: Add the three distances. Each radius is counted twice. 7 plus 8 plus 9 equals 24.
Halve to get the three radii added together. 24 divided by 2 equals 12.
The two smaller coins have the closest centres, 7 centimetres apart. Take their radii away. 12 minus 7 equals 5.
Check: the radii are 3 centimetres, 4 centimetres and 5 centimetres. 3 plus 4 equals 7 and 3 plus 5 equals 8 and 4 plus 5 equals 9.
So the radius of the largest coin is 5 centimetres.

G4A_CIRCLE_033.q: Two round tins, each of radius 7 centimetres, stand on a table touching each other. A ribbon is pulled tight around the two tins together. It goes straight across from one tin to the other on both sides, and it curves around the outer half of each tin. How long is the ribbon? Use pi as 22 over 7.
hints: Break the ribbon into its parts: the straight parts and the curved parts. Find each part and add them up.
Each straight part runs from the widest point of one tin to the widest point of the other, so it is as long as the distance between the two centres. The two curved parts are half circles.

Similar problem: two tins of radius 14 centimetres. The centres are 28 centimetres apart, so the two straight parts are 28 centimetres each. The two half circles make one whole circle of 2 times 22 over 7 times 14, which is 88 centimetres. The ribbon is 28 plus 28 plus 88, which is 144 centimetres long.
steps: The tins touch, so their centres are two radii apart. Each straight part is this long. 7 plus 7 equals 14.
There are two straight parts. 2 times 14 equals 28.
The two curved parts are half circles, which together make one whole circle. 2 times 22 over 7 times 7 equals 44.
Add the straight parts and the curved parts. 28 plus 44 equals 72.
So the ribbon is 72 centimetres long.

G4A_CIRCLE_034.q: The hour hand of a wall clock is 7 centimetres long. How far does the tip of the hour hand travel in one full day of 24 hours? Use pi as 22 over 7.
hints: The tip of the hand moves along a circle. Before you calculate, think about how many times the hour hand goes all the way round in a whole day.
The hour hand takes 12 hours to go once round the clock face. Work out how many times it goes round in 24 hours.

Similar problem: a minute hand 21 centimetres long, over 2 hours. The minute hand goes round once every hour, so twice in 2 hours. One round is 2 times 22 over 7 times 21, which is 132 centimetres, so the tip travels 2 times 132, which is 264 centimetres.
steps: The tip moves on a circle of radius 7 centimetres. Find the distance once round. 2 times 22 over 7 times 7 equals 44.
The hour hand goes once round in 12 hours. Find how many times it goes round in a day. 24 divided by 12 equals 2.
Multiply the distance once round by the number of rounds. 2 times 44 equals 88.
So the tip of the hour hand travels 88 centimetres.

G4A_COUNTING_001.q: How many whole numbers are there from 15 to 42, counting both 15 and 42?
hints: When you count from one number up to another and both ends are included, think about whether subtracting alone counts every number.
Find 42 minus 15 first. Then ask yourself whether the starting number 15 has been counted yet.
A similar problem: from 6 to 10 the numbers are 6, 7, 8, 9, 10. Subtracting gives 10 minus 6, which is 4, and adding 1 for the starting number gives 5 numbers.
steps: Subtract the smaller number from the larger one. 42 minus 15 equals 27.
This counts the jumps. Add 1 so that the starting number 15 is counted too. 27 plus 1 equals 28.
There are 28 whole numbers from 15 to 42.

G4A_COUNTING_002.q: Meera stands in a queue at the school canteen. She is 7th from the front and 5th from the back. How many children are in the queue?
hints: A position from the front and a position from the back both count the same child. Think about what happens if you simply add them.
There are 6 children in front of Meera. Work out how many are behind her, then count Meera once.
A similar problem: Raju is 3rd from the front and 4th from the back. In front of him are 2 children, behind him are 3, and Raju makes 2 plus 3 plus 1, which is 6 children.
steps: Count the children in front of Meera and behind her. 7 minus 1 equals 6 in front, and 5 minus 1 equals 4 behind.
Add them, and add Meera herself once. 6 plus 4 plus 1 equals 11.
There are 11 children in the queue.

G4A_COUNTING_003.q: A straight fence is 40 metres long. A post stands every 5 metres, with a post at each end. How many posts are there?
hints: Posts stand at the ends of the gaps. In a straight line with a post at both ends, compare the number of posts with the number of gaps.
First find how many 5-metre gaps fit into 40 metres.
A similar problem: a 12-metre fence with a post every 4 metres has 12 divided by 4, which is 3 gaps. The posts stand at 0, 4, 8 and 12 metres, so there are 4 posts.
steps: Find the number of gaps between posts. 40 divided by 5 equals 8.
A straight line of gaps has one more post than gaps. 8 plus 1 equals 9.
There are 9 posts.

G4A_COUNTING_004.q: How many 2-digit numbers end in the digit 5?
hints: Think about which digits are allowed in the tens place of a 2-digit number.
