Start listing them: 15, 25, 35, and keep going until the last 2-digit number that ends in 5.
A similar problem: the 2-digit numbers smaller than 60 that end in 2 are 12, 22, 32, 42 and 52. The tens digit runs from 1 to 5, so there are 5 numbers.
steps: The ones digit is fixed as 5. The tens digit can be 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 or 9.
There are 9 such numbers.

G4A_COUNTING_005.q: Riya has 3 different tops and 2 different skirts. An outfit is one top worn with one skirt. How many different outfits can she make?
hints: Every top can be paired with every skirt. Think about how many pairs each top makes.
Take the first top. How many outfits can it make with the 2 skirts? Then do the same for the other tops.
A similar problem: with 4 caps and 2 scarves, each cap can go with 2 scarves, so there are 4 times 2, which is 8 pairs.
steps: Each top can be worn with either of the 2 skirts, so each top gives 2 outfits.
There are 3 tops. 3 times 2 equals 6.
Riya can make 6 different outfits.

G4A_COUNTING_006.q: How many even numbers are there from 1 to 30?
hints: Even and odd numbers take turns as you count. Think about what share of the numbers are even.
The even numbers start 2, 4, 6. Find the last even number in the range and see which place it holds in the list.
A similar problem: from 1 to 10 the even numbers are 2, 4, 6, 8, 10. Every second number is even, so there are 10 divided by 2, which is 5 of them.
steps: From 1 to 30, every second number is even: 2, 4, 6, and so on up to 30.
Half of the 30 numbers are even. 30 divided by 2 equals 15.
There are 15 even numbers from 1 to 30.

G4A_COUNTING_007.q: A carpenter cuts a long wooden plank into 6 pieces. He cuts one piece at a time. How many cuts does he make?
hints: Think about what one cut does to the number of pieces.
Before any cut there is 1 piece. After the first cut there are 2 pieces. Keep going until there are 6.
A similar problem: to cut a ribbon into 3 pieces, the first cut makes 2 pieces and the second cut makes 3 pieces. So 2 cuts are needed.
steps: The plank starts as 1 piece. Every cut adds 1 more piece.
To reach 6 pieces, 5 more pieces are needed. 6 minus 1 equals 5.
The carpenter makes 5 cuts.

G4A_COUNTING_008.q: How many different 2-digit numbers can you make using only the digits 3 and 8? A digit may be used twice in a number.
hints: Think about the choices for the tens place and the choices for the ones place.
Write the numbers that start with 3 first. Then write the ones that start with 8.
A similar problem: with the digits 1, 2 and 5 and repeats allowed, there are 3 choices for the tens place and 3 for the ones place, so 3 times 3 equals 9 numbers.
steps: The tens digit can be 3 or 8, and the ones digit can be 3 or 8.
That gives 2 choices for each place. 2 times 2 equals 4.
The numbers are 33, 38, 83 and 88, so 4 numbers can be made.

G4A_COUNTING_009.q: The pages of a small story book are numbered from 1 to 25. How many digits are printed in all to number the pages?
hints: Some page numbers have one digit and some have two. Count the two groups separately.
Pages 1 to 9 use one digit each. Work out how many pages are left from 10 to 25.
A similar problem: for pages 1 to 12, pages 1 to 9 use 9 digits. Pages 10, 11 and 12 are 3 pages using 2 digits each, which is 6 digits. In all, 9 plus 6 equals 15 digits.
steps: Pages 1 to 9 have one digit each. 9 times 1 equals 9.
Pages 10 to 25 are 16 pages with two digits each. 16 times 2 equals 32.
Add the two groups. 9 plus 32 equals 41.
In all, 41 digits are printed.

G4A_COUNTING_010.q: How many 2-digit numbers have digits that add up to 7?
hints: Work in an organised way: choose the tens digit first, and the ones digit is then decided.
Start with tens digit 1. The ones digit must be 6, giving 16. Now try tens digit 2, and carry on.
A similar problem: 2-digit numbers with digits adding to 4 are 13, 22, 31 and 40. The tens digit runs from 1 to 4, so there are 4 numbers.
steps: The tens digit can be 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 or 7. It cannot be 0.
For each tens digit there is exactly one ones digit that makes the total 7.
The numbers are 16, 25, 34, 43, 52, 61 and 70.
There are 7 such numbers.

G4A_COUNTING_011.q: Kiran writes all the numbers from 1 to 40 in her notebook. How many times does she write the digit 3?
hints: A digit can appear in the ones place or in the tens place. Count each place separately.
First list the numbers that have 3 in the ones place: 3, 13, and so on. Then look at the numbers that have 3 in the tens place.

A similar problem: from 1 to 30, the digit 2 is in the ones place in 2, 12 and 22, which is 3 times. It is in the tens place in 20 to 29, which is 10 times. In all it is written 13 times, and 22 is counted twice because it has two 2s.
steps: In the ones place, 3 appears in 3, 13, 23 and 33. That is 4 times.
In the tens place, 3 appears in 30, 31, 32, and so on up to 39. That is 10 times.
Add the two counts. The number 33 has two 3s, so it is rightly counted in both. 4 plus 10 equals 14.
She writes the digit 3 a total of 14 times.

G4A_COUNTING_012.q: 30 children stand in a line for the morning assembly. Arjun is 12th from the front. What is his position from the back?
hints: Find how many children stand behind him. His place from the back is one more than that.
Arjun is 12th from the front, so take 12 away from 30 to find how many children are behind him.
A similar problem: in a line of 10 children, Sita is 4th from the front. Behind her are 10 minus 4, which is 6 children, so she is 7th from the back.
steps: Find how many children are behind Arjun. 30 minus 12 equals 18.
Counting from the back, those 18 children come first and Arjun is next. 18 plus 1 equals 19.
Arjun is 19th from the back.

G4A_COUNTING_013.q: A square garden has sides of 12 metres. Posts are fixed all around its edge, one at every corner and one every 3 metres along each side. How many posts are needed?
hints: The posts go all the way around and come back to the start. In a closed loop, compare the number of posts with the number of gaps.
Find the distance all the way around the garden first. Then see how many 3-metre gaps fit into it.
A similar problem: a square of side 6 metres with a post every 2 metres has a distance around of 24 metres. That is 24 divided by 2, which is 12 gaps, and going around a loop needs exactly 12 posts.
steps: Find the distance around the garden. 4 times 12 equals 48.
Find the number of 3-metre gaps. 48 divided by 3 equals 16.
Around a closed loop the last gap ends at the first post, so the number of posts equals the number of gaps.
16 posts are needed.

G4A_COUNTING_014.q: Anu, Binu and Charu stand in a row for a photo. In how many different orders can they stand?
hints: Think place by place: who can stand first, then who can stand next, then who is left.
Suppose Anu stands first. Write the orders the other two can stand in. Then let Binu stand first, and then Charu.
A similar problem: two friends, Raj and Sam, can stand as Raj then Sam, or Sam then Raj. There are 2 choices for the first place and 1 for the second, so 2 times 1 equals 2 orders.
steps: Any of the 3 children can stand first.
Once the first is chosen, 2 children are left for the second place, and then 1 for the last place.
Multiply the choices. 3 times 2 times 1 equals 6.
They can stand in 6 different orders.

G4A_COUNTING_015.q: A window has 4 small square panes, arranged as 2 rows of 2. Counting squares of every size, how many squares can you see in the window?
hints: Squares can be of different sizes. Count the small ones, then look for bigger squares made by joining small ones.
Count the small panes first. Then ask whether all four panes together make a square.
A similar problem: a single square pane has just 1 square. A row of 2 panes has 2 small squares and no bigger square, because the two together make a long rectangle. So it has 2 squares.
steps: There are 4 small square panes.
The whole window, made of all 4 panes, is 1 big square.
Add them. 4 plus 1 equals 5.
There are 5 squares in the window.

G4A_COUNTING_016.q: 16 players enter a knockout badminton tournament. In every match the loser goes out and the winner plays on. How many matches are played to find the champion?
hints: Each match sends exactly one player out. Think about how many players must go out before one champion is left.
Count round by round: 16 players play 8 matches in the first round, leaving 8 players. Carry on until one player is left.
A similar problem: with 4 players, the first round has 2 matches and the final is 1 match. That is 2 plus 1, which is 3 matches, and 3 players have gone out.
steps: Count the matches in each round. 8 plus 4 plus 2 plus 1 equals 15.
Another way to see it: each match sends one player out, and 15 players must go out to leave 1 champion.
15 matches are played.

G4A_COUNTING_017.q: How many 2-digit numbers are multiples of 7?
hints: Find the smallest and the largest 2-digit multiples, then count how many multiples lie from one to the other.
The first multiple of 7 with two digits is 14, which is 7 times 2. Find the largest multiple of 7 that is below 100.
A similar problem: the 2-digit multiples of 20 are 20, 40, 60 and 80. They are 20 times 1 up to 20 times 4, so there are 4 of them.
steps: The smallest 2-digit multiple of 7 is 14. 7 times 2 equals 14.
The largest 2-digit multiple of 7 is 98. 7 times 14 equals 98.
Count the multipliers from 2 to 14. 14 minus 2 plus 1 equals 13.
There are 13 two-digit multiples of 7.

G4A_COUNTING_018.q: Sunita walks up from the 1st floor to the 4th floor and climbs 48 steps. Every floor has the same number of steps. How many steps would she climb from the 1st floor to the 7th floor?
hints: Going from one floor to another, count the flights of stairs climbed, not the floor numbers.
From the 1st floor to the 4th floor Sunita climbs 3 flights of stairs. Use this to find the steps in one flight.
A similar problem: going from the 1st floor to the 3rd floor is 2 flights. If that is 20 steps, each flight has 10 steps. From the 1st floor to the 5th floor is 4 flights, which is 40 steps.
steps: From the 1st to the 4th floor there are 3 flights of stairs. 4 minus 1 equals 3.
Find the steps in one flight. 48 divided by 3 equals 16.
From the 1st to the 7th floor there are 6 flights. 6 times 16 equals 96.
She would climb 96 steps.

G4A_COUNTING_019.q: An ice-cream shop has 4 flavours: mango, chocolate, vanilla and strawberry. Rohan picks 2 different flavours for his cup. How many different pairs of flavours can he choose?
hints: A pair is the same whichever flavour is named first. List the pairs in an organised way so that none is repeated.
Start with mango and pair it with each of the other three. Then move to chocolate, pairing it only with flavours not used with it before.
A similar problem: from 3 fruits, apple, banana and cherry, the pairs are apple-banana, apple-cherry and banana-cherry. That is 2 plus 1, which is 3 pairs.
steps: Mango can pair with chocolate, vanilla or strawberry: 3 pairs.
Chocolate can pair with vanilla or strawberry: 2 new pairs. Vanilla can pair with strawberry: 1 new pair.
Add the pairs. 3 plus 2 plus 1 equals 6.
Rohan can choose 6 different pairs.

G4A_COUNTING_020.q: Using each of the digits 2, 0 and 5 exactly once, how many 3-digit numbers can be made?
hints: Look carefully at the hundreds place. One of these digits cannot go there.
A 3-digit number cannot begin with 0. So the hundreds digit is 2 or 5. List the numbers that begin with 2 first.
A similar problem: with the digits 0 and 7 used once each, 07 is just 7, so the only 2-digit number is 70. That is 1 number, not 2.
steps: The hundreds digit can be 2 or 5, but not 0.
Starting with 2: 205 and 250. Starting with 5: 502 and 520.
Count them. 2 times 2 equals 4.
4 three-digit numbers can be made.

G4A_COUNTING_021.q: A big triangle has two straight lines drawn from its top corner down to its base. These lines split it into 3 small triangles side by side. Counting triangles of every size, how many triangles are there in the figure?
hints: Count the small triangles first, then triangles made by joining neighbouring small ones.
There are 3 small triangles. Next, count the triangles made of 2 small triangles that are next to each other.
A similar problem: one line from the top corner to the base splits a triangle into 2 small triangles. Together with the big one, that makes 2 plus 1, which is 3 triangles.
steps: There are 3 small triangles.
Two neighbouring small triangles together make a bigger triangle. This can be done in 2 ways: left with middle, and middle with right.
All three together make the 1 big triangle.
Add them all. 3 plus 2 plus 1 equals 6.
There are 6 triangles in the figure.

G4A_COUNTING_022.q: In a ticket queue at the railway station, Ravi is 8th from the front and Sana is 15th from the front. How many people stand between them?
hints: The people between them hold the positions after Ravi and before Sana. Neither Ravi nor Sana is counted.
List the positions between them, starting 9th, 10th, and stopping just before the 15th.
A similar problem: between the 3rd and the 6th person stand the 4th and the 5th. Subtracting gives 6 minus 3, which is 3, and taking 1 away gives 2 people.
steps: The people between them are at positions 9, 10, 11, 12, 13 and 14.
A quick way: subtract the positions and take away 1. 15 minus 8 minus 1 equals 6.
6 people stand between them.

G4A_COUNTING_023.q: How many numbers from 100 to 200, counting both 100 and 200, end in the digit 0?
hints: Numbers ending in 0 come once in every ten numbers. Be careful with both ends of the range.
List them: 100, 110, 120, and keep going. Check whether 200 belongs in your list.
A similar problem: from 10 to 50, the numbers ending in 0 are 10, 20, 30, 40 and 50. There are 4 jumps of ten, and 4 plus 1 equals 5 numbers.
steps: From 100 to 200 there are 10 jumps of ten, and one more for the starting number. 10 plus 1 equals 11.
There are 11 such numbers.

G4A_COUNTING_024.q: The pages of a book are numbered starting from 1. In all, 129 digits were printed for the page numbers. How many pages does the book have?
hints: Work backwards. Take away the digits used by the one-digit pages, then see how many two-digit pages the remaining digits can number.
Pages 1 to 9 use 9 digits. Subtract these from 129 to find the digits left for pages with two digits.
A similar problem: a booklet uses 29 digits. Pages 1 to 9 use 9, leaving 20 digits. That numbers 20 divided by 2, which is 10 two-digit pages, so the booklet has 9 plus 10, which is 19 pages.
steps: Pages 1 to 9 use 9 digits. Find the digits left. 129 minus 9 equals 120.
Each page from 10 onwards uses 2 digits. 120 divided by 2 equals 60.
Add the one-digit pages and the two-digit pages. 9 plus 60 equals 69.
The book has 69 pages.

G4A_COUNTING_025.q: How many 2-digit numbers have a tens digit that is bigger than the ones digit? For example, 72 is such a number but 27 is not.
hints: Work in an organised way: fix the tens digit and count the ones digits that are smaller than it. Look for a pattern.
With tens digit 1, the only smaller ones digit is 0, giving 10. With tens digit 2, the ones digit can be 0 or 1. Carry on up to tens digit 9.

A similar problem: among numbers from 10 to 39, tens digit 1 gives 1 number, which is 10. Tens digit 2 gives 2 numbers, 20 and 21. And tens digit 3 gives 3 numbers, 30, 31 and 32. That is 1 plus 2 plus 3, which is 6 numbers.
steps: Tens digit 1 gives 1 number, which is 10. Tens digit 2 gives 2 numbers, 20 and 21. Tens digit 3 gives 3 numbers, and so on.
Tens digit 9 gives 9 numbers, from 90 to 98.
Add the counts. 1 plus 2 plus 3 plus 4 plus 5 plus 6 plus 7 plus 8 plus 9 equals 45.
There are 45 such numbers.

G4A_COUNTING_026.q: How many 3-digit numbers have digits that add up to 4?
hints: Work in an organised way: fix the hundreds digit, then count the ways the other two digits can make up the rest.
Start with hundreds digit 1. The other two digits must add up to 3. List these numbers, then move on to hundreds digit 2.
A similar problem: 3-digit numbers with digits adding to 2 are 101, 110 and 200. Hundreds digit 1 gives 2 numbers and hundreds digit 2 gives 1 number, so there are 3.
steps: Hundreds digit 1: the other digits add to 3, giving 103, 112, 121 and 130. That is 4 numbers.
Hundreds digit 2: 202, 211 and 220. That is 3 numbers.
Hundreds digit 3: 301 and 310. Hundreds digit 4: 400. That is 2 numbers and 1 number.
Add the counts. 4 plus 3 plus 2 plus 1 equals 10.
There are 10 such numbers.

G4A_COUNTING_027.q: A square board is divided into 9 small squares, in 3 rows of 3. Counting squares of every size, how many squares are there on the board?
hints: Squares come in different sizes. Count each size separately: the smallest, the middle size, and the largest.
There are 9 small squares. Now count the squares that are 2 small squares wide and 2 tall. One sits in each corner of the board.
A similar problem: a board with 2 rows of 2 has 4 small squares and 1 big square, so 4 plus 1 equals 5 squares.
steps: There are 9 small squares.
Squares that are 2 wide and 2 tall: one fits in each corner of the board, so there are 4.
The whole board is 1 large square.
Add all the sizes. 9 plus 4 plus 1 equals 14.
There are 14 squares on the board.

G4A_COUNTING_028.q: Four small squares are joined in a single row to make a long strip. Counting rectangles of every size, with the small squares counted too, how many rectangles are there in the strip?
hints: A rectangle in the strip is made of 1, 2, 3 or 4 neighbouring squares. Count each length separately.
There are 4 rectangles made of 1 square. Next, count the rectangles made of 2 neighbouring squares: first with second, second with third, and so on.
A similar problem: a strip of 3 squares has 3 rectangles of one square, 2 of two squares and 1 of three squares. That is 3 plus 2 plus 1, which is 6 rectangles.
steps: Rectangles made of 1 square: 4.
Rectangles made of 2 neighbouring squares: 3. Made of 3 neighbouring squares: 2.
The whole strip of 4 squares: 1.
Add them. 4 plus 3 plus 2 plus 1 equals 10.
There are 10 rectangles in the strip.

G4A_COUNTING_029.q: At a birthday party, every child gave one card to every other child. In all, 30 cards were given. How many children were at the party?
hints: Each child gives a card to everyone except themselves. So the total is the number of children times one less than that number.
Try a small party: with 3 children, each gives 2 cards. Work out the total for 4 children, then 5, and keep going until you reach 30.
A similar problem: if 12 cards were given, try 4 children. Each gives 3 cards, and 4 times 3 equals 12. So there were 4 children.
steps: If there are some children, each one gives a card to all the others, which is one fewer than the number of children.
Look for two numbers next to each other that multiply to 30. 6 times 5 equals 30.
So 6 children each gave 5 cards.
There were 6 children at the party.

G4A_COUNTING_030.q: Using the digits 0, 1, 2 and 3, with no digit repeated in a number, how many 3-digit even numbers can be made?
hints: Two places need care: the ones place must make the number even, and the hundreds place cannot be 0. Split into cases by the last digit.
An even number here ends in 0 or 2. First count the numbers that end in 0. The other two places are filled from 1, 2 and 3.

A similar problem: 2-digit even numbers from the digits 0, 3 and 4 with no repeats. Ending in 0: 30 and 40. Ending in 4: only 34, because 04 is not a 2-digit number. That is 2 plus 1, which is 3 numbers.
steps: Ending in 0: the hundreds digit has 3 choices, 1, 2 or 3, and the tens digit then has 2 choices. 3 times 2 equals 6.
Ending in 2: the hundreds digit can only be 1 or 3, and the tens digit then has 2 choices. 2 times 2 equals 4.
Add the two cases. 6 plus 4 equals 10.
10 such numbers can be made.

G4A_COUNTING_031.q: A temple bell takes 6 seconds to ring 4 times, measured from the first ring to the last ring. The rings are evenly spaced. How many seconds does it take to ring 10 times?
hints: The time is spent in the gaps between the rings, not on the rings themselves. Count the gaps.
Between 4 rings there are 3 gaps. Use this to find how long one gap lasts.
A similar problem: a bell takes 8 seconds to ring 3 times. That is 2 gaps, so each gap is 4 seconds. Ringing 6 times has 5 gaps, and that takes 5 times 4, which is 20 seconds.
steps: 4 rings have 3 gaps between them. Find the length of one gap. 6 divided by 3 equals 2.
10 rings have 9 gaps between them. 10 minus 1 equals 9.
Multiply the gaps by the length of each gap. 9 times 2 equals 18.
It takes 18 seconds to ring 10 times.

G4A_COUNTING_032.q: Children stand in a row. Tara is 9th from the left and Uma is 6th from the right. They swap places, and now Tara is 15th from the left. How many children are in the row?
hints: After the swap, Tara stands exactly where Uma stood. So you know one spot's position from both ends.
Uma's old spot is 6th from the right. After the swap Tara is in that spot, and it is 15th from the left. Use both positions for this one spot.
A similar problem: a spot is 4th from the left and 3rd from the right. There are 3 children to its left and 2 to its right, so the row has 3 plus 2 plus 1, which is 6 children.
steps: After swapping, Tara stands in Uma's old spot. That spot is 15th from the left and 6th from the right.
Add the two positions and take away 1, because the spot is counted twice. 15 plus 6 minus 1 equals 20.
There are 20 children in the row.

G4A_COUNTING_033.q: Aman writes all the numbers from 1 to 100. How many times does he write the digit 1?
hints: Count place by place: how often the digit is in the ones place, in the tens place, and in the hundreds place.
In the ones place the digit 1 appears in 1, 11, 21, and so on up to 91. Count these first, then look at the tens place.
A similar problem: from 1 to 50, the digit 4 is in the ones place 5 times, in 4, 14, 24, 34 and 44. It is in the tens place 10 times, from 40 to 49. That makes 15 times.
steps: Tens place: 10, 11, 12, and so on up to 19.
Hundreds place: only in 100. That is 1 time.
Add them. 10 plus 10 plus 1 equals 21.
Aman writes the digit 1 a total of 21 times.

G4A_COUNTING_034.q: How many numbers from 1 to 60 can be divided exactly by 2 or by 3, or by both?
hints: Some numbers can be divided by both 2 and 3. If you count the two groups and add, those numbers get counted twice.
Count the multiples of 2 up to 60, and the multiples of 3 up to 60. Then find how many numbers are in both lists.
A similar problem: from 1 to 12 there are 6 multiples of 2 and 4 multiples of 3. The numbers 6 and 12 are in both lists. So the count is 6 plus 4 minus 2, which is 8.
steps: Count the multiples of 2 and the multiples of 3. 60 divided by 2 equals 30, and 60 divided by 3 equals 20.
Numbers in both lists are the multiples of 6. 60 divided by 6 equals 10.
Add the two lists and take away the numbers counted twice. 30 plus 20 minus 10 equals 40.
There are 40 such numbers.

G4A_COUNTING_035.q: A flag has 3 stripes in a row. Each stripe is painted red, green or blue. Stripes that touch each other must be different colours. How many different flags can be made?
hints: Choose the colours stripe by stripe. Read the rule with care: only stripes that touch must differ.
The first stripe can be any of the 3 colours. The second stripe must differ from the first. Think about how many colours the third stripe can take.
A similar problem: a flag with 2 stripes and 3 colours, where the stripes must differ. The first stripe has 3 choices and the second has 2, so there are 3 times 2, which is 6 flags.
steps: The first stripe can be any of 3 colours.
The second stripe touches the first, so it has 2 choices.
The third stripe touches only the second, so it also has 2 choices. It may match the first stripe.
Multiply the choices. 3 times 2 times 2 equals 12.
12 different flags can be made.

G4A_COUNTING_036.q: How many numbers are in this list? 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24
hints: Count the numbers one at a time. You are counting how many there are, not looking at how big they are.
Point to each number in turn and count: 4 is the first, 8 is the second, and so on.
A similar problem: the list 5, 10, 15 has three numbers, because we count 5 as one, 10 as two and 15 as three.
steps: Count the numbers one by one: 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24.
There are 6 numbers in the list.

G4A_COUNTING_037.q: Ria writes down all the whole numbers from 6 to 10: 6, 7, 8, 9, 10. How many numbers does she write?
hints: Count the numbers Ria writes, one at a time.
Point to each number in the list 6, 7, 8, 9, 10 and count as you go.
A similar problem: the whole numbers from 2 to 4 are 2, 3, 4. Counting them one by one gives 3 numbers.
steps: Count the numbers one by one: 6, 7, 8, 9, 10.
Ria writes 5 numbers.

G4A_COUNTING_038.q: How many whole numbers lie between 10 and 15? Do not count 10 or 15.
hints: Write out the numbers that come after the first number and before the last one, then count them.
The first number after 10 is 11. Keep writing numbers until you reach the one just before 15.
A similar problem: the whole numbers between 3 and 6 are 4 and 5, so there are 2 of them.
steps: Write the numbers that come after 10 and before 15: 11, 12, 13, 14.
Count them. There are 4 whole numbers between 10 and 15.

G4A_COUNTING_039.q: Anu and Bala stand in a line, one behind the other. In how many different orders can they stand?
hints: Write down every order you can think of, then count them.
Start with Anu in front and Bala behind. Is there another way?
A similar problem: a red cup and a blue cup on a shelf can be placed as red then blue, or blue then red. That is 2 orders.
steps: List the orders: Anu in front with Bala behind, or Bala in front with Anu behind.
There are no other ways, so they can stand in 2 different orders.

G4A_COUNTING_040.q: Using the digits 4 and 7 once each, how many different 2-digit numbers can you make?
hints: Write down every number you can make, then count them.
Put 4 in the tens place and 7 in the ones place. Then try the digits the other way round.
A similar problem: with the digits 2 and 5 once each, the numbers are 25 and 52. That is 2 numbers.
steps: Put 4 first and then 7 to make 47. Put 7 first and then 4 to make 74.
There are no other ways, so you can make 2 different numbers.

G4A_COUNTING_041.q: Five children stand in a queue in this order, starting from the front: Asha, Bina, Chetan, Dev, Esha. Who is 3rd in the queue?
hints: Count along the queue from the front, one child at a time.
Asha is 1st because she is at the front. Keep counting: 2nd, 3rd.
A similar problem: in the queue Ravi, Sita, Tara, counting from the front, Ravi is 1st and Sita is 2nd.
steps: Count from the front: Asha is 1st and Bina is 2nd.
The next child is 3rd. So Chetan is 3rd in the queue.

G4A_COUNTING_042.q: Ravi is 4th in a queue. How many children are standing in front of him?
hints: Think about the places in the queue that come before Ravi's place.
The places in front of the 4th place are the 1st, the 2nd and so on. List them.
A similar problem: Sita is 6th in a queue. The children in front of her are 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th and 5th, so 5 children are in front of her.
steps: The places in front of the 4th place are the 1st, 2nd and 3rd places.
So 3 children are standing in front of Ravi. 4 minus 1 equals 3.

G4A_COUNTING_043.q: There are 6 children in a queue. Meena is at the very front. How many children are behind her?
hints: Everyone in the queue except Meena is behind her.
Take Meena away from the 6 children and see how many are left.
A similar problem: 9 children are in a queue and Arun is at the very front. The other children, 9 minus 1, which is 8, are behind him.
steps: Meena is at the front, so all the other children are behind her.
Take Meena away from the 6 children. So 5 children are behind her. 6 minus 1 equals 5.

G4A_COUNTING_044.q: How many even numbers are in this list? 3, 4, 7, 8, 10, 13
hints: An even number can be shared into two equal groups. Even numbers end in 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8.
Go through the list one number at a time and look at the last digit of each.
A similar problem: in the list 1, 2, 5, 6 the even numbers are 2 and 6, so there are 2 even numbers.
steps: Even numbers end in 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8. In the list, these are 4, 8 and 10.
So there are 3 even numbers in the list.

G4A_COUNTING_045.q: Anu, Binu and Charu stand in a row. Writing A for Anu, B for Binu and C for Charu, all the possible orders are: A B C, A C B, B A C, B C A, C A B, C B A. In how many of these orders is Anu first?
hints: Look at the first letter of each order in the list.
Anu is shown by the letter A. Find the orders that begin with A and count them.
A similar problem: in the same list, the orders that begin with C are C A B and C B A, so Charu is first in 2 orders.
steps: Look for the orders that begin with A: they are A B C and A C B.
So Anu is first in 2 of the orders.

G4A_COUNTING_046.q: Count the days from Monday to Thursday, counting both Monday and Thursday. How many days is that?
hints: Say the days in order and count each one as you say it.
Start with Monday as the first day. Keep going until you have said Thursday.
A similar problem: from Friday to Sunday, counting both, the days are Friday, Saturday, Sunday. That is 3 days.
steps: List the days: Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday.
Count them. That is 4 days.

G4A_COUNTING_047.q: Seven chairs stand in a row. They are numbered 1 to 7 in order. Which chair is exactly in the middle?
hints: The middle chair has the same number of chairs on each side of it.
Write the numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 in a row. Cross off one from each end, again and again, until one is left.
A similar problem: for five chairs numbered 1 to 5, cross off 1 and 5, then 2 and 4. Chair 3 is left, with two chairs on each side.
steps: Write the chairs in order: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7.
Chairs 1, 2 and 3 are on one side and chairs 5, 6 and 7 are on the other side.
With three chairs on each side, the middle one is Chair 4.

G4A_DATA_001.q: Rohit's runs in five cricket matches were: Match 1: 34, Match 2: 52, Match 3: 47, Match 4: 25, Match 5: 43. In which match did he score the most runs?
hints: This asks you to find the biggest number in a list and say which match it belongs to.
Compare the tens digits of the five scores first. Which scores have the biggest tens digit?
Example: Scores of Game 1: 18, Game 2: 31, Game 3: 27. The biggest number is 31, so the most runs came in Game 2.
steps: Look at the tens digits: 34, 52, 47, 25 and 43 have tens digits 3, 5, 4, 2 and 4.
The biggest tens digit is 5, so 52 is the biggest score.
52 runs were scored in Match 2, so the answer is Match 2.

G4A_DATA_002.q: In a pictograph, each picture of a book stands for 5 books sold. Monday has 4 pictures, Tuesday has 6 pictures, Wednesday has 3 pictures and Thursday has 5 pictures. On which day were the fewest books sold?
hints: Every picture stands for the same number of books, so think about what the number of pictures tells you.
The day with the fewest pictures has the fewest books. Compare 4, 6, 3 and 5.
Example: Each picture stands for 2 kites. Ravi has 7 pictures, Sita has 2 pictures and Anu has 5 pictures. Sita has the fewest pictures, so Sita has the fewest kites.
steps: Each picture stands for the same number of books, so fewer pictures means fewer books.
The numbers of pictures are 4, 6, 3 and 5. The smallest is 3.
Wednesday has 3 pictures, which is 15 books. 3 times 5 equals 15.
The fewest books were sold on Wednesday.

G4A_DATA_003.q: In a tally chart, each bundle stands for 5 and each single stroke stands for 1. The row for parrots has 3 bundles and 2 single strokes. How many parrots were counted?
hints: A tally chart counts in fives. Work out the bundles first, then add the single strokes.
Find how many the 3 bundles stand for by multiplying 3 by 5.
Example: 2 bundles and 4 single strokes. The bundles give 2 times 5 equals 10, and 10 plus 4 equals 14.
steps: Each bundle stands for 5, so 3 bundles stand for 15. 3 times 5 equals 15.
Add the 2 single strokes. 15 plus 2 equals 17.
17 parrots were counted.

G4A_DATA_004.q: The number of children present in Class 4 was: Monday 38, Tuesday 35, Wednesday 40, Thursday 32. How many more children were present on Wednesday than on Tuesday?
hints: The words 'how many more' ask you to compare two numbers from the list.
Pick out the numbers for Wednesday and Tuesday only. They are 40 and 35.
Example: Monday 26, Tuesday 19. To find how many more on Monday, subtract: 26 minus 19 equals 7.
steps: Wednesday has 40 children and Tuesday has 35 children.
Subtract to find how many more. 40 minus 35 equals 5.
5 more children were present on Wednesday.

G4A_DATA_005.q: A bar graph shows the samosas sold at a stall: Monday 12, Tuesday 15, Wednesday 9, Thursday 15, Friday 11. Which two days have bars of the same height?
hints: Bars of the same height show the same number. Look for a number that appears twice.
Read the five numbers one by one: 12, 15, 9, 15, 11. Which number do you see two times?
Example: Red 7, Blue 4, Green 7, Yellow 6. The number 7 appears twice, so the bars for Red and Green are equally tall.
steps: Bars are equally tall when their numbers are equal.
In the list 12, 15, 9, 15, 11 only the number 15 appears twice.
15 belongs to Tuesday and Thursday, so the equal bars are Tuesday and Thursday.

G4A_DATA_006.q: The children of Class 4 each chose one favourite fruit: Mango 14, Banana 6, Apple 9, Guava 5. How many children chose banana or guava?
hints: You need to put two groups from the table together.
Pick out only the numbers for banana and guava. They are 6 and 5.
Example: Rose 8, Lily 7, Lotus 4. The children who chose rose or lotus are 8 plus 4 equals 12.
steps: Banana was chosen by 6 children and guava by 5 children.
Add the two groups. 6 plus 5 equals 11.
11 children chose banana or guava.

G4A_DATA_007.q: Six children got these marks in a spelling test: 14, 18, 9, 20, 12, 17. How many children got more than 15 marks?
hints: Here you count how many numbers in a list are bigger than a given number.
Go through the marks one at a time and tick each one that is bigger than 15. Start with 14: is it bigger than 15?
Example: Marks 6, 11, 8, 13, 5. The marks more than 10 are 11 and 13, so 2 children got more than 10.
steps: Check each mark against 15.
14, 9 and 12 are less than 15. The marks 18, 20 and 17 are more than 15.
That makes 3 children with more than 15 marks.

G4A_DATA_008.q: Each child in a class chose one favourite game: Cricket 13, Kho-kho 8, Football 7, Carrom 4. How many children are there in the class?
hints: Every child chose exactly one game, so the whole class is all the groups put together.
Add the four numbers. A good start is 13 plus 7, which makes a round number.
Example: Tea 9, Milk 11, Juice 5. All together that is 9 plus 11 plus 5 equals 25 people.
steps: Add cricket and football first. 13 plus 7 equals 20.
Add kho-kho and carrom. 8 plus 4 equals 12.
Put the two sums together. 20 plus 12 equals 32.
There are 32 children in the class.

G4A_DATA_009.q: In a tally chart, a bundle stands for 5 and a single stroke stands for 1. Which of these shows 23?
hints: Think about how many full fives fit into the number, and what is left over.
Count in fives: 5, 10, 15, 20. How many fives is that, and how many more do you need to reach 23?
Example: To show 12, count in fives: 5, 10. That is 2 bundles, and 12 minus 10 equals 2 single strokes.
steps: Four fives make 20. 4 times 5 equals 20.
Find what is left after 20. 23 minus 20 equals 3.
So 23 is shown by 4 bundles and 3 strokes.

G4A_DATA_010.q: In a pictograph, each picture of a sun stands for 2 sunny days. January has 5 pictures, February has 8 pictures, March has 6 pictures and April has 9 pictures. Which month had 16 sunny days?
hints: Each picture stands for more than one day, so the number of pictures is not the number of days.
Work out how many pictures are needed to show 16 days when each picture stands for 2 days.
Example: Each picture stands for 5 pens. To show 20 pens you need 20 divided by 5 equals 4 pictures, so look for the row with 4 pictures.
steps: Each picture stands for 2 days, so 16 days need 8 pictures. 16 divided by 2 equals 8.
The month with 8 pictures is February.
February had 16 sunny days.

G4A_DATA_011.q: The heights of five plants in centimetres are: Rose 34, Tulsi 28, Neem 41, Mint 19, Lily 37. Which plant is the second tallest?
hints: Put the numbers in order from biggest to smallest, then pick the one in second place.
Find the tallest plant first. Which height is the biggest of 34, 28, 41, 19 and 37?
Example: Asha 22, Bina 30, Charu 26. From biggest to smallest: 30, 26, 22. The second biggest is 26, so Charu is second tallest.
steps: From biggest to smallest the heights are 41, 37, 34, 28, 19.
The tallest is 41, Neem. The next is 37.
37 centimetres is the height of Lily, so the second tallest plant is Lily.

G4A_DATA_012.q: The side of a bar graph is marked 0, 10, 20, 30, 40. The top of Tuesday's bar is exactly halfway between the marks 20 and 30. What number does Tuesday's bar show?
hints: When a bar ends between two marks, its value is between those two numbers.
Find the number that is exactly in the middle of 20 and 30. How far apart are 20 and 30?
Example: A bar ends halfway between 40 and 60. The marks are 20 apart, half of 20 is 10, and 40 plus 10 equals 50.
steps: The marks 20 and 30 are 10 apart. 30 minus 20 equals 10.
Half of 10 is 5. 10 divided by 2 equals 5.
Go 5 above 20. 20 plus 5 equals 25.
Tuesday's bar shows 25.

G4A_DATA_013.q: In a pictograph, each picture stands for 3 kites. Ravi's row has 5 pictures and Meena's row has 8 pictures. How many more kites does Meena have than Ravi?
hints: This is a pictograph comparison. Remember that each picture stands for more than one kite.
Find how many more pictures Meena has than Ravi: 8 minus 5.
Example: Each picture stands for 4 balls. Amit has 6 pictures and Sunil has 4 pictures. Amit has 2 more pictures, and 2 times 4 equals 8 more balls.
steps: Meena has 3 more pictures than Ravi. 8 minus 5 equals 3.
Each picture stands for 3 kites. 3 times 3 equals 9.
Meena has 9 more kites than Ravi.

G4A_DATA_014.q: In a pictograph of library books, each picture stands for 5 books. Monday has 4 pictures, Tuesday has 6 pictures and Wednesday has 3 pictures. How many books were borrowed on the three days altogether?
hints: Find the total number of pictures, then change pictures into books.
Add the pictures for the three days: 4 plus 6 plus 3.
Example: Each picture stands for 2 pens. Three rows have 3, 5 and 4 pictures. That is 12 pictures, and 12 times 2 equals 24 pens.
steps: Add the pictures for the three days. 4 plus 6 plus 3 equals 13.
Each picture stands for 5 books. 13 times 5 equals 65.
65 books were borrowed altogether.

G4A_DATA_015.q: In a pictograph, each picture stands for 6 eggs. A farmer's chart has 5 pictures for Monday and 3 pictures for Tuesday. He packs all these eggs in boxes of 12. How many boxes does he fill?
hints: There are two parts here: first find the number of eggs, then share them into boxes.
Find the total number of pictures for the two days, then multiply by 6 to get the eggs.
Example: Each picture stands for 4 buns. There are 6 pictures, so 24 buns. Packed in bags of 8, that is 24 divided by 8 equals 3 bags.
steps: Add the pictures. 5 plus 3 equals 8.
Each picture stands for 6 eggs. 8 times 6 equals 48.
Put the eggs in boxes of 12. 48 divided by 12 equals 4.
He fills 4 boxes.

G4A_DATA_016.q: A sweet shop sold 60 laddoos in four days. The table shows: Monday 12, Tuesday 18, Thursday 14, but the number for Wednesday is smudged. How many laddoos were sold on Wednesday?
hints: You know the whole and three of its four parts. Think about how to find the missing part.
Add the three numbers you can read: 12 plus 18 plus 14.
Example: Total 50, and three days show 10, 15 and 5. These add to 30, so the missing day is 50 minus 30 equals 20.
steps: Add the three known days. 12 plus 18 plus 14 equals 44.
Take this away from the total. 60 minus 44 equals 16.
16 laddoos were sold on Wednesday.

G4A_DATA_017.q: Tickets sold at a mela: on Saturday, 20 adult tickets and 35 child tickets; on Sunday, 28 adult tickets and 30 child tickets. How many more tickets were sold on Sunday than on Saturday?
hints: Each day has two kinds of ticket. Find each day's total before you compare.
Add the adult and child tickets for Saturday: 20 plus 35.
Example: Day 1 has 10 and 12 tickets, total 22. Day 2 has 15 and 14 tickets, total 29. Day 2 sold 29 minus 22 equals 7 more.
steps: Saturday's total. 20 plus 35 equals 55.
Sunday's total. 28 plus 30 equals 58.
Compare the totals. 58 minus 55 equals 3.
3 more tickets were sold on Sunday.

G4A_DATA_018.q: In a pictograph, each picture stands for 4 children and Monday's row has 6 pictures. The chart is drawn again with each picture standing for 8 children. How many pictures will Monday's row have now?
hints: The number of children stays the same. Only the value of each picture changes.
Find how many children Monday's row shows: 6 pictures of 4 children each.
Example: 10 pictures of 2 pens each show 20 pens. If each picture stands for 5 pens, you need 20 divided by 5 equals 4 pictures.
steps: Find the number of children. 6 times 4 equals 24.
Each new picture stands for 8 children. 24 divided by 8 equals 3.
Monday's row will have 3 pictures.

G4A_DATA_019.q: In a pictograph, a full picture stands for 10 coconuts and a half picture stands for 5 coconuts. Monday's row has 3 full pictures and 1 half picture. Tuesday's row has 2 full pictures. How many coconuts were sold on the two days together?
hints: Work out each day's coconuts, counting full pictures and half pictures separately.
For Monday, find 3 full pictures of 10 and then add 5 for the half picture.
Example: A full picture is 4 and a half picture is 2. A row with 2 full pictures and 1 half picture shows 8 plus 2 equals 10.
steps: Monday: 3 full pictures and a half picture. 30 plus 5 equals 35.
Tuesday: 2 full pictures. 2 times 10 equals 20.
Add the two days. 35 plus 20 equals 55.
55 coconuts were sold on the two days.

G4A_DATA_020.q: A tally chart of birds uses bundles of 5 and single strokes. Crows: 2 bundles and 3 strokes. Sparrows: 3 bundles and 1 stroke. Pigeons: 1 bundle and 4 strokes. How many birds were counted in all?
hints: Change each tally row into a number, then add the rows.
Start with crows: 2 bundles are 10, and 3 strokes more.
Example: Row one has 1 bundle and 2 strokes, which is 7. Row two has 2 bundles and 1 stroke, which is 11. Together 7 plus 11 equals 18.
steps: Crows. 10 plus 3 equals 13.
Sparrows. 15 plus 1 equals 16.
Pigeons. 5 plus 4 equals 9.
Add the three rows. 13 plus 16 plus 9 equals 38.
38 birds were counted in all.

G4A_DATA_021.q: A bar graph shows kites sold: Monday 14, Tuesday 9, Wednesday 17, Thursday 11. Friday's bar is twice as tall as Tuesday's bar. How many kites were sold on the five days altogether?
hints: One value is not given directly. Find it from the clue, then add all five days.
Find Friday's number first. It is twice Tuesday's number, which is 9.
Example: Monday 5, Tuesday 8, and Wednesday is twice Monday. Wednesday is 10, and the total is 5 plus 8 plus 10 equals 23.
steps: Friday is twice Tuesday. 2 times 9 equals 18.
Add Monday to Thursday. 14 plus 9 plus 17 plus 11 equals 51.
Add Friday. 51 plus 18 equals 69.
69 kites were sold altogether.

G4A_DATA_022.q: 40 children each chose one favourite game. Cricket was chosen by 16, football by 10 and badminton by 8. All the others chose kabaddi. How many children chose kabaddi?
hints: The whole group is known. The children who are left over after three games chose the fourth game.
Add the children who chose cricket, football and badminton: 16 plus 10 plus 8.
Example: 30 children; 12 chose red and 9 chose blue, the rest chose green. 12 plus 9 equals 21, so green got 30 minus 21 equals 9.
steps: Add the three known games. 16 plus 10 plus 8 equals 34.
Take this away from all the children. 40 minus 34 equals 6.
6 children chose kabaddi.

G4A_DATA_023.q: Meera read 12 pages on Monday, 0 pages on Tuesday, 9 pages on Wednesday and 15 pages on Thursday. What is the average number of pages she read per day over these four days?
hints: An average shares the total equally over all the days, even a day when nothing was read.
Add the pages for all four days: 12 plus 0 plus 9 plus 15.
Example: Goals in three matches are 4, 0 and 2. The total is 6, and 6 divided by 3 matches equals 2 goals per match.
steps: Add the pages. 12 plus 0 plus 9 plus 15 equals 36.
There are 4 days, and Tuesday counts as a day too.
Share the total equally. 36 divided by 4 equals 9.
The average is 9 pages per day.

G4A_DATA_024.q: A bar graph shows cups of tea sold: Monday 22, Tuesday 17, Wednesday 25, Thursday 19. Which list puts the days in order from the shortest bar to the tallest bar?
hints: The shortest bar shows the smallest number and the tallest bar shows the biggest number.
Find the smallest of 22, 17, 25 and 19. That day comes first.
Example: Sunday 8, Monday 5, Tuesday 9. From smallest to biggest the numbers are 5, 8, 9, so the order is Monday, Sunday, Tuesday.
steps: From smallest to biggest the numbers are 17, 19, 22, 25.
17 is Tuesday, 19 is Thursday, 22 is Monday and 25 is Wednesday.
The order from shortest to tallest is Tuesday, Thursday, Monday, Wednesday.

G4A_DATA_025.q: A school has three clubs. Art: 9 girls and 6 boys. Music: 7 girls and 11 boys. Chess: 5 girls and 12 boys. Which club has the most children?
hints: Each club has girls and boys. Find each club's total before comparing.
Add the girls and boys in the Art club: 9 plus 6.
Example: Team P has 4 girls and 9 boys, 13 in all. Team Q has 8 girls and 6 boys, 14 in all. Team Q has more children.
steps: Art club. 9 plus 6 equals 15.
Music club. 7 plus 11 equals 18.
Chess club. 5 plus 12 equals 17.
18 is the biggest total, so the club with the most children is Music.

G4A_DATA_026.q: Children chose their favourite fruit: Mango 18, Apple 9, Banana 12, Orange 6, Grapes 3. Which fruit was chosen by exactly twice as many children as orange?
hints: Twice as many means two times a number. Find that number, then look for it in the list.
Orange was chosen by 6 children. Work out 2 times 6.
Example: Tea 4, Milk 8, Juice 10. Twice as many as tea is 2 times 4 equals 8, and that is milk.
steps: Orange was chosen by 6 children.
Twice as many as 6. 2 times 6 equals 12.
12 children chose banana, so the answer is Banana.

G4A_DATA_027.q: Hardik played 5 cricket matches. His average score was 32 runs per match. How many runs did he score in the 5 matches altogether?
hints: An average tells you what each match would have if the total were shared equally. Here you go back from the average to the total.
Think of every one of the 5 matches as having 32 runs.
Example: The average of 4 matches is 20 runs. The total is 4 times 20 equals 80 runs.
steps: The average is the total shared equally among the matches.
So the total is the average multiplied by the number of matches. 32 times 5 equals 160.
He scored 160 runs altogether.

G4A_DATA_028.q: The rainfall in a town, in millimetres, was: Monday 6, Tuesday 10, Wednesday 4, Thursday 12, Friday 8. On how many days was the rainfall more than the average for the five days?
hints: There are two jobs here: find the average first, then compare each day with it.
Add the five numbers and divide the total by 5 to get the average.
Example: Values 3, 9, 6. The average is 18 divided by 3 equals 6. Only 9 is more than 6, so 1 value is above the average.
steps: Add the rainfall. 6 plus 10 plus 4 plus 12 plus 8 equals 40.
Find the average. 40 divided by 5 equals 8.
Compare each day with 8: only 10 and 12 are more than 8. Friday's 8 is equal to the average, not more.
The rainfall was more than the average on 2 days.

G4A_DATA_029.q: Ananya's average mark in 4 tests was 18. After the 5th test, her average for all 5 tests became 20. How many marks did she get in the 5th test?
hints: An average multiplied by the number of tests gives the total. Compare the total before and after.
Find Ananya's total marks in the first 4 tests: 4 times 18.
Example: The average of 2 tests is 10, so the total is 20. After a 3rd test the average is 12, so the total is 36. The 3rd test was 36 minus 20 equals 16 marks.
steps: Total of the first 4 tests. 4 times 18 equals 72.
Total of all 5 tests. 5 times 20 equals 100.
The difference is the 5th test. 100 minus 72 equals 28.
She got 28 marks in the 5th test.

G4A_DATA_030.q: A pictograph shows old newspapers collected by two classes. Class 4 A has 7 pictures and Class 4 B has 4 pictures. Each picture stands for the same number of newspapers. Class 4 A collected 21 more newspapers than Class 4 B. How many newspapers did Class 4 A collect?
hints: The value of one picture is not given. Use the extra pictures and the extra newspapers to find it.
Class 4 A has 7 minus 4 equals 3 more pictures. These 3 pictures stand for the 21 extra newspapers.
Example: Row one has 6 pictures, row two has 4, and row one shows 10 more. The 2 extra pictures stand for 10, so each picture is 5 and row one shows 6 times 5 equals 30.
steps: Class 4 A has 3 more pictures. 7 minus 4 equals 3.
These 3 pictures stand for 21 newspapers. 21 divided by 3 equals 7.
Class 4 A has 7 pictures of 7 newspapers each. 7 times 7 equals 49.
Class 4 A collected 49 newspapers.

G4A_DATA_031.q: Class 4 has 42 children, and 23 of them are girls. 15 children come to school by bus, and 9 of these are girls. How many boys do not come by bus?
hints: Sort the children two ways: girls or boys, and bus or no bus. Find the boys' numbers step by step.
Find how many boys are in the class: 42 minus 23.
Example: 30 children, 18 girls, so 12 boys. 10 come by bus and 6 of them are girls, so 4 bus boys. Boys not by bus: 12 minus 4 equals 8.
steps: Boys in the class. 42 minus 23 equals 19.
Boys who come by bus. 15 minus 9 equals 6.
Boys who do not come by bus. 19 minus 6 equals 13.
13 boys do not come by bus.

G4A_DATA_032.q: Vikram found the average of five numbers to be 20. Then he saw that he had copied one number as 25 when it was really 15. What is the correct average?
hints: A slip in one number changes the total, and the change is shared among all five numbers.
Find the total Vikram used: 5 times 20.
Example: The average of 4 numbers is 10, so the total is 40. One number was written as 12 instead of 4, so the true total is 40 minus 8 equals 32 and the true average is 32 divided by 4 equals 8.
steps: The total Vikram used. 5 times 20 equals 100.
The number was 10 too big, so take 10 off. 100 minus 10 equals 90.
Share the correct total among the five numbers. 90 divided by 5 equals 18.
The correct average is 18.

G4A_DATA_033.q: A shop sold school bags: Monday 14, Tuesday 18, Wednesday 10. On Saturday it sold as many bags as on Monday and Tuesday together. On Sunday it sold half as many bags as on Saturday. How many bags did it sell on these five days altogether?
hints: Two of the five numbers are hidden in clues. Find them one at a time, then add everything.
Find Saturday's number first: add Monday's 14 and Tuesday's 18.
Example: Monday 4, Tuesday 6. Saturday equals both together, 10, and Sunday is half of that, 5. The total is 4 plus 6 plus 10 plus 5 equals 25.
steps: Saturday. 14 plus 18 equals 32.
Sunday is half of Saturday. 32 divided by 2 equals 16.
Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday together. 14 plus 18 plus 10 equals 42.
Add all five days. 42 plus 32 plus 16 equals 90.
The shop sold 90 bags altogether.

G4A_DATA_034.q: Four friends have 8, 14, 11 and 7 marbles. They share the marbles so that all four have the same number. How many marbles must the friend who had 14 give away?
hints: Sharing equally gives everyone the average. Find what each friend ends up with.
Add all the marbles: 8 plus 14 plus 11 plus 7.
Example: Three friends have 1, 9 and 2 sweets. The total is 12, so each gets 12 divided by 3. The friend with 9 keeps that equal share and gives away the other 5 sweets.
steps: Add all the marbles. 8 plus 14 plus 11 plus 7 equals 40.
Share equally among 4 friends. 40 divided by 4 equals 10.
The friend with 14 keeps 10. 14 minus 10 equals 4.
That friend must give away 4 marbles.

G4A_DATA_035.q: Riya and Kabir each drew a pictograph of their stamps. In Riya's chart each picture stands for 5 stamps and there are 12 pictures. In Kabir's chart each picture stands for 8 stamps and there are 7 pictures. Who has more stamps, and by how many?
hints: The two charts use different values for a picture, so you cannot compare the pictures directly.
Change Riya's pictures into stamps: 12 pictures of 5 stamps each.
Example: Chart one has 6 pictures of 2, which is 12. Chart two has 3 pictures of 5, which is 15. Chart two shows 15 minus 12 equals 3 more.
steps: Riya's stamps. 12 times 5 equals 60.
Kabir's stamps. 7 times 8 equals 56.
Compare. 60 minus 56 equals 4.
Riya has more stamps, by 4.

G4A_DATA_036.q: Class 4 A has 20 children and their average mark in a test is 30. Class 4 B has 30 children and their average mark in the same test is 40. What is the average mark of all 50 children together?
hints: An average depends on how many children are in each group. Find the total marks of each class before you find the average of everyone.
Class 4 A scored 20 times 30 marks in all. Work out the total for Class 4 B in the same way, then add the two totals.

A similar one: 10 children average 6 and 30 children average 10. The totals are 10 times 6 equals 60 and 30 times 10 equals 300, which make 360. Then 360 divided by 40 equals 9, not the halfway number 8.
steps: Find the total marks of Class 4 A. 20 times 30 equals 600.
Find the total marks of Class 4 B. 30 times 40 equals 1200.
Add to get the total marks of all 50 children. 600 plus 1200 equals 1800.
Share the total among 50 children. 1800 divided by 50 equals 36.
The average mark of all 50 children is 36.

G4A_DATA_037.q: A bar graph shows the books sold at a fair. The bottom line of the graph stands for 20 books, not 0, and each square above the bottom line stands for 5 more books. Saturday's bar is 3 squares tall and Sunday's bar is 6 squares tall. How many books were sold on the two days altogether?
hints: Check where the graph starts. A bar's height in squares only tells you how far it is above the bottom line.
Saturday's bar is 3 squares above a line that already stands for 20 books. Find Saturday's number first, then do the same for Sunday.
A similar one: the bottom line stands for 10 and each square stands for 2. Bars of 4 squares and 5 squares show 10 plus 8 equals 18 and 10 plus 10 equals 20, so together 18 plus 20 equals 38.
steps: Saturday's bar is 3 squares above 20. 20 plus 3 times 5 equals 35.
Sunday's bar is 6 squares above 20. 20 plus 6 times 5 equals 50.
Add the two days. 35 plus 50 equals 85.
Altogether 85 books were sold.

G4A_DATA_038.q: In a class of 40 children, 24 like cricket and 20 like football. 6 children like neither game. How many children like both games?
hints: Some children have been counted twice, once for each game. First find how many children like at least one game.
Take away the 6 children who like neither game from 40. Compare that number with 24 plus 20.
A similar one: 30 children, 18 like mango, 15 like banana and 5 like neither. So 25 like at least one fruit. The lists have 18 plus 15 equals 33 names, and 33 minus 25 equals 8 children like both.
steps: Find the children who like at least one game. 40 minus 6 equals 34.
Add the two lists. 24 plus 20 equals 44.
The lists have 44 names but only 34 children, so the extra names are children counted twice. 44 minus 34 equals 10.
10 children like both games.

G4A_DATA_039.q: The average of five whole numbers is 8. Which of these statements is certainly true?
options: At least one of the numbers is exactly 8
At least one of the numbers is 8 or more
Three of the numbers are more than 8
None of the numbers is more than 16
hints: A statement is certainly true only if it holds for every possible set of numbers. Try to find a set that breaks each statement.
The five numbers must add up to 5 times 8 equals 40. Try some unusual sets with this total, such as 0, 0, 0, 0 and 40.

A similar one: three whole numbers have an average of 5, so they add up to 15. The set 1, 1, 13 has no 5 in it and only one number above 5. But all three cannot be below 5, because then the total would be less than 15.
steps: The five numbers add up to 40. 5 times 8 equals 40.
The set 0, 0, 0, 0, 40 has an average of 8. It has no 8 in it, only one number above 8, and a number above 16. So three of the statements can be broken.
If every number were less than 8, the total would be less than 40. That cannot happen.
So the statement that is certainly true is: at least one of the numbers is 8 or more.

G4A_DATA_040.q: Riya wants to draw a pictograph for the kites sold on four days: Monday 12, Tuesday 18, Wednesday 30 and Thursday 42. Every picture must stand for the same number of kites, and she will use only whole pictures. She wants to draw as few pictures as possible. How many pictures will she draw altogether?
hints: Fewer pictures means each picture must stand for more kites. But every day's number must be made of whole pictures.
Look for the largest number that divides 12, 18, 30 and 42 exactly. That is the most one picture can stand for.
A similar one: for 8, 12 and 20 the largest number that divides all three is 4. With 4 for each picture, the rows have 2, 3 and 5 pictures, so 10 pictures altogether.
steps: Each picture must stand for a number that divides 12, 18, 30 and 42 exactly. The largest such number is 6.
Find the pictures for each day. 12 divided by 6 equals 2. 18 divided by 6 equals 3. 30 divided by 6 equals 5. 42 divided by 6 equals 7.
Add the pictures. 2 plus 3 plus 5 plus 7 equals 17.
She will draw 17 pictures altogether.

G4A_DATA_041.q: A shop's sales of school bags were: Monday 20, Tuesday 35, Wednesday 25 and Friday 40. Thursday's number is smudged. The owner remembers that Thursday's number was exactly equal to the average of all five days. How many bags were sold on Thursday?
hints: If one day's number is the same as the average, it does not pull the average up or down. Think about what that says about the other four days.
Add the four numbers you know: 20, 35, 25 and 40. Then think about the average of just these four days.

A similar one: the known days are 10, 14 and 18 and the missing day equals the average of all four. The three known days total 42, so their average is 14. The missing day is 14, and the check works: 56 divided by 4 equals 14.
steps: Add the four known days. 20 plus 35 plus 25 plus 40 equals 120.
A day that equals the average leaves the average unchanged, so Thursday equals the average of the other four days. 120 divided by 4 equals 30.
Check with all five days. 150 divided by 5 equals 30.
30 bags were sold on Thursday.

G4A_DATA_042.q: Riya is reading a storybook. The table shows the total number of pages she had read by the end of each day: Monday 12, Tuesday 30, Wednesday 41, Thursday 65, Friday 80. On which day did she read the most pages?
hints: The table gives running totals, not the pages read on each day. Think about how to get one day's reading from two totals.
On Tuesday she went from 12 pages to 30 pages. Subtract to find Tuesday's pages, then do the same for every day.

A similar one: running totals of 5, 14 and 20 over three days mean 5 pages, then 14 minus 5 equals 9 pages, then 20 minus 14 equals 6 pages. The middle day has the most, even though the last total is the biggest.
steps: On Monday she read 12 pages.
Find the pages for Tuesday and Wednesday. 30 minus 12 equals 18. 41 minus 30 equals 11.
Find the pages for Thursday and Friday. 65 minus 41 equals 24. 80 minus 65 equals 15.
The largest of 12, 18, 11, 24 and 15 is 24.
She read the most pages on Thursday.

G4A_DATA_043.q: Kabir took five spelling tests. His average mark in the first three tests was 10. His average mark in the last three tests was 16. His average mark in all five tests was 12. How many marks did he get in the third test?
hints: The third test belongs to both groups: the first three tests and the last three tests. Use totals, not averages.
Find the total of the first three tests and the total of the last three tests. Then find the total of all five tests.

A similar one with three tests: the first two average 4, total 8, the last two average 7, total 14, and all three average 5, total 15. The middle test is counted twice in 8 plus 14 equals 22, so it is 22 minus 15 equals 7.
steps: Find the total of the first three tests. 3 times 10 equals 30.
Find the total of the last three tests. 3 times 16 equals 48.
Find the total of all five tests. 5 times 12 equals 60.
Adding the two groups counts the third test twice. 30 plus 48 equals 78.
Take away the real total to leave the third test. 78 minus 60 equals 18.
He got 18 marks in the third test.

G4A_DATA_044.q: Ravi took five tests, each out of 20 marks. In four of them he got 12, 15, 9 and 18. He has forgotten the fifth mark, but he remembers that his average for the five tests was exactly equal to his mark in one of the five tests. What is the forgotten mark?
hints: The average of five marks must come out as a whole number here, because it equals one of the marks. Test the possible totals one at a time.
The four known marks add up to 54. The total of all five must be a number that 5 divides exactly. Which totals are possible if the fifth mark is 20 or less?

A similar one: known marks 7, 10 and 4, total 21, with one mark out of 10 missing, and the average of the four equals one of the marks. Totals that 4 divides are 24 and 28. A missing 3 gives an average of 6, which is not one of the marks. A missing 7 gives an average of 7, which is. So the missing mark is 7.
steps: Add the four known marks. 12 plus 15 plus 9 plus 18 equals 54.
The total of five marks must divide exactly by 5. With a fifth mark from 0 to 20, the total can be 55, 60, 65 or 70, so the fifth mark is 1, 6, 11 or 16.
The averages would be 11, 12, 13 or 14.
Only 12 is one of his marks, and it goes with a total of 60. 60 minus 54 equals 6.
The forgotten mark is 6.

G4A_DATA_045.q: Each of the 30 children in a class voted for exactly two different fruits out of mango, apple, banana and guava. Mango got 20 votes, apple got 15 votes and banana got 14 votes. How many votes did guava get?
hints: Count votes, not children. Each child gave more than one vote.
Find the total number of votes: 30 children with 2 votes each. Then add the votes for mango, apple and banana.
A similar one: 20 children each vote for two games out of three. That makes 40 votes. If cricket gets 18 and football gets 13, then kho-kho gets 40 minus 18 minus 13 equals 9 votes.
steps: Each child gave 2 votes, so find the total votes. 30 times 2 equals 60.
Add the votes for the three known fruits. 20 plus 15 plus 14 equals 49.
The rest of the votes went to guava. 60 minus 49 equals 11.
Guava got 11 votes.

G4A_DATA_046.q: Five different whole numbers have an average of 11. The greatest of them is 14. What is the smallest value that the smallest number could have?
hints: To make one number as small as possible, make all the others as large as they are allowed to be.
The five numbers add up to 5 times 11 equals 55. The greatest is 14 and the numbers are all different, so what are the largest values the next three can take?

A similar one: four different whole numbers have an average of 9 and the greatest is 12. The total is 36. The largest the next two can be is 11 and 10, and 12 plus 11 plus 10 equals 33, so the smallest can go down to 36 minus 33 equals 3.
steps: Find the total of the five numbers. 5 times 11 equals 55.
To make the smallest number as small as possible, make the other four as large as possible: 14, 13, 12 and 11. 14 plus 13 plus 12 plus 11 equals 50.
What is left is the smallest number. 55 minus 50 equals 5.
The smallest number could be as small as 5.

G4A_DATA_047.q: Asha and Bina each drew a pictograph of their stamps. In Asha's chart each picture stands for 6 stamps. In Bina's chart each picture stands for 4 stamps. Together the two girls drew 22 pictures, and the pictures show 108 stamps altogether. How many pictures did Asha draw?
hints: Try pretending every picture is worth the smaller amount, then see how many stamps are still missing.
If all 22 pictures stood for 4 stamps, they would show 22 times 4 equals 88 stamps. How many more stamps are needed, and how much extra does each of Asha's pictures bring?

A similar one: 9 pictures show 33 stamps, some worth 5 and some worth 3. If all were worth 3, that is 27 stamps, which is 6 short. Each picture worth 5 adds 2 extra, so 6 divided by 2 equals 3 pictures are worth 5.
steps: Suppose all 22 pictures stood for 4 stamps. 22 times 4 equals 88.
Find how many stamps are still missing. 108 minus 88 equals 20.
Each of Asha's pictures stands for 2 more stamps than that, so divide. 20 divided by 2 equals 10.
Check: 10 pictures of 6 stamps and 12 pictures of 4 stamps. 60 plus 48 equals 108.
Asha drew 10 pictures.

G4A_DATA_048.q: The children of Class 4 were asked how many pets they have at home. The table shows: 0 pets, 6 children; 1 pet, 10 children; 2 pets, 2 children; 3 pets, 2 children. What is the average number of pets per child?
hints: The table has two kinds of numbers: how many pets, and how many children. Decide which numbers to use to count the pets and which to count the children.
The 2 children with 3 pets have 2 times 3 equals 6 pets between them. Find the pets for each row like this, then add them.

A similar one: 4 children have 0 books, 2 children have 3 books and 4 children have 6 books. The books are 0 plus 6 plus 24 equals 30 and the children are 4 plus 2 plus 4 equals 10, so the average is 30 divided by 10 equals 3 books.
steps: Count the pets in each row: children times pets. 6 times 0 equals 0. 10 times 1 equals 10. 2 times 2 equals 4. 2 times 3 equals 6.
Add to get all the pets. 0 plus 10 plus 4 plus 6 equals 20.
Count all the children. 6 plus 10 plus 2 plus 2 equals 20.
Share the pets among the children. 20 divided by 20 equals 1.
The average is 1 pet per child.

G4A_DATA_049.q: Asha and Bina took the same 5 tests. Asha's average mark was 3 more than Bina's average mark. Asha scored 85 marks altogether. How many marks did Bina score altogether?
hints: A difference in averages is a difference for every test. Think about how that grows over all the tests.
Being 3 ahead on average over 5 tests means being ahead by 3 marks five times. Find how many marks that is in total.
A similar one: over 4 tests Ravi's average is 2 more than Sam's, and Ravi's total is 48. Ravi is ahead by 4 times 2 equals 8 marks in total, so Sam scored 48 minus 8 equals 40.
steps: Asha is 3 marks ahead on average in each of 5 tests. Find her lead in total. 5 times 3 equals 15.
Take that lead away from Asha's total. 85 minus 15 equals 70.
Check with averages: Asha's is 17 and Bina's is 14, which is 3 less. 85 divided by 5 equals 17. 70 divided by 5 equals 14.
Bina scored 70 marks altogether.

G4A_DATA_050.q: On a bar graph of sweets sold, the bar for Monday shows 45 sweets and is 9 centimetres tall. Tuesday's bar is 4 centimetres shorter than Monday's bar. How many sweets does Tuesday's bar show?
hints: Centimetres on the graph and sweets are different units. Find what 1 centimetre stands for before comparing the bars.
A bar 9 centimetres tall shows 45 sweets. Divide to find how many sweets 1 centimetre stands for.
A similar one: a bar 8 centimetres tall shows 48 books, so 1 centimetre stands for 6 books. A bar 3 centimetres shorter is 5 centimetres tall and shows 5 times 6 equals 30 books.
steps: Find what 1 centimetre stands for. 45 divided by 9 equals 5.
Find the height of Tuesday's bar in centimetres. 9 minus 4 equals 5.
Change Tuesday's height into sweets. 5 times 5 equals 25.
Tuesday's bar shows 25 sweets.

G4A_DATA_051.q: A pictograph shows the books read by four friends. Each picture stands for 3 books. Asha's row has 6 pictures, Bala's row has 4 pictures and Charu's row has 9 pictures. Dev's row is torn off. The four friends read 72 books altogether. How many more pictures did Dev's row have than Bala's row?
hints: Work in one unit at a time. The total is in books, but the rows and the question are in pictures.
The three rows you can see have 6, 4 and 9 pictures. Change the 72 books into pictures so that you can compare.

A similar one: each picture stands for 5 pens, the rows you can see have 3 and 6 pictures, and the total is 70 pens. 70 pens is 14 pictures, so the hidden row has 14 minus 9 equals 5 pictures. That is 2 more than the row with 3.
steps: Change the total into pictures. 72 divided by 3 equals 24.
Count the pictures in the three rows you can see. 6 plus 4 plus 9 equals 19.
Find the pictures in Dev's row. 24 minus 19 equals 5.
Compare Dev's row with Bala's row. 5 minus 4 equals 1.
Dev's row had 1 more picture than Bala's row.

G4A_DECIMALS_001.q: In the number 536.429, which digit is in the hundredths place?
hints: Places after the decimal point have their own names. Say them in order as you move to the right of the point.
The first digit after the point is in the tenths place. Which place comes next?
A similar one: in 0.917, the digits after the point are 9 in the tenths, 1 in the hundredths, and 7 in the thousandths. So the thousandths digit there is 7.
steps: After the decimal point the places are tenths, hundredths and thousandths. In 536.429 that is 4 tenths, 2 hundredths and 9 thousandths.
The digit in the hundredths place is 2.

G4A_DECIMALS_002.q: Which decimal means seven and nine hundredths?
hints: The word and stands for the decimal point. The last word tells you the place where the number must end.
Hundredths are the second place after the point. If there are no tenths, that place still needs a digit.
A similar one: four and three hundredths. That is 4 wholes, 0 tenths and 3 hundredths, written 4.03.
steps: Seven is the whole-number part, so the number starts with 7 and a decimal point.
Nine hundredths means 9 in the second place after the point, with 0 in the tenths place. 7 plus 9 over 100 equals 7.09.
Seven and nine hundredths is 7.09.

G4A_DECIMALS_003.q: What is 4 plus 3 over 10, plus 7 over 1000?
hints: Each fraction tells you which decimal place its digit goes in. A place that is not mentioned gets a zero.
3 over 10 puts a 3 in the tenths place. Which place does 7 over 1000 use, and what goes in the place between?
A similar one: 2 plus 5 over 100, plus 9 over 1000. There are no tenths, so a 0 goes there: 2.059.
steps: 4 is the whole-number part, and 3 over 10 puts 3 in the tenths place.
There are no hundredths, so that place gets 0. 7 over 1000 puts 7 in the thousandths place.
The number is 4.307. 4 plus 0.3, plus 0.007, equals 4.307.

G4A_DECIMALS_004.q: Which of these numbers is greater than 4.3 but less than 4.4?
hints: Give all the numbers the same number of decimal places so that they are easy to compare.
Think of 4.3 as 4.30 and 4.4 as 4.40. Which number sits between 4.30 and 4.40?
A similar one: a number between 2.6 and 2.7. Write them as 2.60 and 2.70; then 2.64 lies between them.
steps: Write the two ends with two decimal places: 4.30 and 4.40.
4.35 is more than 4.30 and less than 4.40.
The number between 4.3 and 4.4 is 4.35.

G4A_DECIMALS_005.q: Riya walks 1.6 kilometres to school and then 0.85 kilometres from school to the library. How far does she walk in all?
hints: When you add decimals, line up the decimal points so that tenths are added to tenths.
Write 1.6 as 1.60 so that both numbers have two decimal places. Then add.
A similar one: 2.7 plus 0.45. Write 2.7 as 2.70. Then 2.70 plus 0.45 equals 3.15.
steps: Write both distances with two decimal places: 1.60 and 0.85.
Add, keeping the decimal points in line. 1.60 plus 0.85 equals 2.45.
Riya walks 2.45 kilometres in all.

G4A_DECIMALS_006.q: A rope is 5 metres long. A piece 1.35 metres long is cut off. How long is the rope that is left?
hints: A whole number can be written with a decimal point and zeros after it. That makes the subtraction easy to line up.
Write 5 as 5.00 and put 1.35 under it with the points in line.
A similar one: 8 minus 2.45. Write 8 as 8.00. Then 8.00 minus 2.45 equals 5.55.
steps: Write 5 metres as 5.00 metres.
Subtract, keeping the decimal points in line. 5.00 minus 1.35 equals 3.65.
The rope that is left is 3.65 metres long.

G4A_DECIMALS_007.q: One pencil costs 4.50 rupees. What is the cost of 10 such pencils?
hints: Multiplying by 10 makes every digit worth ten times as much.
When a decimal is multiplied by 10, each digit moves one place to the left. Move the digits of 4.50.
A similar one: one eraser costs 2.75 rupees. For 10 erasers each digit moves one place to the left, giving 27.50 rupees.
steps: Multiply 4.50 rupees by 10. Each digit moves one place to the left. 4.50 times 10 equals 45.00.
10 pencils cost 45.00 rupees.

hints: A fraction is easy to write as a decimal when its bottom number is 10 or 100.
What can you multiply 20 by to make 100? Multiply the top by the same number.
A similar one: 9 over 25. Multiply the top and bottom by 4 to get 36 over 100, which is 0.36.
steps: Multiply the top and bottom by 5 to make hundredths. 7 times 5, over 20 times 5, equals 35 over 100.
35 hundredths is written 0.35. 35 over 100 equals 0.35.

G4A_DECIMALS_009.q: A ribbon 7.2 metres long is cut into 6 equal pieces. How long is each piece?
hints: This is equal sharing, so divide. Divide as you would with whole numbers and keep the decimal point in its place.
7.2 is 72 tenths. Share 72 tenths into 6 equal groups.
A similar one: 8.4 metres cut into 4 equal pieces. 84 tenths divided by 4 equals 21 tenths, so each piece is 2.1 metres.
steps: 7.2 metres is 72 tenths of a metre.
Divide by 6. 72 divided by 6 equals 12.
12 tenths is 1.2, so each piece is 1.2 metres long. 7.2 divided by 6 equals 1.2.

G4A_DECIMALS_010.q: Aman has 8 rupees and 5 paise. How is this amount written in rupees?
hints: 100 paise make 1 rupee, so paise are hundredths of a rupee and always take two decimal places.
5 paise is 5 hundredths of a rupee. Which digit goes in the tenths place?
A similar one: 3 rupees and 7 paise. 7 paise is 7 hundredths of a rupee, so it is written 3.07 rupees.
steps: 1 paisa is one hundredth of a rupee, so 5 paise is 0.05 rupees. 5 divided by 100 equals 0.05.
Add the 8 rupees. The amount is 8.05 rupees. 8 plus 0.05 equals 8.05.

G4A_DECIMALS_011.q: In a long-jump contest, Anil jumped 3.38 metres, Bharat jumped 3.045 metres, Chirag jumped 3.4 metres and Dinesh jumped 3.405 metres. Who came second?
hints: To compare decimals, give them all the same number of decimal places. More digits does not mean a bigger number.
Write every jump with three decimal places, for example 3.4 as 3.400. Then compare from the left.
A similar one: 2.5, 2.48 and 2.507. With three decimal places they are 2.500, 2.480 and 2.507. The greatest is 2.507, then 2.500, then 2.480.
steps: Write every jump with three decimal places: 3.380, 3.045, 3.400 and 3.405.
All have 3 wholes, so compare the parts after the point: 405 is the most, then 400, then 380, then 045.
The longest jump is 3.405 metres by Dinesh, and the next longest is 3.4 metres, so Chirag came second.

G4A_DECIMALS_012.q: In the number 5.252, how many times as large is the value of the first 2 as the value of the second 2?
hints: The same digit has different values in different places. Each place is 10 times as large as the place to its right.
Name the place of each 2. Then count how many places apart they are.
A similar one: in 4.66, the first 6 is 0.6 and the second 6 is 0.06. They are one place apart, so 0.6 is 10 times as large as 0.06.
steps: The first 2 is in the tenths place, so its value is 0.2.
The second 2 is in the thousandths place, so its value is 0.002.
From thousandths to tenths is two places to the left, and each place is 10 times as large. 10 times 10 equals 100.
The first 2 is 100 times as large as the second 2.

G4A_DECIMALS_013.q: Three parcels weigh 2.5 kilograms, 0.375 kilograms and 14 kilograms. What is their total weight?
hints: The numbers have different numbers of decimal places. Line up the decimal points before adding.
Write them as 2.500, 0.375 and 14.000. A whole number has its decimal point at the end.
A similar one: 1.2 plus 0.45, plus 6. Write 1.20 plus 0.45, plus 6.00, which gives 7.65.
steps: Give every weight three decimal places: 2.500, 0.375 and 14.000.
Add the first two. 2.500 plus 0.375 equals 2.875.
Add the 14 wholes. 2.875 plus 14.000 equals 16.875.
The total weight is 16.875 kilograms.

G4A_DECIMALS_014.q: By how much is 10 greater than 3.607?
hints: By how much greater asks for the difference, so subtract. Give the whole number the same decimal places as the other number.
Write 10 as 10.000 and put 3.607 under it with the decimal points in line.
A similar one: 5 minus 1.208. Write 5.000 minus 1.208, which gives 3.792.
steps: Write 10 as 10.000.
Subtract with the decimal points in line. 10.000 minus 3.607 equals 6.393.
Check by adding back: 6.393 plus 3.607 equals 10. So 10 is greater than 3.607 by 6.393.

G4A_DECIMALS_015.q: One cricket ball weighs 0.16 kilograms. What is the weight of 25 such balls?
hints: Equal weights repeated many times means multiplication. Multiply as whole numbers, then put the decimal point back.
Work out 16 times 25 first. Since 0.16 has two decimal places, the answer needs two decimal places.
A similar one: balls of 0.12 kilograms each, 50 balls. 12 times 50 equals 600, and with two decimal places that is 6.00, so 6 kilograms.
steps: Multiply without the decimal point. 16 times 25 equals 400.
0.16 has two decimal places, so the answer has two decimal places. 0.16 times 25 equals 4.00.
25 balls weigh 4 kilograms.

hints: This question multiplies and divides by 10, 100 or 1000. Multiplying makes the digits move to the left, and dividing makes them move to the right.
Work from left to right. First multiply 0.045 by 1000, which moves every digit three places to the left. Then divide that result by 10.
A similar example: 0.07 times 1000, divided by 100. Multiplying by 1000 moves the digits three places to the left, giving 70. Dividing by 100 moves them two places to the right, giving 0.7.
steps: Multiply by 1000 first. Every digit moves three places to the left. 0.045 times 1000 equals 45.
Now divide by 10. Every digit moves one place to the right. 45 divided by 10 equals 4.5.
The answer is 4.5.

G4A_DECIMALS_017.q: The box times 100 equals 3.7. Which number goes in the box?
hints: The box was multiplied by 100 to give 3.7. To find the box, undo the multiplying.
Divide 3.7 by 100. Dividing by 100 moves every digit two places to the right.
A similar one: the box times 10 equals 5.2. Undo it by dividing by 10: 5.2 divided by 10 equals 0.52.
steps: Undo the multiplication by dividing: the box is 3.7 divided by 100.
Move every digit two places to the right, filling the empty place with 0. 3.7 divided by 100 equals 0.037.
Check: 0.037 times 100 equals 3.7. The number in the box is 0.037.

G4A_DECIMALS_018.q: Which of these is the greatest? 0.58, 3 over 5, 5 over 8, or 0.65?
hints: Fractions and decimals are hard to compare when mixed. Put them all in the same form first.
Change 3 over 5 and 5 over 8 into decimals. For 3 over 5, think of tenths.
A similar one: which is greater, one quarter or 0.3? One quarter equals 0.25, and 0.25 is less than 0.30, so 0.3 is greater.
steps: Change 3 over 5 to a decimal. 3 over 5 equals 6 over 10, which is 0.6.
Change 5 over 8 to a decimal. One eighth is 0.125, so five eighths is 0.625.
