G4A_PUZZLES_004.q: In a picture puzzle, a star plus a star makes 14. A star plus a moon makes 10. What is the moon worth?
hints: Start with the clue that has only one kind of shape. Once you know that shape, use it in the other clue.
Two stars make 14. Find what one star is worth.
A similar problem: a sun plus a sun makes 12, so a sun is 6. A sun plus a cloud makes 8, so the cloud is 8 minus 6 equals 2.
steps: Two equal stars make 14, so find one star. 14 divided by 2 equals 7.
A star plus a moon makes 10. 10 minus 7 equals 3.
The moon is worth 3.

G4A_PUZZLES_005.q: Amit is taller than Bina. Bina is taller than Chetan. Divya is shorter than Chetan. Who is the tallest of the four?
hints: Put the children in order of height, using one clue at a time.
Write the names in a line from tallest to shortest. Start with Amit and Bina, then fit Chetan in.
A similar problem: Ria is taller than Sam, and Sam is taller than Tia. From tallest to shortest the order is Ria, Sam, Tia, so Ria is the tallest.
steps: Amit is taller than Bina, and Bina is taller than Chetan. So the order is Amit, Bina, Chetan.
Divya is shorter than Chetan, so she comes last: Amit, Bina, Chetan, Divya.
The tallest is Amit.

G4A_PUZZLES_006.q: In a magic square, every row adds up to 21. One row has the numbers 4 and 11 and one missing number. What is the missing number?
hints: The three numbers in the row must add up to the magic total. Two of them are known.
Add 4 and 11. Then find how much more is needed to reach 21.
A similar problem: a row must add up to 15 and has 2 and 9. Those make 11, so the missing number is 15 minus 11 equals 4.
steps: Add the two numbers you know. 4 plus 11 equals 15.
Find what is needed to reach 21. 21 minus 15 equals 6.
The missing number is 6.

G4A_PUZZLES_007.q: Two signs are missing: 8 blank 4 blank 2 equals 10. Which two signs, in this order, make it true?
hints: Try each pair of signs in turn and work out the answer it gives.
The answer 10 is a little more than 8. Think about which first sign makes 8 bigger, and what the second sign must then do.
A similar problem: for 9 blank 3 blank 2 equals 8, the answer is a little less than 9, so try minus first: 9 minus 3 equals 6. Then 6 must become 8, so add 2. The signs there are minus then plus.
steps: Try plus first. 8 plus 4 equals 12.
Now 12 must become 10, so subtract 2. 12 minus 2 equals 10.
The signs are plus then minus.

G4A_PUZZLES_008.q: A palindrome number reads the same forwards and backwards, like 353. Which of these is a palindrome number?
hints: Read each number from right to left and compare it with the number read from left to right.
In a 4-digit palindrome, the first digit matches the last digit and the second digit matches the third. Check each number for this.
A similar problem: 4004 read backwards is 4004, so it is a palindrome. 4040 read backwards is 0404, so it is not.
steps: Write each number backwards: 1212 becomes 2121, 1122 becomes 2211, and 2121 becomes 1212. These all change.
1221 written backwards is still 1221.
The palindrome number is 1221.

G4A_PUZZLES_009.q: In this magic square, every row, every column and both diagonals add up to the same total. Row 1: 16, 2, P. Row 2: 6, Q, 14. Row 3: 8, 18, 4. What is P plus Q?
hints: Find the magic total from a line that has no letter in it. Then use it on the lines that have a letter.
Row 3 has no letter. Add its numbers to find the magic total, then look at Row 1.

A similar problem: a magic square has rows 8, 1, R and 3, S, 7 and 4, 9, 2. Row 3 adds to 15. So R equals 15 minus 8 minus 1, which is 6 and S equals 15 minus 3 minus 7, which is 5, and R plus S equals 11.
steps: Find the magic total from Row 3. 8 plus 18 plus 4 equals 30.
Use Row 1 to find P. 30 minus 16 minus 2 equals 12.
Use Row 2 to find Q. 30 minus 6 minus 14 equals 10.
Add P and Q. 12 plus 10 equals 22.
P plus Q equals 22.

G4A_PUZZLES_010.q: In the sum 3 P plus P 8 equals 82, the letter P stands for the same digit both times. 3 P and P 8 are two-digit numbers. Which digit is P?
hints: Look at the ones column first. The ones digits must add up to a number that ends in the ones digit of the answer.
In the ones column, P plus 8 must end in 2. Which digit added to 8 gives a number ending in 2?
A similar problem: in 1 R plus R 6 equals 49, the ones column says R plus 6 must end in 9, so R is 3. Check the whole sum: 13 plus 36 equals 49. It is true, so R is 3.
steps: In the ones column, P plus 8 must end in 2. Since 4 plus 8 equals 12, P could be 4.
Check the whole sum with P as 4. 34 plus 48 equals 82.
The sum is true, so P is 4.

G4A_PUZZLES_011.q: P and Q are digits. The two-digit numbers P Q and Q P add up to 77, and P is 1 more than Q. What is the number P Q?
hints: When a two-digit number is added to its reverse, each column adds the same two digits. Find what the two digits add up to.
In the ones column, Q plus P must give 7. Now find two digits that add up to 7 where one is 1 more than the other.
A similar problem: R S plus S R equals 99 and R is 1 more than S. The digits add up to 9, so they are 5 and 4. R is the bigger one, so R S is 54.
steps: In each column the digits P and Q are added, and the total is 77, so P plus Q equals 7.
Two digits that add up to 7 and differ by 1 are 4 and 3.
P is the bigger digit, so P is 4 and Q is 3.
Check the sum. 43 plus 34 equals 77.
The number P Q is 43.

G4A_PUZZLES_012.q: I think of a number. I double it and then add 3. The answer is 17. What number did I think of?
hints: Work backwards from the answer, undoing each step in the opposite order.
The last thing done was adding 3. Undo that first by taking 3 away from 17.
A similar problem: I double a number and add 5 to get 25. Undo the adding: 25 minus 5 equals 20. Undo the doubling: 20 divided by 2 equals 10. The number was 10.
steps: Undo the adding of 3. 17 minus 3 equals 14.
Undo the doubling. 14 divided by 2 equals 7.
Check. 7 times 2 plus 3 equals 17.
The number was 7.

G4A_PUZZLES_013.q: Isha, Jay, Kiran and Lata each have one pet: a cat, a dog, a parrot and a rabbit. Jay has the cat. Kiran has the rabbit. Isha does not have the dog. Which pet does Lata have?
hints: Cross off the pets that are already taken, then use the last clue to decide between the pets that are left.
Jay and Kiran have the cat and the rabbit. Which two pets are left for Isha and Lata?
A similar problem: Om, Pia and Raj have a ball, a kite and a top. Om has the ball. Pia does not have the kite. So Pia has the top, and Raj has the kite.
steps: Jay has the cat and Kiran has the rabbit, so the dog and the parrot are left for Isha and Lata.
Isha does not have the dog, so Isha has the parrot.
The only pet left for Lata is the dog.

G4A_PUZZLES_014.q: I am a 2-digit number less than 50. I am a multiple of 7. My digits add up to 6. Which number am I?
hints: Use the clue that leaves the fewest numbers first, list them, then test each with the other clue.
List the 2-digit multiples of 7 that are less than 50. Then add the digits of each one.
A similar problem: a 2-digit multiple of 9 less than 40 whose digits differ by 5. The multiples are 18, 27 and 36. Only 27 has digits that differ by 5, so the number is 27.
steps: The 2-digit multiples of 7 below 50 are 14, 21, 28, 35, 42 and 49.
Their digit totals are 5, 3, 10, 8, 6 and 13.
Only one has digits adding up to 6. The number is 42.

G4A_PUZZLES_015.q: A pencil and an eraser together cost 12 rupees. Two pencils and an eraser together cost 19 rupees. How much does the eraser cost?
hints: Compare the two purchases. Look at what the second one has that the first one does not.
The second purchase has exactly one more pencil than the first. Find how much more it costs.
A similar problem: a pen and a cap cost 10 rupees, and two pens and a cap cost 16 rupees. The extra pen costs 16 minus 10 equals 6 rupees, so the cap costs 10 minus 6 equals 4 rupees.
steps: The second purchase has one extra pencil. Find its cost. 19 minus 12 equals 7.
A pencil and an eraser cost 12 rupees together. 12 minus 7 equals 5.
The eraser costs 5 rupees.

G4A_PUZZLES_016.q: The three-digit number 2 R 5 is multiplied by 3 and the answer is 735. R stands for one digit. Which digit is R?
hints: A multiplication can be undone by division. Find the whole number first, then read off the hidden digit.
Divide 735 by 3 to find the number 2 R 5.
A similar problem: 1 R 4 times 2 equals 368. Dividing, 368 divided by 2 equals 184, so 1 R 4 is 184 and R is 8.
steps: Undo the multiplication. 735 divided by 3 equals 245.
So 2 R 5 is 245, and R is the tens digit.
R is 4.

G4A_PUZZLES_017.q: Five children ran a race. Dev finished after Farah but before Esha. Hari finished between Dev and Esha. Gita finished last. Who came second?
hints: Draw five blanks for the five places and fit the children in, one clue at a time.
Start with the first clue: Farah is ahead of Dev, and Dev is ahead of Esha. Then find where Hari fits.
A similar problem: in a race of three, Mina finished before Nitu, and Omar finished before Mina. The order is Omar, Mina, Nitu, so Mina came second.
steps: From the first clue, the order is Farah, then Dev, then Esha.
Hari is between Dev and Esha: Farah, Dev, Hari, Esha.
Gita is last: Farah, Dev, Hari, Esha, Gita.
The child who came second is Dev.

G4A_PUZZLES_018.q: On a dice, the dots on opposite faces always add up to 7. Neha can see three faces showing 1, 2 and 3. What is the total of the dots on the three faces she cannot see?
hints: Each face Neha can see has a hidden face opposite it. Use the rule for opposite faces.
The face opposite 1 must make 7 with it. Find that face, then do the same for 2 and 3.
A similar problem: if the faces seen are 2, 4 and 6, the hidden faces are 7 minus 2 equals 5, 7 minus 4 equals 3 and 7 minus 6 equals 1. Their total is 5 plus 3 plus 1 equals 9.
steps: Find the face opposite each face she can see. 7 minus 1 equals 6, 7 minus 2 equals 5, 7 minus 3 equals 4.
Add the hidden faces. 6 plus 5 plus 4 equals 15.
The hidden faces total 15.

G4A_PUZZLES_019.q: In this magic square, every row, every column and both diagonals add up to the same total. Some boxes are blank. Row 1: P, 16, 9. Row 2: blank, 11, blank. Row 3: 13, blank, Q. What is the value of Q?
hints: Look for a line of three boxes that has no blank and no letter. It may be a diagonal. That line gives the magic total.
The diagonal from the top right corner to the bottom left corner is 9, 11, 13. Add these to find the magic total, then use Row 1 to find P.

A similar problem: Row 1 is R, 7, 6. Row 2 is blank, 5, blank. Row 3 is 4, blank, S. The diagonal 6, 5, 4 gives a total of 15. So R equals 15 minus 7 minus 6, which is 2, and the other diagonal gives S equals 15 minus 2 minus 5, which is 8.
steps: The diagonal 9, 11, 13 is complete. Find the magic total. 9 plus 11 plus 13 equals 33.
Use Row 1 to find P. 33 minus 16 minus 9 equals 8.
The other diagonal is P, 11, Q. Use it to find Q. 33 minus 8 minus 11 equals 14.
Q is 14.

G4A_PUZZLES_020.q: A two-digit number ending in 3 is multiplied by a two-digit number ending in 4. Which of these can be the product?
hints: You cannot find the exact numbers, so test each choice instead. Check its last digit, and check whether its size is possible.
The last digit of the product comes from 3 times 4. Which choices end in the right digit? Then think about the smallest and largest products possible.

A similar problem: a two-digit number ending in 2 times a two-digit number ending in 6 must end in 2, because 2 times 6 equals 12. The smallest such product is 12 times 16 equals 192 and the largest is 92 times 96 equals 8832. So 1472 is possible, it is 32 times 46, but 9992 is too big.
steps: Find the last digit of the product. 3 times 4 equals 12.
So the product ends in 2. This rules out 1037.
Find the smallest and largest possible products. 13 times 14 equals 182, 93 times 94 equals 8742.
172 is smaller than 182 and 9872 is bigger than 8742, so neither is possible.
The one left is possible. 43 times 24 equals 1032.
The product can be 1032.

G4A_PUZZLES_021.q: In the sum P plus P plus P equals Q P, the letters P and Q stand for two different digits, and Q P is a two-digit number. What is P plus Q?
hints: Look at the ones digit. Three times the digit P gives a number that ends in P again. Very few digits can do that.
Test the digits one by one: 3 times 1 equals 3, 3 times 2 equals 6, and so on. Look for a two-digit answer whose ones digit is the digit you started with.

A similar problem: R plus R plus R plus R plus R plus R equals 2 R, where 2 R is a two-digit number that starts with 2. Six times R must end in R and lie in the twenties. Since 6 times 4 equals 24, R is 4.
steps: Three times P must end in the digit P and must be a two-digit number.
Testing the digits, only 5 works. 5 plus 5 plus 5 equals 15.
So P is 5 and Q P is 15, which makes Q equal to 1.
Add the two digits. 5 plus 1 equals 6.
P plus Q equals 6.

G4A_PUZZLES_022.q: I am a 3-digit number. My hundreds digit is double my ones digit. My tens digit equals my hundreds digit plus my ones digit. My three digits add up to 12. Which number am I?
hints: Every digit can be described using the ones digit. Try small values for the ones digit and see which one fits all the clues.
If the ones digit is 1, the hundreds digit is 2 and the tens digit is 2 plus 1 equals 3. Do these digits add up to 12? If not, try ones digit 2.

A similar problem: the hundreds digit is three times the ones digit, the tens digit is their total, and the digits add up to 8. With ones digit 1, the hundreds digit is 3 and the tens digit is 4. Since 3 plus 4 plus 1 equals 8, the number is 341.
steps: Try ones digit 1: hundreds digit 2, tens digit 3. The digits add up to 6, which is too small.
Try ones digit 2: hundreds digit 4, tens digit 6. 4 plus 6 plus 2 equals 12.
All the clues fit.
The number is 462.

G4A_PUZZLES_023.q: A farmer has hens and goats. Together they have 10 heads and 28 legs. How many goats does the farmer have?
hints: Each animal has one head, so you know how many animals there are. Suppose they were all hens and see how many legs are missing.
There are 10 animals. If all 10 were hens, how many legs would there be? Compare that with 28.
A similar problem: 5 heads and 14 legs. If all 5 were hens there would be 10 legs. The 4 extra legs come from goats, which have 2 more legs each, so there are 4 divided by 2 equals 2 goats.
steps: There are 10 animals. Suppose all were hens with 2 legs each. 10 times 2 equals 20.
Find the extra legs. 28 minus 20 equals 8.
Each goat has 2 more legs than a hen. 8 divided by 2 equals 4.
Check with 4 goats and 6 hens. 4 times 4 plus 6 times 2 equals 28.
The farmer has 4 goats.

G4A_PUZZLES_024.q: The digits of a 2-digit number add up to 9. When the two digits swap places, the new number is 27 more than the first number. What is the first number?
hints: List the 2-digit numbers that fit the first clue. Then test each one with the second clue.
Numbers whose digits add up to 9 are 18, 27, and so on. The swapped number is bigger, so the first number has the smaller digit in the tens place. Test each by swapping and subtracting.
A similar problem: the digits add up to 7 and the swapped number is 9 more. Test 16: 61 minus 16 equals 45. Test 25: 52 minus 25 equals 27. Test 34: 43 minus 34 equals 9. So the number is 34.
steps: Numbers with digits adding up to 9 and a smaller tens digit are 18, 27, 36 and 45.
Swap the digits of each and subtract. 81 minus 18 equals 63, 72 minus 27 equals 45, 63 minus 36 equals 27, 54 minus 45 equals 9.
Only one of them grows by 27 when its digits swap.
The first number is 36.

G4A_PUZZLES_025.q: A laddoo is hidden in one of three boxes. Each box has a label. The label on Box 1 says: The laddoo is in this box. The label on Box 2 says: The laddoo is not in this box. The label on Box 3 says: The laddoo is not in Box 1. Only one of the three labels is true. Where is the laddoo?
hints: Suppose the laddoo is in one box, and count how many labels would then be true. Do this for each box in turn.
Suppose the laddoo is in Box 1. Is the label on Box 1 true? Is the label on Box 2 true? Count the true labels and compare with what the question says.

A similar problem: a coin is in one of two tins, and you are told that both labels are untrue. The label on Tin 1 says: The coin is in Tin 2. The label on Tin 2 says: The coin is in this tin. If the coin were in Tin 2, both labels would be true. If it is in Tin 1, both labels are untrue, just as you were told. So the coin is in Tin 1.
steps: If the laddoo is in Box 1: the labels on Box 1 and Box 2 are both true. That is two true labels, so this does not fit.
If the laddoo is in Box 3: the labels on Box 2 and Box 3 are both true. That is two true labels again.
If the laddoo is in Box 2: the label on Box 1 is untrue, the label on Box 2 is untrue, and the label on Box 3 is true. Exactly one label is true.
The laddoo is in Box 2.

G4A_QUADS_001.q: A quadrilateral has all four sides equal, but none of its angles is a right angle. What is it called?
hints: Two of these shapes have four equal sides. What makes them different from each other is their angles.
A square has four equal sides and four right angles. Which shape has four equal sides but leans over, so its angles are not right angles?
A similar one: a quadrilateral with opposite sides equal and four right angles, but with its length different from its breadth, is a rectangle.
steps: Four equal sides are found in a square and in a rhombus.
A square always has four right angles, so it does not fit here.
A shape with four equal sides and no right angles is a rhombus.

G4A_QUADS_002.q: One angle of a parallelogram is 70 degrees. What is the size of the angle next to it?
hints: In a parallelogram, opposite angles are equal, and two angles that are next to each other add up to 180 degrees.
The angle next to the 70 degree angle makes 180 degrees together with it. Take 70 degrees away from 180 degrees.
A similar one: if one angle of a parallelogram is 65 degrees, the angle next to it is 180 degrees minus 65 degrees, which is 115 degrees.
steps: Angles next to each other in a parallelogram add up to 180 degrees.
Take the known angle away from 180 degrees. 180 minus 70 equals 110.
The angle next to it is 110 degrees.

G4A_QUADS_003.q: The perimeter of a rhombus is 52 centimetres. How long is each side?
hints: Think about what is special about the sides of a rhombus. The perimeter is all the sides added together.
A rhombus has four equal sides, so the perimeter is 4 times one side. Share 52 centimetres into 4 equal parts.
A similar one: a rhombus with perimeter 36 centimetres has sides of 36 divided by 4, which is 9 centimetres each.
steps: All four sides of a rhombus are equal, so the perimeter is 4 times one side.
Divide the perimeter by 4. 52 divided by 4 equals 13.
Each side is 13 centimetres.

G4A_QUADS_004.q: A square handkerchief has sides of 25 centimetres. Lace is stitched all around its edge. The lace costs 3 rupees for every centimetre. What does the lace cost?
hints: Lace that goes all around the edge is as long as the perimeter. Find that length first, then the cost.
A square has 4 equal sides, so the perimeter is 4 times 25 centimetres.
A similar one: ribbon at 2 rupees a centimetre around a square of side 10 centimetres. The perimeter is 40 centimetres, so the ribbon costs 40 times 2, which is 80 rupees.
steps: Length of lace equals perimeter of the square. 4 times 25 equals 100.
Each centimetre costs 3 rupees. 100 times 3 equals 300.
The lace costs 300 rupees.

G4A_QUADS_005.q: A wire is bent into a square of side 18 centimetres. The same wire is then bent into a rectangle whose length is twice its breadth. What is the area of the rectangle?
hints: The wire does not change length, so the square and the rectangle have the same perimeter. Use the perimeter to find the sides of the rectangle.
The wire is 4 times 18 centimetres long. In the rectangle, the length is 2 breadths, so going around it is 2 plus 1 plus 2 plus 1, which is 6 breadths.

A similar one: a square of side 6 centimetres uses 24 centimetres of wire. For a rectangle with length twice its breadth, 6 breadths make 24 centimetres, so the breadth is 4 centimetres, the length is 8 centimetres and the area is 32 square centimetres.
steps: Length of the wire equals perimeter of the square. 4 times 18 equals 72.
Around the rectangle there are 6 breadths, because each length is 2 breadths. 72 divided by 6 equals 12.
The breadth is 12 centimetres, so the length is twice that. 2 times 12 equals 24.
Area equals length times breadth. 24 times 12 equals 288.
The area of the rectangle is 288 square centimetres.

G4A_QUADS_006.q: A rectangular garden is 20 metres long and 14 metres wide. A path 2 metres wide runs all around it on the outside. What is the area of the path?
hints: The garden and the path together make a bigger rectangle. The path is the bigger rectangle with the garden taken out.
The path adds 2 metres at both ends of the length and 2 metres at both ends of the width. Find the length and width of the big rectangle.

A similar one: a lawn 10 metres by 6 metres with a 1 metre path outside. The big rectangle is 12 metres by 8 metres, area 96 square metres. The lawn is 60 square metres, so the path is 36 square metres.
steps: The path adds 2 metres on each side, so 4 metres to the length and 4 metres to the width. 20 plus 4 equals 24. 14 plus 4 equals 18.
Area of the garden with the path. 24 times 18 equals 432.
Area of the garden alone. 20 times 14 equals 280.
Area of the path. 432 minus 280 equals 152.
The area of the path is 152 square metres.

G4A_QUADS_007.q: A floor is 6 metres long and 4 metres wide. It is covered with square tiles of side 50 centimetres, with no gaps. How many tiles are needed?
hints: The floor is measured in metres and the tile in centimetres. Use the same unit for both, then count how many tiles fit along the length and along the width.
Two tiles of 50 centimetres make 1 metre. So how many tiles fit along 6 metres, and how many along 4 metres?
A similar one: a floor 5 metres by 3 metres with 50 centimetre tiles. Ten tiles fit along the length and 6 along the width, so 10 times 6 equals 60 tiles are needed.
steps: Two tiles of 50 centimetres make 1 metre. Along the 6 metre length. 6 times 2 equals 12.
Along the 4 metre width. 4 times 2 equals 8.
Tiles needed equals tiles in a row times number of rows. 12 times 8 equals 96.
The floor needs 96 tiles.

G4A_QUADS_008.q: A square sheet of paper has sides of 12 centimetres. It is cut into two equal rectangles by one straight cut. What is the perimeter of each rectangle?
hints: Picture the cut going across the middle of the square. Work out the length and the breadth of one of the pieces.
The cut halves one pair of sides. Each rectangle is 12 centimetres long. How wide is it?
A similar one: a square of side 10 centimetres cut into two equal rectangles gives pieces 10 centimetres by 5 centimetres. Each has a perimeter of 10 plus 5 plus 10 plus 5, which is 30 centimetres.
steps: The cut goes through the middle, so each rectangle is 12 centimetres long and half of 12 centimetres wide. 12 divided by 2 equals 6.
Add the four sides of one rectangle. 12 plus 6 plus 12 plus 6 equals 36.
The perimeter of each rectangle is 36 centimetres.

G4A_QUADS_009.q: Think about these four shapes: square, rectangle, rhombus and parallelogram. How many of them always have four right angles?
hints: Go through the shapes one by one. The word always matters: ask whether every shape of that kind must have right angles.
A square and a rectangle have right angles at every corner. Can a rhombus or a parallelogram lean over to one side?
A similar one: how many of the same four shapes always have opposite sides equal? The square, rectangle, rhombus and parallelogram all do, so the count is 4.
steps: A square always has four right angles. So does a rectangle.
A rhombus can lean over, like a diamond, so its angles need not be right angles.
A parallelogram can lean over too, so its angles need not be right angles.
Only the square and the rectangle always have four right angles, so the count is 2.

G4A_QUADS_010.q: A rectangle is 20 centimetres long and 15 centimetres wide. Its length is made 5 centimetres longer and its width is made 5 centimetres shorter. What happens to its area?
hints: Do not guess from the fact that 5 is added and 5 is taken away. Work out the area before and the area after, and compare them.
The new rectangle is 25 centimetres long and 10 centimetres wide. Find its area, and the area of the first rectangle.

A similar one: a rectangle 10 centimetres by 8 centimetres has area 80 square centimetres. Make it 2 centimetres longer and 2 centimetres narrower: 12 centimetres by 6 centimetres has area 72 square centimetres. The area decreases by 8 square centimetres.
steps: Area at the start. 20 times 15 equals 300.
New length and width. 20 plus 5 equals 25. 15 minus 5 equals 10.
New area. 25 times 10 equals 250.
Compare the two areas. 300 minus 250 equals 50.
The new area is smaller, so it decreases by 50 square centimetres.

G4A_QUADS_011.q: A hall is 12 metres long and 9 metres wide. Carpet for the whole floor costs 150 rupees for each square metre. A wooden strip along all four walls costs 40 rupees for each metre. What is the total cost?
hints: Carpet covers the floor, so it needs the area. A strip along the walls goes around the edge, so it needs the perimeter.
Find the area of the floor with 12 times 9, and the perimeter with 12 plus 9 plus 12 plus 9. Then find each cost separately.

A similar one: a room 5 metres by 4 metres. Carpet at 100 rupees a square metre costs 20 times 100, which is 2,000 rupees. A strip at 10 rupees a metre costs 18 times 10, which is 180 rupees. Together that is 2,180 rupees.
steps: Area of the floor, and the cost of the carpet. 12 times 9 equals 108. 108 times 150 equals 16200.
Perimeter of the floor, and the cost of the strip. 2 times, 12 plus 9, equals 42. 42 times 40 equals 1680.
Add the two costs. 16200 plus 1680 equals 17880.
The total cost is 17,880 rupees.

G4A_QUADS_012.q: A rectangular field is 30 metres long and 20 metres wide. Fence posts are fixed all around it, 5 metres apart, with one post at each corner. How many posts are needed?
hints: The posts go around a closed loop. On a closed loop, the number of posts is the same as the number of gaps between them.
Find the perimeter of the field. Then see how many gaps of 5 metres fit into it.
A similar one: a square plot of side 10 metres with posts 5 metres apart. The perimeter is 40 metres, so there are 40 divided by 5, which is 8 gaps and 8 posts.
steps: Distance around the field. 2 times, 30 plus 20, equals 100.
Number of 5 metre gaps around the field. 100 divided by 5 equals 20.
Around a closed loop every gap ends at a post, and the last gap ends at the first post, so posts and gaps are equal in number.
The field needs 20 posts.

G4A_QUADS_013.q: A wire 40 centimetres long is bent to make a rectangle. Each side is a whole number of centimetres, and the length is greater than the breadth. What is the difference between the largest area and the smallest area the rectangle can have?
hints: The wire is the perimeter, so the length and the breadth always add up to the same number. Try different pairs and watch how the area changes.

Half of 40 centimetres is 20 centimetres, so length plus breadth equals 20 centimetres. Start with 19 centimetres and 1 centimetre, then 18 centimetres and 2 centimetres, and see which way the area moves. Remember the length must stay greater than the breadth.

Similar problem: a 20 centimetre wire, so length plus breadth equals 10 centimetres. The thinnest rectangle is 9 by 1 with area 9 square centimetres. The fattest allowed is 6 by 4 with area 24 square centimetres, because 5 by 5 has equal sides. The difference is 24 minus 9, which is 15 square centimetres.
steps: The length and breadth together are half the wire. 40 divided by 2 equals 20.
The smallest area comes from the thinnest rectangle, 19 centimetres by 1 centimetre. 19 times 1 equals 19.
The area grows as the sides get closer. The closest pair with the length still greater is 11 centimetres and 9 centimetres. 11 times 9 equals 99.
Subtract the smallest area from the largest. 99 minus 19 equals 80.
So the difference is 80 square centimetres.

G4A_QUADS_014.q: A wire is bent into a square of side 15 centimetres. The same wire is then bent into a rectangle whose length is 4 centimetres more than the side of the square. What happens to the area enclosed by the wire?
hints: The wire does not change, so the perimeter stays the same. But the same perimeter does not always enclose the same area. Find both areas and compare.
The perimeter is 4 times 15 centimetres. If the length becomes 19 centimetres, work out what the breadth has to be so the perimeter stays the same.

Similar problem: a square of side 10 centimetres becomes a rectangle 3 centimetres longer. The length is 13 centimetres, and since length plus breadth must still be 20 centimetres, the breadth is 7 centimetres. The area goes from 100 square centimetres to 13 times 7, which is 91 square centimetres, so it decreases by 9 square centimetres.
steps: The wire is as long as the perimeter of the square. 4 times 15 equals 60.
The length is 19 centimetres. Length and breadth together are half the wire, so find the breadth. 30 minus 19 equals 11.
Find the area of the rectangle. 19 times 11 equals 209.
Compare with the area of the square. 15 times 15 equals 225.
The area becomes smaller. 225 minus 209 equals 16.
So the area decreases by 16 square centimetres.

G4A_QUADS_015.q: A rectangular park is 30 metres long and 20 metres wide. Two straight paths, each 2 metres wide, run right across the middle of the park. One path runs along the length and the other runs across the width, so they cross each other in the middle. What is the total area covered by the paths?
hints: Each path is a long thin rectangle. Think carefully about the small piece of ground where the two paths cross.
Find the area of the path that is 30 metres long, and the area of the path that is 20 metres long. Then find the size of the square where they lie on top of each other.

Similar problem: a field 20 metres by 10 metres with two crossing paths 1 metre wide. The paths are 20 square metres and 10 square metres. The crossing square is 1 square metre and belongs to both, so the total is 20 plus 10 minus 1, which is 29 square metres.
steps: Find the area of the path along the length. 30 times 2 equals 60.
Find the area of the path across the width. 20 times 2 equals 40.
Where they cross, a square of side 2 metres belongs to both paths. 2 times 2 equals 4.
Add the two paths and take the crossing square away once. 60 plus 40 minus 4 equals 96.
So the paths cover 96 square metres.

G4A_QUADS_016.q: A square garden has a path 1 metre wide all around it on the outside. The area of the path is 40 square metres. How long is each side of the garden?
hints: The path is made of four strips along the sides of the garden and four little squares at the corners. Work backwards from the area of the path.
Each corner piece is a square of side 1 metre. Take the four corner squares away from 40 square metres first, and see what is left for the four strips.

Similar problem: the path has area 24 square metres. The four corners take 4 square metres, leaving 20 square metres for four strips. Each strip is 5 square metres and 1 metre wide, so it is 5 metres long. The garden has sides of 5 metres.
steps: The four corners of the path are squares of side 1 metre. 4 times 1 equals 4.
Take the corners away to find the area of the four strips. 40 minus 4 equals 36.
Each strip has the same area. 36 divided by 4 equals 9.
A strip of 9 square metres that is 1 metre wide is 9 metres long, as long as a side of the garden.
So each side of the garden is 9 metres.

G4A_QUADS_017.q: A rectangle has an area of 24 square centimetres. Its length is made 2 times as long and its breadth is made 3 times as long. What is the area of the new rectangle?
hints: You are not told the length or the breadth. Choose any pair that gives the right area and see what happens. Then try another pair to check.
Try a rectangle 6 centimetres by 4 centimetres. Make the length 2 times as long and the breadth 3 times as long, then multiply.

Similar problem: a rectangle of area 5 square centimetres, say 5 centimetres by 1 centimetre. Make the length 3 times and the breadth 2 times as long: 15 centimetres by 2 centimetres. The new area is 30 square centimetres, which is 6 times the old area.
steps: Pick a rectangle with area 24 square centimetres, such as 6 centimetres by 4 centimetres.
Make the length 2 times as long and the breadth 3 times as long. 6 times 2 equals 12 and 4 times 3 equals 12.
Find the new area. 12 times 12 equals 144.
The area has been multiplied by 2 and then by 3, which is 6 times. This is true for any rectangle of area 24 square centimetres. 24 times 6 equals 144.
So the area of the new rectangle is 144 square centimetres.

G4A_QUADS_018.q: A rectangle is drawn on paper. If its length were made 3 centimetres longer, with the breadth unchanged, its area would grow by 21 square centimetres. If instead its breadth were made 2 centimetres longer, with the length unchanged, its area would grow by 20 square centimetres. What is the perimeter of the rectangle?
hints: When one side of a rectangle grows, the extra area is a thin strip. Think about the two sides of that strip.
The first strip is 3 centimetres one way and as long as the breadth the other way, and its area is 21 square centimetres. Use this to find the breadth.

Similar problem: making the length 2 centimetres longer adds 10 square centimetres, so the breadth is 10 divided by 2, which is 5 centimetres. Making the breadth 4 centimetres longer adds 32 square centimetres, so the length is 32 divided by 4, which is 8 centimetres. The perimeter is 2 times, 8 plus 5, which is 26 centimetres.
steps: The first extra strip is 3 centimetres by the breadth. 21 divided by 3 equals 7.
The second extra strip is 2 centimetres by the length. 20 divided by 2 equals 10.
So the rectangle is 10 centimetres long and 7 centimetres wide.
Find the perimeter. 2 times, 10 plus 7, equals 34.
So the perimeter of the rectangle is 34 centimetres.

G4A_QUADS_019.q: Rahul has 36 square tiles, each of side 1 centimetre. He lays all 36 tiles flat, with no gaps, to make one rectangle. A square counts as a rectangle here, and a 4 by 9 rectangle is the same as a 9 by 4 rectangle. How many different rectangles can he make?
hints: The number of tiles is the area of the rectangle. Each rectangle is a pair of whole numbers that multiply to give that area.
List the pairs in order: 1 by something, 2 by something, 3 by something, and stop when the pairs begin to repeat the other way round.
Similar problem: 16 tiles. The pairs are 1 by 16, 2 by 8 and 4 by 4. After that, 8 by 2 is a repeat. So 16 tiles make 3 different rectangles, even though 16 has more factors than that.
steps: Each rectangle uses all 36 tiles, so its two sides multiply to give 36.
List the pairs in order. 1 times 36, 2 times 18, 3 times 12, 4 times 9, 6 times 6.
After 6 by 6 the pairs repeat the other way round, such as 9 by 4.
Count the pairs: 1 by 36, 2 by 18, 3 by 12, 4 by 9 and 6 by 6.
So Rahul can make 5 different rectangles.

G4A_QUADS_020.q: A big square is divided by straight lines into 3 rows of 3 equal small squares, like a noughts and crosses board. How many squares of all sizes are there in the drawing?
hints: The small squares are not the only squares. Bigger squares can be made from blocks of small squares, and those bigger squares can overlap each other.
Count by size: first the squares made of 1 small square, then those made of a 2 by 2 block, then the 3 by 3 block. For the 2 by 2 blocks, think about where the top left corner can be.
Similar problem: a square divided into 2 rows of 2 small squares. There are 4 small squares and 1 big square, so there are 5 squares of all sizes.
steps: Count the small squares. 3 times 3 equals 9.
Count the squares made of a 2 by 2 block. Such a block can start in 2 places across and 2 places down. 2 times 2 equals 4.
There is 1 square made of the whole 3 by 3 block.
Add them all. 9 plus 4 plus 1 equals 14.
So there are 14 squares of all sizes.

G4A_QUADS_021.q: Five equal small squares are joined side by side in one straight row to make a long strip. Look at every shape made of one small square or of several neighbouring small squares. How many of these shapes are rectangles that are not squares?
hints: Count by length: shapes that are 2 squares long, 3 squares long, and so on. Shapes of the same length can overlap. Think about which shapes are squares.
A shape 2 squares long can start at the 1st, 2nd, 3rd or 4th small square. Count those, then do the same for shapes 3, 4 and 5 squares long.

Similar problem: a strip of 3 small squares. Shapes 2 squares long: 2 of them. Shapes 3 squares long: 1. The single small squares are squares, so they are left out. That gives 2 plus 1, which is 3 rectangles that are not squares.
steps: A shape made of just 1 small square is a square, so it is not counted.
Shapes 2 squares long: 4 of them. Shapes 3 squares long: 3 of them.
Shapes 4 squares long: 2 of them. The whole strip, 5 squares long: 1.
Add them. 4 plus 3 plus 2 plus 1 equals 10.
So 10 of the shapes are rectangles that are not squares.

G4A_QUADS_022.q: Which of these statements about quadrilaterals is true?
options: A quadrilateral with four equal sides is always a square
A quadrilateral with four right angles always has four equal sides
A quadrilateral with two pairs of equal sides is always a parallelogram
A quadrilateral with four equal sides always has its opposite sides parallel
hints: A statement with the word always is true only if no shape at all breaks it. For each statement, try to think of one quadrilateral that breaks it.
Think about a rhombus that leans over, a long rectangle and a kite. Test each statement on these three shapes.

Similar problem: is this statement true? A quadrilateral with four right angles is always a square. A rectangle 5 centimetres by 2 centimetres has four right angles, but its sides are not all equal. One shape that breaks the statement is enough, so it is not always true.
steps: A leaning rhombus has four equal sides but no right angles, so four equal sides do not always make a square.
A long rectangle has four right angles but its sides are not all equal.
A kite has two pairs of equal sides, but the equal sides are next to each other, and it is not a parallelogram.
A quadrilateral with four equal sides is a rhombus, or a square, which is a special rhombus. In every rhombus the opposite sides are parallel.
So the true statement is: a quadrilateral with four equal sides always has its opposite sides parallel.

G4A_QUADS_023.q: The four angles of a quadrilateral add up to 360 degrees. Which of these can a quadrilateral not have?
options: Two right angles and one acute angle
hints: Use the total of 360 degrees. For each choice, either find four angles that fit and add up to 360 degrees, or explain why the total can never be reached.
Start with three obtuse angles: try 100 degrees, 100 degrees and 100 degrees, and see what is left for the fourth angle. Then think about four angles that are each less than 90 degrees.

Similar problem: can a triangle have three acute angles? Yes: 60 degrees, 60 degrees and 60 degrees add up to 180 degrees. Can a triangle have two right angles? No: 90 degrees plus 90 degrees already makes 180 degrees, leaving nothing for the third angle.
steps: A square has four right angles, so four right angles are possible.
Three obtuse angles are possible: 100 degrees, 100 degrees, 100 degrees and 60 degrees. 100 plus 100 plus 100 plus 60 equals 360.
Two right angles and one acute angle are possible: 90 degrees, 90 degrees, 80 degrees and 100 degrees. 90 plus 90 plus 80 plus 100 equals 360.
Four acute angles are each less than 90 degrees, so together they are less than 360 degrees. 4 times 90 equals 360.
So a quadrilateral cannot have four acute angles.

G4A_QUADS_024.q: A square sheet of paper is cut into 4 equal rectangular strips by three straight cuts, all parallel to one side of the square. Each strip has a perimeter of 40 centimetres. What is the area of the square sheet?
hints: Picture one strip. Its long side is a whole side of the square, and its short side is one quarter of a side. Work backwards from the perimeter of a strip.
Half of the strip's perimeter is one long side plus one short side, which is 20 centimetres. The long side is 4 times the short side.

Similar problem: a square is cut into 2 equal rectangles, each with perimeter 18 centimetres. Long side plus short side equals 9 centimetres, and the long side is 2 times the short side, so they are 6 centimetres and 3 centimetres. The square has side 6 centimetres and area 36 square centimetres.
steps: Half the perimeter of a strip is its long side plus its short side. 40 divided by 2 equals 20.
The long side is 4 times the short side, so 20 centimetres is 5 equal parts. 20 divided by 5 equals 4.
The long side of a strip is the side of the square. 4 times 4 equals 16.
Find the area of the square. 16 times 16 equals 256.
So the area of the square sheet is 256 square centimetres.

G4A_QUADS_025.q: The length of a rectangle is 3 times its breadth. Both are whole numbers of centimetres. Which of these can be the area of the rectangle?
hints: If the breadth is some number, the length is 3 times that number. Think about what the area must then look like.
The area is 3 times breadth times breadth. So divide each area by 3 and ask: is the result a number multiplied by itself?

Similar problem: the length is 2 times the breadth. Then the area is 2 times breadth times breadth. An area of 50 square centimetres works, because 50 divided by 2 is 25, which is 5 times 5, giving a rectangle 10 centimetres by 5 centimetres. An area of 40 square centimetres does not, because 40 divided by 2 is 20, which is not a number times itself.
steps: The area is length times breadth, which is 3 times breadth times breadth.
Divide each area by 3. 54 divided by 3 equals 18, 36 divided by 3 equals 12, 96 divided by 3 equals 32, 75 divided by 3 equals 25.
Only 25 is a number multiplied by itself. 5 times 5 equals 25.
So the breadth is 5 centimetres and the length is 15 centimetres. 15 times 5 equals 75.
So the area can be 75 square centimetres.

G4A_QUADS_026.q: A square sheet of card has sides of 10 centimetres. A small square of side 4 centimetres is cut away from one corner of the sheet. What is the perimeter of the card that is left?
hints: Cutting a piece away makes the area smaller, but the perimeter is a different thing. Walk around the edge of the new shape and add up every edge, including the new ones.
The new shape has six edges. Two of the old edges are now 4 centimetres shorter, and there are two new edges inside the notch. Find the length of each.

Similar problem: a rectangle 8 centimetres by 5 centimetres with a 2 centimetre square cut from one corner. The edges are 8, 5, 6, 3 and two new edges of 2 centimetres each. They add up to 26 centimetres, the same as the perimeter of the whole rectangle.
steps: Two edges of the card are still 10 centimetres long.
The two edges that met at the cut corner are now shorter. 10 minus 4 equals 6.
The notch adds two new edges of 4 centimetres each.
Add all six edges. 10 plus 10 plus 6 plus 6 plus 4 plus 4 equals 40.
So the perimeter of the card that is left is 40 centimetres.

G4A_RATIO_001.q: A class has 12 boys and 18 girls. What is the ratio of boys to girls in its simplest form?
hints: Write the two numbers in the order the question names them. Then divide both by the same number until nothing more divides both.
Boys come first, so start with 12 is to 18. Both numbers can be divided by 6.
Example: 15 boys and 20 girls give 15 is to 20. Dividing both by 5 gives 3 is to 4.
steps: Boys to girls is 12 is to 18.
Both numbers can be divided by 6: 12 divided by 6 equals 2 and 18 divided by 6 equals 3.
So the ratio in its simplest form is 2 is to 3.

G4A_RATIO_002.q: What is the ratio 20 is to 35 in its simplest form?
hints: To simplify a ratio, divide both numbers by the same number: the biggest one that divides both.
Both 20 and 35 are in the 5 times table. Divide each by 5.
Example: in 18 is to 30 both numbers can be divided by 6, giving 3 is to 5.
steps: The biggest number that divides both 20 and 35 is 5.
20 divided by 5 equals 4 and 35 divided by 5 equals 7.
So 20 is to 35 in its simplest form is 4 is to 7.

G4A_RATIO_003.q: 4 notebooks cost 60 rupees. How many rupees does 1 notebook cost?
hints: When you know the cost of several equal things, divide to find the cost of one.
Share 60 rupees equally among the 4 notebooks.
Example: if 5 pens cost 40 rupees, one pen costs 40 divided by 5, which is 8 rupees.
steps: All 4 notebooks cost the same, so divide the total by 4.
60 divided by 4 equals 15.
So 1 notebook costs 15 rupees.

G4A_RATIO_004.q: A bag holds 3 red balls and 5 blue balls. What is the ratio of red balls to all the balls in the bag?
hints: Read carefully what is being compared. Here one colour is compared with the whole bag, so you need the total.
First add to find all the balls in the bag.
Example: with 2 green and 7 yellow balls there are 9 balls in all, so green to all is 2 is to 9.
steps: All the balls: 3 plus 5 equals 8.
Red balls come first, then all the balls.
So the ratio is 3 is to 8.

G4A_RATIO_005.q: Which of these ratios is equal to 2 is to 3?
hints: Two ratios are equal when both numbers of one are multiplied, or divided, by the same number to get the other.
Multiply both 2 and 3 by 2, then by 3, and see which result is in the list.
Example: 1 is to 4 is equal to 3 is to 12, because 1 times 3 equals 3 and 4 times 3 equals 12.
steps: Multiply both numbers of 2 is to 3 by 3.
2 times 3 equals 6 and 3 times 3 equals 9.
So 6 is to 9 is equal to 2 is to 3.

G4A_RATIO_006.q: To make lemonade, Sana mixes 1 cup of lemon juice with 4 cups of water. If she uses 3 cups of lemon juice, how many cups of water does she need?
hints: The mix must stay the same, so whatever you multiply the juice by, multiply the water by the same number.
The juice has gone from 1 cup to 3 cups. That is 3 times as much.
Example: 1 cup of rice needs 2 cups of water, so 5 cups of rice need 5 times 2, which is 10 cups of water.
steps: The juice is 3 times as much as before.
So the water must be 3 times as much too.
4 times 3 equals 12, so she needs 12 cups of water.

G4A_RATIO_007.q: A car travels 60 kilometres in 1 hour. At the same speed, how many kilometres does it travel in 3 hours?
hints: At a steady speed, the car covers the same distance in every hour. More hours means more distance.
It covers 60 kilometres in each hour, and there are 3 hours. Multiply.
Example: a bus that travels 40 kilometres in 1 hour travels 40 times 4, which is 160 kilometres in 4 hours.
steps: In 1 hour the car travels 60 kilometres.
In 3 hours it travels 3 times as far: 60 times 3 equals 180.
So it travels 180 kilometres.

G4A_RATIO_008.q: 10 rupees buys 2 samosas. At the same price, how many samosas does 50 rupees buy?
hints: Find how many times bigger the money is. The number of samosas grows by the same number of times.
How many tens are there in 50? Each ten buys 2 samosas.
Example: if 20 rupees buys 3 bananas, then 80 rupees is 4 times as much money and buys 3 times 4, which is 12 bananas.
steps: 50 divided by 10 equals 5, so 50 rupees is 5 times as much money as 10 rupees.
The samosas are 5 times as many: 2 times 5 equals 10.
So 50 rupees buys 10 samosas.

G4A_RATIO_009.q: Sweets are shared between two children in the ratio 3 is to 7. Into how many equal parts are the sweets divided altogether?
hints: A ratio tells you how many equal parts each person gets. The total number of parts comes from putting them together.
One child gets 3 parts and the other gets 7 parts. Put them together.
Example: sharing in the ratio 4 is to 5 means 4 plus 5, which is 9 equal parts altogether.
steps: The first child gets 3 parts and the second child gets 7 parts.
3 plus 7 equals 10.
So the sweets are divided into 10 equal parts altogether.

G4A_RATIO_010.q: A tailor needs 2 metres of cloth to make 1 shirt. How many shirts can he make from 14 metres of cloth?
hints: Each shirt uses up the same amount of cloth. Find how many such amounts fit into the whole cloth.
How many 2s are there in 14? Divide.
Example: if 1 kurta needs 3 metres, then 15 metres make 15 divided by 3, which is 5 kurtas.
steps: Each shirt needs 2 metres of cloth.
14 divided by 2 equals 7.
So he can make 7 shirts.

G4A_RATIO_011.q: What is the ratio of 50 paise to 2 rupees in its simplest form?
hints: Before writing a ratio, both amounts must be in the same unit.
Change 2 rupees into paise. One rupee is 100 paise.
Example: 20 centimetres to 1 metre. Since 1 metre is 100 centimetres, the ratio is 20 is to 100, and dividing both by 20 gives 1 is to 5.
steps: 2 rupees is 200 paise.
The ratio is 50 is to 200.
Divide both by 50: 50 divided by 50 equals 1 and 200 divided by 50 equals 4.
So the ratio in its simplest form is 1 is to 4.

G4A_RATIO_012.q: A kabaddi club has 20 children. 8 of them are girls. What is the ratio of girls to boys in its simplest form?
hints: Check which two groups are being compared. You may need to work out one of them first.
Find the number of boys: 20 minus 8.
Example: of 24 children, 6 are girls, so 18 are boys. Girls to boys is 6 is to 18, and dividing both by 6 gives 1 is to 3.
steps: Boys: 20 minus 8 equals 12.
Girls to boys is 8 is to 12.
Divide both by 4: 8 divided by 4 equals 2 and 12 divided by 4 equals 3.
So the ratio in its simplest form is 2 is to 3.

G4A_RATIO_013.q: 5 kilograms of rice costs 300 rupees. At the same price, how many rupees do 8 kilograms of rice cost?
hints: Find the cost of one unit first, then multiply by the number you need.
Find the cost of 1 kilogram: 300 divided by 5.
Example: if 4 kilograms of dal costs 200 rupees, then 1 kilogram costs 50 rupees, and 7 kilograms cost 50 times 7, which is 350 rupees.
steps: 1 kilogram costs 300 divided by 5, which is 60 rupees.
8 kilograms cost 8 times as much: 60 times 8 equals 480.
So 8 kilograms of rice cost 480 rupees.

G4A_RATIO_014.q: 120 rupees is shared among Amit, Bina and Chetan in the ratio 1 is to 2 is to 3. How many rupees does Chetan get?
hints: Add the numbers in the ratio to find the total number of equal parts. Then find the value of one part.
The parts are 1 plus 2 plus 3 in all. Divide 120 rupees by that total.
Example: 450 rupees shared in the ratio 1 is to 3 is to 5 has 9 parts of 50 rupees each, so the last person gets 5 times 50, which is 250 rupees.
steps: Total parts: 1 plus 2 plus 3 equals 6.
One part is 120 divided by 6, which is 20 rupees.
Chetan gets 3 parts: 3 times 20 equals 60.
So Chetan gets 60 rupees.

G4A_RATIO_015.q: The ratio of pencils to pens in a box is 4 is to 3. There are 28 pencils. How many pencils and pens are there altogether?
hints: Use the amount you know to find the size of one part. Then use the parts to find what is asked.
The pencils are 4 parts and there are 28 of them. Find one part: 28 divided by 4.
Example: books to copies are 5 is to 2 and there are 30 books. One part is 30 divided by 5, which is 6, and there are 7 parts in all, so there are 7 times 6, which is 42 things altogether.
steps: One part is 28 divided by 4, which is 7.
Pens are 3 parts: 3 times 7 equals 21.
Altogether: 28 plus 21 equals 49.
So there are 49 pencils and pens altogether.

G4A_RATIO_016.q: A train covers 240 kilometres in 4 hours. At the same speed, how many hours does it take to cover 420 kilometres?
hints: Find how far the train goes in one hour. Then see how many such hours are needed for the new distance.
Find the distance covered in 1 hour: 240 divided by 4.
Example: a bus covers 150 kilometres in 3 hours, so 50 kilometres each hour. For 450 kilometres it takes 450 divided by 50, which is 9 hours.
steps: In 1 hour the train covers 240 divided by 4, which is 60 kilometres.
Time for 420 kilometres: 420 divided by 60 equals 7.
So the train takes 7 hours.

G4A_RATIO_017.q: A recipe for 6 people needs 300 grams of flour. How many grams of flour are needed for 4 people?
hints: Find the amount for one person first, then multiply by the number of people you are cooking for.
Flour for 1 person: 300 divided by 6.
Example: a recipe for 5 people uses 400 grams of rice, so 80 grams each. For 3 people it needs 80 times 3, which is 240 grams.
steps: For 1 person: 300 divided by 6 equals 50 grams.
For 4 people: 50 times 4 equals 200.
So 200 grams of flour are needed.

G4A_RATIO_018.q: 45 mangoes are shared between Kiran and Leela in the ratio 4 is to 5. How many more mangoes does Leela get than Kiran?
hints: Find the size of one part. Then see how many more parts one person has than the other.
There are 4 plus 5 parts in all. Divide 45 by that.
Example: 40 sweets shared in the ratio 3 is to 5 make 8 parts of 5 sweets each. The second child has 2 parts more, which is 2 times 5, or 10 sweets more.
steps: Total parts: 4 plus 5 equals 9.
One part is 45 divided by 9, which is 5 mangoes.
Leela has 5 parts and Kiran has 4 parts, so Leela has 1 part more.
So Leela gets 5 more mangoes.

G4A_RATIO_019.q: On a map, 2 centimetres stands for 10 kilometres. Two towns are 7 centimetres apart on the map. How many kilometres apart are they really?
hints: Find what 1 centimetre on the map stands for. Then multiply by the number of centimetres.
If 2 centimetres stands for 10 kilometres, find what 1 centimetre stands for: 10 divided by 2.
Example: if 3 centimetres stands for 12 kilometres, then 1 centimetre stands for 4 kilometres, and 5 centimetres stands for 4 times 5, which is 20 kilometres.
steps: 1 centimetre stands for 10 divided by 2, which is 5 kilometres.
7 centimetres stands for 7 times 5, which is 35 kilometres.
So the towns are really 35 kilometres apart.

G4A_RATIO_020.q: What is the ratio 18 is to 24 is to 30 in its simplest form?
hints: A ratio with three numbers is simplified the same way as one with two: divide all of them by the biggest number that divides every one.
18, 24 and 30 are all in the 6 times table. Divide each by 6.
Example: in 10 is to 20 is to 25 all three numbers can be divided by 5, giving 2 is to 4 is to 5.
steps: The biggest number that divides 18, 24 and 30 is 6.
18 divided by 6 equals 3, 24 divided by 6 equals 4 and 30 divided by 6 equals 5.
So the simplest form is 3 is to 4 is to 5.

G4A_RATIO_021.q: Which of these ratios is not equal to 4 is to 6?
hints: Simplify each ratio, or build each one from the given ratio by multiplying or dividing both numbers by the same number.
4 is to 6 in its simplest form is 2 is to 3. Now simplify each ratio in the list.
Example: is 9 is to 12 equal to 3 is to 5? Dividing 9 and 12 by 3 gives 3 is to 4, so they are not equal.
steps: 4 is to 6 simplifies to 2 is to 3.
8 is to 12 and 12 is to 18 both simplify to 2 is to 3 as well.
6 is to 8 simplifies to 3 is to 4, which is different.
So the ratio that is not equal to 4 is to 6 is 6 is to 8.

G4A_RATIO_022.q: A machine fills 45 bottles in 9 minutes. At the same rate, how many bottles does it fill in 1 hour?
hints: Find how many bottles are filled in one minute. Watch the units: the question changes from minutes to an hour.
Bottles in 1 minute: 45 divided by 9. Then remember how many minutes make 1 hour.
Example: a tap fills 24 buckets in 8 minutes, so 3 each minute. In half an hour, which is 30 minutes, it fills 3 times 30, which is 90 buckets.
steps: In 1 minute the machine fills 45 divided by 9, which is 5 bottles.
1 hour is 60 minutes.
5 times 60 equals 300.
So the machine fills 300 bottles in 1 hour.

G4A_RATIO_023.q: The ratio of Arun's stamps to Bela's stamps is 3 is to 5. Bela has 12 more stamps than Arun. How many stamps does Arun have?
hints: The extra stamps match the extra parts in the ratio. Use that to find the size of one part.
Bela has 5 minus 3, which is 2 parts more than Arun, and those 2 parts are 12 stamps.
Example: the ratio is 2 is to 5 and the second person has 15 more. The 3 extra parts are 15, so one part is 5, and the first person has 2 times 5, which is 10.
steps: Bela has 5 minus 3, which is 2 parts more than Arun.
Those 2 parts are 12 stamps, so one part is 12 divided by 2, which is 6 stamps.
Arun has 3 parts: 3 times 6 equals 18.
So Arun has 18 stamps.

G4A_RATIO_024.q: The length and breadth of a rectangular playground are in the ratio 5 is to 3. The length is 40 metres. What is the perimeter of the playground in metres?
hints: Use the ratio to find the missing side first. Then go all the way round the rectangle.
The length is 5 parts and measures 40 metres. Find one part: 40 divided by 5.
Example: length to breadth is 4 is to 1 and the length is 20 metres. One part is 5 metres, so the breadth is 5 metres and the perimeter is 20 plus 5 plus 20 plus 5, which is 50 metres.
steps: One part is 40 divided by 5, which is 8 metres.
The breadth is 3 parts: 3 times 8 equals 24 metres.
One length and one breadth: 40 plus 24 equals 64 metres.
The perimeter is twice that: 64 times 2 equals 128, so the perimeter is 128 metres.

G4A_RATIO_025.q: Asha's money and Bina's money are in the ratio 2 is to 3. Bina's money and Chitra's money are in the ratio 3 is to 4. Asha has 40 rupees. How many rupees does Chitra have?
hints: Work along the chain one link at a time: use the first ratio to find the middle person, then the second ratio to find the last.
Asha's 2 parts are 40 rupees. Find one part, then Bina's 3 parts.

Example: Pia to Qadir is 1 is to 2 and Qadir to Rita is 2 is to 5. If Pia has 10 rupees, then Qadir has 20 rupees, one part of the second ratio is 10 rupees, and Rita has 5 times 10, which is 50 rupees.
steps: Asha's 2 parts are 40 rupees, so one part is 40 divided by 2, which is 20 rupees.
Bina has 3 parts: 3 times 20 equals 60 rupees.
In the second ratio Bina's 3 parts are 60 rupees, so one part is 60 divided by 3, which is 20 rupees.
Chitra has 4 parts: 4 times 20 equals 80, so Chitra has 80 rupees.

G4A_RATIO_026.q: A bag has 20 marbles, red and green, in the ratio 2 is to 3. Then 4 more red marbles are put in. What is the new ratio of red marbles to green marbles?
hints: A ratio gives parts, not actual numbers. Find the actual numbers first, make the change, then write the new ratio.
There are 2 plus 3, which is 5 parts in 20 marbles. Find one part, then the number of red and of green marbles.
Example: 15 sweets, orange to lemon 2 is to 3, so 6 orange and 9 lemon. Add 6 orange: now there are 12 orange and 9 lemon, which is 12 is to 9, or 4 is to 3.
steps: Total parts: 2 plus 3 equals 5, so one part is 20 divided by 5, which is 4 marbles.
Red: 2 times 4 equals 8. Green: 3 times 4 equals 12.
After 4 more red marbles: 8 plus 4 equals 12 red, and still 12 green.
12 is to 12 simplifies, so the new ratio is 1 is to 1.

G4A_RATIO_027.q: 3 pens cost the same as 5 pencils. One pencil costs 6 rupees. How many rupees do 4 pens cost?
hints: Use the thing whose price you know to find the price of the other thing. Then find the cost of the number asked.
Find the cost of 5 pencils: 5 times 6. That is also the cost of 3 pens.
Example: 2 erasers cost the same as 6 sharpeners at 3 rupees each, which is 18 rupees. So one eraser costs 9 rupees, and 5 erasers cost 5 times 9, which is 45 rupees.
steps: 5 pencils cost 5 times 6, which is 30 rupees.
So 3 pens cost 30 rupees, and 1 pen costs 30 divided by 3, which is 10 rupees.
4 pens cost 4 times 10, which is 40.
So 4 pens cost 40 rupees.

G4A_RATIO_028.q: 96 sweets are shared among three children in the ratio 1 is to 3 is to 4. What is the difference between the largest share and the smallest share?
hints: Find the size of one part. Then compare the biggest share with the smallest by counting how many parts apart they are.
There are 1 plus 3 plus 4 parts in all. Divide 96 by that.
Example: 60 sweets in the ratio 1 is to 2 is to 3 make 6 parts of 10 sweets. The largest share is 2 parts more than the smallest, so the difference is 2 times 10, which is 20.
steps: Total parts: 1 plus 3 plus 4 equals 8.
One part is 96 divided by 8, which is 12 sweets.
The largest share is 4 parts and the smallest is 1 part, so they are 3 parts apart.
3 times 12 equals 36, so the difference is 36 sweets.

G4A_RATIO_029.q: Hari walks 3 kilometres in 45 minutes. At the same speed, how many kilometres does he walk in 2 hours?
hints: Find the time for 1 kilometre. Change the hours into minutes so that the units match.
Time for 1 kilometre: 45 divided by 3 minutes. And 2 hours is 120 minutes.
Example: Mina cycles 4 kilometres in 20 minutes, so 1 kilometre takes 5 minutes. In 1 hour, which is 60 minutes, she cycles 60 divided by 5, which is 12 kilometres.
steps: 1 kilometre takes 45 divided by 3, which is 15 minutes.
2 hours is 120 minutes.
120 divided by 15 equals 8.
So Hari walks 8 kilometres in 2 hours.

G4A_RATIO_030.q: To make green paint, a painter mixes 2 tins of blue with every 3 tins of yellow. He has 12 tins of blue and 15 tins of yellow. What is the greatest number of tins of green paint he can make?
hints: Each lot of the mix uses up some of each colour. See which colour runs out first; that colour decides how many lots can be made.
The blue is enough for 12 divided by 2 lots. The yellow is enough for 15 divided by 3 lots. Which is smaller?
Example: a drink needs 1 cup of syrup for every 4 cups of water. With 3 cups of syrup and 8 cups of water, the water allows only 2 lots, so the most is 2 times 5, which is 10 cups of drink.
steps: The blue is enough for 12 divided by 2, which is 6 lots. The yellow is enough for 15 divided by 3, which is 5 lots.
The yellow runs out first, so only 5 lots can be made.
Each lot is 2 plus 3, which is 5 tins of green paint.
5 times 5 equals 25, so he can make 25 tins of green paint.

G4A_RATIO_031.q: Asha and Bina have stickers in the ratio 5 is to 3. Asha gives 6 of her stickers to Bina, and now the two girls have the same number of stickers. How many stickers did Asha have at first?
hints: When one girl gives stickers to the other, one number goes down and the other goes up. Think about how much the gap between them changes.
Asha has 2 parts more than Bina. Giving away 6 stickers lowers Asha by 6 and raises Bina by 6. How big must the gap have been for them to end up equal?
A similar one: Ravi and Sam have marbles in the ratio 7 is to 3, and when Ravi gives Sam 10 they are equal. The gap was 2 times 10, which is 20 marbles, or 4 parts, so one part is 5 and Ravi had 35.
steps: Giving 6 stickers closes the gap from both sides, so the gap at first was twice 6. 2 times 6 equals 12.
The gap is 5 minus 3, which is 2 parts, so find one part. 12 divided by 2 equals 6.
Asha had 5 parts. 5 times 6 equals 30.
Check: Asha 30 and Bina 18 become 24 and 24.
Asha had 30 stickers at first.

G4A_RATIO_032.q: 8 workers can paint a school in 12 days, all working at the same speed. They start the job, and after 4 days 8 more workers join them. How many more days will it take to finish the painting?
hints: Think of the whole job as a number of days of work for one worker. Then see how much is left after the first 4 days.
8 workers for 12 days is 8 times 12, which is 96 days of work for one worker. Find how much of that the 8 workers finish in 4 days.
A similar one: 6 workers need 10 days, so the job is 60 worker-days. After 5 days, 30 worker-days are left. If the team grows to 10 workers, the rest takes 30 divided by 10, which is 3 days.
steps: Measure the whole job in worker-days. 8 times 12 equals 96.
Find the work done in the first 4 days. 8 times 4 equals 32.
Find the work still left. 96 minus 32 equals 64.
Now there are 8 plus 8, which is 16 workers to share it. 64 divided by 16 equals 4.
It will take 4 more days.

G4A_RATIO_033.q: 70 rupees is shared among Asha, Bina and Chitra. Asha's share and Bina's share are in the ratio 2 is to 3. Bina's share and Chitra's share are in the ratio 4 is to 5. How many rupees does Chitra get?
hints: Bina appears in both ratios but with different numbers of parts. Make Bina's number the same in both before joining the ratios.
Bina is 3 in the first ratio and 4 in the second. Find a number that both 3 and 4 divide, and rewrite each ratio so Bina has that many parts.

A similar one: P is to Q, as 1 is to 2 and Q is to R, as 3 is to 4. Make Q equal to 6 in both: 3 is to 6 and 6 is to 8. So P is to Q is to R, as 3 is to 6 is to 8, which is 17 parts. If the total is 34 rupees, each part is 2 rupees and R gets 16 rupees.
steps: Make Bina's part the same in both ratios. Use 12, which both 3 and 4 divide.
Rewrite the ratios: 2 is to 3 becomes 8 is to 12 and 4 is to 5 becomes 12 is to 15. So the three shares are 8 is to 12 is to 15.
Count the parts. 8 plus 12 plus 15 equals 35.
Find one part. 70 divided by 35 equals 2.
Chitra has 15 parts. 15 times 2 equals 30.
Chitra gets 30 rupees.

G4A_RATIO_034.q: A box has red and blue beads in the ratio 2 is to 3. Meena adds 8 red beads and no blue beads. Now the ratio of red beads to blue beads is 2 is to 1. How many blue beads are in the box?
hints: Only the red beads change. Rewrite the two ratios so that the blue beads have the same number of parts in both.
Blue is 3 parts in 2 is to 3 but 1 part in 2 is to 1. Multiply the second ratio so that blue is 3 parts there too.

A similar one: red to blue is 1 is to 2, and after adding 15 red it is 2 is to 1. Write 2 is to 1 as 4 is to 2 so blue stays 2 parts. Red has grown from 1 part to 4 parts, so 3 parts are 15 beads, one part is 5, and blue is 2 parts, which is 10.
steps: Blue does not change, so write 2 is to 1 as 6 is to 3. Now blue is 3 parts before and after.
Red grows from 2 parts to 6 parts. 6 minus 2 equals 4.
Those 4 parts are the 8 beads added. Find one part. 8 divided by 4 equals 2.
Blue is 3 parts. 3 times 2 equals 6.
Check: 4 red and 6 blue become 12 red and 6 blue, which is 2 is to 1.
There are 6 blue beads in the box.

G4A_RATIO_035.q: A piggy bank holds only 1 rupee, 2 rupee and 5 rupee coins. The numbers of 1 rupee, 2 rupee and 5 rupee coins are in the ratio 3 is to 2 is to 1. The coins are worth 96 rupees altogether. How many 5 rupee coins are there?
hints: The ratio compares how many coins there are, not how much money they are worth. Find the value of one small group of coins.
Take one group of 3 one-rupee coins, 2 two-rupee coins and 1 five-rupee coin. Work out how many rupees that group is worth.

A similar one: 1 rupee and 5 rupee coins in the ratio 2 is to 1 are worth 35 rupees. One group of 2 one-rupee coins and 1 five-rupee coin is worth 7 rupees, so there are 35 divided by 7, which is 5 groups, and 5 five-rupee coins.
steps: Take one group: 3 coins of 1 rupee, 2 coins of 2 rupees and 1 coin of 5 rupees. Find its value. 3 times 1, plus 2 times 2, plus 1 times 5, equals 12.
Find how many such groups make 96 rupees. 96 divided by 12 equals 8.
Each group has one 5 rupee coin, so count them. 8 times 1 equals 8.
There are 8 coins of 5 rupees.

G4A_RATIO_036.q: A carpenter takes 12 minutes to cut a long wooden pole into 4 pieces. Each cut takes the same time. How many minutes will he take to cut another pole of the same kind into 8 pieces?
hints: Count the cuts, not the pieces. Picture the pole and mark where the saw goes.
To get 4 pieces from one pole you need only 3 cuts. Find how long one cut takes.
A similar one: 10 minutes to cut a rope into 3 pieces means 2 cuts of 5 minutes each. For 6 pieces you need 5 cuts, so 5 times 5 equals 25 minutes, not 20.
steps: 4 pieces need 3 cuts. 4 minus 1 equals 3.
Find the time for one cut. 12 divided by 3 equals 4.
8 pieces need 7 cuts. 8 minus 1 equals 7.
Find the time for 7 cuts. 7 times 4 equals 28.
He will take 28 minutes.

G4A_RATIO_037.q: A temple bell rings 4 times in 6 seconds, measured from the first ring to the last ring. The gaps between the rings are all equal. How many seconds will the bell take, from the first ring to the last, to ring 12 times?
hints: The time is spent in the gaps between the rings. Count the gaps, not the rings.
4 rings have only 3 gaps between them. Find how long one gap lasts.
A similar one: a bell takes 10 seconds to ring 3 times, so there are 2 gaps of 5 seconds each. To ring 9 times there are 8 gaps, so it takes 8 times 5, which is 40 seconds.
steps: 4 rings have 3 gaps. 4 minus 1 equals 3.
Find the length of one gap. 6 divided by 3 equals 2.
12 rings have 11 gaps. 12 minus 1 equals 11.
Find the time for 11 gaps. 11 times 2 equals 22.
It will take 22 seconds.

G4A_RATIO_038.q: Jug A holds 8 cups of lemonade made with lemon juice and water in the ratio 1 is to 3. Jug B holds 8 cups of lemonade made with lemon juice and water in the ratio 1 is to 1. Both jugs are poured into one big pot. What is the ratio of lemon juice to water in the pot?
hints: You cannot add the numbers in two ratios unless the parts are the same size. Find the actual cups of juice and water in each jug.
In Jug A the 8 cups are split into 1 plus 3, which is 4 parts, so each part is 2 cups. Find the cups of juice and of water in Jug A, then in Jug B.
A similar one: 6 cups mixed 1 is to 2 has 2 cups of juice and 4 cups of water. Another 6 cups mixed 1 is to 1 has 3 and 3. Together that is 5 cups of juice and 7 cups of water, a ratio of 5 is to 7.
steps: Jug A: 4 parts make 8 cups, so each part is 2 cups. It has 2 cups of juice and 6 cups of water.
Jug B: 2 parts make 8 cups, so each part is 4 cups. It has 4 cups of juice and 4 cups of water.
Add the juice, and add the water. 2 plus 4 equals 6, 6 plus 4 equals 10.
Simplify 6 is to 10 by dividing both numbers by 2.
The ratio of lemon juice to water is 3 is to 5.

G4A_RATIO_039.q: In a class, the ratio of boys to girls is exactly 4 is to 5. Which of these could be the number of children in the class?
hints: Think about how many equal parts the class is split into. The whole class must be made of whole parts.
Boys are 4 parts and girls are 5 parts. Add these to find how many parts make the whole class, and look for a number that can be split into that many equal parts.
A similar one: if cats to dogs is 2 is to 5, there are 7 parts, so the total must be a multiple of 7. A total of 28 gives 8 cats and 20 dogs. A total of 20 cannot be split into 7 equal whole parts.
steps: The class is 4 parts boys and 5 parts girls. 4 plus 5 equals 9.
So the number of children must be a multiple of 9.
Of 36, 40, 32 and 25, only 36 is a multiple of 9. 36 divided by 9 equals 4.
Check: 16 boys and 20 girls is 4 is to 5.
The class could have 36 children.

G4A_RATIO_040.q: An auto-rickshaw fare is a fixed starting charge plus the same amount for every kilometre. A 3 kilometre ride costs 50 rupees and a 5 kilometre ride costs 70 rupees. How much does a 10 kilometre ride cost?
hints: Doubling the distance does not double the fare here, because part of the fare is the same for every ride. Compare the two rides you know.
The 5 kilometre ride is 2 kilometres longer than the 3 kilometre ride and costs 20 rupees more. Find the cost of one extra kilometre.

A similar one: 2 kilometres costs 35 rupees and 4 kilometres costs 55 rupees. The extra 2 kilometres cost 20 rupees, so each kilometre is 10 rupees and the starting charge is 35 minus 20, which is 15 rupees. An 8 kilometre ride costs 15 plus 80, which is 95 rupees.
steps: The extra 2 kilometres cost the extra money. 70 minus 50 equals 20.
Find the cost of one kilometre. 20 divided by 2 equals 10.
Find the starting charge from the 3 kilometre ride. 50 minus 3 times 10 equals 20.
Find the fare for 10 kilometres. 20 plus 10 times 10 equals 120.
A 10 kilometre ride costs 120 rupees.

G4A_RATIO_041.q: Ravi and Sita share 60 sweets in the ratio 7 is to 3. Ravi wants both of them to have the same number of sweets. How many sweets must Ravi give to Sita?
hints: Find each child's share first. Then remember that every sweet Ravi gives away also adds one to Sita.
There are 7 plus 3, which is 10 parts, so each part is 6 sweets. Find Ravi's sweets and Sita's sweets, and what each should have when they are equal.
A similar one: 40 sweets shared 3 is to 1 gives 30 and 10. Equal shares would be 20 each, so the giver hands over 30 minus 20, which is 10 sweets, or half of the gap of 20.
steps: Find one part. 60 divided by 10 equals 6.
Find the two shares. 7 times 6 equals 42, 3 times 6 equals 18.
Equal shares would be half of 60 each. 60 divided by 2 equals 30.
Ravi must come down from 42 to 30. 42 minus 30 equals 12.
Ravi must give 12 sweets to Sita.

G4A_RATIO_042.q: Two-thirds of Asha's stickers is the same number as one-half of Bina's stickers. What is the ratio of Asha's stickers to Bina's stickers?
hints: Try real numbers. Pick a number for the equal amount and work back to each girl's stickers.
Suppose the equal amount is 6 stickers. If two-thirds of Asha's stickers is 6, how many does Asha have? If half of Bina's is 6, how many does Bina have?
A similar one: half of P equals one-quarter of Q. If the equal amount is 5, then P is 10 and Q is 20, so P is to Q is 1 is to 2. The one who needs the smaller fraction has more.
steps: Choose an easy number for the equal amount, such as 6.
Two-thirds of Asha's stickers is 6, so one-third is 3 and Asha has 9.
Half of Bina's stickers is 6, so Bina has 12.
Simplify 9 is to 12 by dividing both numbers by 3.
The ratio of Asha's stickers to Bina's stickers is 3 is to 4.

G4A_RATIO_043.q: 4 hens lay 12 eggs in 3 days. If every hen lays eggs at the same steady rate, how many eggs will 6 hens lay in 5 days?
hints: Two things change at once: the number of hens and the number of days. Find what one hen does in one day.
4 hens for 3 days is 4 times 3, which is 12 hen-days. They lay 12 eggs in that time, so how many eggs does one hen lay in one day?
A similar one: 2 hens lay 8 eggs in 4 days. That is 8 hen-days, so 1 egg for each hen each day. Then 5 hens in 3 days lay 5 times 3, which is 15 eggs.
steps: Count the hen-days in the first case. 4 times 3 equals 12.
Find the eggs for one hen in one day. 12 divided by 12 equals 1.
Count the hen-days in the second case. 6 times 5 equals 30.
At 1 egg for each hen-day, find the eggs. 30 times 1 equals 30.
6 hens will lay 30 eggs in 5 days.

G4A_RATIO_044.q: Some sweets are shared between Anu and Bala in the ratio 3 is to 4, with none left over. There are more than 40 but fewer than 50 sweets, and Bala gets more than 25 sweets. How many sweets does Anu get?
hints: The total must split into equal whole parts. List the totals that are possible, then test each one against the other clue.
There are 3 plus 4, which is 7 parts, so the total is a multiple of 7. Which multiples of 7 lie between 40 and 50?

A similar one: a ratio of 2 is to 3 with a total between 22 and 32 means a total of 25 or 30. If the bigger share is more than 16, the total is 30 with shares 12 and 18, because 25 gives only 10 and 15.
steps: The total is a multiple of 3 plus 4, which is 7. Between 40 and 50, the multiples of 7 are 42 and 49.
With 42 sweets each part is 6, so Bala gets 24. That is not more than 25.
With 49 sweets each part is 7, so Bala gets 28. That is more than 25.
Anu gets 3 parts of 7. 3 times 7 equals 21.
Anu gets 21 sweets.

G4A_RATIO_045.q: In a school club, the ratio of girls to all the children in the club is 3 is to 8. There are 40 boys in the club. How many girls are there?
hints: Read carefully what the two numbers in the ratio stand for. One of them is the whole club, not the boys.
Out of every 8 children, 3 are girls. How many of every 8 are boys? Use that with the 40 boys.
A similar one: girls to all children is 2 is to 7 and there are 30 boys. Boys are 7 minus 2, which is 5 parts, so each part is 6 and there are 2 times 6, which is 12 girls.
steps: The whole club is 8 parts and girls are 3 parts, so find the boys' parts. 8 minus 3 equals 5.
The 40 boys are 5 parts. Find one part. 40 divided by 5 equals 8.
Girls are 3 parts. 3 times 8 equals 24.
Check: 24 girls out of 64 children is 3 is to 8.
There are 24 girls.

G4A_RATIO_046.q: Asha cycles 5 kilometres in the same time that Bala cycles 4 kilometres. They start together on a 30 kilometre ride and keep these steady speeds. When Asha finishes the ride, how many kilometres does Bala still have to go?
hints: The gap between them keeps growing as they ride. Find how far Bala has gone by the time Asha finishes.
30 kilometres is 6 lots of 5 kilometres. In each of those lots of time, how far does Bala go?

A similar one: Ravi runs 3 kilometres while Sam runs 2 kilometres. When Ravi finishes 12 kilometres, that is 4 lots, so Sam has run 4 times 2, which is 8 kilometres and still has 12 minus 8, or 4 kilometres to go.
steps: Find how many lots of 5 kilometres Asha rides. 30 divided by 5 equals 6.
In each lot of time Bala rides 4 kilometres. 6 times 4 equals 24.
Find how far Bala still has to go. 30 minus 24 equals 6.
Bala still has 6 kilometres to go.

G4A_SEQUENCES_001.q: Look at this number pattern: 2, 50, 5, 46, 8, 42, 11, 38, and so on. What is the 15th number in the pattern?
hints: Two patterns are mixed together here, taking turns. Separate them before you count positions.
The 1st, 3rd, 5th and 7th numbers are 2, 5, 8, 11. Decide which of the two patterns the 15th number belongs to, and what position it has inside that pattern.

Similar problem: in 1, 30, 3, 28, 5, 26, and so on, the 9th number is in the rising pattern 1, 3, 5, and so on. The 1st, 3rd, 5th, 7th and 9th places hold its first five numbers, so the 9th number is 9.
steps: Split the pattern. Odd places: 2, 5, 8, 11, and so on, going up by 3. Even places: 50, 46, 42, 38, and so on, going down by 4.
The 15th place is an odd place, so it belongs to the pattern that goes up by 3.
The odd places 1, 3, 5, and so on, up to 15, are 8 places, so we need the 8th number of 2, 5, 8, 11, and so on.
The 8th number is 2 plus 7 jumps of 3. 2 plus 7 times 3 equals 23.
The 15th number in the pattern is 23.

G4A_SEQUENCES_002.q: The pattern 4, 9, 14, 19, and so on, goes up by 5 each time and ends at 99. How many of its numbers are even?
hints: First see which numbers in the pattern are even and which are odd. Then count only the ones you need, taking care with the first and the last.
The pattern goes even, odd, even, odd: 4, 9, 14, 19. The even ones end in 4. Find where they start and where they stop.
Similar problem: 3, 8, 13, 18, and so on, up to 48. The even numbers are 8, 18, 28, 38, 48, which is 5 numbers.
steps: Adding 5 changes even to odd and odd to even, so the numbers take turns: 4 is even, 9 is odd, 14 is even, and so on.
The even numbers are the ones ending in 4: 4, 14, 24, and so on, up to 94.
From 4 to 94 in jumps of 10 there are 9 jumps, so there are 10 numbers. 9 plus 1 equals 10.
10 of the numbers in the pattern are even.

G4A_SEQUENCES_003.q: A number pattern goes up and down like this: 1, 2, 3, 4, 3, 2, 1, 2, 3, 4, 3, 2, 1, 2, 3, 4, and so on. What is the 100th number in the pattern?
hints: Find the block of numbers that repeats again and again. Be careful about exactly where one block ends and the next begins.
The pattern starts 1, 2, 3, 4, 3, 2 and then the next block begins with 1 again. Count how many numbers are in one block.

Similar problem: 1, 2, 3, 2, 1, 2, 3, 2, 1, and so on, has the repeating block 1, 2, 3, 2 with 4 numbers. For the 30th number, 30 divided by 4 leaves remainder 2, so it is the 2nd number of the block, which is 2.
steps: The repeating block is 1, 2, 3, 4, 3, 2. The next 1 starts a new block, so a block has 6 numbers, not 7.
