100 divided by 6 is 16 with remainder 4, so 16 full blocks use up 96 numbers. 16 times 6 equals 96.
The 100th number is the 4th number of the next block: 1, 2, 3, 4.
The 100th number in the pattern is 4.

G4A_SEQUENCES_004.q: What is the value of 20 minus 19, plus 18 minus 17, plus 16 minus 15, and so on, down to plus 2 minus 1? The numbers go down one at a time from 20 to 1, and the signs take turns.
hints: Do not work from left to right through all twenty numbers. Look for small groups that are easy to work out.
Look at the numbers two at a time: 20 minus 19, then 18 minus 17. What is each pair worth?
Similar problem: 8 minus 7, plus 6 minus 5, plus 4 minus 3, plus 2 minus 1. Each of the pairs 8 minus 7, 6 minus 5, 4 minus 3 and 2 minus 1 is worth 1, and there are 4 pairs, so the value is 4.
steps: Group the numbers in pairs: 20 minus 19, then 18 minus 17, and so on down to 2 minus 1.
Each pair is worth 1.
There are 20 numbers, so there are 10 pairs. 20 divided by 2 equals 10.
10 pairs of 1 make 10, so the value is 10.

G4A_SEQUENCES_005.q: Farid arranges dots in rows to make a triangle. The 1st row has 1 dot, the 2nd row has 2 dots, the 3rd row has 3 dots, and so on. He has 60 dots and makes as many complete rows as he can. How many dots are left over?
hints: Keep a running total of the dots used as each new row is added, and stop before the total goes past the dots he has.
After 4 rows he has used 1 plus 2 plus 3 plus 4 equals 10 dots. Keep adding rows and watch the total.
Similar problem: with 25 dots, the running totals are 1, 3, 6, 10, 15, 21, and the next would be 28, which is too many. So 6 rows use 21 dots and 25 minus 21 equals 4 dots are left over.
steps: Running totals of dots after each row: 1, 3, 6, 10, 15, 21, 28, 36, 45, 55.
After 10 rows he has used 55 dots. An 11th row needs 11 more dots, which would make 66, more than 60.
So he makes 10 complete rows and uses 55 dots. 60 minus 55 equals 5.
5 dots are left over.

G4A_SEQUENCES_006.q: Arun saves 5 rupees on the first day. Every day after that he saves 3 rupees more than he saved the day before. On which day does the total money he has saved first become more than 100 rupees?
hints: There are two different amounts here: what he saves on one day, and the total so far. The question is about the total.
Write the daily savings: 5, 8, 11, 14, and so on, and beside them keep a running total: 5, 13, 24, and so on.
Similar problem: saving 2 rupees on day 1 and 2 rupees more each day, when does the total pass 25 rupees? Daily: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10. Totals: 2, 6, 12, 20, 30. The total first passes 25 on the 5th day.
steps: Daily savings in rupees: 5, 8, 11, 14, 17, 20, 23, 26.
After the 7th day the total is 98, which is still not more than 100.
On the 8th day he adds 26 and the total becomes 124. 98 plus 26 equals 124.
The total first becomes more than 100 rupees on the 8th day.

G4A_SEQUENCES_007.q: Find the rule in this pattern: 2, 6, 4, 12, 10, 30, 28, and so on. What is the 10th number in the pattern?
hints: Look at how each number becomes the next. The same change does not happen every time, so check the steps in turn.
From 2 to 6 is times 3. From 6 to 4 is take away 2. See whether those two steps keep taking turns.
Similar problem: 1, 2, 5, 10, 13, 26, and so on, uses times 2 and then add 3 in turn. After 26 comes 29, then 58, so the 8th number is 58.
steps: The rule takes turns: multiply by 3, then subtract 2. For example 2 times 3 equals 6, 6 minus 2 equals 4, 4 times 3 equals 12 and 12 minus 2 equals 10.
Seven numbers are given. The 8th is 28 times 3. 28 times 3 equals 84.
The 9th is 84 minus 2. 84 minus 2 equals 82.
The 10th is 82 times 3. 82 times 3 equals 246.
The 10th number in the pattern is 246.

G4A_SEQUENCES_008.q: Pattern A is 5, 9, 13, 17, and so on, and goes up by 4 each time. Pattern B is 2, 9, 16, 23, and so on, and goes up by 7 each time. The number 9 is in both patterns. What is the next number that is in both patterns?
hints: A number in both patterns must be reachable from 9 by jumps of one size and also by jumps of the other size.
From 9, pattern A moves in jumps of 4 and pattern B moves in jumps of 7. How far from 9 must you go before both kinds of jump land on the same number?

Similar problem: 1, 3, 5, and so on, up by 2, and 1, 4, 7, and so on, up by 3, share the number 1. Jumps of 2 and jumps of 3 first meet 6 further on, so the next shared number is 1 plus 6, which is 7.
steps: Both patterns contain 9. From there A goes up in 4s and B goes up in 7s.
They meet again when the distance from 9 is a multiple of both 4 and 7. The smallest such distance is 28.
28 is the distance, not the number, so add it to 9. 9 plus 28 equals 37.
The next number in both patterns is 37.

G4A_SEQUENCES_009.q: A number pattern goes up by the same amount each time. Its 5th number is 23 and its 8th number is 35. What is the 1st number of the pattern?
hints: First find the size of one jump from the two numbers you know. Then walk backwards, counting jumps, not numbers.
From the 5th number to the 8th number there are 3 jumps, and the numbers rise from 23 to 35. Find the size of one jump.
Similar problem: the 3rd number is 14 and the 6th number is 29. Three jumps make 15, so one jump is 5. From the 3rd back to the 1st is 2 jumps, so the 1st number is 14 minus 10, which is 4.
steps: From the 5th number to the 8th number is 3 jumps, and the numbers rise by 12. 35 minus 23 equals 12.
So one jump is 4. 12 divided by 3 equals 4.
From the 5th number back to the 1st number is 4 jumps, not 5. 4 times 4 equals 16.
Go back 16 from 23. Check: 7, 11, 15, 19, 23, 27, 31, 35. 23 minus 16 equals 7.
The 1st number of the pattern is 7.

hints: The square of a number is the number multiplied by itself.
Here you need 12 times 12. Try splitting it into 12 times 10 and 12 times 2.
Example: the square of 11 is 11 times 11. 11 times 10 equals 110 and 11 times 1 equals 11, so 110 plus 11 equals 121.
steps: The square of 12 means 12 multiplied by itself.
12 times 10 equals 120 and 12 times 2 equals 24.
120 plus 24 equals 144, so the square of 12 is 144. 12 times 12 equals 144.

G4A_SQUARES_002.q: Which of these numbers is a perfect square?
hints: A perfect square is what you get when a whole number is multiplied by itself. Run through the squares you know.
Try the squares near these numbers: 6 times 6, 7 times 7, 8 times 8 and 9 times 9. Does any of them match a number in the list?
Example: among 30, 36, 40 and 42, only 36 is a perfect square, because 6 times 6 equals 36.
steps: List the squares near these numbers: 6 times 6 equals 36, 7 times 7 equals 49, 8 times 8 equals 64 and 9 times 9 equals 81.
48, 56 and 72 are not in that list.
64 is 8 times 8, so the perfect square is 64.

G4A_SQUARES_003.q: A square carrom board is marked with 81 small squares, in equal rows and columns. How many small squares are there in each row?
hints: When the rows and columns are equal, the total is a number multiplied by itself. You are looking for that number.
Ask yourself: which number times itself makes 81? Try 8 times 8 and 9 times 9.
Example: 49 tiles laid in equal rows and columns have 7 in each row, because 7 times 7 equals 49.
steps: Equal rows and columns means the number in each row, multiplied by itself, is 81.
8 times 8 equals 64, which is too small, and 9 times 9 equals 81, which fits.
So there are 9 small squares in each row. 9 times 9 equals 81.

G4A_SQUARES_004.q: A number ends in the digit 7. Which digit does its square end in?
hints: The last digit of a square depends only on the last digit of the number being squared.
So you only need to work out 7 times 7 and look at its last digit.
Example: a number ending in 4, such as 14 or 24, has a square ending in 6, because 4 times 4 equals 16.
steps: Only the last digit matters, so look at 7 times 7.
7 times 7 equals 49, which ends in 9.
Check with 17: 17 times 17 equals 289, which also ends in 9. So the square ends in 9.

G4A_SQUARES_005.q: What is the next perfect square after 49?
hints: Perfect squares come from squaring the counting numbers in order: 1 times 1, 2 times 2, 3 times 3 and so on.
First find which number is squared to give 49. Then square the next counting number.
Example: 25 is 5 times 5, so the next perfect square after 25 is 6 times 6, which is 36.
steps: 49 is 7 times 7.
The next counting number after 7 is 8.
8 times 8 equals 64, so the next perfect square after 49 is 64.

G4A_SQUARES_006.q: Ravi plants mango saplings in a square field: 11 rows with 11 saplings in each row. How many saplings does he plant?
hints: Rows of equal size are counted by multiplying the number of rows by the number in each row.
Here you need 11 times 11. Try 11 times 10 first, then add one more 11.
Example: 13 rows with 13 plants in each row have 13 times 13 plants. 13 times 10 equals 130 and 13 times 3 equals 39, so 130 plus 39 equals 169.
steps: Saplings equals rows, times saplings in each row. 11 times 11.
11 times 10 equals 110, and one more 11 makes 110 plus 11, which is 121.
So Ravi plants 121 saplings.

hints: The small 2 means the number is multiplied by itself. Square each number first, then add.
Work out 5 times 5 and 3 times 3 separately.
Example: 4 squared plus 2 squared is 16 plus 4, which is 20.
steps: 5 squared means 5 times 5, which is 25.
3 squared means 3 times 3, which is 9.
25 plus 9 equals 34, so 5 squared plus 3 squared equals 34.

hints: To square a number that ends in zero, square the front digit and remember that each zero appears twice.
30 times 30 is 3 times 3 with two zeros placed after it.
Example: the square of 20 is 20 times 20. 2 times 2 equals 4, and then two zeros give 400.
steps: The square of 30 is 30 times 30.
3 times 3 equals 9.
One zero from each 30 gives two zeros, so 30 times 30 equals 900.

G4A_SQUARES_009.q: What is the greatest two-digit perfect square?
hints: List the perfect squares in order and look for the last one that still has two digits.
Try 9 times 9 and 10 times 10. Which of them has two digits?
Example: the greatest one-digit perfect square is 9, because 3 times 3 equals 9 and the next one, 4 times 4 equals 16, has two digits.
steps: 9 times 9 equals 81, which has two digits.
10 times 10 equals 100, which has three digits.
So the greatest two-digit perfect square is 81.

G4A_SQUARES_010.q: What is the smallest number that must be taken away from 30 to leave a perfect square?
hints: Taking away makes the number smaller, so look for the nearest perfect square below the number.
Which perfect square is just below 30? Try 5 times 5 and 6 times 6.
Example: for 70, the nearest perfect square below is 8 times 8, which is 64, so 70 minus 64, which is 6, must be taken away.
steps: 5 times 5 equals 25, which is below 30, and 6 times 6 equals 36, which is above 30.
The nearest perfect square below 30 is 25.
30 minus 25 equals 5, so 5 must be taken away.

G4A_SQUARES_011.q: Which of these numbers is the square of an odd number?
hints: Find which number was squared to make each one, then check whether that number is odd or even.
36 is 6 times 6 and 64 is 8 times 8. Now find the numbers for 49 and 100.
Example: among 16, 25 and 144, the square of an odd number is 25, because 25 is 5 times 5 and 5 is odd.
steps: 36 is 6 times 6, 64 is 8 times 8 and 100 is 10 times 10. The numbers 6, 8 and 10 are even.
49 is 7 times 7, and 7 is odd.
So the square of an odd number is 49.

G4A_SQUARES_012.q: What is the difference between the square of 6 and the number 6 itself?
hints: First find the square. Then the word difference tells you to subtract.
Work out 6 times 6 first.
Example: for 5, the square is 5 times 5, which is 25, and the difference is 25 minus 5, which is 20.
steps: The square of 6 is 6 times 6, which is 36.
Difference means subtract: 36 minus 6 equals 30.
So the difference is 30.

G4A_SQUARES_013.q: How many perfect squares are there between 50 and 150?
hints: List the perfect squares in order and pick out the ones that lie between the two numbers.
The first square above 50 is 8 times 8, which is 64. Keep going with 9 times 9, 10 times 10 and so on, until you pass 150.
Example: between 10 and 40 the perfect squares are 16, 25 and 36, so there are 3 of them.
steps: 7 times 7 equals 49, which is just below 50, so start from 8 times 8, which is 64.
13 times 13 equals 169, which is more than 150, so stop there.
The squares are 64, 81, 100, 121 and 144, so there are 5.

G4A_SQUARES_014.q: Which of these digits can never be the last digit of a perfect square?
hints: The last digit of a square depends only on the last digit of the number squared, so there are just ten cases to check.
Square each digit from 0 to 9 and write down the last digit each time: 0, 1, 4, 9, and so on.
Example: can a perfect square end in 3? The squares of 0 to 9 end in 0, 1, 4, 9, 6, 5, 6, 9, 4 and 1. There is no 3, so a perfect square never ends in 3.
steps: Their last digits are 0, 1, 4, 9, 6, 5, 6, 9, 4 and 1.
4, 5 and 6 are in this list, but 7 is not.
So a perfect square can never end in 7.

hints: Square each number first, then subtract. Do not subtract first.
Work out 10 times 10 and 6 times 6.
Example: 7 squared minus 3 squared is 49 minus 9, which is 40.
steps: 10 squared means 10 times 10, which is 100.
6 squared means 6 times 6, which is 36.
100 minus 36 equals 64, so 10 squared minus 6 squared equals 64.

G4A_SQUARES_016.q: The sum 1 plus 3 plus 5 plus 7 plus 9 plus 11 is the square of which number?
hints: Add the odd numbers, then ask which number times itself gives that total.
Add in pairs: 1 with 11, 3 with 9, and 5 with 7.
Example: 1 plus 3 plus 5 plus 7 equals 16, and 16 is 4 times 4, so that sum is the square of 4. Notice that there were 4 odd numbers.
steps: 1 plus 11 equals 12, 3 plus 9 equals 12 and 5 plus 7 equals 12.
The total is 12 plus 12 plus 12, which is 36.
36 is 6 times 6.
So the sum is the square of 6.

G4A_SQUARES_017.q: A teacher has 150 children on the playground. She makes them stand in the biggest possible square, with the same number in every row and every column. How many children are left out?
hints: The children standing in the square make a perfect square number. Find the biggest perfect square that is not more than the number of children.
Try 12 times 12 and 13 times 13. Which one is still no more than 150?
Example: with 90 children, the biggest square is 9 times 9, which is 81, so 90 minus 81, which is 9 children, are left out.
steps: 12 times 12 equals 144 and 13 times 13 equals 169.
169 is more than 150, so the biggest square uses 144 children.
150 minus 144 equals 6, so 6 children are left out.

G4A_SQUARES_018.q: A gardener has 200 rose plants. He wants to plant all of them in a square, with the same number in every row and every column. What is the least number of extra plants he must buy?
hints: He is adding plants, so look for the nearest perfect square above the number he has.
Try 14 times 14 and 15 times 15. Which is the first one above 200?
Example: with 90 plants, the next perfect square is 10 times 10, which is 100, so he must buy 100 minus 90, which is 10 more.
steps: 14 times 14 equals 196, which is less than 200, so it cannot hold all the plants.
15 times 15 equals 225, which is the first perfect square above 200.
225 minus 200 equals 25, so he must buy 25 extra plants.

G4A_SQUARES_019.q: What is the square root of 400 added to the square root of 49?
hints: Find each square root on its own first, then add them.
Which number times itself gives 400? Think of 2 times 2 equals 4 and the zeros.
Example: the square root of 900 is 30 and the square root of 16 is 4, so together they make 30 plus 4, which is 34.
steps: 20 times 20 equals 400, so the square root of 400 is 20.
7 times 7 equals 49, so the square root of 49 is 7.
20 plus 7 equals 27, so the sum is 27.

G4A_SQUARES_020.q: 441 soldiers stand in a square, with the same number in each row and each column. Every soldier in the front row holds a flag. How many flags are there?
hints: The front row has as many soldiers as the side of the square. Find the number that times itself gives the total.
20 times 20 equals 400, which is a little too small. The total ends in 1, so try a number ending in 1.
Example: 169 soldiers in a square stand 13 in each row, because 13 times 13 equals 169, so the front row would hold 13 flags.
steps: The number in each row, multiplied by itself, is 441.
20 times 20 equals 400, which is too small, so try the next number.
21 times 21 equals 441.
The front row has 21 soldiers, so there are 21 flags.

G4A_SQUARES_021.q: Which of these numbers is not a perfect square?
hints: Check each number: is there a whole number that, multiplied by itself, gives it?
Work out the squares from 11 times 11 to 14 times 14 and tick off the ones in the list.
Example: among 81, 90 and 100, the one that is not a perfect square is 90, since 9 times 9 equals 81 and 10 times 10 equals 100 and nothing falls in between.
steps: 11 times 11 equals 121, 12 times 12 equals 144, 13 times 13 equals 169 and 14 times 14 equals 196.
121, 144 and 196 are in this list.
164 falls between 144 and 169, so 164 is not a perfect square.

G4A_SQUARES_022.q: The squares of two numbers that come one after the other are 144 and 169. What is the sum of the two numbers?
hints: Work backwards from each square to the number that was squared. Then add those numbers.
Which number times itself gives 144? Try 12.
Example: if the squares are 81 and 100, the numbers are 9 and 10, and their sum is 9 plus 10, which is 19.
steps: 12 times 12 equals 144, so the first number is 12.
13 times 13 equals 169, so the second number is 13.
12 plus 13 equals 25, so the sum of the two numbers is 25.

G4A_SQUARES_023.q: Only one of these numbers is a perfect square. Use the last digits to find it.
hints: A perfect square can end only in 0, 1, 4, 5, 6 or 9. Any number ending in 2, 3, 7 or 8 can be ruled out straight away.
Look at the last digit of each number. Which ones end in 2, 3, 7 or 8?
Example: among 352, 361, 377 and 388, only 361 can be a perfect square, and indeed 19 times 19 equals 361.
steps: 1232 ends in 2, 1443 ends in 3 and 1687 ends in 7.
No perfect square ends in 2, 3 or 7, so these three are ruled out.
1521 ends in 1, and 39 times 39 equals 1521.
So the perfect square is 1521.

G4A_SQUARES_024.q: What is 1 squared plus 2 squared plus 3 squared plus 4 squared?
hints: Square each number on its own, then add the four squares.
Write the squares in a row: 1, 4, and then 3 times 3 and 4 times 4.
Example: 1 squared plus 2 squared plus 3 squared is 1 plus 4 plus 9, which is 14.
steps: The squares are 1, 4, 9 and 16.
Add them: 1 plus 4 plus 9 plus 16 equals 30.
So 1 squared plus 2 squared plus 3 squared plus 4 squared equals 30.

G4A_SQUARES_025.q: Tara has made a square with 64 small tiles. She wants to add tiles to make the next bigger square. How many more tiles does she need?
hints: Find the side of the square she has, make the side one tile longer, and compare the two totals.
64 is 8 times 8, so her square has 8 tiles on each side. The next bigger square has 9 tiles on each side.
Example: going from a 5 by 5 square of 25 tiles to a 6 by 6 square of 36 tiles needs 36 minus 25, which is 11 more tiles.
steps: 64 is 8 times 8, so the square has 8 tiles on each side.
The next bigger square has 9 tiles on each side: 9 times 9 equals 81.
81 minus 64 equals 17, so she needs 17 more tiles.

G4A_SQUARES_026.q: The square of a number is 225. What is the square of the number that is 1 more?
hints: First find the number whose square is given. Then add 1 to that number and square it.
Which number times itself gives 225? It ends in 5, so try 15.
Example: if the square of a number is 100, the number is 10, and the square of 11 is 11 times 11, which is 121.
steps: 15 times 15 equals 225, so the number is 15.
One more than 15 is 16.
16 times 16 equals 256, so the square is 256.

G4A_SQUARES_027.q: How many perfect squares are there from 1 to 100, counting both 1 and 100?
hints: Each perfect square comes from one counting number. Count how many counting numbers have a square that is not more than the limit.
1 times 1 equals 1, which is the first one. Which number squared gives exactly 100?
Example: from 1 to 50 the perfect squares are 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36 and 49. They are the squares of 1 to 7, so there are 7.
steps: 1 times 1 equals 1 and 10 times 10 equals 100.
So the squares of 1, 2, 3 and so on, up to 10, all lie from 1 to 100.
That makes 10 perfect squares.

hints: Square each number, then subtract. Splitting each number around 50 makes the squaring easier.
51 times 51 is 51 times 50 and one more 51. Work that out first.
Example: 21 squared minus 19 squared is 441 minus 361, which is 80.
steps: 51 times 51 is 51 times 50 plus 51: 2550 plus 51 equals 2601. 51 times 51 equals 2601.
49 times 49 is 49 times 50 minus 49: 2450 minus 49 equals 2401. 49 times 49 equals 2401.
2601 minus 2401 equals 200, so 51 squared minus 49 squared equals 200.

G4A_SQUARES_029.q: What is the smallest number by which 48 must be divided so that the result is a perfect square?
hints: Try dividing by small numbers in order, and check each result against the perfect squares you know.
Start with 48 divided by 2, which is 24. Is 24 a perfect square? If not, try the next number.
Example: for 50, try 50 divided by 2, which is 25. Since 25 is 5 times 5, the smallest number to divide 50 by is 2.
steps: 48 itself is not a perfect square, so dividing by 1 is no help.
48 divided by 2 equals 24, and 24 is not a perfect square.
48 divided by 3 equals 16, and 16 is 4 times 4, a perfect square.
So the smallest number to divide by is 3.

G4A_SQUARES_030.q: What is the smallest number that must be subtracted from 1000 to get a perfect square?
hints: Subtracting makes the number smaller, so find the largest perfect square below the number.
30 times 30 equals 900. Now try 31 times 31 and 32 times 32 to see which is the last one below 1000.
Example: for 500, 22 times 22 equals 484, which is the largest perfect square below it, so 500 minus 484, which is 16, must be subtracted.
steps: 31 times 31 equals 961 and 32 times 32 equals 1024.
1024 is more than 1000, so the largest perfect square below 1000 is 961.
1000 minus 961 equals 39, so 39 must be subtracted.

G4A_SQUARES_031.q: How many whole numbers lie between 15 squared and 16 squared?
hints: Work out the two squares, then count the numbers strictly between them. The two squares themselves are not counted.
15 times 15 equals 225 and 16 times 16 equals 256. Now count from 226 up to 255.
Example: between 3 times 3, which is 9, and 4 times 4, which is 16, lie 10, 11, 12, 13, 14 and 15. That is 6 numbers, one less than 16 minus 9, which is 7.
steps: 15 times 15 equals 225 and 16 times 16 equals 256.
The gap is 256 minus 225, which is 31.
The numbers in between run from 226 to 255, which is one fewer than the gap.
31 minus 1 equals 30, so 30 whole numbers lie between them.

G4A_SQUARES_032.q: A farmer plants his young trees in a square, with the same number in each row and each column, and has 5 trees left over. To make the next bigger square he would need 20 more trees. How many trees does he have?
hints: His trees lie between two perfect squares that come one after the other. Work out how far apart those two squares are.
He is 5 above one square and 20 below the next, so the two squares are 5 plus 20, which is 25 apart. Which two neighbouring squares differ by 25?
Example: with 3 left over and 4 short of the next square, the squares are 3 plus 4, which is 7 apart. 9 and 16 differ by 7, so there are 9 plus 3, which is 12 trees.
steps: The two squares are 5 plus 20, which is 25 apart.
12 times 12 equals 144 and 13 times 13 equals 169, and 169 minus 144 equals 25.
He has 5 more than the smaller square, 144.
144 plus 5 equals 149, so he has 149 trees.

G4A_SQUARES_033.q: Asha has two square sheets of stamps. One sheet has 9 rows of 9 stamps and the other has 12 rows of 12 stamps. She rearranges all the stamps into one big square. How many stamps are in each row of the big square?
hints: Count all the stamps first. Then find the number that, multiplied by itself, gives that total.
The first sheet has 9 times 9 stamps and the second has 12 times 12. Add the two.
Example: sheets of 3 rows of 3 and 4 rows of 4 hold 9 plus 16, which is 25 stamps, and 25 is 5 times 5, so the big square has 5 in each row.
steps: 9 times 9 equals 81 and 12 times 12 equals 144.
81 plus 144 equals 225 stamps in all.
15 times 15 equals 225.
So the big square has 15 stamps in each row.

G4A_SQUARES_034.q: I am a two-digit perfect square. The sum of my two digits is 13. Which number am I?
hints: List all the two-digit perfect squares, then add the digits of each one.
The two-digit perfect squares are 16, 25, 36, 49, 64 and 81. Start adding their digits: 1 plus 6 equals 7, 2 plus 5 equals 7, and carry on.
Example: the two-digit perfect square whose digits add up to 10 is 64, because 6 plus 4 equals 10 and 8 times 8 equals 64.
steps: The two-digit perfect squares are 16, 25, 36, 49, 64 and 81.
Their digit sums are 7, 7, 9, 13, 10 and 9.
Only one of them has digits adding to 13: 4 plus 9 equals 13.
So the number is 49.

G4A_SQUARES_035.q: What is the smallest perfect square that can be divided exactly by both 6 and 8?
hints: The number must be in both times tables and also be a number times itself. Go through the perfect squares in order and test each one.
Squares of odd numbers cannot be divided by 8, so test the even ones: 4, 16, 36, 64, 100 and onward. Can 36 be divided by 8? Can 64 be divided by 6?
Example: the smallest perfect square that can be divided exactly by both 2 and 3 is 36, because 4, 9, 16 and 25 each miss one of them.
steps: Test the even perfect squares in order: 4, 16, 36, 64, 100, 144.
36 divided by 6 equals 6, but 36 cannot be divided exactly by 8. 64 divided by 8 equals 8, but 64 cannot be divided exactly by 6.
4, 16 and 100 cannot be divided exactly by 6.
144 divided by 6 equals 24 and 144 divided by 8 equals 18, so the smallest such perfect square is 144.

G4A_SQUARES_036.q: Most numbers have an even number of factors. For example, 12 has six factors: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 12. How many numbers from 1 to 50 have an odd number of factors?
hints: Factors come in pairs that multiply to give the number. Think about when a factor is paired with itself.
For 12 the pairs are 1 and 12, 2 and 6, 3 and 4. Now try 16: the pairs are 1 and 16, 2 and 8, and then 4 with itself. What kind of number has a factor paired with itself?
A similar one, from 1 to 20: only 1, 4, 9 and 16 have a factor that pairs with itself, so 4 numbers have an odd number of factors.
steps: Factors come in pairs, such as 2 and 6 for 12, so most numbers have an even number of factors.
A pair has the same number twice only when the number is a perfect square, such as 4 times 4 for 16. Then the count of factors is odd.
List the perfect squares from 1 to 50: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36 and 49.
So 7 numbers from 1 to 50 have an odd number of factors.

G4A_SQUARES_037.q: Look at the pattern: 1 plus 3 equals 4, 1 plus 3 plus 5 equals 9, 1 plus 3 plus 5 plus 7 equals 16. What is the sum of all the odd numbers from 1 to 39?
hints: Each sum in the pattern is a perfect square. Work out which square goes with how many odd numbers are added.
Two odd numbers give 2 times 2, three give 3 times 3, four give 4 times 4. So count how many odd numbers there are from 1 to 39.
A similar one: the odd numbers from 1 to 19. There are 10 of them, because 19 plus 1 equals 20 and half of 20 is 10. So the sum is 10 times 10, which is 100.
steps: In the pattern, adding the first 2, 3 or 4 odd numbers gives 2 times 2, 3 times 3 or 4 times 4. The sum is the count of odd numbers multiplied by itself.
Count the odd numbers from 1 to 39. Add 1 to the last number and halve. 40 divided by 2 equals 20.
Multiply the count by itself. 20 times 20 equals 400.
The sum is 400.

G4A_SQUARES_038.q: The squares of two numbers that come one after the other differ by 37. What is the larger of the two numbers?
hints: Look at how far apart neighbouring squares are: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25. Find a rule that links the gap to the two numbers.
The gap between 3 times 3 and 4 times 4 is 7, which is 3 plus 4. The gap between 4 times 4 and 5 times 5 is 9, which is 4 plus 5. Which two neighbouring numbers add up to 37?
A similar one: two neighbouring squares differ by 21. The two numbers add up to 21, so they are 10 and 11. Check: 121 minus 100 equals 21. The larger is 11.
steps: Neighbouring squares differ by the sum of the two numbers. For example, 25 minus 16 equals 9 and 4 plus 5 equals 9.
So the two numbers add up to 37 and are next to each other. 18 plus 19 equals 37.
Check with the squares. 361 minus 324 equals 37.
The larger number is 19.

G4A_SQUARES_039.q: 144 children stand in a square formation, with the same number in every row and every column. Each child standing on the outside edge of the square holds a flag. How many children hold a flag?
hints: Find how many children stand in each row. Then count the edge carefully: the corner children belong to two sides.
144 is 12 times 12, so each side has 12 children. If you add four sides of 12, which children get counted twice?
A similar one: 25 children in a square stand 5 to a side. Four sides of 5 make 20, but the 4 corner children were counted twice, so 20 minus 4, which is 16 children, are on the edge.
steps: Find the number of children on each side. 12 times 12 equals 144.
Four sides of 12 would count each corner child twice. 4 times 12 equals 48.
Take away the 4 corners that were counted twice. 48 minus 4 equals 44.
44 children hold a flag.

G4A_SQUARES_040.q: A square floor is covered with 225 tiles, in equal rows and columns. The tiles along both diagonals, from each corner to the opposite corner, are red, and all the other tiles are white. How many red tiles are there?
hints: Find how many tiles are in each row. Then think about whether the two diagonals share a tile.
225 is 15 times 15. Each diagonal has 15 tiles. With an odd number like 15, the two diagonals cross on one tile in the middle.
A similar one: a floor of 7 rows of 7 tiles. Each diagonal has 7 tiles and they share the middle tile, so there are 7 plus 7 minus 1, which is 13 red tiles.
steps: Find the number of tiles in each row. 15 times 15 equals 225.
Each diagonal has 15 tiles. 15 plus 15 equals 30.
Because 15 is odd, the diagonals cross on the middle tile, which was counted twice. 30 minus 1 equals 29.
There are 29 red tiles.

G4A_SQUARES_041.q: Some numbers can be made by adding two perfect squares. For example, 13 equals 4 plus 9. Which of these numbers can not be made by adding two perfect squares?
hints: For each number, try taking away each perfect square that is smaller than it. See whether what is left is also a perfect square.
The perfect squares to use are 1, 4, 9, 16 and 25. For 20, try 20 minus 16, which is 4. Is 4 a perfect square? Test the other numbers in the same way.

A similar one: can 11 be made? 11 minus 1 equals 10, 11 minus 4 equals 7 and 11 minus 9 equals 2, and none of 10, 7 and 2 is a perfect square. So 11 cannot be made, but 10 can, because 1 plus 9 equals 10.
steps: The perfect squares to use are 1, 4, 9, 16 and 25.
Three of the numbers can be made. 4 plus 16 equals 20, 4 plus 25 equals 29, 9 plus 25 equals 34.
For 21, take away each square: 20, 17, 12 and 5 are left. None of these is a perfect square.
The number that cannot be made is 21.

G4A_SQUARES_042.q: Soldiers stand in a square formation, with the same number in every row and every column. Then 3 full rows and 3 full columns of soldiers march away, and the soldiers who remain still form a square. In all, 69 soldiers marched away. How many soldiers were there at first?
hints: The soldiers who leave are the difference between a big square and a smaller square. Test square numbers.
If each side had 10 soldiers, the square left would have sides of 7, and 100 minus 49, which is 51, would leave. That is too few, so try bigger squares.
A similar one: 2 rows and 2 columns leave, 36 soldiers in all. Try sides of 10 and 8: 100 minus 64 equals 36. So there were 100 soldiers at first.
steps: The square at first has some number on each side, and the square left has 3 fewer on each side.
Test sides of 12 and 9. 144 minus 81 equals 63.
Test sides of 13 and 10. 169 minus 100 equals 69.
This matches the 69 soldiers who marched away.
There were 169 soldiers at first.

G4A_SQUARES_043.q: In each of these, the two numbers add up to 60. Which product is the greatest?
hints: Compare each product with the one where the two numbers are equal. Try the same idea with small numbers first.
Try numbers that add up to 10: 5 times 5 equals 25, 4 times 6 equals 24, 3 times 7 equals 21. What happens to the product as the two numbers move further apart?

A similar one with numbers that add up to 20: 10 times 10 equals 100, 9 times 11 equals 99, 8 times 12 equals 96 and 7 times 13 equals 91. The equal pair gives the greatest product, and each step apart makes it smaller.
steps: All four pairs add up to 60, so compare how far apart the two numbers are.
With small numbers that add up to 10, the products get smaller as the numbers move apart. 5 times 5 equals 25, 4 times 6 equals 24, 3 times 7 equals 21.
The same happens here. 30 times 30 equals 900, 29 times 31 equals 899, 28 times 32 equals 896, 27 times 33 equals 891.
The greatest product is 30 times 30.

G4A_SQUARES_044.q: Look at the pattern: 11 times 11 equals 121, 111 times 111 equals 12321, 1111 times 1111 equals 1234321. What is the sum of the digits of 11111 times 11111?
hints: Look at how the digits in each answer climb up and come back down. Predict the next answer before adding its digits.
The answers climb to 2, then 3, then 4, and come back down to 1. Write the answer that climbs to 5, then add all its digits.
A similar one: 1111 times 1111 equals 1234321. Its digits add up to 1 plus 2 plus 3 plus 4 plus 3 plus 2 plus 1, which makes 16, and that is 4 times 4.
steps: The answers climb by one digit each time and come back down: 121, 12321, 1234321.
So the next answer climbs to 5 and comes back down. 11111 times 11111 equals 123454321.
Add the digits going up, then the digits going down. 1 plus 2 plus 3 plus 4 plus 5 equals 15, 4 plus 3 plus 2 plus 1 equals 10.
Add the two parts. 15 plus 10 equals 25.
The sum of the digits is 25.

G4A_SQUARES_045.q: Kabir's age this year is a perfect square. Nine years from now, his age will be a perfect square again. How old is Kabir this year?
hints: Write out the perfect squares in order and look at the gaps between neighbours.
The squares are 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49. Test each one as Kabir's age: add 9 and see whether you land on another square.
A similar one with a gap of 5: 1 plus 5 equals 6, which is not a square, but 4 plus 5 equals 9, which is. So the age would be 4.
steps: List the perfect squares: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49.
Add 9 to each and look for another square: 10, 13, 18, 25, 34, 45, 58.
Only 25 is a perfect square, and it comes from 16. 16 plus 9 equals 25.
After 16 the gaps between squares are more than 9, so there is no other answer.
Kabir is 16 years old this year.

G4A_SQUARES_046.q: By which smallest number must 12 be multiplied so that the answer is a perfect square greater than 100?
hints: First find the smallest multiplier that gives any perfect square. Then check the extra condition, and look for the next multiplier if you need to.
12 is 2 times 2 times 3. Multiplying by 3 gives 36, a perfect square, but 36 is not greater than 100. To keep a perfect square, multiply 36 by another perfect square.

A similar one: the smallest multiplier of 8 that gives a square greater than 50. Multiplying 8 by 2 gives the square of 4, which is too small. Multiply that by 4 and you have 8 times 8, which is 64, and that is greater than 50. So the multiplier is 8.
steps: 12 is 2 times 2 times 3, so it needs one more 3 to become a perfect square. 12 times 3 equals 36.
36 is not greater than 100. To stay a perfect square, multiply 36 by the next perfect square, 4. 36 times 4 equals 144.
Find the multiplier of 12 that gives 144. 144 divided by 12 equals 12.
The smallest number to multiply by is 12.

G4A_SQUARES_047.q: Anu picks any odd number greater than 1, squares it and then subtracts 1. What is the greatest number that will always divide her answer exactly, whatever odd number she picks?
hints: Try several odd numbers, not just one. Look for what all the answers have in common.
With 3 the answer is 9 minus 1, which is 8. With 5 it is 25 minus 1, which is 24. Try 7 and 9 too, then look for the greatest number that divides every answer.
A similar one: pick any even number, square it, and ask what always divides the answer. From 2, 4 and 6 you get 4, 16 and 36. The greatest number dividing all of these is 4.
steps: Try the first few odd numbers. 3 times 3 minus 1 equals 8, 5 times 5 minus 1 equals 24, 7 times 7 minus 1 equals 48, 9 times 9 minus 1 equals 80.
Look for numbers that divide 8, 24, 48 and 80 exactly. The divisor cannot be more than 8, because the first answer is 8.
8 divides all four. 24 divided by 8 equals 3, 48 divided by 8 equals 6, 80 divided by 8 equals 10.
The greatest number that always divides her answer is 8.

G4A_SQUARES_048.q: The year 2025 is a perfect square, because 45 times 45 equals 2025. How many years after 2025 is the next year that is a perfect square?
hints: The next perfect square comes from the next whole number. You do not need to multiply it out if you know how far apart neighbouring squares are.
The next square is 46 times 46. The gap between the squares of two neighbouring numbers is the sum of those two numbers. Which two numbers do you add here?
A similar one: 20 times 20 equals 400. The next square is 21 times 21, and the gap is 20 plus 21, which is 41, so the next square is 441.
steps: The next perfect square after 45 times 45 is 46 times 46.
Neighbouring squares differ by the sum of the two numbers. 45 plus 46 equals 91.
Check by multiplying. 46 times 46 equals 2116, 2116 minus 2025 equals 91.
The next perfect-square year is 91 years after 2025.

G4A_TIME_001.q: A train leaves Pune station at 17 20 on the 24-hour clock. What is this time on the 12-hour clock?
hints: On the 24-hour clock, hours bigger than 12 are afternoon or evening times.
Take 12 away from the hours: 17 minus 12. The minutes stay the same.
Example: 14 35 on the 24-hour clock. 14 minus 12 equals 2, so it is 2 35 p m.
steps: 17 is more than 12, so the time is after noon and is a p m time.
Take 12 away from the hours. 17 minus 12 equals 5.
The minutes stay as 20, so the time is 5 20 p m.

G4A_TIME_002.q: How many days are there altogether in the months of June and July?
hints: You need to remember how many days each month has. The knuckle trick or the rhyme 'Thirty days has September' can help.
June has 30 days. How many days does July have?
Example: December has 31 days and January has 31 days. Together they have 31 plus 31 equals 62 days.
steps: June has 30 days.
July has 31 days.
Add them. 30 plus 31 equals 61.
June and July have 61 days altogether.

G4A_TIME_003.q: How many days are there in February 2028?
hints: February is the only month whose length changes. It depends on whether the year is a leap year.
A year like this is a leap year if 4 divides it exactly. Try dividing 2028 by 4.
Example: For February 2023, divide 2023 by 4. It leaves a remainder of 3, so 2023 is not a leap year and its February has 28 days.
steps: Check whether 4 divides 2028 exactly. 2028 divided by 4 equals 507.
There is no remainder, so 2028 is a leap year.
In a leap year February has one extra day, so February 2028 has 29 days.

G4A_TIME_004.q: A film is 135 minutes long. How long is that in hours and minutes?
hints: One hour is 60 minutes. See how many full hours fit into the minutes, and what is left.
Two hours are 120 minutes. Is 135 more than 120? How much more?
Example: 80 minutes. One hour is 60 minutes, and 80 minus 60 equals 20, so 80 minutes is 1 hour 20 minutes.
steps: Two full hours fit into 135 minutes. 2 times 60 equals 120.
Find the minutes left over. 135 minus 120 equals 15.
135 minutes is 2 hours 15 minutes.

G4A_TIME_005.q: Today is Wednesday. What day of the week will it be 10 days from today?
hints: The days of the week repeat every 7 days. Take out the full weeks first.
7 days from Wednesday is Wednesday again. How many days are left out of 10 after taking away 7?
Example: Today is Monday. 9 days later: 7 days bring Monday again, and 2 more days give Wednesday.
steps: After 7 days it is Wednesday again.
Days still to count. 10 minus 7 equals 3.
Three days after Wednesday: Thursday, Friday, Saturday.
It will be Saturday.

G4A_TIME_006.q: Arjun's school starts at 8:00 a m and ends at 1 30 p m. How long is his school day?
hints: The time passes 12 noon, so count in two parts: up to noon, and after noon.
Find how long it is from 8:00 a m to 12 noon.
Example: From 9:00 a m to 2 15 p m. From 9:00 a m to noon is 3 hours, and from noon to 2 15 p m is 2 hours 15 minutes, so 5 hours 15 minutes in all.
steps: From 8:00 a m to 12 noon. 12 minus 8 equals 4.
From 12 noon to 1 30 p m is 1 hour 30 minutes.
4 hours and 1 hour 30 minutes make 5 hours 30 minutes.

G4A_TIME_007.q: Dadi's favourite TV serial starts at a quarter to 7 in the evening. What is this time on the 24-hour clock?
hints: First write the time with hours and minutes, then change it to the 24-hour clock.
A quarter to 7 means 15 minutes before 7 o'clock. Which hour is it still in, and how many minutes past?
Example: A quarter to 4 in the afternoon is 3 45 p m. Adding 12 to the hours gives 15 45.
steps: A quarter to 7 is 15 minutes before 7 o'clock, which is 6 45.
It is evening, so the time is 6 45 p m.
For a p m time, add 12 to the hours. 6 plus 12 equals 18.
On the 24-hour clock the time is 18 45.

G4A_TIME_008.q: A train journey from Kanyakumari to Jammu takes exactly 3 days. How many hours is that?
hints: Think about how many hours make one full day, counting day and night together.
One day has 24 hours. Find 3 lots of 24.
Example: 2 days are 2 times 24 equals 48 hours.
steps: One full day has 24 hours.
Multiply by 3 days. 3 times 24 equals 72.
The journey takes 72 hours.

G4A_TIME_009.q: A night bus leaves Bengaluru at 9 30 p m. The journey to Chennai takes 6 hours 45 minutes. At what time does the bus reach Chennai?
hints: The journey crosses midnight, so the answer will be an am time on the next day. Add the hours and the minutes in parts.
Add the 6 hours first. Going 6 hours on from 9 30 p m passes midnight: where do you land?
Example: Leave at 10 40 p m and travel 3 hours 30 minutes. Three hours later it is 1 40 a m, and 30 more minutes make 2 10 a m.
steps: Add 6 hours to 9 30 p m: it becomes 3 30 a m the next day.
Now add 45 minutes. 30 minutes take the time to 4:00 a m.
The remaining minutes. 45 minus 30 equals 15.
The bus reaches Chennai at 4 15 a m.

G4A_TIME_010.q: A train leaves Mumbai at 22 40 and reaches Goa at 05:10 the next morning. How long is the journey?
hints: The journey crosses midnight. Split it into the part before midnight and the part after midnight.
Find how long it is from 22 40 to midnight, which is 24:00.
Example: From 23 15 to 02:30 the next day. Up to midnight is 45 minutes, and after midnight is 2 hours 30 minutes, so 3 hours 15 minutes in all.
steps: From 22 40 to midnight is 1 hour 20 minutes.
From midnight to 05:10 is 5 hours 10 minutes.
Add: 1 hour 20 minutes and 5 hours 10 minutes make 6 hours 30 minutes.
The journey takes 6 hours 30 minutes.

G4A_TIME_011.q: In a certain month, the 5th is a Tuesday. What day of the week is the 23rd of the same month?
hints: The same day of the week comes again every 7 days. Jump forward in sevens from the date you know.
Add 7 to the 5th again and again to find other Tuesdays: 5, 12, and so on.
Example: The 3rd is a Monday. The 10th and 17th are also Mondays, so the 20th, three days later, is a Thursday.
steps: The Tuesdays are 7 days apart. 5 plus 7 plus 7 equals 19.
So the 19th is a Tuesday.
Days from the 19th to the 23rd. 23 minus 19 equals 4.
Four days after Tuesday: Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday.
The 23rd is a Saturday.

G4A_TIME_012.q: How many days after 20 February 2024 is 5 March 2024?
hints: Count the days left in February, then the days in March. Check how long February is in that year.
2024 can be divided exactly by 4, so it is a leap year. How many days does its February have?
Example: From 25 February 2023 to 4 March 2023. February 2023 has 28 days, so 3 days are left in February, and 4 more in March make 7 days.
steps: 2024 is a leap year, so February has 29 days.
Days left in February after the 20th. 29 minus 20 equals 9.
Add the 5 days of March. 9 plus 5 equals 14.
5 March 2024 is 14 days after 20 February 2024.

G4A_TIME_013.q: Anil practises the tabla for 40 minutes every day. For how long does he practise in one week?
hints: Find the total minutes for the week, then change the minutes into hours and minutes.
A week has 7 days. Find 7 lots of 40 minutes.
Example: 50 minutes a day for 3 days is 150 minutes. Two hours are 120 minutes, so that is 2 hours 30 minutes.
steps: Minutes in one week. 7 times 40 equals 280.
Four hours are 240 minutes. 4 times 60 equals 240.
Minutes left over. 280 minus 240 equals 40.
He practises for 4 hours 40 minutes in one week.

G4A_TIME_014.q: A month has 30 days, and its 1st day is a Saturday. How many Sundays are there in this month?
hints: Find the date of the first Sunday, then keep jumping forward 7 days until the month ends.
If the 1st is a Saturday, the first Sunday is the very next day, the 2nd.
Example: A month of 30 days begins on a Monday. Its first Sunday is the 7th, and the others are the 14th, 21st and 28th, so that month has 4 Sundays.
steps: The 1st is a Saturday, so the 2nd is the first Sunday.
Add 7 each time: the Sundays are the 2nd, 9th, 16th, 23rd and 30th.
The 30th is still inside the month.
There are 5 Sundays in this month.

G4A_TIME_015.q: Kavya's train leaves at 14 10. She wants to reach the station 25 minutes before the train leaves, and it takes her 35 minutes to travel from home to the station. What is the latest time she can leave home?
hints: Work backwards from the train time. Both the early arrival and the travel time come before the train leaves.
Add the two amounts of time she needs before 14 10: 25 minutes and 35 minutes.
Example: A bus leaves at 16 30. Rahul wants to be 10 minutes early and needs 20 minutes to get there. He needs 30 minutes in all, so he leaves at 16:00, which is 4:00 p m.
steps: Total time needed before the train leaves. 25 plus 35 equals 60.
60 minutes is 1 hour.
One hour before 14 10 is 13 10.
Change to the 12-hour clock. 13 minus 12 equals 1.
The latest she can leave home is 1 10 p m.

G4A_TRIANGLES_001.q: A triangle has sides 5 centimetres, 5 centimetres and 8 centimetres. What kind of triangle is it?
options: These sides cannot make a triangle
hints: Triangles are named by how many of their sides are equal. Compare the three lengths.
Two of the lengths are 5 centimetres and the third is 8 centimetres. How many sides are equal?
A similar one: a triangle with sides 7 centimetres, 4 centimetres and 6 centimetres has three different lengths, so it is a scalene triangle.
steps: The two shorter sides together are 10 centimetres, which is more than 8 centimetres, so the sides do make a triangle. 5 plus 5 equals 10.
Exactly two sides are equal: 5 centimetres and 5 centimetres.
A triangle with exactly two equal sides is an isosceles triangle.

G4A_TRIANGLES_002.q: The angles of a triangle are 35 degrees, 55 degrees and 90 degrees. What kind of triangle is it?
hints: Triangles can be named by their biggest angle. Is it less than 90 degrees, exactly 90 degrees, or more than 90 degrees?
The biggest of the three angles is 90 degrees. What is an angle of 90 degrees called?
A similar one: a triangle with angles 30 degrees, 40 degrees and 110 degrees has one angle bigger than 90 degrees, so it is an obtuse-angled triangle.
steps: The biggest angle is 90 degrees.
An angle of 90 degrees is a right angle.
A triangle with one right angle is a right-angled triangle.

G4A_TRIANGLES_003.q: All three sides of a triangle have different lengths. By its sides, what is the triangle called?
hints: There are three names for triangles by their sides: one for three equal sides, one for two equal sides, and one for no equal sides.
This triangle has no two sides the same. Which of the three names is for that?
A similar one: a triangle with sides 6 centimetres, 6 centimetres and 6 centimetres has all sides equal, so it is called an equilateral triangle.
steps: Three equal sides make an equilateral triangle, and two equal sides make an isosceles triangle.
This triangle has no equal sides at all.
A triangle with three different sides is a scalene triangle.

G4A_TRIANGLES_004.q: An isosceles triangle has two equal sides of 9 centimetres each. Its third side is 6 centimetres. What is its perimeter?
hints: The perimeter is the distance all the way around, so add all three sides.
The three sides are 9 centimetres, 9 centimetres and 6 centimetres. Add them.
A similar one: equal sides of 5 centimetres each and a third side of 4 centimetres give a perimeter of 5 plus 5 plus 4, which is 14 centimetres.
steps: The three sides are 9 centimetres, 9 centimetres and 6 centimetres.
Add them. 9 plus 9 plus 6 equals 24.
The perimeter is 24 centimetres.

G4A_TRIANGLES_005.q: A triangle has angles 100 degrees, 40 degrees and 40 degrees. Which name describes it best?
hints: The name has two parts. One part comes from the biggest angle. The other part comes from how many angles, and so how many sides, are equal.
The biggest angle is 100 degrees. Is that less than, equal to, or more than 90 degrees? Then look at the two angles of 40 degrees.
A similar one: a triangle with angles 90 degrees, 45 degrees and 45 degrees has a right angle and two equal angles, so it is a right-angled isosceles triangle.
steps: The biggest angle is 100 degrees, which is more than 90 degrees, so the triangle is obtuse-angled.
Two angles are equal, both 40 degrees. The sides opposite equal angles are equal, so two sides are equal.
It is an obtuse-angled isosceles triangle.

G4A_TRIANGLES_006.q: Which of these sets of lengths cannot be the sides of a triangle?
hints: Three lengths make a triangle only when the two shorter ones together are longer than the longest one.
For each set, add the two shorter lengths and compare the total with the longest length. Watch for a total that is only equal, not greater.
A similar one: 2 centimetres, 3 centimetres and 7 centimetres cannot make a triangle, because 2 plus 3 equals 5, which is less than 7 and the short sides cannot meet.
steps: 3 plus 4 equals 7, which is more than 5, and 6 plus 6 equals 12, which is more than 11. These two sets make triangles.
7 plus 8 equals 15, which is more than 14, so this set makes a triangle too.
4 plus 5 equals 9, which is only equal to the longest side, 9. The two short sides would lie flat along the long side.
The set that cannot make a triangle is 4 centimetres, 5 centimetres, 9 centimetres.

G4A_TRIANGLES_007.q: In a right-angled triangle, one of the two acute angles is twice the other. What is the smallest angle of the triangle?
hints: The three angles of a triangle add up to 180 degrees. In a right-angled triangle one angle is 90 degrees, so think about what is left for the other two.
The two acute angles together make 90 degrees. One is twice the other, so think of them as 1 part and 2 parts.

A similar one: in a right-angled triangle one acute angle is 4 times the other. Five equal parts make 90 degrees, so one part is 18 degrees. The angles are 18 degrees and 72 degrees, and the smallest is 18 degrees.
steps: The two acute angles together. 180 minus 90 equals 90.
One angle is 1 part and the other is 2 parts, so 3 parts make 90 degrees. 90 divided by 3 equals 30.
The acute angles are 30 degrees and 60 degrees.
The smallest angle is 30 degrees.

G4A_TRIANGLES_008.q: The perimeter of an isosceles triangle is 40 centimetres. The side that is different from the other two is 12 centimetres. How long is each of the equal sides?
hints: The perimeter is the sum of the three sides. Take away the side you know, and what is left belongs to the two equal sides.
Take 12 centimetres away from 40 centimetres. The rest is shared equally between the two equal sides.
A similar one: perimeter 26 centimetres and a different side of 6 centimetres. The two equal sides share 26 minus 6, which is 20 centimetres, so each is 10 centimetres.
steps: Take the different side away from the perimeter. 40 minus 12 equals 28.
The two equal sides share this equally. 28 divided by 2 equals 14.
Each equal side is 14 centimetres.

G4A_TRIANGLES_009.q: All three angles of a triangle are equal. What is the sum of any two of its angles?
hints: The three angles of any triangle add up to 180 degrees. If they are all equal, you can find one of them.
Share 180 degrees equally among three angles to find each one. Then add two of them.
A similar one: a right-angled triangle has two equal angles. They share 180 minus 90, which is 90 degrees, so each is 45 degrees, and those two together make 90 degrees.
steps: The three equal angles add up to 180 degrees, so find one angle. 180 divided by 3 equals 60.
Add two of the angles. 60 plus 60 equals 120.
The sum of any two angles is 120 degrees.

G4A_TRIANGLES_010.q: Two sides of a triangle are 7 centimetres and 10 centimetres. The third side is a whole number of centimetres. What is the greatest length the third side can have?
hints: In a triangle, any two sides together must be longer than the third side. Use this to find how long the third side is allowed to be.
Add the two sides you know. The third side must be shorter than this total, not equal to it.
A similar one: with sides 4 centimetres and 6 centimetres, the third side must be shorter than 4 plus 6, which is 10 centimetres. The greatest whole number is 9 centimetres.
steps: Add the two known sides. 7 plus 10 equals 17.
The third side must be shorter than 17 centimetres. At exactly 17 centimetres the two sides would lie flat along it.
The greatest whole number less than 17 is 16.
The greatest length of the third side is 16 centimetres.

G4A_TRIANGLES_011.q: Jay has four sticks of lengths 3 centimetres, 5 centimetres, 7 centimetres and 10 centimetres. He picks three sticks at a time to make a triangle. How many different triangles can he make?
hints: List every way of choosing three sticks from the four. Then test each choice: the two shorter sticks together must be longer than the longest one.
There are four ways to choose three sticks: leave out one stick each time. Begin with 3, 5 and 7, and compare 3 plus 5 with 7.

A similar one: sticks of 1 centimetre, 2 centimetres, 3 centimetres and 4 centimetres. Of the four choices, only 2, 3 and 4 works, because 2 plus 3 equals 5, which is more than 4. So 1 triangle can be made.
steps: Sticks 3, 5, 7: 3 plus 5 equals 8, which is more than 7, so this makes a triangle.
Sticks 3, 5, 10: 3 plus 5 equals 8, which is less than 10, so no triangle.
Sticks 3, 7, 10: 3 plus 7 equals 10, which is only equal to 10, so no triangle.
Sticks 5, 7, 10: 5 plus 7 equals 12, which is more than 10, so this makes a triangle.
He can make 2 different triangles.

G4A_TRIANGLES_012.q: In an isosceles triangle, the angle between the two equal sides is 3 times each of the other two angles. How big is that angle?
hints: In an isosceles triangle the two angles opposite the equal sides are equal. Think of the angles as equal parts that add up to 180 degrees.
Call each of the two equal angles 1 part. The angle between the equal sides is then 3 parts. How many parts are there altogether?
A similar one: if the top angle is twice each base angle, the angles are 2 parts, 1 part and 1 part. Four parts make 180 degrees, so one part is 45 degrees and the top angle is 90 degrees.
steps: The two equal angles are 1 part each, and the angle between the equal sides is 3 parts. 3 plus 1 plus 1 equals 5.
Five parts make 180 degrees, so find one part. 180 divided by 5 equals 36.
The angle between the equal sides is 3 parts. 3 times 36 equals 108.
That angle is 108 degrees.

G4A_TRIANGLES_013.q: In a triangle, the second angle is 20 degrees more than the first angle, and the third angle is 20 degrees more than the second. What is the largest angle?
hints: The three angles add up to 180 degrees. Describe the second and third angles by how much more they are than the first.
The second angle is the first plus 20 degrees, and the third is the first plus 40 degrees. So three times the first angle, plus 60 degrees, makes 180 degrees.

A similar one: the second angle is 10 degrees more than the first and the third is 10 degrees more than the second. Three times the first plus 30 degrees is 180 degrees, so the first is 50 degrees and the largest is 70 degrees.
steps: The third angle is 20 degrees plus 20 degrees, which is 40 degrees, more than the first.
Take the extra 20 degrees and 40 degrees away from 180 degrees. What is left is three times the first angle. 180 minus 20 minus 40 equals 120.
Find the first angle. 120 divided by 3 equals 40.
The largest angle is the third one. 40 plus 40 equals 80.
The largest angle is 80 degrees.

G4A_TRIANGLES_014.q: An isosceles triangle has a perimeter of 50 centimetres. One of its sides is 12 centimetres long. Which of these can be the lengths of its other two sides?
hints: There are two things to check: two of the three sides must be equal, and the two shorter sides together must be longer than the longest side.
The 12 centimetre side could be one of the equal pair, or it could be the side that is different. Work out the sides in each case and test whether they can close into a triangle.

A similar one: an isosceles triangle with perimeter 20 centimetres and one side 4 centimetres. Sides 4, 4 and 12 cannot close, because 4 plus 4 is less than 12. Sides 4, 8 and 8 can, so the other sides are 8 centimetres and 8 centimetres.
steps: If 12 centimetres is one of the equal sides, the sides are 12, 12 and 26. 50 minus 12 minus 12 equals 26.
But 12 plus 12 equals 24, which is less than 26, so those sides cannot close into a triangle.
If 12 centimetres is the different side, the equal sides share the rest. 50 minus 12, then divided by 2, equals 19.
Check: 12 plus 19 is more than 19, so the triangle closes. The other two sides are 19 centimetres and 19 centimetres.

G4A_TRIANGLES_015.q: Which of these statements about triangles is true?
options: A triangle can have two obtuse angles
An equilateral triangle can be right-angled
A scalene triangle can have two equal angles
A right-angled triangle can be isosceles
hints: Test each statement with two facts: the three angles of a triangle add up to 180 degrees, and equal sides sit opposite equal angles.
For each statement, try to write down three angles that would fit it and still add up to 180 degrees. If you cannot, the statement is not true.
A similar test: can a triangle have two right angles? 90 degrees plus 90 degrees is already 180 degrees, which leaves nothing for the third angle. So it cannot.
steps: Two obtuse angles would add up to more than 180 degrees, so a triangle cannot have them.
An equilateral triangle has three angles of 60 degrees, so it never has a right angle.
Two equal angles give two equal sides, and a scalene triangle has no equal sides.
Angles of 90 degrees, 45 degrees and 45 degrees add up to 180 degrees and two of them are equal. So the true statement is: A right-angled triangle can be isosceles.

G4A_TRIANGLES_016.q: Meera has a thin straw 12 centimetres long. She cuts it into three pieces, each a whole number of centimetres long, and joins the pieces end to end to make a triangle. How many different triangles can she make? Triangles with the same three side lengths count as one.
hints: Three lengths make a triangle only when the two shorter ones together are longer than the longest one. List the ways to split the straw in an orderly way and test each.
The longest piece must be shorter than half of 12 centimetres, so it can be at most 5 centimetres. Start with a longest piece of 5 centimetres and find the other two.

Similar problem: a 10 centimetre straw. The longest piece must be less than 5 centimetres, so try 4 centimetres: the other two add up to 6 centimetres, giving 2, 4, 4 and 3, 3, 4. A longest piece of 3 centimetres would need the others to add up to 7 centimetres, which is too much. So a 10 centimetre straw gives 2 triangles.
steps: The two shorter sides together must be longer than the longest side, so the longest side is less than 6 centimetres.

Longest side 5 centimetres: the other two add up to 7 centimetres. They can be 2 centimetres and 5 centimetres, or 3 centimetres and 4 centimetres. 2 plus 5 plus 5 equals 12, and 3 plus 4 plus 5 equals 12.
Longest side 4 centimetres: the other two add up to 8 centimetres, so they must be 4 centimetres and 4 centimetres. 4 plus 4 plus 4 equals 12.
A longest side of 3 centimetres or less cannot reach a total of 12 centimetres.
So Meera can make 3 different triangles.

G4A_TRIANGLES_017.q: Two sides of a triangle are 6 centimetres and 11 centimetres long. The third side is a whole number of centimetres. How many different lengths can the third side have?
hints: The third side cannot be too short or too long. Find the shortest and the longest whole number it can be, then count carefully.
The third side must be longer than 11 minus 6 and shorter than 11 plus 6. Decide whether those two end numbers themselves are allowed.

Similar problem: sides of 4 centimetres and 9 centimetres. The third side must be more than 5 centimetres and less than 13 centimetres, so it can be 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11 or 12 centimetres. That is 7 different lengths.
steps: The third side must be longer than the difference of the other two. 11 minus 6 equals 5.
The third side must be shorter than the sum of the other two. 11 plus 6 equals 17.
A side of exactly 5 centimetres or exactly 17 centimetres would make the three sides lie flat, so the third side can be 6 centimetres up to 16 centimetres.
Count the whole numbers from 6 to 16. 16 minus 6 plus 1 equals 11.
So the third side can have 11 different lengths.

G4A_TRIANGLES_018.q: In an isosceles triangle, one angle is 4 times another angle. The triangle has no obtuse angle. What is the smallest angle of the triangle?
hints: An isosceles triangle has two equal angles. The equal angles could be the two small ones or the two big ones. Try both and see which fits everything the question says.
Call the small angle one part. Then the angles are either 1, 1 and 4 parts, or 1, 4 and 4 parts. All the parts together make 180 degrees.

Similar problem: in an isosceles triangle one angle is 2 times another and no angle is a right angle. Parts 1, 1, 2 give 45 degrees, 45 degrees, 90 degrees, which has a right angle. Parts 1, 2, 2 give 5 parts, which make 180 degrees, so one part is 36 degrees. The smallest angle is 36 degrees.
steps: First case: the two equal angles are the small ones. The parts are 1, 1 and 4. 180 divided by 6 equals 30.
That gives 30 degrees, 30 degrees and 120 degrees. But 120 degrees is obtuse, so this case is not allowed.
Second case: the two equal angles are the big ones. The parts are 1, 4 and 4. 180 divided by 9 equals 20.
That gives 20 degrees, 80 degrees and 80 degrees. No angle is obtuse, so this is the triangle.
So the smallest angle is 20 degrees.

G4A_TRIANGLES_019.q: Two triangles are both isosceles, and each of them has an angle of 40 degrees. The two triangles do not have the same set of angles. What is the difference between the largest angle of one triangle and the largest angle of the other?
hints: In an isosceles triangle, a given angle can be one of the two equal angles, or it can be the angle that is different. That gives two different triangles.
First let 40 degrees be one of the two equal angles and find the third angle. Then let 40 degrees be the different angle and find the two equal ones.

Similar problem with 20 degrees: if 20 degrees is one of the equal angles, the angles are 20 degrees, 20 degrees, 140 degrees. If 20 degrees is the different angle, the others are 80 degrees each. The largest angles are 140 degrees and 80 degrees, and their difference is 60 degrees.
steps: If 40 degrees is one of the two equal angles, the third angle is what is left from 180 degrees. 180 minus 40 minus 40 equals 100.
If 40 degrees is the different angle, the two equal angles share what is left. 180 minus 40, then divided by 2, equals 70.
So the triangles have angles 40 degrees, 40 degrees, 100 degrees and 40 degrees, 70 degrees, 70 degrees.
Subtract the two largest angles. 100 minus 70 equals 30.
So the difference between the two largest angles is 30 degrees.

G4A_TRIANGLES_020.q: An isosceles triangle has one side of 5 centimetres and another side of 11 centimetres. What is its perimeter?
hints: The third side must be equal to one of the two sides you know. Try each choice, and check that the three sides can really make a triangle.
If the third side is 5 centimetres, the sides are 5, 5 and 11. Add the two short sides and compare with the long side.

Similar problem: an isosceles triangle with sides 4 centimetres and 9 centimetres. Sides 4, 4, 9 cannot meet because 4 plus 4 is less than 9. Sides 4, 9, 9 can. The perimeter is 4 plus 9 plus 9, which is 22 centimetres.
steps: An isosceles triangle has two equal sides, so the third side is either 5 centimetres or 11 centimetres.
Try 5 centimetres: the two short sides together must be longer than the longest side. 5 plus 5 equals 10.
10 centimetres is shorter than 11 centimetres, so sides of 5, 5 and 11 cannot make a triangle.
So the third side is 11 centimetres. Add the three sides. 5 plus 11 plus 11 equals 27.
So the perimeter is 27 centimetres.

G4A_TRIANGLES_021.q: Aman has a big box of sticks. Every stick is 3 centimetres, 4 centimetres or 8 centimetres long, and there are plenty of each length. He makes a triangle using three sticks as its three sides. The sticks may have the same length. How many different triangles can he make?
hints: List every way to choose three lengths: all the same, two the same, and all different. Then test each choice to see whether it can really make a triangle.
Start with the three choices where all sticks are equal. Then take two equal sticks with one different stick, and check that the two shorter sticks together are longer than the longest.

Similar problem: sticks of 2 centimetres and 5 centimetres only. The choices are 2, 2, 2 and 5, 5, 5 and 2, 2, 5 and 2, 5, 5. In 2, 2, 5 the short sticks add up to only 4 centimetres, so it is out. That leaves 3 triangles.
steps: All three sticks equal: 3, 3, 3 and 4, 4, 4 and 8, 8, 8. All three make triangles.
Two equal and one different: 3, 3, 4 and 3, 4, 4 and 3, 8, 8 and 4, 8, 8 make triangles.
But 3, 3, 8 and 4, 4, 8 do not, because the two short sticks are not longer than the long one. 3 plus 3 equals 6, and 4 plus 4 equals 8.
All different: 3, 4, 8 does not make a triangle either. 3 plus 4 equals 7.
Count the choices that are left. 3 plus 4 equals 7.
So Aman can make 7 different triangles.

G4A_TRIANGLES_022.q: The three angles of a triangle are whole numbers of degrees, and all three are different. What is the largest size the smallest angle can have?
hints: To make the smallest angle as big as possible, the three angles should be as close to each other as they can be while staying different.
If all three were equal they would be 60 degrees each. They must be different, so think about three whole numbers very close to 60 that add up to 180.
Similar problem: three different whole numbers add up to 30. Equal shares would be 10 each. The closest different numbers are 9, 10 and 11, so the smallest can be at most 9.
steps: If the three angles were equal, each would be 60 degrees. 180 divided by 3 equals 60.
The angles must be different, so the smallest must be less than 60 degrees.
Try 59 degrees for the smallest. The other two must add up to 121 degrees, and 60 degrees and 61 degrees do that. 59 plus 60 plus 61 equals 180.
So the largest size the smallest angle can have is 59 degrees.

G4A_TRIANGLES_023.q: Which of these statements is true for every triangle?
options: Its largest angle is more than 60 degrees
It has at least two acute angles
Its two smallest angles add up to less than 90 degrees
Exactly one of its angles is 60 degrees or more
hints: A statement is true for every triangle only if no triangle at all breaks it. For each statement, try to think of a triangle that breaks it.
Test each statement on some special triangles: the equilateral triangle, a right-angled triangle, and an isosceles triangle with angles 40 degrees, 70 degrees, 70 degrees.

Similar problem: is 'every triangle has an angle of less than 60 degrees' always true? Test the equilateral triangle: its angles are 60 degrees, 60 degrees, 60 degrees, and none is less than 60 degrees. One triangle that breaks the statement is enough, so it is not always true.
steps: The equilateral triangle has angles 60 degrees, 60 degrees, 60 degrees. Its largest angle is not more than 60 degrees, and its two smallest angles add up to 120 degrees.
A triangle with angles 40 degrees, 70 degrees, 70 degrees has two angles of 60 degrees or more, not exactly one.
Could a triangle have two angles that are not acute? Two angles of 90 degrees or more already use up the whole 180 degrees, leaving nothing for the third angle. 90 plus 90 equals 180.
So at most one angle can be right or obtuse, and the other two must be acute.
The statement true for every triangle is: it has at least two acute angles.

G4A_TRIANGLES_024.q: Five equilateral triangles, each with sides of 4 centimetres, are placed in a row. The first points up, the second points down, the third points up, and so on. Each triangle shares one whole side with the next triangle, so together they make one flat shape with no gaps. What is the perimeter of this shape?
hints: The perimeter is only the outside edge. Every side that two triangles share is inside the shape, and it is hidden for both of those triangles.
Count how many sides are shared between neighbours in a row of five triangles. Each shared side removes one side from each of two triangles.

Similar problem: three equilateral triangles of side 5 centimetres in a row. All sides together make 9 sides. There are 2 shared sides, and each hides 2 sides, so 9 minus 4 equals 5 sides stay outside. The perimeter is 5 times 5, which is 25 centimetres.
steps: Five separate triangles have 15 sides in all. 5 times 3 equals 15.
In a row of five triangles there are 4 places where two neighbours share a side.
Each shared side hides one side of each neighbour, so 8 sides are hidden. 4 times 2 equals 8.
Count the sides left on the outside and multiply by 4 centimetres. 15 minus 8, then times 4, equals 28.
So the perimeter of the shape is 28 centimetres.

G4A_TRIANGLES_025.q: The sides of a triangle are three consecutive whole numbers of centimetres, such as 5 centimetres, 6 centimetres and 7 centimetres. What is the smallest perimeter such a triangle can have?
hints: Start from the smallest consecutive numbers, but check each time that the three lengths can really close up into a triangle.
Try 1 centimetre, 2 centimetres and 3 centimetres first. Add the two shorter sides and compare the total with the longest side.

Similar problem: the sides are three consecutive even numbers. Try 2, 4, 6: 2 plus 4 is only equal to 6, so they lie flat. Try 4, 6, 8: 4 plus 6 equals 10, which is more than 8, so it is a triangle. The smallest perimeter is 4 plus 6 plus 8, which is 18 centimetres.
steps: Try the smallest set, 1 centimetre, 2 centimetres and 3 centimetres. The two shorter sides only equal the longest side, so they lie flat. 1 plus 2 equals 3.
Try the next set, 2 centimetres, 3 centimetres and 4 centimetres. The two shorter sides are longer than the longest side. 2 plus 3 equals 5.
So 2, 3, 4 is the smallest such triangle. Add its sides. 2 plus 3 plus 4 equals 9.
So the smallest perimeter is 9 centimetres.

G4A_TRIANGLES_026.q: The perimeter of a triangle is 30 centimetres, and each side is a whole number of centimetres. What is the greatest length its longest side can have?
hints: The longest side cannot take too much of the perimeter. The other two sides together must still be longer than it.
Suppose the longest side is 15 centimetres. Work out what is left for the other two sides together, and compare.

Similar problem: perimeter 20 centimetres. If the longest side were 10 centimetres, the other two would add up to 10 centimetres and lie flat. With 9 centimetres, the other two add up to 11 centimetres, which is more. So the greatest longest side is 9 centimetres.
steps: The other two sides together must be longer than the longest side.
Try 15 centimetres. The other two sides add up to 15 centimetres, which is only equal, so they lie flat. 30 minus 15 equals 15.
Try 14 centimetres. The other two sides add up to 16 centimetres, which is more than 14 centimetres. 30 minus 14 equals 16.
Sides such as 14 centimetres, 14 centimetres and 2 centimetres make a real triangle.
So the greatest length of the longest side is 14 centimetres.

G4A_TRIANGLES_027.q: A triangle is right-angled. One of its angles is 4 times another of its angles, and all three angles are whole numbers of degrees. What is the smallest angle of the triangle?
hints: One angle is 90 degrees. Decide which two angles are in the '4 times' relation: could the right angle be one of them? Use the clue about whole numbers.
If 90 degrees were 4 times another angle, that angle would be 90 divided by 4. Check whether that is a whole number. If not, the relation is between the two acute angles.

Similar problem: in a right-angled triangle, one acute angle is 5 times the other acute angle. The two acute angles add up to 90 degrees, and they make 6 equal parts. One part is 90 divided by 6, which is 15 degrees, so the angles are 15 degrees, 75 degrees and 90 degrees.
steps: If the right angle were 4 times another angle, that angle would not be a whole number. 90 divided by 4 equals 22 and a half.
So the relation is between the two acute angles. Together they make 90 degrees. 180 minus 90 equals 90.
One acute angle is 1 part and the other is 4 parts, 5 parts in all. 90 divided by 5 equals 18.
The angles are 18 degrees, 72 degrees and 90 degrees. 18 plus 72 plus 90 equals 180.
So the smallest angle is 18 degrees.

G4A_TRIANGLES_028.q: Two sides of a triangle are 9 centimetres and 4 centimetres. The third side is a whole number of centimetres, and the perimeter of the triangle is a multiple of 7. How long is the third side?
hints: Two things must both be true: the three sides must be able to make a triangle, and the perimeter must be in the 7 times table. Find the possible third sides first.
The third side must be more than 9 minus 4 and less than 9 plus 4. For each allowed length, the perimeter is 13 plus that length.

Similar problem: sides 5 centimetres and 8 centimetres, perimeter a multiple of 10. The third side is between 3 centimetres and 13 centimetres, so the perimeter is between 16 centimetres and 26 centimetres. The only multiple of 10 there is 20, so the third side is 20 minus 13, which is 7 centimetres.
steps: The third side must be more than 5 centimetres and less than 13 centimetres. 9 minus 4 equals 5, and 9 plus 4 equals 13.
So the third side is from 6 centimetres to 12 centimetres, and the perimeter is from 19 centimetres to 25 centimetres. 13 plus 6 equals 19, and 13 plus 12 equals 25.
The only multiple of 7 from 19 to 25 is 21.
Take away the two known sides. 21 minus 9 minus 4 equals 8.
So the third side is 8 centimetres.

G4A_TRIANGLES_029.q: Triangle A B C is isosceles. Angle A is 50 degrees. Angle B is bigger than angle A and also bigger than angle C. What is angle C?
hints: This is about an isosceles triangle, which has two equal angles. Use what the question says about angle B to work out which two angles are the equal pair.
Angle B is bigger than each of the other two angles, so it cannot be equal to either of them. Ask yourself which two angles are left to be the equal pair.

Here is a similar problem. Triangle P Q R is isosceles, angle P is 40 degrees, and angle Q is bigger than both other angles. Angle Q cannot be in the equal pair, so angle R equals angle P, which is 40 degrees. Then angle Q is 180 minus 40 minus 40, which is 100 degrees.
steps: An isosceles triangle has two equal angles.
Angle B is bigger than angle A and bigger than angle C, so angle B is not equal to either of them. The equal pair must be angle A and angle C.
Check that this fits: angle B would be 180 minus 50 minus 50, which is 80 degrees, which is bigger than 50 degrees.
So angle C is equal to angle A, which is 50 degrees.

G4A_TRIANGLES_030.q: Two angles of a triangle add up to 110 degrees. The bigger of these two angles is 30 degrees more than the smaller one. What kind of triangle is it?
hints: To name a triangle you need all three angles. Find the two angles described, then do not forget the third one.
Take the extra 30 degrees away from 110 degrees. What is left is twice the smaller angle.

Similar problem: two angles add up to 100 degrees and differ by 20 degrees. Taking 20 from 100 leaves 80, so the smaller is 40 degrees and the bigger is 60 degrees. The third angle is 180 minus 100, which is 80 degrees. All three are different, so that triangle is scalene.
steps: Take away the extra 30 degrees. What is left is two equal shares. 110 minus 30, then divided by 2, equals 40.
So the two angles are 40 degrees and 70 degrees. 40 plus 30 equals 70.
Find the third angle. 180 minus 110 equals 70.
The angles are 40 degrees, 70 degrees and 70 degrees. Two of them are equal.
So it is an isosceles triangle.

G4A_UNITS_001.q: A cycle track is 4 kilometres 75 metres long. What is its length in kilometres?
hints: Kilometres are bigger than metres, so the metres become a decimal part of a kilometre. Remember how many metres make 1 kilometre.
1 kilometre equals 1000 metres, so divide the 75 metres by 1000 to turn it into kilometres. Then join it to the 4 kilometres.
A similar one: 2 kilometres 40 metres. 40 divided by 1000 equals 0.04, so 2 kilometres 40 metres equals 2.04 kilometres.
steps: 1 kilometre equals 1000 metres, so to change metres into kilometres we divide by 1000.
Change the 75 metres into kilometres. 75 divided by 1000 equals 0.075.
Add the 4 whole kilometres. The track is 4.075 kilometres long. 4 plus 0.075 equals 4.075.

G4A_UNITS_002.q: Meera's water bottle holds 1.2 litres. She drinks 350 millilitres. How many millilitres of water are left in the bottle?
hints: The two amounts are in different units. Make the units the same before you subtract.
Change 1.2 litres into millilitres: multiply by 1000. Then take away what Meera drank.
A similar one: a jug holds 1.5 litres and 400 millilitres is poured out. 1.5 litres equals 1500 millilitres, and 1500 minus 400 equals 1100 millilitres are left.
steps: Change litres into millilitres: 1 litre equals 1000 millilitres. 1.2 times 1000 equals 1200.
Take away the 350 millilitres that Meera drank. 1200 minus 350 equals 850.
850 millilitres of water are left in the bottle.

G4A_UNITS_003.q: A new pencil is 14 centimetres 6 millimetres long. After a month of sharpening it is 12 centimetres 9 millimetres long. How many millimetres shorter has it become?
hints: Both lengths mix centimetres and millimetres. It is easiest to write each one in millimetres only.
