G5A_OPERATIONS2_007.q: Which number, when multiplied by 9, gives 108?
hints: A missing number in a multiplication is found by dividing.
Divide 108 by 9. It may help to see 108 as 90 and 18.
A similar one: the number that gives 91 when multiplied by 7 is 91 divided by 7 equals 13, because 70 divided by 7 equals 10 and 21 divided by 7 equals 3.
steps: To undo multiplying by 9, divide by 9.
Divide 108 by 9. 108 divided by 9 equals 12.
The number is 12. 12 times 9 equals 108.

G5A_OPERATIONS2_008.q: One dozen is 12. A fruit seller has 60 bananas. How many dozens of bananas is that?
hints: Counting how many equal groups fit into a number is a division.
Divide 60 by 12. You can count up in twelves: 12, 24, 36 and so on, until you reach 60.
A similar one: 36 bananas are 36 divided by 12 equals 3 dozens.
steps: A dozen is a group of 12, so divide 60 by 12.
Count in twelves: 12, 24, 36, 48, 60. That is 5 groups.
There are 5 dozens of bananas.

G5A_PERCENTAGE_001.q: The price of a cricket bat is raised by 20 percent. A month later, the new price is cut by 20 percent. Compared with the price at the very beginning, the final price is:
hints: The two percentages are taken of different prices. Try a simple starting price and follow it through.
Start with 100 rupees. After a 20 percent rise the price is 120 rupees. The 20 percent cut is now taken from 120 rupees.
Similar problem: a price goes up by 10 percent and then down by 10 percent. From 100 rupees it goes to 110 rupees, then drops by 11 rupees to 99 rupees, which is 1 percent less than at the start.
steps: Take a starting price of 100 rupees. A 20 percent rise makes it 120 rupees.
The 20 percent cut is 20 percent of 120 rupees, which is 24 rupees.
The final price is 96 rupees.
96 rupees is 4 rupees below 100 rupees, so the final price is 4 percent less than at the beginning.

G5A_PERCENTAGE_002.q: The fare for a bus trip was raised by 20 percent. Later the new fare was reduced by 10 percent, and it is now 594 rupees. What was the fare before the two changes?
hints: Work backwards, undoing the last change first. Each percentage belongs to the fare just before that change.
After the 10 percent reduction, the fare is 90 percent of the raised fare. So 594 rupees is 90 percent of the raised fare.

Similar problem: a price rises by 25 percent and then falls by 20 percent to 300 rupees. 300 rupees is 80 percent of the raised price, so the raised price is 375 rupees. 375 rupees is 125 percent of the first price, so the first price was 300 rupees.
steps: 594 rupees is 90 percent of the raised fare, so the raised fare was 660 rupees.
660 rupees is 120 percent of the first fare.
So the first fare was 550 rupees.
Check: 550 rupees raised by 20 percent is 660 rupees, and 660 rupees less 10 percent is 594 rupees. The fare was 550 rupees.

G5A_PERCENTAGE_003.q: Anil's weight is 25 percent more than Binu's weight. By what percent is Binu's weight less than Anil's weight?
hints: The two percentages have different bases. 'Less than Anil's' means compare with Anil's weight.
Let Binu weigh 100 units. Then Anil weighs 125 units. The gap of 25 units must now be compared with 125.
Similar problem: Tina's height is 50 percent more than Uma's. If Uma is 100 units, Tina is 150 units. Uma is 50 units less out of 150, which is one-third less, about 33 percent, not 50 percent.
steps: Let Binu's weight be 100 units. Anil's weight is 25 percent more, which is 125 units.
Binu is 25 units lighter than Anil.
Compare the 25 units with Anil's 125 units. 25 over 125 times 100 equals 20.
Binu's weight is 20 percent less than Anil's weight.

G5A_PERCENTAGE_004.q: Farida has 400 rupees and Gopal has 500 rupees. Which one of these statements is true?
options: Farida has 25 percent less money than Gopal.
Gopal has 20 percent more money than Farida.
Farida has 80 percent less money than Gopal.
Gopal has 25 percent more money than Farida.
hints: 'More than Farida' is measured against Farida's money. 'Less than Gopal' is measured against Gopal's money.
The difference is 100 rupees. Work out what percent 100 rupees is of 400 rupees, and what percent it is of 500 rupees.

Similar problem: Hema has 200 rupees and Isha has 300 rupees. The gap is 100 rupees. Isha has 100 out of 200 more, which is 50 percent more than Hema. Hema has 100 out of 300 less, which is one-third less than Isha.
steps: The difference between them is 100 rupees.
Measured against Farida's 400 rupees, the difference is 25 percent.
Measured against Gopal's 500 rupees, the difference is 20 percent.
So Farida has 20 percent less than Gopal, and the true statement is: Gopal has 25 percent more money than Farida.

G5A_PERCENTAGE_005.q: Meera spent 40 percent of her money on a school bag. Then she spent 25 percent of the money that was left on a water bottle. She now has 315 rupees. How much money did Meera have at first?
hints: The second percentage is of what was left, not of all the money. Work backwards from 315 rupees.
After the bottle, 75 percent of the money left after the bag remained. So 315 rupees is 75 percent of that amount.

Similar problem: Ravi spends 50 percent of his money, then 20 percent of the rest, and has 80 rupees. 80 rupees is 80 percent of what was left after the first spend, so that was 100 rupees. 100 rupees is 50 percent of the start, so he began with 200 rupees.
steps: 315 rupees is 75 percent of the money left after the bag, so that amount was 420 rupees.
After the bag, 60 percent of all her money was left, so 420 rupees is 60 percent of the starting amount.
So she started with 700 rupees.
Check: 40 percent of 700 rupees is 280 rupees, leaving 420 rupees. 25 percent of 420 rupees is 105 rupees, leaving 315 rupees. Meera had 700 rupees at first.

G5A_PERCENTAGE_006.q: In a test, Asha scored 30 percent of the total marks and was 15 marks short of the pass mark. Bala scored 45 percent of the total marks and got 30 marks more than the pass mark. What were the total marks of the test?
hints: Both scores are compared with the same pass mark. Think about how far apart the two children's marks are.
Asha is 15 below the pass mark and Bala is 30 above it. How many marks apart are they? That gap is also 45 percent minus 30 percent of the total.

Similar problem: Chetan gets 40 percent and is 10 marks short of passing. Dev gets 60 percent and is 20 marks above the pass mark. They are 30 marks apart, which is 20 percent of the total, so the total is 150 marks.
steps: Asha is 15 below the pass mark and Bala is 30 above it, so Bala has 45 marks more than Asha.
In percent, Bala has 15 percent of the total more than Asha.
So 15 percent of the total is 45 marks, and 1 percent is 3 marks.
The total is 300 marks.

G5A_PERCENTAGE_007.q: A school bag has a marked price of 1,500 rupees. Shop A takes 20 percent off the marked price and then adds 5 percent tax on the reduced price. Shop B adds 5 percent tax to the marked price and then takes 20 percent off that total. Which statement is true?
options: Shop A charges 1,260 rupees and Shop B charges 1,275 rupees.
hints: A percentage change is a multiplication. Think about whether the order of two multiplications matters, then check with the numbers.
Work out Shop A first: take 20 percent off 1,500 rupees, then add 5 percent of the reduced price.

Similar problem: on 1,000 rupees, taking 10 percent off and then adding 10 percent gives 900 rupees and then 990 rupees. Adding 10 percent first and then taking 10 percent off gives 1,100 rupees and then 990 rupees. Both orders end at 990 rupees.
steps: Shop A: 20 percent off 1,500 rupees leaves 1,200 rupees.
5 percent tax on 1,200 rupees is 60 rupees, so Shop A charges 1,260 rupees.
Shop B: 5 percent tax on 1,500 rupees is 75 rupees, making 1,575 rupees.
20 percent off 1,575 rupees is 315 rupees, so Shop B charges 1,260 rupees as well.
Both shops charge 1,260 rupees.

G5A_PERCENTAGE_008.q: A restaurant bill of 1,155 rupees already includes a 5 percent tax on the price of the food. How many rupees of tax are in the bill?
hints: The tax was worked out on the food price, not on the final bill. Ask what percent of the food price the whole bill is.
The bill is the food price, 100 percent, plus the tax, 5 percent, so 1,155 rupees is 105 percent of the food price.
Similar problem: a bill of 660 rupees includes 10 percent tax. 660 rupees is 110 percent of the price, so 1 percent is 6 rupees, the price is 600 rupees and the tax is 60 rupees.
steps: The bill is 100 percent plus 5 percent equals 105 percent of the food price.
So 1 percent of the food price is 11 rupees.
The tax is 5 percent of the food price. 5 times 11 equals 55.
Check: food 1,100 rupees plus tax 55 rupees makes 1,155 rupees. The tax is 55 rupees.

G5A_PERCENTAGE_009.q: In a class, 40 percent of the children are girls and the rest are boys. 30 percent of the girls and 50 percent of the boys wear glasses. What percent of the whole class wears glasses?
hints: Each percentage is of a different group. Picture a class of 100 children and count.
In a class of 100 there are 40 girls and 60 boys. Find 30 percent of the 40 girls first.

Similar problem: 20 percent of a club are adults. 50 percent of the adults and 10 percent of the children wear caps. Out of 100 members, 10 adults and 8 children wear caps, so 18 percent of the club wears caps.
steps: Picture a class of 100 children: 40 girls and 60 boys.
Girls with glasses: 30 percent of 40 is 12.
Boys with glasses: 50 percent of 60 is 30.
Altogether 42 children out of 100 wear glasses, which is 42 percent.

G5A_PERCENTAGE_010.q: A class has 40 children, and 30 percent of them are girls. Some boys move to another class, and no girls leave. Now 40 percent of the children in the class are girls. How many boys moved?
hints: The number of girls stays the same, but the class gets smaller. The new percentage belongs to the new class size.
First find the number of girls: 30 percent of 40. These same girls are 40 percent of the smaller class.

Similar problem: a club has 60 children and 20 percent are girls, so there are 12 girls. Some boys leave and the girls become 25 percent of the club. 12 is 25 percent of 48, so the club now has 48 children and 60 minus 48 equals 12 boys left.
steps: There are 12 girls.
After the boys move, these 12 girls are 40 percent of the class.
So 10 percent of the new class is 3 children, and the new class has 30 children.
The number of boys who moved is 10.

G5A_PERCENTAGE_011.q: Each side of a square playground is made 50 percent longer. By what percent does the area of the playground increase?
hints: Area uses the side twice, so the increase counts twice over. Try a square with an easy side length.
Take a side of 10 metres, so the area is 100 square metres. Find the new side and the new area.
Similar problem: each side of a square is doubled, which is a 100 percent increase. A side of 10 metres becomes 20 metres and the area goes from 100 to 400 square metres, an increase of 300 percent.
steps: Take a square of side 10 metres. Its area is 100 square metres.
50 percent longer means the side becomes 15 metres.
The new area is 225 square metres.
The area grows by 125 square metres on 100, which is an increase of 125 percent.

G5A_PERCENTAGE_012.q: Rohan's mother puts 6,000 rupees in a bank that pays simple interest of 5 percent per year. How much money will she have in all after 18 months?
hints: The rate is for one year, so the time must be in years. Also check whether the question wants the interest or the total.
18 months is one and a half years. Find the interest for one year first: 5 percent of 6,000 rupees.
Similar problem: 4,000 rupees at 10 percent per year for 6 months. One year's interest is 400 rupees, so half a year gives 200 rupees, and the total is 4,200 rupees.
steps: The interest for one year is 300 rupees.
18 months is one and a half years, so the interest is 300 rupees plus 150 rupees equals 450 rupees.
Add the interest to the money put in. 6000 plus 450 equals 6450.
She will have 6,450 rupees in all.

G5A_PERCENTAGE_013.q: In a school election there were only two candidates, and every vote went to one of them. The winner got 60 percent of the votes and won by 240 votes. How many votes were cast in all?
hints: 'Won by 240' is the gap between the two candidates. Find that gap as a percent of all the votes.
The other candidate got 100 percent minus 60 percent equals 40 percent of the votes. What percent of the votes is the gap between them?

Similar problem: a winner gets 55 percent of the votes and wins by 50 votes. The other candidate gets 45 percent, so the gap is 10 percent of the votes. 10 percent is 50 votes, so 500 votes were cast.
steps: The other candidate got 40 percent of the votes.
The winner's lead is 20 percent of the votes.
20 percent of the votes is 240, so 10 percent is 120.
In all, 1,200 votes were cast.

G5A_PERCENTAGE_014.q: Exactly 35 percent of the children in a class are girls. What is the smallest number of children the class could have?
hints: The number of girls must be a whole number. Write the percentage as a fraction in its simplest form.
35 percent is 35 out of 100. Divide the top and the bottom by the same number until you cannot go any further.
Similar problem: exactly 12 percent of the beads in a box are red. 12 out of 100 simplifies to 3 out of 25, so the smallest box has 25 beads, 3 of them red.
steps: 35 percent means 35 out of every 100.
Simplify by dividing the top and the bottom by 5. 35 over 100 equals 7 over 20.
7 and 20 share no factor, so the girls are 7 out of every 20 children.
The smallest class has 20 children, 7 of them girls.

G5A_PERCENTAGE_015.q: A shop has an offer on notebooks: 'Buy 4, get 1 more free.' Riya takes 5 notebooks of the same price and pays for 4. What percent discount is she really getting on the 5 notebooks?
hints: A discount is measured against the full price of everything taken home.
Give each notebook an easy price, such as 10 rupees. What is the full price of 5 notebooks, and how much does Riya save?
Similar problem: 'Buy 2, get 1 free.' With 10 rupee items, the 3 items are worth 30 rupees and you save 10 rupees. That is one-third of the full price, about 33 percent, not 50 percent.
steps: Let each notebook cost 10 rupees. The 5 notebooks are worth 50 rupees.
Riya pays for 4 notebooks, which is 40 rupees, so she saves 10 rupees.
Compare the saving with the full price of 50 rupees. 10 over 50 times 100 equals 20.
The discount is 20 percent.

G5A_PLACEVALUE_001.q: Find the difference between the greatest 5-digit even number with all its digits different and the smallest 5-digit odd number with all its digits different.
hints: Build each number one place at a time, and check both conditions, all digits different, and even or odd, before you subtract.
The greatest 5-digit number with different digits is 98,765, but it is odd. Change only the ones digit to make it even while keeping the digits different.
Similar problem with 4-digit numbers: the greatest even one with different digits is 9,876 and the smallest odd one with different digits is 1,023. Their difference is 9,876 minus 1,023 equals 8,853.
steps: The greatest 5-digit number with all digits different is 98,765. It is odd, so lower the ones digit to the next unused even digit: 98,764.
The smallest 5-digit number with all digits different is 10,234. It is even, so raise the ones digit to the next unused odd digit: 10,235.
Subtract the two numbers. 98764 minus 10235 equals 88529.
The difference is 88,529.

G5A_PLACEVALUE_002.q: In a 5-digit number, the digit in the thousands place is 4. When the thousands digit and the tens digit swap places, the number becomes greater by 2,970. What is the digit in the tens place of the original number?
hints: Think about how much each of the two digits is worth before and after the swap. The other three digits do not change at all.
If the tens digit is 1 more than the thousands digit, the swap adds 1,000 and takes away 10. Work out that change first.

Similar problem: the hundreds digit is 2, and swapping it with the ones digit makes the number greater by 297. Each 1 of difference changes the number by 100 minus 1 equals 99, and 297 divided by 99 equals 3, so the ones digit is 2 plus 3 equals 5.
steps: Only the thousands and tens digits change. If the tens digit is 1 more than the thousands digit, the swap adds 1,000 and removes 10, a gain of 990.
Find how many more the tens digit is than the thousands digit. 2970 divided by 990 equals 3.
The number became greater, so the tens digit is the bigger one: 3 more than 4. 4 plus 3 equals 7.
Check with 54,372: after the swap it is 57,342, and 57,342 minus 54,372 equals 2,970. The digit in the tens place is 7.

G5A_PLACEVALUE_003.q: A dairy sold 45 million 6 thousand packets of milk last year. This year it sold 9 lakh 95 thousand more packets than last year. How many packets did it sell this year, written in the Indian system?
hints: Write both numbers in the same system before adding. Decide how many lakhs make one million.
1 million is 10 lakh, so 45 million is 450 lakh, which is 4 crore 50 lakh. Now write the whole of last year's number in the Indian system.

Similar problem: 12 million 4 thousand plus 3 lakh 98 thousand. 12 million is 1 crore 20 lakh. The thousands give 4 plus 98 equals 102 thousand, which is 1 lakh 2 thousand. The lakhs give 20 plus 3 plus 1 equals 24 lakh. The sum is 1 crore 24 lakh 2 thousand.
steps: 1 million is 10 lakh, so 45 million is 450 lakh, which is 4 crore 50 lakh.
So last year's number is 4 crore 50 lakh 6 thousand.
Add the thousands: 6 thousand plus 95 thousand equals 101 thousand, which is 1 lakh 1 thousand.
Add the lakhs, with the 1 lakh carried over. 50 plus 9 plus 1 equals 60.
This year the dairy sold 4 crore 60 lakh 1 thousand packets.

G5A_PLACEVALUE_004.q: Every whole number from 1 to 100 is written in Roman numerals. Which number needs the most letters?
hints: A bigger number does not always need more letters. Look at the tens part and the ones part separately, and ask which of each is the longest.
Write the ones from 1 to 9 in Roman numerals: I, I I, I I I, I V, V, V I, V I I, V I I I, I X. Which one has the most letters? Then do the same for the tens.
Similar problem for 1 to 39: the longest ones part is V I I I, for 8, and the longest tens part is X X X, for 30, so the longest numeral is X X X V I I I, which is 38 and has 7 letters.
steps: Among the ones, 8 is the longest: V I I I has 4 letters.
Among the tens, 80 is the longest: L X X X has 4 letters. 90 is just X C.
Join them: 88 is L X X X V I I I. 4 plus 4 equals 8.
No other number from 1 to 100 has as many as 8 letters, so the answer is 88.

G5A_PLACEVALUE_005.q: Every whole number from 1 to 100 is written in Roman numerals. How many of them do not use the letter X?
hints: X can come from the tens part of a number, but it can also hide in the ones part. Check both.
First decide which tens are written without X. Remember that 40 is X L and 90 is X C.

Similar problem: how many numbers from 1 to 20 do not use the letter V? The ones parts with V are 4, 5, 6, 7 and 8, so five numbers up to 10 are out and five more between 11 and 20 are out. That leaves 20 minus 10 equals 10 numbers.
steps: X appears in the tens part for 10 to 49, X, X X, X X X, X L, and for 60 to 99, L X, L X X, L X X X, X C. So only 1 to 9, 50 to 59 and 100, which is C, are left to check.
X also appears when the ones digit is 9, because 9 is I X. So 9 and 59 are out as well.
Count what is left: 1 to 8 gives 8 numbers, 50 to 58 gives 9 numbers, and 100 gives 1 more. 8 plus 9 plus 1 equals 18.
So 18 of the numbers do not use the letter X.

G5A_PLACEVALUE_006.q: How many whole numbers become 4,700 when rounded to the nearest hundred, but do not become 4,700 when rounded to the nearest ten?
hints: Find the full list of numbers for each kind of rounding. Then think about which numbers are in the first list but not in the second.
The numbers that round to 4,700 to the nearest hundred run from 4,650 to 4,749. Count how many numbers that is.

Similar problem: rounding to the nearest thousand gives 6,000 for 5,500 to 6,499, which is 1,000 numbers. Rounding to the nearest hundred gives 6,000 for 5,950 to 6,049, which is 100 numbers. So 1,000 minus 100 equals 900 numbers round to 6,000 the first way but not the second.
steps: To the nearest hundred, 4,700 comes from 4,650 up to 4,749. That is 100 numbers.
To the nearest ten, 4,700 comes from 4,695 up to 4,704. That is 10 numbers.
All 10 of those numbers are also in the first list, so take them away. 100 minus 10 equals 90.
So 90 whole numbers round to 4,700 to the nearest hundred but not to the nearest ten.

G5A_PLACEVALUE_007.q: Kabir and Zoya count their marbles. Rounded to the nearest ten, Kabir has 80 marbles and Zoya has 50 marbles. What is the smallest possible difference between the numbers of marbles they really have?
hints: Each rounded number hides a range of real numbers. Think about which real numbers would bring the two children closest together.
List the numbers that round to 80: they run from 75 to 84. Now find the range of numbers that round to 50.

Similar problem: two numbers round to 60 and 20 to the nearest ten. The smallest the first can be is 55 and the greatest the second can be is 24, so the smallest possible difference is 55 minus 24 equals 31.
steps: Kabir's real number can be anything from 75 to 84. Zoya's can be anything from 45 to 54.
For the smallest difference, take Kabir's smallest number and Zoya's greatest number: 75 and 54. 55 would round up to 60, so 54 is her greatest.
Subtract. 75 minus 54 equals 21.
The smallest possible difference is 21 marbles.

G5A_PLACEVALUE_008.q: Anaya writes every whole number from 1 to 200. How many times does she write the digit 7?
hints: Count digits, not numbers. It helps to count the ones place and the tens place separately.
Start with the ones place: 7, 17, 27 and so on. How many of these are there up to 200?

Similar problem: how many times is the digit 3 written from 1 to 100? In the ones place it appears 10 times, 3, 13, and so on, up to 93. In the tens place it appears 10 times, 30 to 39. That is 10 plus 10 equals 20 times, and 33 is rightly counted twice.
steps: Count the 7's in the ones place: 7, 17, 27, and so on, up to 197. There is one in every ten numbers, so there are 20.
Count the 7's in the tens place: 70 to 79 and 170 to 179. 10 plus 10 equals 20.
No number up to 200 has 7 in the hundreds place.
Add the two counts. Numbers such as 77 are counted twice, which is right because they have two 7's. 20 plus 20 equals 40.
Anaya writes the digit 7 a total of 40 times.

G5A_PLACEVALUE_009.q: How many 3-digit numbers have digits whose product is 12? For example, 143 is one of them, because 1 times 4 times 3 equals 12.
hints: First find every set of three digits that multiply to 12. Then count how many numbers each set can make.
Start with the sets that include the digit 1: the other two digits must multiply to 12. Then look for a set without any 1.

Similar problem: digits with product 8. The sets are 1, 1, 8, which gives 3 numbers; 1, 2, 4, which gives 6 numbers; and 2, 2, 2, which gives 1 number. So there are 3 plus 6 plus 1 equals 10 such numbers.
steps: List the sets of three digits that multiply to 12: 1, 2, 6 and 1, 3, 4 and 2, 2, 3.
Three different digits can be arranged in 6 ways. So 1, 2, 6 gives 6 numbers and 1, 3, 4 gives 6 numbers.
The set 2, 2, 3 has a repeated digit, so it gives only 3 numbers: 223, 232 and 322.
Add them up. 6 plus 6 plus 3 equals 15.
There are 15 such numbers.

G5A_PLACEVALUE_010.q: I am a 4-digit number. My thousands digit is twice my ones digit. My hundreds digit is 3 more than my tens digit. The sum of my four digits is 20. Which number am I?
hints: Use the clue that leaves the fewest possibilities first, then test each possibility against the other clues.
The thousands digit is twice the ones digit. List every pair of digits that fits this clue.

Similar problem: a 3-digit number whose hundreds digit is 3 times its ones digit, with tens digit 4 and digit sum 12. The ones digit can be 1, 2 or 3. Trying each: 3 plus 4 plus 1 equals 8, then 6 plus 4 plus 2 equals 12, so the number is 642.
steps: The thousands digit is twice the ones digit, so the thousands and ones digits can only be 2 and 1, 4 and 2, 6 and 3, or 8 and 4.
These pairs add up to 3, 6, 9 and 12. The four digits total 20, so the hundreds and tens digits must add up to 17, 14, 11 or 8.

The hundreds digit is 3 more than the tens digit. A sum of 11 fits, with 7 and 4. A sum of 17 would need 10 and 7, and 10 is not a digit. Sums of 14 and 8 cannot be split into two whole numbers that are 3 apart.
So the digits are 6, 7, 4 and 3. Check the sum. 6 plus 7 plus 4 plus 3 equals 20.
The number is 6743.

G5A_PLACEVALUE_011.q: What is the smallest 6-digit number that can be made using only the digits 0, 3, 5 and 8, if each of these digits must be used at least once?
hints: There are six places but only four digits, so some digit must repeat. Think about which digit is best to repeat when the number should be small.
The first digit cannot be 0. Choose the smallest digit that can go first, then think about the next places.
Similar problem: the smallest 5-digit number using only 0, 2 and 7, each at least once. Start with 2, then use 0 as often as possible, keeping the last place for 7. The number is 20007.
steps: The first digit cannot be 0, so start with the smallest other digit: 3.
To keep the number small, fill the next places with 0, the smallest digit. Digits may repeat, so 0 can be used again and again.
The digits 5 and 8 must each appear once. Put them in the last two places, smaller one first.
That leaves three places for 0, so the number is 300058.

G5A_PLACEVALUE_012.q: What is the greatest 4-digit number in which all four digits are different and add up to 12?
hints: Make the digits on the left as big as you can, but keep checking both conditions as you go.
Start with 9 in the thousands place. What must the other three digits add up to?

Similar problem: the greatest 3-digit number with different digits adding up to 10. Start with 9, leaving 1 for the other two digits. They must be different, so they are 1 and 0, and the number is 910.
steps: Make the thousands digit as big as possible: 9. The other three digits must add up to 3.
The hundreds digit cannot be 3, because then the last two digits would both be 0, and the digits must all be different.
So the hundreds digit is 2, leaving 1 for the last two digits: 1 and 0, bigger one first.
The greatest such number is 9210.

G5A_PLACEVALUE_013.q: Which of these statements is true for every 4-digit number?
options: The sum of the place values of all its digits is equal to the number itself
The face value of each digit is smaller than its place value
The place value of the hundreds digit is greater than the place value of the tens digit
The sum of the face values of all its digits is equal to the number itself
hints: A statement is true for every number only if no number can break it. Try to break each one with a tricky number, such as one with zeros in it.
Test each statement on 3,050. Write the face value and the place value of each of its four digits first.

Similar idea with 3-digit numbers: is 'the place value of the hundreds digit is always more than 100' true? Test 100 itself: the place value of its 1 is exactly 100, not more. One number that breaks a statement is enough to rule it out.
steps: Test each statement with a tricky number such as 3,050. Its face values are 3, 0, 5, 0 and its place values are 3,000, 0, 50, 0.

The face values add up to 8, not 3,050. The ones digit 0 has face value 0 and place value 0, so its face value is not smaller. The hundreds digit has place value 0, which is not greater than the tens digit's 50.
The place values add up to the number. This is just the expanded form, so it happens for every number. 3000 plus 0 plus 50 plus 0 equals 3050.
So the statement that is always true is: the sum of the place values of all its digits is equal to the number itself.

G5A_PLACEVALUE_014.q: A 2-digit number is 27 more than the number made by writing its digits in the opposite order. The reversed number is also a 2-digit number. How many such numbers are there?
hints: Try one or two examples of a number minus its reverse and look for a pattern in the answers.
Work out 41 minus 14 and 52 minus 25. What do you notice about the gap between the digits each time?

Similar problem with 45 more: 45 divided by 9 equals 5, so the tens digit is 5 more than the ones digit. The numbers are 61, 72, 83 and 94. 50 is left out because its reverse is not a 2-digit number. So there are 4 of them.
steps: Try examples: 41 minus 14 equals 27 and 52 minus 25 equals 27. A 2-digit number minus its reverse is always 9 times the gap between its digits.
Find the gap between the digits. 27 divided by 9 equals 3.
So the tens digit is 3 more than the ones digit: 30, 41, 52, 63, 74, 85, 96.
The reverse of 30 is 03, which is not a 2-digit number, so 30 is left out.
That leaves 41, 52, 63, 74, 85 and 96, so there are 6 such numbers.

G5A_PLACEVALUE_015.q: How many 3-digit numbers have exactly one digit that is 0?
hints: Decide where the single 0 can be, and remember that the other digits must then not be 0.
The hundreds digit can never be 0. Start with the case where the 0 is in the tens place: how many choices are there for each of the other two digits?

Similar problem: how many 2-digit numbers have exactly one digit that is 5? Tens digit 5 with a ones digit that is not 5 gives 9 numbers. Ones digit 5 with a tens digit that is not 5 or 0 gives 8 numbers. Total: 9 plus 8 equals 17.
steps: The hundreds digit can never be 0, so the single 0 is either in the tens place or in the ones place.
0 in the tens place only: the hundreds digit has 9 choices, 1 to 9, and the ones digit has 9 choices, 1 to 9. 9 times 9 equals 81.
0 in the ones place only: again 9 choices for the hundreds digit and 9 for the tens digit. 9 times 9 equals 81.
Add the two cases. 81 plus 81 equals 162.
So 162 three-digit numbers have exactly one 0.

G5A_PLACEVALUE_016.q: A number has all its digits different. Rounded to the nearest thousand, it becomes 60,000. What is the greatest number it could be?
hints: First find the range of numbers that round to 60,000. Then look for the greatest one in that range that also fits the other condition.
The greatest number that rounds to 60,000 to the nearest thousand is 60,499. Check its digits one by one.

Similar problem: all digits different, and the number rounds to 7,000 to the nearest thousand. The greatest number that rounds to 7,000 is 7,499, but 9 repeats. Lowering the last digit to the next unused one gives 7,498.
steps: Numbers that round to 60,000 to the nearest thousand run from 59,500 to 60,499.
The greatest of these is 60,499, but it uses the digit 9 twice.
Keep 6, 0, 4 and 9 in the first four places and lower the ones digit to the biggest digit not yet used: 8.
The greatest such number is 60,498.

G5A_PLACEVALUE_017.q: Using each of the digits 2, 5 and 7 exactly once, six different 3-digit numbers can be made. What is the sum of all six numbers?
hints: You could add six numbers, but there is a quicker way: think about how often each digit appears in each place.
List the six numbers and look only at the hundreds place. How many times does each of 2, 5 and 7 appear there?

Similar problem with the digits 1, 2 and 3: each digit appears twice in each place, so every place adds up to 2 times open bracket 1 plus 2 plus 3 close bracket, equals 12. The sum is 12 hundreds plus 12 tens plus 12 ones equals 1,332.
steps: The six numbers are 257, 275, 527, 572, 725 and 752. Each digit appears exactly twice in the hundreds place, twice in the tens place and twice in the ones place.
So each place adds up to twice the sum of the digits. 2 times open bracket 2 plus 5 plus 7 close bracket, equals 28.
Add the three places: 28 hundreds, 28 tens and 28 ones. 2800 plus 280 plus 28 equals 3108.
The sum of all six numbers is 3,108.

G5A_PLACEVALUE_018.q: A palindrome is a number that reads the same forwards and backwards, such as 3,553. How many 4-digit palindromes are even numbers?
hints: In a palindrome, some digits are copies of others. Work out how many digits you are really free to choose.
The last digit decides whether a number is even. In a 4-digit palindrome, which other digit is the same as the last digit?

Similar problem: how many 3-digit palindromes are multiples of 5? The last digit must be 0 or 5, and it equals the first digit, which cannot be 0. So the first digit is 5, which is 1 choice, and the middle digit is free, which is 10 choices: 1 times 10 equals 10.
steps: A 4-digit palindrome is decided by its first two digits: the third digit copies the second and the fourth copies the first.
For an even number the last digit must be even. It is the same as the first digit, which cannot be 0, so it is 2, 4, 6 or 8: 4 choices.
The second digit can be any digit from 0 to 9: 10 choices.
Multiply the choices. 4 times 10 equals 40.
There are 40 even 4-digit palindromes.

G5A_PROFITLOSS_001.q: A shopkeeper bought a toy car for 40 rupees and sold it for 55 rupees. How much profit did he make?
hints: Profit is how much more the selling price is than the cost price.
Take the cost price, 40 rupees, away from the selling price, 55 rupees.
Similar problem: a kite bought for 30 rupees and sold for 50 rupees gives a profit of 50 minus 30 equals 20 rupees.
steps: The cost price is 40 rupees and the selling price is 55 rupees.
Profit equals selling price minus cost price. 55 minus 40 equals 15.
The profit is 15 rupees.

G5A_PROFITLOSS_002.q: Meena bought a bag for 250 rupees and sold it for 220 rupees. How much loss did she make?
hints: A loss happens when the selling price is less than the cost price. The loss is the difference.
Take the selling price, 220 rupees, away from the cost price, 250 rupees.
Similar problem: a lamp bought for 500 rupees and sold for 460 rupees gives a loss of 500 minus 460 equals 40 rupees.
steps: The cost price is 250 rupees and the selling price is 220 rupees, which is less.
Loss equals cost price minus selling price. 250 minus 220 equals 30.
The loss is 30 rupees.

G5A_PROFITLOSS_003.q: A fruit seller buys a basket of mangoes for 300 rupees. He wants to make a profit of 50 rupees. At what price should he sell the basket?
hints: To make a profit, the selling price must be more than the cost price.
Add the profit he wants, 50 rupees, to the cost price, 300 rupees.
Similar problem: something that cost 200 rupees must be sold for 200 plus 40 equals 240 rupees to make a profit of 40 rupees.
steps: Selling price equals cost price plus profit. 300 plus 50 equals 350.
He should sell the basket for 350 rupees.

G5A_PROFITLOSS_004.q: Ravi bought a cricket bat for 500 rupees. He sold it to a friend at a loss of 80 rupees. For how much did he sell the bat?
hints: A loss means the selling price is less than the cost price.
Take the loss, 80 rupees, away from the cost price, 500 rupees.
Similar problem: something that cost 600 rupees and is sold at a loss of 50 rupees is sold for 600 minus 50 equals 550 rupees.
steps: Selling price equals cost price minus loss. 500 minus 80 equals 420.
He sold the bat for 420 rupees.

G5A_PROFITLOSS_005.q: A shopkeeper sold a pen for 90 rupees and made a profit of 20 rupees. How much had he paid for the pen?
hints: With a profit, the cost price is less than the selling price.
Take the profit, 20 rupees, away from the selling price, 90 rupees.
Similar problem: a cap sold for 60 rupees with a profit of 15 rupees had cost 60 minus 15 equals 45 rupees.
steps: Cost price equals selling price minus profit. 90 minus 20 equals 70.
He had paid 70 rupees for the pen.

G5A_PROFITLOSS_006.q: Sita sold a storybook for 150 rupees. She made a loss of 30 rupees. How much had she paid for the storybook?
hints: With a loss, the cost price is more than the selling price.
Add the loss, 30 rupees, to the selling price, 150 rupees.
Similar problem: a toy sold for 200 rupees at a loss of 40 rupees had cost 200 plus 40 equals 240 rupees.
steps: Cost price equals selling price plus loss. 150 plus 30 equals 180.
She had paid 180 rupees for the storybook.

G5A_PROFITLOSS_007.q: A shopkeeper sells a toy for more money than he paid for it. What does he make?
hints: Think about whether the shopkeeper ends up with more money or less money than he spent.
He gets back everything he paid and some extra. What is that extra money called?
Similar problem: Anu buys a ball for 10 rupees and sells it for 8 rupees. She gets back less than she paid, so she makes a loss.
steps: The selling price is more than the cost price.
The extra money the shopkeeper gets is called profit.
So he makes a profit.

G5A_PROFITLOSS_008.q: Mohan bought a cycle for 900 rupees and later sold it for 900 rupees. What did he make?
options: neither a profit nor a loss
hints: Compare the selling price with the cost price.
Work out the selling price less the cost price: 900 minus 900.
Similar problem: Tara buys a book for 50 rupees and sells it for 50 rupees. The two prices are equal, so she makes no profit and no loss.
steps: The cost price is 900 rupees and the selling price is 900 rupees.
The two prices are equal, so nothing is gained and nothing is lost. 900 minus 900 equals 0.
Mohan made neither a profit nor a loss.

G5A_PROFITLOSS_009.q: A shopkeeper bought a water bottle for 80 rupees and sold it for 100 rupees. What was his profit?
hints: Profit is the selling price less the cost price.
Take 80 rupees away from 100 rupees.
Similar problem: a notebook bought for 45 rupees and sold for 60 rupees gives a profit of 60 minus 45 equals 15 rupees.
steps: The cost price is 80 rupees and the selling price is 100 rupees.
Profit equals selling price minus cost price. 100 minus 80 equals 20.
His profit was 20 rupees.

G5A_PROFITLOSS_010.q: A fruit seller paid 200 rupees for a box of apples. Which of these selling prices gives him a profit?
hints: A profit needs a selling price that is more than the cost price.
Compare each price with 200 rupees. Which one is greater than 200 rupees?
Similar problem: something that cost 50 rupees gives a profit when it is sold for 65 rupees, because 65 is more than 50, but not when it is sold for 45 rupees.
steps: The cost price is 200 rupees. A profit needs a selling price above 200 rupees.
180 rupees and 150 rupees are less than 200 rupees, and 200 rupees is equal to it.
Only 240 rupees is more than 200 rupees, so 240 rupees gives a profit.

G5A_SEQUENCES_001.q: What is the 9th term of the sequence 3, 4, 7, 11, 18, 29, and so on?
hints: If the differences do not make a simple pattern, look at how each term is linked to the terms just before it.
Look at 3, 4, 7. Then look at 4, 7, 11. How could you make the third number from the first two each time?

Similar problem: 2, 5, 7, 12, 19, 31, and so on. Each term is the sum of the two before it: 2 plus 5 equals 7, and 5 plus 7 equals 12. So the 7th term is 19 plus 31 equals 50 and the 8th term is 31 plus 50 equals 81.
steps: Each term is the sum of the two terms before it: 3 plus 4 equals 7, 4 plus 7 equals 11, 7 plus 11 equals 18, 11 plus 18 equals 29.
The 7th term is the sum of the 5th and 6th terms. 18 plus 29 equals 47.
The 8th term is the sum of the 6th and 7th terms. 29 plus 47 equals 76.
The 9th term is the sum of the 7th and 8th terms. 47 plus 76 equals 123.
The 9th term is 123.

G5A_SEQUENCES_002.q: In the sequence 5, 40, 8, 35, 11, 30, 14, 25, and so on, what is the sum of the 15th term and the 16th term?
hints: The terms go up, then down, then up again. Try looking at every second term on its own.
The 1st, 3rd, 5th and 7th terms are 5, 8, 11, 14. The 2nd, 4th, 6th and 8th terms are 40, 35, 30, 25. Which place in its own pattern does the 15th term have?
Similar problem: 2, 50, 6, 45, 10, 40, and so on. The odd positions go 2, 6, 10, 14, 18, so the 9th term is 18. The even positions go 50, 45, 40, 35, 30, so the 10th term is 30. Their sum is 48.
steps: The odd positions hold 5, 8, 11, 14, and so on: add 3. The even positions hold 40, 35, 30, 25, and so on: subtract 5.
The 15th term is the 8th number of the first pattern, which is 7 steps after 5. 5 plus 7 times 3 equals 26.
The 16th term is the 8th number of the second pattern, which is 7 steps after 40. 40 minus 7 times 5 equals 5.
Add them. 26 plus 5 equals 31.
The sum of the 15th and 16th terms is 31.

G5A_SEQUENCES_003.q: Tara counts aloud like this: 1, 2, 3, 4, 3, 2, 1, 2, 3, 4, 3, 2, 1, 2, and so on, going up to 4 and back down to 1 again and again. What is the 100th number she says?
hints: Find the block of numbers that repeats exactly, with no number shared between one block and the next.
Write out the first 13 numbers and mark where the pattern starts again. Take care: does the 1 belong to the end of one block or the start of the next?

Similar problem: 1, 2, 3, 2, 1, 2, 3, 2, 1, and so on. The repeating block is 1, 2, 3, 2, which has 4 numbers. For the 50th number, 50 divided by 4 equals 12 remainder 2, so it is the 2nd number of the block, which is 2.
steps: The repeating block is 1, 2, 3, 4, 3, 2. It has 6 numbers, and after it the next block starts again with 1.
Find how many whole blocks fit into 100 numbers. 100 divided by 6 equals 16 remainder 4.
After 16 whole blocks, 96 numbers have been said. The 100th number is the 4th number of the next block.
The 4th number of the block 1, 2, 3, 4, 3, 2 is 4, so the 100th number is 4.

G5A_SEQUENCES_004.q: A sequence starts 100, 93, 86, 79, and so on, and goes down by 7 each time. How many terms of the sequence are greater than 0?
hints: Work out how many times 7 can be taken away before the terms drop below 0. Then think about how steps and terms are related.
100 divided by 7 is 14 remainder 2. So after 14 steps down the term is 2. Is that term still greater than 0? And how many terms are there if 14 steps have been taken?

Similar problem: 50, 44, 38, and so on, going down by 6. 50 divided by 6 is 8 remainder 2, so after 8 steps the term is 2. Counting the first term as well, there are 8 plus 1 equals 9 terms greater than 0.
steps: See how many 7's can be taken from 100. 100 divided by 7 equals 14 remainder 2.
So after 14 steps down, the term is 2, which is still greater than 0. One more step would give a number below 0.
The terms are the starting term and then one term for each step. 14 plus 1 equals 15.
So 15 terms are greater than 0.

G5A_SEQUENCES_005.q: What is the value of 100 minus 99 plus 98 minus 97 plus 96 minus 95 plus, and so on, plus 4 minus 3 plus 2 minus 1?
hints: Working from left to right would take very long. Look for small groups of neighbouring terms that are easy to work out.
Put brackets round the terms two at a time: open bracket 100 minus 99 close bracket, plus open bracket 98 minus 97 close bracket, plus, and so on. What is each bracket worth?

Similar problem: 20 minus 19 plus 18 minus 17 plus, and so on, plus 2 minus 1. Each pair such as open bracket 20 minus 19 close bracket is worth 1. There are 20 numbers, so 10 pairs, and the value is 10.
steps: Group the terms in pairs: open bracket 100 minus 99 close bracket, plus open bracket 98 minus 97 close bracket, plus, and so on, plus open bracket 4 minus 3 close bracket, plus open bracket 2 minus 1 close bracket.
Each pair is worth 1.
There are 100 numbers, so there are 50 pairs.
Add up the pairs. 50 times 1 equals 50.
The value is 50.

G5A_SEQUENCES_006.q: In the sequence 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 4, 4, 4, 4, and so on, each whole number n is written n times. What is the 50th term?
hints: Work out the position where each number is written for the last time. The running total of 1 plus 2 plus 3 plus, and so on, helps.
The last 1 is at position 1, the last 2 at position 1 plus 2 equals 3, the last 3 at position 1 plus 2 plus 3 equals 6. Keep adding until the total passes 50.
Similar problem: the 20th term. 1 plus 2 plus 3 plus 4 plus 5 equals 15, so the last 5 is at position 15. The next six positions, 16 to 21, hold 6's. So the 20th term is 6.
steps: Add 1 plus 2 plus 3 plus, and so on, to find where each number ends. The 9's end at position 45.
The next ten terms are all 10's. They end at position 55.
Position 50 lies between 46 and 55.
So the 50th term is 10.

G5A_SEQUENCES_007.q: A sequence starts with 7. The rule is: if a term is odd, add 5 to get the next term; if a term is even, halve it to get the next term. So the sequence begins 7, 12, 6, 3, and so on. What is the 50th term?
hints: Keep applying the rule until you see a group of terms coming round again. Note exactly where the repeating part begins.
Carry on from 3: it is odd, so add 5 to get 8. Then 4, then 2, then 1. What comes after 1, and have you seen that number before?

Similar problem: start with 5; if odd add 3, if even halve. The sequence is 5, 8, 4, 2, 1, 4, 2, 1, and so on. The block 4, 2, 1 repeats from the 3rd term. For the 21st term, 21 minus 2 equals 19 terms lie in the repeating part, and 19 divided by 3 leaves remainder 1, so it is the 1st number of the block, which is 4.
steps: Continue the sequence: 7, 12, 6, 3, 8, 4, 2, 1, 6, 3, 8, 4, 2, 1, and so on. The block 6, 3, 8, 4, 2, 1 repeats, starting from the 3rd term.
The first two terms are not in the repeating part, so set them aside. 50 minus 2 equals 48.
The block has 6 numbers. See how many whole blocks fit into 48 terms. 48 divided by 6 equals 8.
Exactly 8 whole blocks fit, so the 50th term is the last number of a block.
The last number of the block 6, 3, 8, 4, 2, 1 is 1, so the 50th term is 1.

G5A_SPEED_001.q: Asha cycles at a steady speed of 12 kilometres per hour. How far does she cycle in 3 hours?
hints: Speed tells you how far something goes in one hour. Distance is speed multiplied by time.
Asha goes 12 kilometres in the first hour, 12 kilometres in the second and 12 kilometres in the third.
A similar one: a cyclist going 10 kilometres per hour for 2 hours covers 10 times 2 equals 20 kilometres.
steps: Distance is speed multiplied by time.
Multiply 12 kilometres per hour by 3 hours. 12 times 3 equals 36.
Asha cycles 36 kilometres.

G5A_SPEED_002.q: A snail crawls 5 centimetres every minute. How far does it crawl in 8 minutes?
hints: The snail covers the same distance every minute. Distance is speed multiplied by time.
The speed is 5 centimetres each minute and the time is 8 minutes. Multiply them.
A similar one: an ant that walks 4 centimetres every minute walks 4 times 6 equals 24 centimetres in 6 minutes.
steps: Distance is speed multiplied by time.
Multiply 5 centimetres each minute by 8 minutes. 5 times 8 equals 40.
The snail crawls 40 centimetres.

G5A_SPEED_003.q: Ravi swims at a steady speed of 2 metres every second. How long does he take to swim 50 metres?
hints: Time is distance divided by speed.
Ask how many lots of 2 metres fit into 50 metres. Each lot takes 1 second.
A similar one: a swimmer who covers 2 metres every second swims 30 metres in 30 divided by 2 equals 15 seconds.
steps: Time is distance divided by speed.
Divide 50 metres by 2 metres each second. 50 divided by 2 equals 25.
Ravi takes 25 seconds.

G5A_SPEED_004.q: Rahul walks at a steady speed of 4 kilometres per hour. How long does he take to walk 12 kilometres?
hints: Time is distance divided by speed.
Ask how many lots of 4 kilometres fit into 12 kilometres. Each lot takes 1 hour.
A similar one: walking at 5 kilometres per hour, a walk of 10 kilometres takes 10 divided by 5 equals 2 hours.
steps: Time is distance divided by speed.
Divide 12 kilometres by 4 kilometres per hour. 12 divided by 4 equals 3.
Rahul takes 3 hours.

G5A_SPEED_005.q: A boat travels 45 kilometres along a river in 3 hours at a steady speed. What is the speed of the boat?
hints: Speed is the distance covered in one unit of time. Speed is distance divided by time.
The boat covers 45 kilometres in 3 hours. Share 45 kilometres equally among the 3 hours.
A similar one: a boat that travels 40 kilometres in 4 hours has a speed of 40 divided by 4 equals 10 kilometres per hour.
steps: Speed is distance divided by time.
Divide 45 kilometres by 3 hours. 45 divided by 3 equals 15.
The speed of the boat is 15 kilometres per hour.

G5A_SPEED_006.q: A horse gallops 600 metres in 2 minutes at a steady speed. How many metres does it gallop in one minute?
hints: The distance covered in one minute is the speed. Speed is distance divided by time.
The horse covers 600 metres in 2 minutes. Share 600 metres equally between the 2 minutes.
A similar one: a horse that gallops 800 metres in 2 minutes covers 800 divided by 2 equals 400 metres in one minute.
steps: Speed is distance divided by time.
Divide 600 metres by 2 minutes. 600 divided by 2 equals 300.
The horse gallops 300 metres in one minute.

G5A_SPEED_007.q: A toy car moves 10 centimetres every second. How long does it take to move 80 centimetres?
hints: Time is distance divided by speed.
Ask how many lots of 10 centimetres fit into 80 centimetres. Each lot takes 1 second.
A similar one: a toy car that moves 10 centimetres every second takes 60 divided by 10 equals 6 seconds to move 60 centimetres.
steps: Time is distance divided by speed.
Divide 80 centimetres by 10 centimetres each second. 80 divided by 10 equals 8.
The toy car takes 8 seconds.

G5A_SPEED_008.q: Kavya walks 100 metres in 50 seconds at a steady speed. What is her speed in metres per second?
hints: Speed is the distance covered in one unit of time. Speed is distance divided by time.
Kavya covers 100 metres in 50 seconds. Share 100 metres equally among the 50 seconds.
A similar one: someone who walks 90 metres in 30 seconds has a speed of 90 divided by 30 equals 3 metres per second.
steps: Speed is distance divided by time.
Divide 100 metres by 50 seconds. 100 divided by 50 equals 2.
Kavya's speed is 2 metres per second.

G5A_SPEED_009.q: A lorry travels at a steady speed of 40 kilometres per hour for 5 hours. What distance does it cover?
hints: Speed tells you how far something goes in one hour. Distance is speed multiplied by time.
The lorry goes 40 kilometres in every one of the 5 hours. Multiply 40 by 5.
A similar one: a lorry going 30 kilometres per hour for 4 hours covers 30 times 4 equals 120 kilometres.
steps: Distance is speed multiplied by time.
Multiply 40 kilometres per hour by 5 hours. 40 times 5 equals 200.
The lorry covers 200 kilometres.

G5A_SPEED_010.q: Four friends each cycled for exactly 1 hour. Ravi covered 14 kilometres, Sana covered 11 kilometres, Tina covered 16 kilometres and Uday covered 9 kilometres. Who cycled at the greatest speed?
hints: When everyone travels for the same time, the fastest is the one who goes the furthest.
Each friend cycled for 1 hour, so the distance each one covered is also the speed in kilometres per hour. Compare the four distances.
A similar one: in 1 hour Meena walks 5 kilometres and Arjun walks 4 kilometres. Meena covers more in the same time, so Meena is faster.
steps: All four cycled for the same time, 1 hour, so compare the distances.
The distances are 14 kilometres, 11 kilometres, 16 kilometres and 9 kilometres. The greatest is 16 kilometres.
So Tina cycled at the greatest speed.

G5A_TRIANGLES_001.q: How many of these five sets of lengths can be the three sides of a triangle? Set 1: 3 centimetres, 4 centimetres, 7 centimetres. Set 2: 5 centimetres, 5 centimetres, 9 centimetres. Set 3: 2 centimetres, 6 centimetres, 9 centimetres. Set 4: 4 centimetres, 7 centimetres, 10 centimetres. Set 5: 6 centimetres, 6 centimetres, 12 centimetres.
hints: Imagine fixing the longest stick on the table and hinging the two shorter sticks at its ends. When can their tips meet above it?
For each set, add the two shorter lengths and compare the total with the longest length. Think hard about the sets where they are exactly equal.

A similar check: 2 centimetres, 3 centimetres, 5 centimetres cannot make a triangle, because 2 plus 3 is exactly 5 and the short sticks lie flat on the long one. But 3 centimetres, 3 centimetres, 5 centimetres can, because 3 plus 3 is more than 5.
steps: Three lengths make a triangle only when the two shorter ones together are more than the longest.
Set 1: 3 plus 4 equals 7, only equal, so no. Set 2: 5 plus 5 equals 10, more than 9, so yes. Set 3: 2 plus 6 equals 8, less than 9, so no.
Set 4: 4 plus 7 equals 11, more than 10, so yes. Set 5: 6 plus 6 equals 12, only equal, so no.
Only Set 2 and Set 4 make triangles, so the answer is 2.

G5A_TRIANGLES_002.q: Mira has five sticks of lengths 2 centimetres, 3 centimetres, 4 centimetres, 5 centimetres and 7 centimetres. She picks three sticks at a time and tries to make a triangle with them as its sides. How many different triangles can she make?
hints: Not every choice of three sticks will close up into a triangle. List the choices in an orderly way so that none is missed, and test each one.
Start with the choices that use the 2 centimetre stick: 2, 3, 4 and 2, 3, 5 and 2, 3, 7 and so on. For each, compare the two shorter sticks together with the longest.

A similar task with sticks of 1 centimetre, 2 centimetres, 3 centimetres and 4 centimetres: the choices are 1, 2, 3 and 1, 2, 4 and 1, 3, 4 and 2, 3, 4. Only 2, 3, 4 works, because 2 plus 3 is more than 4, so just 1 triangle can be made.
steps: There are 10 ways to choose three of the five sticks. A choice makes a triangle only if the two shorter sticks together are longer than the longest.
With the 2 centimetre stick: 2, 3, 4 works and 2, 4, 5 works. But 2, 3, 5 and 2, 5, 7 are only equal, and 2, 3, 7 and 2, 4, 7 are too short.
Without the 2 centimetre stick: 3, 4, 5 and 3, 5, 7 and 4, 5, 7 work, but 3, 4, 7 is only equal.
So Mira can make 5 triangles.

G5A_TRIANGLES_003.q: Two sides of a triangle are 4 centimetres and 9 centimetres long. The third side is a whole number of centimetres. How many different lengths can the third side have?
hints: The third side cannot be too long or too short. Find both limits, then count the whole numbers strictly between them.
If the third side is the longest, it must be less than 4 plus 9. If 9 centimetres is the longest, then 4 plus the third side must be more than 9.

A similar triangle has sides 3 centimetres and 8 centimetres. The third side must be more than 5 centimetres and less than 11 centimetres, so it can be 6, 7, 8, 9 or 10 centimetres: that is 5 different lengths.
steps: The third side must be shorter than the other two together. 4 plus 9 equals 13.
With 4 centimetres it must beat the 9 centimetre side, so it must be longer than their difference. 9 minus 4 equals 5.
So the third side is more than 5 centimetres and less than 13 centimetres: it can be 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11 or 12 centimetres.
Counting these gives 7 different lengths.

G5A_TRIANGLES_004.q: Three villages P, Q and R do not lie in one straight line. Straight roads join each pair of villages. Road P Q is 7 kilometres long and road Q R is 12 kilometres long. Which of these could be the length of road P R?
hints: The three roads form a triangle. Think about going from P to R directly, and going from P to R by way of Q.
The direct road P R must be shorter than going round through Q, which is 7 kilometres plus 12 kilometres. It also cannot be too short: 7 kilometres and P R together must be more than 12 kilometres.

A similar map: road A B is 6 kilometres and road B C is 10 kilometres, with the three villages not in a line. Road A C must be more than 4 kilometres and less than 16 kilometres, so 15 kilometres is possible but 16 kilometres and 4 kilometres are not.
steps: The direct road must be shorter than the way round through Q. 7 plus 12 equals 19.
Roads P Q and P R together must be longer than road Q R, so P R is longer than the difference. 12 minus 7 equals 5.
So P R is more than 5 kilometres and less than 19 kilometres. Exactly 19 kilometres or exactly 5 kilometres would put the villages in a straight line.
Of the lengths offered, only 18 kilometres fits.

G5A_TRIANGLES_005.q: How many different triangles have sides that are whole numbers of centimetres and a perimeter of 13 centimetres? Triangles with the same three side lengths count as one triangle.
hints: Not every three numbers that add up to 13 make a triangle. Decide first how long the longest side is allowed to be.
The longest side must be shorter than the other two together, so it must be less than half of 13. It also cannot be less than 5 centimetres, or the three sides could not reach 13 centimetres.
A similar count for perimeter 9 centimetres: the longest side must be less than 4 and a half, so it is 3 or 4. That gives 3, 3, 3 and 4, 4, 1 and 4, 3, 2, which is 3 triangles.
steps: The longest side must be less than the other two together, so it is less than half of 13 centimetres: at most 6 centimetres. It is at least 5 centimetres, because three sides of 4 centimetres or less cannot add up to 13 centimetres.
Longest side 6 centimetres: the other two add up to 7 centimetres, giving 6, 6, 1 and 6, 5, 2 and 6, 4, 3.
Longest side 5 centimetres: the other two add up to 8 centimetres, giving 5, 5, 3 and 5, 4, 4.
Count them: there are 5 triangles.

G5A_TRIANGLES_006.q: An isosceles triangle has sides that are whole numbers of centimetres and a perimeter of 20 centimetres. How many different triangles like this are there?
hints: Choose the length of the two equal sides and the third side is then fixed. But not every choice closes up into a triangle.
If each equal side is 3 centimetres, the third side is 14 centimetres. Can two sides of 3 centimetres reach across 14 centimetres? Find which lengths of the equal sides do work.

A similar count for perimeter 12 centimetres: equal sides of 4 centimetres give 4, 4, 4 and equal sides of 5 centimetres give 5, 5, 2. Equal sides of 3 centimetres give 3, 3, 6, which lies flat. So there are 2 triangles.
steps: If each equal side is a certain length, the third side is 20 centimetres less twice that length.
The two equal sides together must be longer than the third side, so together they are more than half of 20 centimetres: each equal side is more than 5 centimetres.
The third side must be at least 1 centimetre, so each equal side is at most 9 centimetres.
The equal sides can be 6, 7, 8 or 9 centimetres, giving 6, 6, 8 and 7, 7, 6 and 8, 8, 4 and 9, 9, 2: that is 4 triangles.

G5A_TRIANGLES_007.q: One angle of an isosceles triangle is 40 degrees. Which answer gives every possible size of the largest angle of the triangle?
hints: An isosceles triangle has two equal angles. The question does not say whether the 40 degree angle is one of the equal pair or the odd one out.
First let 40 degrees be one of the two equal angles and find the third angle. Then let 40 degrees be the odd one out and find the two equal angles.

A similar triangle: one angle of an isosceles triangle is 50 degrees. If the equal angles are 50 degrees each, the third is 80 degrees. If 50 degrees is the odd one, the others are 65 degrees each. So the largest angle is 65 degrees or 80 degrees.
steps: If 40 degrees is one of the two equal angles, the third angle is what is left. 180 minus 40 minus 40 equals 100.
If 40 degrees is the odd one out, the two equal angles share the rest. 180 minus 40 equals 140.
Halve it to find each equal angle. 140 divided by 2 equals 70.
The triangle is 40 degrees, 40 degrees, 100 degrees or 40 degrees, 70 degrees, 70 degrees, so its largest angle is 70 degrees or 100 degrees.

G5A_TRIANGLES_008.q: Two sides of an isosceles triangle are 4 centimetres and 9 centimetres long. What is the perimeter of the triangle?
hints: The third side must equal one of the two given sides. Before adding up, check that each choice really makes a triangle.
Try the third side as 4 centimetres: can sides of 4 centimetres and 4 centimetres reach across a side of 9 centimetres? Then try the third side as 9 centimetres.

A similar triangle: an isosceles triangle has sides 3 centimetres and 8 centimetres. Sides 3, 3, 8 cannot meet, because 3 plus 3 is less than 8. So the sides are 3, 8, 8 and the perimeter is 19 centimetres.
steps: The third side is equal to one of the others, so it is 4 centimetres or 9 centimetres.
With 4 centimetres, 4 centimetres and 9 centimetres: 4 plus 4 equals 8, which is less than 9, so these sides cannot meet to make a triangle.
With 4 centimetres, 9 centimetres and 9 centimetres: 4 plus 9 is more than 9, so this triangle can be made.
Add the three sides: the perimeter is 22 centimetres.

G5A_TRIANGLES_009.q: One exterior angle of a triangle is 110 degrees. Of the two interior angles that are not next to this exterior angle, one is 20 degrees bigger than the other. What is the largest interior angle of the triangle?
hints: A triangle has three interior angles. Make sure you know all three before deciding which is the largest.
An exterior angle equals the two far interior angles added together, so those two add up to 110 degrees. The interior angle next to the exterior angle lies with it on a straight line.

A similar triangle: an exterior angle is 100 degrees and the two far interior angles differ by 10 degrees, so they are 45 degrees and 55 degrees. The interior angle next to the exterior angle is 80 degrees, and that is the largest.
steps: The two far interior angles add up to the exterior angle, 110 degrees, and one is 20 degrees more than the other.
Take away the extra 20 degrees and halve to find the smaller one. Open bracket 110 minus 20 close bracket, divided by 2 equals 45.
So those two angles are 45 degrees and 65 degrees.
The third interior angle lies beside the exterior angle on a straight line. 180 minus 110 equals 70.
The interior angles are 45 degrees, 65 degrees and 70 degrees, so the largest interior angle is 70 degrees.

G5A_TRIANGLES_010.q: In a triangle, the largest angle is equal to the sum of the other two angles. One of those two angles is 4 times the other. What is the smallest angle of the triangle?
hints: Begin with the first sentence alone. If one angle equals the other two added together, what part of the whole 180 degrees must it be?
The largest angle and the other two together make 180 degrees, and the other two together equal the largest. So the largest angle is half of 180 degrees.

A similar triangle: the largest angle equals the sum of the other two, and one of those is twice the other. The largest is 90 degrees, and the other two share 90 degrees as 1 part and 2 parts, so they are 30 degrees and 60 degrees.
steps: The largest angle equals the other two together, so it is half of the total. 180 divided by 2 equals 90.
The other two angles add up to 90 degrees, and one is 4 times the other, so together they are 5 equal parts.
Find one part. 90 divided by 5 equals 18.
The angles are 18 degrees, 72 degrees and 90 degrees, so the smallest angle is 18 degrees.

G5A_TRIANGLES_011.q: At each corner of a triangle, one exterior angle is drawn. What is the smallest number of these three exterior angles that can be obtuse?
hints: An exterior angle and the interior angle beside it lie on a straight line. Think about what kind of interior angle gives an obtuse exterior angle.
If an interior angle is acute, the exterior angle beside it is more than 90 degrees. Now ask how many acute angles a triangle must have.

A similar idea: a triangle with interior angles 100 degrees, 50 degrees and 30 degrees has exterior angles 80 degrees, 130 degrees and 150 degrees. Only the corner with the obtuse interior angle has an acute exterior angle.
steps: An exterior angle is 180 degrees less the interior angle beside it, so it is obtuse exactly when that interior angle is acute.
A triangle cannot have two angles of 90 degrees or more, because those two alone would already reach 180 degrees.
So every triangle has at least two acute interior angles, and each of them gives an obtuse exterior angle.
A triangle such as 100 degrees, 50 degrees, 30 degrees has exactly two obtuse exterior angles, so the smallest number is 2.

G5A_TRIANGLES_012.q: A triangle has a base of 20 centimetres, and the height drawn to that base is 9 centimetres. Another side of the same triangle is 12 centimetres long. What is the height drawn to the 12 centimetre side?
hints: Any side of a triangle can be used as the base, with its own height. Think about what stays the same whichever side you choose.
Use the first base and height to find the area: half of 20 times 9. The 12 centimetre side and its height must give the same area.

A similar triangle has base 10 centimetres with height 6 centimetres, so its area is 30 square centimetres. If another side is 8 centimetres, then half of 8 times its height is 30, so 4 times the height is 30 and the height is 7 and a half centimetres.
steps: Find the area using the first base and height. One half times 20 times 9 equals 90.
The area is 90 square centimetres whichever side is used as the base.
With the 12 centimetre side as base, half of 12 times the height is 90, so 12 times the height is 180.
Divide by 12: the height drawn to the 12 centimetre side is 15 centimetres.

G5A_TRIANGLES_013.q: A triangle has sides that are whole numbers of centimetres and a perimeter of 24 centimetres. What is the greatest possible length of its longest side?
hints: When one side gets longer, the other two together get shorter, because the perimeter is fixed. Find the point where they can no longer meet.
If the longest side is 12 centimetres, the other two sides together are also 12 centimetres. Can they rise above the long side to make a triangle?

A similar triangle with perimeter 16 centimetres: a longest side of 8 centimetres leaves 8 centimetres for the other two, which would lie flat. A longest side of 7 centimetres leaves 9 centimetres, and 7, 7, 2 works. So the greatest is 7 centimetres.
steps: The longest side must be shorter than the other two sides together.
A longest side of 12 centimetres leaves exactly 12 centimetres for the other two, so they would lie flat along it and make no triangle.
A longest side of 11 centimetres leaves 13 centimetres for the other two, which is more than 11 centimetres. For example, 11 centimetres, 11 centimetres and 2 centimetres make a triangle.
So the greatest possible length of the longest side is 11 centimetres.

G5A_VARIATION_001.q: Asha and Bina collect stickers. The numbers of stickers they have are in the ratio 5 is to 3. Asha gives 12 of her stickers to Bina, and now the two girls have the same number of stickers. How many stickers did Asha have at first?
hints: When one friend gives to the other, the total does not change, but the gap between them closes from both sides.
Asha has 5 parts and Bina has 3 parts, so the gap is 2 parts. Giving 12 stickers closes a gap that is twice as big as 12.

Similar problem: two boys have marbles in the ratio 7 is to 3. The first gives 10 marbles to the second and they become equal. The gap was 2 times 10 equals 20 marbles, which is 4 parts, so one part is 5 and the first boy had 7 times 5 equals 35 marbles.
steps: Giving 12 stickers takes Asha down by 12 and Bina up by 12, so the gap between them was 24.
The gap is 5 minus 3 equals 2 parts, so one part is 12 stickers.
Asha had 5 parts. 5 times 12 equals 60.
Check: 60 and 36 become 48 and 48. Asha had 60 stickers at first.

G5A_VARIATION_002.q: Meena and Tara share some money in the ratio 5 is to 1. Meena then gives 15 rupees to Tara, and the ratio of Meena's money to Tara's money becomes 2 is to 1. How much money does Meena have now?
hints: The total money stays the same when one person gives to the other. Make both ratios describe the same total number of parts.
5 is to 1 has 6 parts in all, but 2 is to 1 has only 3. Rewrite 2 is to 1 as 4 is to 2 so that both ratios have 6 parts.

Similar problem: two friends have money in the ratio 3 is to 1. The first gives 8 rupees to the second and the ratio becomes 1 is to 1, which is 2 is to 2 with the same 4 parts. The first went from 3 parts to 2 parts, so one part is 8 rupees and the first now has 2 times 8 equals 16 rupees.
steps: The total does not change. 5 is to 1 is 6 parts, so write the new ratio 2 is to 1 as 4 is to 2, which is also 6 parts.
Meena goes from 5 parts to 4 parts, so one part is the 15 rupees she gave.
Meena now has 4 parts. 4 times 15 equals 60.
Check: 75 rupees and 15 rupees become 60 rupees and 30 rupees, which is 2 is to 1. Meena has 60 rupees now.

G5A_VARIATION_003.q: In a chess club the ratio of boys to girls is 3 is to 4. Then 6 more boys join, and no girls join or leave. The ratio of boys to girls becomes 6 is to 7. How many children are in the club now?
hints: The number of girls does not change, so make the girls' part the same number in both ratios.
Girls are 4 parts in the first ratio and 7 parts in the second. Rewrite both ratios so that the girls are 28 parts.

Similar problem: red to blue beads are 2 is to 3. After 4 more red beads are added the ratio is 5 is to 6. With blue as 6 parts both times, the ratios are 4 is to 6 and 5 is to 6, so one part is 4 beads and there are now 11 times 4 equals 44 beads.
steps: The number of girls stays the same, so write both ratios with the girls as 28 parts: 3 is to 4 equals 21 is to 28 and 6 is to 7 equals 24 is to 28.
Boys go from 21 parts to 24 parts. These 3 parts are the 6 new boys, so one part is 2 children.
Now there are 24 plus 28 equals 52 parts. 52 times 2 equals 104.
There are 104 children in the club now.

G5A_VARIATION_004.q: In Class 5 B, the ratio of the children who walk to school to all the children in the class is 3 is to 8. There are 40 children who do not walk to school. How many children walk to school?
hints: Check what the second number in the ratio stands for: is it another group, or the whole class?
Out of every 8 children, 3 walk, so 8 minus 3 equals 5 do not walk. The 40 children match those 5 parts.

Similar problem: the ratio of red balloons to all the balloons is 2 is to 7, and 30 balloons are not red. Not red is 7 minus 2 equals 5 parts, so one part is 6 and there are 2 times 6 equals 12 red balloons.
steps: The ratio compares the walkers with the whole class: 3 parts walk out of 8 parts in all.
So 8 minus 3 equals 5 parts do not walk, and these are the 40 children.
The walkers are 3 parts. 3 times 8 equals 24.
24 children walk to school.

G5A_VARIATION_005.q: Anu, Bela and Chitra share 372 rupees. Anu's share to Bela's share is 3 is to 4, and Bela's share to Chitra's share is 6 is to 5. How much does Chitra get?
hints: Bela appears in both ratios. Make Bela's number the same in both before joining them into one ratio.
Bela is 4 in one ratio and 6 in the other. Change both ratios so that Bela is 12.

Similar problem: P to Q is 1 is to 2 and Q to R is 3 is to 4, and they share 170 rupees. With Q as 6, the ratios are 3 is to 6 and 6 is to 8, so P is to Q is to R equals 3 is to 6 is to 8. That is 17 parts of 10 rupees each, so R gets 8 times 10 equals 80 rupees.
steps: Bela must have the same number in both ratios: 3 is to 4 equals 9 is to 12 and 6 is to 5 equals 12 is to 10.
So Anu is to Bela is to Chitra equals 9 is to 12 is to 10, which is 31 parts.
One part is 12 rupees.
Chitra gets 10 parts, which is 120 rupees.

G5A_VARIATION_006.q: Half of Kavi's savings is equal to one-third of Lata's savings. Together they have saved 150 rupees. How much has Kavi saved?
hints: If half of one amount equals only a third of another amount, think about which of the two amounts must be larger.
Call the equal amount one block. Kavi's savings are 2 blocks, because half of them is 1 block. How many blocks are Lata's savings?
Similar problem: one-third of Raj's marbles equals one-quarter of Sam's marbles, and together they have 70. Raj has 3 blocks and Sam has 4 blocks, so one block is 10 and Raj has 30 marbles.
steps: Call the equal amount 1 block. Half of Kavi's savings is 1 block, so Kavi has 2 blocks.
One-third of Lata's savings is 1 block, so Lata has 3 blocks.
Together they have 5 blocks worth 150 rupees, so one block is 30 rupees.
Kavi has 2 blocks, which is 60 rupees.

G5A_VARIATION_007.q: 12 workers can build a wall in 20 days. They all work for 5 days, and then 3 of the workers leave. The others finish the wall at the same pace. How many days does the wall take from start to finish?
hints: Measure the whole job in worker-days: the work one worker does in one day.
The wall needs 12 times 20 worker-days. Find how many of them are used up in the first 5 days.

Similar problem: 10 workers need 12 days. After 2 days, 5 of them leave. The job is 120 worker-days, 20 are done, and 100 are left for 5 workers, which takes 20 more days. From start to finish that is 2 plus 20 equals 22 days.
steps: The whole wall is 240 worker-days of work.
In the first 5 days, 12 workers do 60 worker-days, so 180 are left.
Now 9 workers remain, so they need 20 more days.
From start to finish the wall takes 25 days.

G5A_VARIATION_008.q: A hostel has enough rice to feed 40 students for 30 days. After 10 days, 10 more students join the hostel. For how many more days will the rice last?
hints: Count the rice in student-days: the rice one student eats in one day. First work out how much is left when the new students arrive.
After 10 days, the 40 students still have rice for 20 days. How many student-days of rice is that?
Similar problem: food lasts 20 campers for 15 days. After 5 days, 5 more campers come. The food left is 20 times 10 equals 200 camper-days, and 25 campers finish it in 8 days.
steps: After 10 days, the rice left would feed 40 students for 20 more days.
That is 800 student-days of rice.
Now there are 50 students.
The rice will last 16 more days.

G5A_VARIATION_009.q: A taxi charges a fixed amount for every trip plus the same amount for each kilometre. A 5 kilometre trip costs 110 rupees and an 8 kilometre trip costs 155 rupees. How much does a 12 kilometre trip cost?
hints: Because of the fixed amount, the cost is not simply so many rupees per kilometre. Compare the two trips to see what the extra kilometres cost.
The 8 kilometre trip is 3 kilometres longer than the 5 kilometre trip and costs 45 rupees more. What does each extra kilometre cost?

Similar problem: a cab costs 70 rupees for 2 kilometres and 110 rupees for 6 kilometres. The extra 4 kilometres cost 40 rupees, so each kilometre is 10 rupees and the fixed amount is 50 rupees. A 10 kilometre trip costs 50 plus 100 equals 150 rupees.
steps: The extra 3 kilometres cost 45 rupees, so each kilometre costs 15 rupees.
For 5 kilometres the kilometres cost 75 rupees, so the fixed amount is 35 rupees.
12 kilometres cost 180 rupees for the kilometres.
Adding the fixed amount, the 12 kilometre trip costs 215 rupees.

G5A_VARIATION_010.q: A 30-litre mixture has milk and water in the ratio 7 is to 3. How many litres of water must be added so that the ratio of milk to water becomes 3 is to 2?
hints: Only water is added, so the amount of milk stays the same. Build the new ratio around the milk.
First find the litres of milk and of water in the 30 litres: 7 parts and 3 parts out of 10 parts.

Similar problem: 40 litres of juice and water are in the ratio 3 is to 1, so there are 30 litres of juice and 10 litres of water. For a ratio of 3 is to 2 with 30 litres of juice, the water must be 20 litres, so 10 litres of water are added.
steps: One part is 3 litres, so there are 21 litres of milk and 9 litres of water.
The milk stays at 21 litres. In the ratio 3 is to 2 the milk is 3 parts, so one part is 7 litres.
The water must be 2 parts, which is 14 litres.
Water to add: 5 litres.

G5A_VARIATION_011.q: Jar P holds 20 litres of milk and water mixed in the ratio 3 is to 1. Jar Q holds 30 litres of milk and water mixed in the ratio 2 is to 3. Both jars are emptied into one big drum. What is the ratio of milk to water in the drum?
hints: Ratios cannot be added directly when the jars hold different amounts. Work in litres.
Find the litres of milk and of water in Jar P: 3 parts and 1 part out of 20 litres.

Similar problem: 10 litres mixed 4 is to 1 has 8 litres of milk and 2 litres of water. 20 litres mixed 1 is to 1 has 10 litres of each. Together that is 18 litres of milk and 12 litres of water, a ratio of 3 is to 2.
steps: Jar P: 4 parts are 20 litres, so it has 15 litres of milk and 5 litres of water.
Jar Q: 5 parts are 30 litres, so it has 12 litres of milk and 18 litres of water.
In the drum there are 15 plus 12 equals 27 litres of milk and 5 plus 18 equals 23 litres of water.
The ratio of milk to water in the drum is 27 is to 23.

G5A_VARIATION_012.q: A money box has only 1 rupee, 2 rupee and 5 rupee coins. The numbers of 1 rupee, 2 rupee and 5 rupee coins are in the ratio 5 is to 3 is to 2. The total value of all the coins is 210 rupees. How many 5 rupee coins are in the box?
hints: The ratio counts coins, but 210 rupees is a value. Find the value of one small group of coins first.
Take one group of 5 one-rupee coins, 3 two-rupee coins and 2 five-rupee coins. How many rupees is this group worth?

Similar problem: 1 rupee and 5 rupee coins are in the ratio 3 is to 1 and are worth 64 rupees in all. One group of 3 one-rupee coins and 1 five-rupee coin is worth 8 rupees, so there are 8 groups and 8 five-rupee coins.
steps: One group has 5 coins of 1 rupee, 3 coins of 2 rupees and 2 coins of 5 rupees. It is worth 21 rupees.
The number of such groups is 10.
Each group has 2 coins of 5 rupees. 2 times 10 equals 20.
There are 20 five-rupee coins in the box.

G5A_VARIATION_013.q: The ages of a mother and her daughter Riya are in the ratio 7 is to 2. In 5 years' time, their ages will be in the ratio 8 is to 3. How old is the mother now?
hints: Both of them grow older by the same number of years, so the difference between their ages never changes.
In 7 is to 2 the difference is 5 parts, and in 8 is to 3 the difference is also 5 parts. So the parts are the same size in both ratios.

Similar problem: a father's and a son's ages are in the ratio 5 is to 1. In 6 years they will be in the ratio 3 is to 1, which is 6 is to 2. The difference is 4 parts both times, so one part is 6 years and the father is 5 times 6 equals 30 now.
steps: The difference in ages stays the same. It is 7 minus 2 equals 5 parts now and 8 minus 3 equals 5 parts later, so the parts are the same size.
The mother goes from 7 parts to 8 parts in 5 years, so one part is 5 years.
The mother is 7 parts now. 7 times 5 equals 35.
Check: 35 and 10 become 40 and 15, which is 8 is to 3. The mother is 35 years old now.

G5A_VARIATION_014.q: 3 men or 6 boys can paint a school hall in 20 days. How many days will 2 men and 4 boys take to paint the same hall, working together?
hints: Change all the workers into one kind first, so that the whole team is counted in the same unit.
3 men do the same work as 6 boys, so 1 man works like 2 boys. How many boys is the team of 2 men and 4 boys worth?
Similar problem: 2 men or 6 boys finish a job in 12 days. One man equals 3 boys, so 1 man and 6 boys equal 9 boys. The job is 6 times 12 equals 72 boy-days, so they take 8 days.
steps: 3 men do the work of 6 boys, so 1 man does the work of 2 boys.
2 men and 4 boys are like 4 plus 4 equals 8 boys.
The hall needs 120 boy-days of work.
8 boys take 15 days.

G5A_VARIATION_015.q: Kiran and Leela had money in the ratio 3 is to 2. Each of them spent 40 rupees on a book. Now the ratio of Kiran's money to Leela's money is 2 is to 1. How much money did Kiran have at first?
hints: Both spend the same amount, so the difference between their money does not change.
In 3 is to 2 the difference is 1 part, and in 2 is to 1 the difference is also 1 part. So the parts are the same size before and after.
