hints: Every triangle's three angles make 180 degrees altogether. You know two of them, so the third is whatever is left over.
First add the two angles you know, 75 degrees and 74 degrees. Then think about how far that total is from 180 degrees.
Similar example: two angles of a triangle are 25 degrees and 110 degrees. 25 plus 110 equals 135, and 180 minus 135 equals 45. The third angle is 45 degrees.
steps: Add the two angles you know. 75 plus 74 equals 149.
All three angles of a triangle add up to 180 degrees.
Take the total away from 180 degrees. The third angle is 31 degrees. 180 minus 149 equals 31.

Q_CH19_013_V06.q: What is the supplement of an angle of 169 degrees?
hints: This is about supplementary angles. Two angles are supplementary when together they make a straight line.
Supplementary angles add up to 180 degrees. So take 169 degrees away from 180 degrees.
Similar example: the supplement of 70 degrees is 180 degrees minus 70 degrees, which is 110 degrees. Check: 70 degrees plus 110 degrees equals 180 degrees.
steps: Supplementary angles add up to 180 degrees.
Take the given angle away from 180 degrees. 180 degrees minus 169 degrees equals 11 degrees.
Check by adding: 169 degrees plus 11 degrees equals 180 degrees. The supplement of 169 degrees is 11 degrees.

Q_CH19_014.q: The vertex angle of an isosceles triangle is 50 degrees. Each base angle is:
hints: This is a missing-angle problem. An isosceles triangle has one vertex angle and two equal base angles, and the three angles add up to 180 degrees.
First take the vertex angle of 50 degrees away from 180 degrees to find what the two base angles share.

Here is a similar problem. The vertex angle of an isosceles triangle is 40 degrees. The two base angles share 180 minus 40, which is 140 degrees. They are equal, so each one is 140 divided by 2, which is 70 degrees.
steps: The three angles add up to 180 degrees, so the two base angles together make 180 minus 50, which is 130 degrees.
The base angles are equal, so each is half of 130 degrees. 130 divided by 2 equals 65.
So each base angle is 65 degrees.

Q_CH19_014_V01.q: What is the supplement of an angle of 72 degrees?
hints: This is about supplementary angles. Two angles are supplementary when together they make a straight line.
Supplementary angles add up to 180 degrees. So take 72 degrees away from 180 degrees.
Similar example: the supplement of 70 degrees is 180 degrees minus 70 degrees, which is 110 degrees. Check: 70 degrees plus 110 degrees equals 180 degrees.
steps: Supplementary angles add up to 180 degrees.
Take the given angle away from 180 degrees. 180 degrees minus 72 degrees equals 108 degrees.
Check by adding: 72 degrees plus 108 degrees equals 180 degrees. The supplement of 72 degrees is 108 degrees.

Q_CH19_015.q: In a right-angled triangle, the side opposite to the right angle is called the:
hints: The side opposite the biggest angle is always the longest side.
90 degrees is the biggest angle in a right triangle, so the side opposite it is the longest.
This longest side is called the hypotenuse.
steps: In a right triangle, the side opposite 90 degrees is the longest.
This side is called the hypotenuse.

Q_CH19_016.q: How many axes of symmetry does a scalene triangle have?
hints: An axis of symmetry is a fold line that makes the two halves of a shape match exactly. For a triangle, think about which sides would have to land on each other.
Remember what scalene means: all three sides have different lengths. Imagine folding the triangle through each corner and ask whether the two halves would match.

Here is a similar problem. How many axes of symmetry does a triangle with exactly two equal sides have? Folding through the corner where the two equal sides meet lays one equal side on the other, so that fold line is an axis of symmetry. A fold through either of the other corners would put a longer side on a shorter one. So it has 1 axis of symmetry.
steps: An axis of symmetry is a fold line that makes the two halves match exactly.
In a triangle, a fold through a corner makes matching halves only when the two sides that meet at that corner are equal.
A scalene triangle has three different sides, so no two sides are equal and no fold gives matching halves. So a scalene triangle has 0 axes of symmetry.

Q_CH19_017.q: A triangle has sides 8 centimetres, 11 centimetres, and 15 centimetres. Its perimeter is:
hints: This is a perimeter problem. The perimeter of a shape is the total distance around it.
Add the three sides. Start with 8 plus 11, then add 15 to that.
Here is a similar problem. A triangle has sides 6 centimetres, 9 centimetres and 13 centimetres. 6 plus 9 equals 15, and 15 plus 13 equals 28. Its perimeter is 28 centimetres.
steps: The perimeter is the sum of the three sides.
First add two of the sides: 8 plus 11 equals 19.
Then add the third side: 19 plus 15 equals 34. So the perimeter is 34 centimetres.

Q_CH19_017_V04.q: A rectangle is 29 centimetres long and 14 centimetres wide. What is its area?
hints: This asks for area, the space inside the rectangle. Think about how the length and the width work together to cover it.
The area of a rectangle is length times width. Set up 29 times 14 and work it out.
Here is a similar one: a rectangle 9 centimetres long and 4 centimetres wide. Area equals 9 times 4, which is 36 square centimetres.
steps: The area of a rectangle is length times width.
Split 14 into 10 and 4. Multiply 29 by 10. 29 times 10 equals 290.
Now multiply 29 by 4. 29 times 4 equals 116.
Add the two parts. So the area is 406 square centimetres. 290 plus 116 equals 406.

Q_CH19_017_V06.q: A rectangle is 5 centimetres long and 3 centimetres wide. What is its perimeter?
hints: This asks for perimeter, the distance all the way round the rectangle. Remember that a rectangle has two lengths and two widths.
Add the length and the width first: 5 plus 3. Then think about how many of each side there are.
Here is a similar one: a rectangle 9 centimetres long and 5 centimetres wide. 9 plus 5 equals 14. Double it: 14 times 2 equals 28 centimetres.
steps: Perimeter is the distance all the way round. Start by adding the length and the width. 5 plus 3 equals 8.
There are two lengths and two widths, so double it. The perimeter is 16 centimetres. 8 times 2 equals 16.

Q_CH19_017_V10.q: Each side of a square is 6 centimetres long. What is the area of the square?
hints: This asks for the area of a square, the space inside it. All the sides of a square are equal.
For a square, area is side times side. Set up 6 times 6.
Here is a similar one: a square with side 5 centimetres. Area equals 5 times 5, which is 25 square centimetres.
steps: The area of a square is side times side.
6 times 6 means 6 groups of 6. Add them up. 6 plus 6 plus 6 plus 6 plus 6 plus 6 equals 36.
So the area is 36 square centimetres. 6 times 6 equals 36.

Q_CH19_018.q: The perimeter of a triangle is 36 centimetres. Two sides are 12 centimetres and 9 centimetres. What is the third side?
hints: This is a perimeter problem worked backwards. The perimeter is the total of all three sides, and you know two of them.
First add the two sides you know, 12 centimetres and 9 centimetres. The third side is whatever is still needed to reach 36 centimetres.

Here is a similar problem. The perimeter of a triangle is 40 centimetres and two sides are 14 centimetres and 10 centimetres. The two known sides add up to 14 plus 10, which is 24 centimetres. The third side is 40 minus 24, which is 16 centimetres.
steps: The perimeter is the sum of the three sides, so the three sides add up to 36 centimetres.
The two known sides add up to 12 plus 9, which is 21 centimetres.
The third side is what is left: 36 minus 21 equals 15. So the third side is 15 centimetres.

Q_CH19_018_V08.q: A rectangle is 29 centimetres long and 15 centimetres wide. What is its perimeter?
hints: This asks for perimeter, the distance all the way round the rectangle. Remember that a rectangle has two lengths and two widths.
Add the length and the width first: 29 plus 15. Then think about how many of each side there are.
Here is a similar one: a rectangle 9 centimetres long and 5 centimetres wide. 9 plus 5 equals 14. Double it: 14 times 2 equals 28 centimetres.
steps: Perimeter is the distance all the way round. Start by adding the length and the width. 29 plus 15 equals 44.
There are two lengths and two widths, so double it. The perimeter is 88 centimetres. 44 times 2 equals 88.

Q_CH19_019.q: A right-angled triangle has legs of 6 centimetres and 8 centimetres. What is its area?
hints: This is an area problem for a right-angled triangle. The two legs meet at the right angle, so one is the base and the other is the height. The triangle is half of the rectangle made with them.
Multiply the two legs, 6 times 8, to get the area of the rectangle. Then remember that the triangle is half of it.

Here is a similar problem. A right-angled triangle has legs of 10 centimetres and 6 centimetres. The rectangle made with them has area 10 times 6, which is 60 square centimetres. The triangle is half of that, so its area is 30 square centimetres.
steps: The legs meet at the right angle, so one leg is the base and the other is the height.
Base times height is 6 times 8, which is 48.
The triangle is half of that rectangle: 48 divided by 2 equals 24. So the area is 24 square centimetres.

Q_CH19_020.q: A median of a triangle is a line segment joining a vertex to the blank of the opposite side.
hints: This is about the meaning of a word. The word median is related to the word middle.
Picture a line drawn from one corner of a triangle across to the opposite side. Think about which special point on that side would cut the side into two equal parts.

Here is an example. In triangle P Q R, side Q R is 10 centimetres long. The point M on Q R is 5 centimetres from Q and 5 centimetres from R. The line from P to M is a median of the triangle, because M cuts Q R into two equal parts.
steps: A median starts at a vertex of the triangle and goes across to the opposite side.
It meets that side exactly in the middle, cutting it into two equal parts. The point in the middle of a side is called its midpoint.
So a median joins a vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side.

Q_CH19_021.q: How many medians does a triangle have?
hints: A median joins a vertex of a triangle to the middle of the opposite side. Think about how many different vertices a median can start from.
Count the vertices of a triangle. One median can be drawn from each vertex.
Here is a similar problem. How many diagonals does a rectangle have? A diagonal joins two opposite corners. A rectangle has 4 corners, which make 2 pairs of opposite corners, so it has 2 diagonals.
steps: A median joins a vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side.
A triangle has 3 vertices, and each vertex has exactly one opposite side, so each vertex gives one median.
So a triangle has 3 medians.

Q_CH19_022.q: In a triangle with angles 40 degrees, 60 degrees, and 80 degrees, which side is the longest?
hints: In any triangle, the longest side is always opposite the largest angle.
The largest angle here is 80 degrees.
So the longest side is opposite 80 degrees.
steps: The rule: the longest side is opposite the largest angle.
The largest angle is 80 degrees. The longest side is opposite 80 degrees.

Q_CH19_023.q: Can a triangle have two right angles?
options: Yes, if it's a big triangle
Yes, in a right-angled isosceles triangle
No, because 90 degrees plus 90 degrees equals 180 degrees, leaving 0 degrees for the third angle
Yes, if the sides are very long
hints: If two angles were 90 degrees each, their sum is 180 degrees. But the total for all three angles must be 180 degrees!
That leaves 180 degrees minus 180 degrees, which is 0 degrees, for the third angle. An angle of 0 degrees doesn't exist!
So no, a triangle cannot have two right angles.
steps: If two angles are 90 degrees each: 90 degrees plus 90 degrees equals 180 degrees.
The third angle is 180 degrees minus 180 degrees, which is 0 degrees. This is impossible!
A triangle cannot have two right angles.

Q_CH19_024.q: The perimeter of an equilateral triangle is 45 centimetres. What is the length of each side?
hints: This is a perimeter problem worked backwards. An equilateral triangle has three equal sides, and the perimeter is the total of all three.
The three equal sides add up to 45 centimetres. Think about how to share 45 centimetres equally among 3 sides.
Here is a similar problem. The perimeter of an equilateral triangle is 36 centimetres. Its three sides are equal, so each side is 36 divided by 3, which is 12 centimetres.
steps: An equilateral triangle has 3 equal sides, and together they make the perimeter of 45 centimetres.
Share 45 centimetres equally among the 3 sides: 45 divided by 3 equals 15.
So each side is 15 centimetres long.

Q_CH19_025.q: A right-angled triangle has a base of 12 centimetres and area of 42 square centimetres. What is its height?
hints: The area is half of base times height. We know the area and the base, so find the height.
42 equals half of 12 times h. So 42 equals 6 h.
h equals 42 divided by 6, which is 7 centimetres.
steps: The area is half of base times height. 42 equals half of 12 times h.
42 equals 6 h.
h equals 42 divided by 6, which is 7 centimetres.

Q_CH19_025_V07.q: Each side of a square is 22 centimetres long. What is the area of the square?
hints: This asks for the area of a square, the space inside it. All the sides of a square are equal.
For a square, area is side times side. Set up 22 times 22.
Here is a similar one: a square with side 7 centimetres. Area equals 7 times 7, which is 49 square centimetres.
steps: The area of a square is side times side.
Split 22 into 20 and 2. Multiply 22 by 20. 22 times 20 equals 440.
Now multiply 22 by 2. 22 times 2 equals 44.
Add the two parts. So the area is 484 square centimetres. 440 plus 44 equals 484.

Q_CH20_001.q: The sum of all angles of a quadrilateral is:
hints: A quadrilateral is a shape with four sides and four angles. There is a fixed total for its four angles, and a triangle can help you find it.
Draw a line from one corner of a quadrilateral to the opposite corner. Count how many triangles you get, and remember that the angles of one triangle add up to 180 degrees.

Similar example: a six-sided shape can be cut into 4 triangles by lines from one corner. Each triangle's angles add to 180 degrees, so the angles of the six-sided shape add to 4 times 180 degrees, which is 720 degrees.
steps: Draw one diagonal across the quadrilateral. It cuts the shape into 2 triangles.
The angles of each triangle add up to 180 degrees, and together the two triangles make up all four angles of the quadrilateral. 2 times 180 degrees equals 360 degrees.
The sum of all angles of a quadrilateral is 360 degrees.

Q_CH20_001_V02.q: What is the complement of an angle of 18 degrees?
hints: This is about complementary angles. Two angles are complementary when together they make a right angle.
Complementary angles add up to 90 degrees. So take 18 degrees away from 90 degrees.
Similar example: the complement of 20 degrees is 90 degrees minus 20 degrees, which is 70 degrees. Check: 20 degrees plus 70 degrees equals 90 degrees.
steps: Complementary angles add up to 90 degrees.
Take the given angle away from 90 degrees. 90 degrees minus 18 degrees equals 72 degrees.
Check by adding: 18 degrees plus 72 degrees equals 90 degrees. The complement of 18 degrees is 72 degrees.

Q_CH20_001_V08.q: What is the supplement of an angle of 98 degrees?
hints: This is about supplementary angles. Two angles are supplementary when together they make a straight line.
Supplementary angles add up to 180 degrees. So take 98 degrees away from 180 degrees.
Similar example: the supplement of 70 degrees is 180 degrees minus 70 degrees, which is 110 degrees. Check: 70 degrees plus 110 degrees equals 180 degrees.
steps: Supplementary angles add up to 180 degrees.
Take the given angle away from 180 degrees. 180 degrees minus 98 degrees equals 82 degrees.
Check by adding: 98 degrees plus 82 degrees equals 180 degrees. The supplement of 98 degrees is 82 degrees.

Q_CH20_001_V09.q: Two angles of a triangle are 32 degrees and 73 degrees. What is the third angle?
hints: This uses the angle sum of a triangle: the three angles together make 180 degrees. Find the part that is missing.
First add the two angles you know, 32 degrees and 73 degrees. Then think about how far that total is from 180 degrees.
Similar example: two angles of a triangle are 55 degrees and 45 degrees. 55 plus 45 equals 100, and 180 minus 100 equals 80. The third angle is 80 degrees.
steps: Add the two angles you know. 32 plus 73 equals 105.
All three angles of a triangle add up to 180 degrees.
Take the total away from 180 degrees. The third angle is 75 degrees. 180 minus 105 equals 75.

Q_CH20_002.q: How many axes of symmetry does a rectangle, that is not a square, have?
hints: An axis of symmetry is a fold line that makes the two halves land exactly on top of each other. Picture folding a rectangular sheet of paper.
Try each possible fold: across the middle from side to side, down the middle from top to bottom, and along each corner-to-corner line. Count only the folds where the halves match exactly.

Similar example: an equilateral triangle can be folded from any corner to the middle of the opposite side, and the halves match each time. There are three corners, so an equilateral triangle has 3 axes of symmetry.
steps: Fold the rectangle across the middle so the top edge meets the bottom edge. The halves match, so this is one axis of symmetry.
Fold it down the middle so the left edge meets the right edge. The halves match again, so this is a second axis.
Fold it along a corner-to-corner line. The corners do not land on each other, because the length and the breadth are different. So the diagonals are not axes of symmetry.
A rectangle that is not a square has 2 axes of symmetry.

Q_CH20_002_V06.q: Each side of a square is 4 centimetres long. What is the perimeter of the square?
hints: This asks for perimeter, the distance all the way round the square. All four sides are the same length.
A square has 4 equal sides. So you need 4 lots of 4 centimetres.
Here is a similar one: a square with side 11 centimetres. Perimeter equals 4 times 11, which is 44 centimetres.
steps: A square has 4 equal sides, so the perimeter is 4 times side.
4 times 4 means 4 groups of 4. Add them up. 4 plus 4 plus 4 plus 4 equals 16.
So the perimeter is 16 centimetres. 4 times 4 equals 16.

Q_CH20_003.q: The perimeter of a square with side 11 centimetres is:
hints: Perimeter is the distance around the shape. A square has four sides that are all the same length.
Add up the four equal sides of 11 centimetres, or use multiplication to do it faster.
Similar example: a square has a side of 7 centimetres. Its perimeter is 4 times 7, which is 28 centimetres.
steps: A square has 4 equal sides, so the perimeter is 4 times the side.
Multiply 11 by 4. 4 times 11 equals 44.
The perimeter is 44 centimetres.

Q_CH20_003_V05.q: Each side of a square is 8 centimetres long. What is the area of the square?
hints: This asks for the area of a square, the space inside it. All the sides of a square are equal.
For a square, area is side times side. Set up 8 times 8.
Here is a similar one: a square with side 5 centimetres. Area equals 5 times 5, which is 25 square centimetres.
steps: The area of a square is side times side.
8 times 8 means 8 groups of 8. Add them up. 8 plus 8 plus 8 plus 8 plus 8 plus 8 plus 8 plus 8 equals 64.
So the area is 64 square centimetres. 8 times 8 equals 64.

Q_CH20_004.q: The area of a square with side 9 metres is:
hints: Area is the space inside the square. Look at both the number and the unit in each choice, because area is measured in square units.
Multiply the side by itself. Then choose the unit that goes with area.
Similar example: a square has a side of 7 metres. Its area is 7 times 7, which is 49 square metres, written 49 s q m.
steps: The area of a square is side times side. 9 times 9 equals 81.
The side is in metres, so the area is in square metres, written s q m. The unit m on its own measures length, not area.
The area is 81 square metres.

Q_CH20_005.q: A rectangle has length 12 centimetres and breadth 7 centimetres. Its perimeter is:
hints: Perimeter is the distance all the way around. A rectangle has two lengths and two breadths, and the answer is a length, not an area.
Add the length and the breadth, 12 and 7. That is halfway round, so think about what to do next.
Similar example: a rectangle has length 15 centimetres and breadth 6 centimetres. Length plus breadth is 15 plus 6, which is 21 centimetres, and the perimeter is 2 times 21, which is 42 centimetres.
steps: Add the length and the breadth. 12 plus 7 equals 19.
The rectangle has two lengths and two breadths, so double 19. 2 times 19 equals 38.
The perimeter is 38 centimetres.

Q_CH20_006.q: A rectangle has length 15 centimetres and breadth 8 centimetres. Its area is:
hints: Area is the space inside the rectangle. It is found by multiplying the length by the breadth.
Multiply 15 by 8. You can split 15 into 10 and 5 and multiply each part by 8.
Similar example: a rectangle has length 12 centimetres and breadth 9 centimetres. 10 times 9 equals 90 and 2 times 9 equals 18, so the area is 90 plus 18, which is 108 square centimetres.
steps: The area of a rectangle is length times breadth, so multiply 15 by 8.
Split 15 into 10 and 5. 10 times 8 equals 80 and 5 times 8 equals 40, and 80 plus 40 equals 120.
The area is 120 square centimetres.

Q_CH20_006_V04.q: A rectangle is 6 centimetres long and 3 centimetres wide. What is its area?
hints: This asks for area, the space inside the rectangle. Think about how the length and the width work together to cover it.
The area of a rectangle is length times width. Set up 6 times 3 and work it out.
Here is a similar one: a rectangle 12 centimetres long and 5 centimetres wide. Area equals 12 times 5, which is 60 square centimetres.
steps: The area of a rectangle is length times width.
6 times 3 means 6 groups of 3. Add them up. 3 plus 3 plus 3 plus 3 plus 3 plus 3 equals 18.
So the area is 18 square centimetres. 6 times 3 equals 18.

Q_CH20_007.q: Find the side of a square whose perimeter is numerically equal to its area.
hints: For a square, the perimeter is 4 times the side and the area is the side times the side. You need a side for which these two numbers come out the same.
Test the sides offered in the choices. For each one, work out 4 times the side and the side times itself, and compare the two results.

Similar example: is the perimeter of a square of side 5 equal in number to its area? The perimeter is 4 times 5, which is 20 and the area is 5 times 5, which is 25. They are not equal, so 5 is not such a side. Test other sides in the same way.
steps: The perimeter of a square is 4 times the side, and the area is the side times the side. Test each side that is offered.
Side 8: the perimeter is 4 times 8, which is 32 and the area is 8 times 8, which is 64. These are not equal.
Side 6: the perimeter is 4 times 6, which is 24 and the area is 6 times 6, which is 36. These are not equal.
Side 4: the perimeter is 16 and the area is also 16. These are equal. 4 times 4 equals 16.
The side of the square is 4.

Q_CH20_007_V02.q: A rectangle is 14 centimetres long and 6 centimetres wide. What is its area?
hints: This asks for area, the space inside the rectangle. Think about how the length and the width work together to cover it.
The area of a rectangle is length times width. Set up 14 times 6 and work it out.
Here is a similar one: a rectangle 11 centimetres long and 7 centimetres wide. Area equals 11 times 7, which is 77 square centimetres.
steps: The area of a rectangle is length times width.
Split 14 into 10 and 4. Multiply the 10 by 6. 6 times 10 equals 60.
Now multiply the 4 by 6. 6 times 4 equals 24.
Add the two parts. So the area is 84 square centimetres. 60 plus 24 equals 84.

Q_CH20_007_V06.q: A rectangle is 13 centimetres long and 3 centimetres wide. What is its perimeter?
hints: This asks for perimeter, the distance all the way round the rectangle. Remember that a rectangle has two lengths and two widths.
Add the length and the width first: 13 plus 3. Then think about how many of each side there are.
Here is a similar one: a rectangle 9 centimetres long and 5 centimetres wide. 9 plus 5 equals 14. Double it: 14 times 2 equals 28 centimetres.
steps: Perimeter is the distance all the way round. Start by adding the length and the width. 13 plus 3 equals 16.
There are two lengths and two widths, so double it. The perimeter is 32 centimetres. 16 times 2 equals 32.

Q_CH20_008.q: Which of the following can be the length and breadth of a rectangle whose perimeter is 32 metres?
hints: The perimeter is two lengths and two breadths. So first work out what one length and one breadth must add up to.
Halve the perimeter, 32 metres. Then add the two numbers in each choice and see which pair gives that half.
Similar example: a rectangle has a perimeter of 20 metres, so length plus breadth is 20 divided by 2, which is 10 metres. The pair 6.5 metres and 3.5 metres fits, because 6.5 plus 3.5 equals 10.
steps: Half the perimeter is one length plus one breadth. 32 divided by 2 equals 16.
Test 18 metres and 14 metres: 18 plus 14 equals 32. That is the whole perimeter, not half of it, so this pair is too big.
Test 8 metres and 7 metres: 8 plus 7 equals 15, which is 1 short of 16.
Test 10.5 metres and 5.5 metres. They add to 16, so this pair fits.
The length and breadth can be 10.5 metres, 5.5 metres.

Q_CH20_008_V04.q: A rectangle is 19 centimetres long and 16 centimetres wide. What is its perimeter?
hints: This asks for perimeter, the distance all the way round the rectangle. Remember that a rectangle has two lengths and two widths.
Add the length and the width first: 19 plus 16. Then think about how many of each side there are.
Here is a similar one: a rectangle 20 centimetres long and 6 centimetres wide. 20 plus 6 equals 26. Double it: 26 times 2 equals 52 centimetres.
steps: Perimeter is the distance all the way round. Start by adding the length and the width. 19 plus 16 equals 35.
There are two lengths and two widths, so double it. The perimeter is 70 centimetres. 35 times 2 equals 70.

Q_CH20_009.q: Find the perimeter of a rectangle whose length is, 2 m plus 5 n, and breadth is, m minus 3 n.
hints: P equals 2 times, L plus B. First find L plus B.
L plus B equals, 2 m plus 5 n, plus, m minus 3 n, which is 3 m plus 2 n
P equals 2 times, 3 m plus 2 n, which is 6 m plus 4 n
steps: L plus B equals, 2 m plus 5 n, plus, m minus 3 n, which is 3 m plus 2 n. 2 m plus m equals 3 m. 5 n minus 3 n equals 2 n.
P equals 2 times, 3 m plus 2 n, which is 6 m plus 4 n

Q_CH20_010.q: The length and breadth of a rectangle are, 3 a minus 5, centimetres and, a plus 5, centimetres. If the perimeter is 40 centimetres, find a.
hints: P equals 2 times, L plus B. So 40 equals 2 times, open bracket, 3 a minus 5, plus a plus 5, close bracket.
40 equals 2 times 4 a. So 40 equals 8 a.
A equals 40 divided by 8, which is 5.
steps: L plus B equals, 3 a minus 5, plus, a plus 5, which is 4 a. 3 a plus a equals 4 a. Minus 5 plus 5 equals 0.
P equals 2 times, 4 a, which is 8 a, which is 40
A equals 5. L equals 3 times 5 minus 5, which is 10 centimetres. B equals 5 plus 5, which is 10 centimetres.

Q_CH20_011.q: Sam ran ten rounds around a rectangular field. The field is 350 metres long and 120 metres wide. What total distance did Sam run?
hints: One round of the field is its perimeter. Find the distance for one round first, then for all the rounds, and check the units in the choices.
Add the length and the width, 350 metres and 120 metres, and double the total to get one round.

Similar example: a field is 200 metres long and 150 metres wide. One round is 2 times, 200 plus 150, which is 700 metres. Five rounds are 5 times 700, which is 3500 metres. Since 1000 metres is 1 kilometre, that is 3.5 kilometres.
steps: Add the length and the width of the field. 350 plus 120 equals 470.
Double it to get one full round of the field. 2 times 470 equals 940.
Sam ran ten rounds, so multiply one round by 10. 10 times 940 equals 9400.
The distance is 9400 metres. Since 1000 metres is 1 kilometre, divide by 1000 to change it to kilometres. 9400 divided by 1000 equals 9.4.
Sam ran 9.4 kilometres.

Q_CH20_011_V04.q: A circle has a radius of 21 centimetres. What is its area? Use pi as 22 over 7.
hints: This asks for the area of a circle, the space inside it. The rule uses pi and the radius.
Area equals pi times radius times radius. Put 21 in for the radius and 22 over 7 for pi. Try dividing 21 by 7 first.
A similar example: a circle with radius 7 centimetres. Area equals 22 over 7 times 7 times 7. First 7 divided by 7 equals 1. Then 22 times 1 times 7 equals 154. The area is 154 square centimetres.
steps: The area of a circle is pi times radius times radius. The radius is 21 centimetres.
Divide 21 by 7 first to make the sum easy. 21 divided by 7 equals 3.
Now multiply 22 by 3, then by 21. 22 times 3 times 21 equals 1386.
The area is 1386 square centimetres. 22 over 7 times 21 times 21 equals 1386.

Q_CH20_011_V05.q: A circle has a radius of 35 centimetres. What is its circumference? Use pi as 22 over 7.
hints: This asks for the circumference, the distance all the way around the circle. The rule uses pi and the radius.
Circumference equals 2 times pi times radius. Put 35 in for the radius and 22 over 7 for pi. Try dividing 35 by 7 first.

A similar example: a circle with radius 21 centimetres. Circumference equals 2 times 22 over 7 times 21. First 21 divided by 7 equals 3. Then 2 times 22 times 3 equals 132. The circumference is 132 centimetres.
steps: The circumference of a circle is 2 times pi times radius. The radius is 35 centimetres.
Divide 35 by 7 first to make the sum easy. 35 divided by 7 equals 5.
Now multiply 2 by 22, then by 5. 2 times 22 times 5 equals 220.
The circumference is 220 centimetres. 2 times 22 over 7 times 35 equals 220.

Q_CH20_012.q: The length and breadth of a rectangle add up to 12 centimetres and they differ by 2 centimetres. Find the area.
hints: Before you can find the area you need the length and the breadth. You know their sum and their difference, so find the two numbers first.
Look for two numbers that add up to 12 and are 2 apart. One way is to take the difference away from the sum and halve what is left, which gives the smaller number.

Similar example: the length and breadth add up to 14 centimetres and differ by 2 centimetres. Taking 2 from 14 leaves 12, and half of 12 is 6, so the breadth is 6 centimetres and the length is 6 plus 2, which is 8 centimetres. The area is 8 times 6, which is 48 square centimetres.
steps: Take the difference from the sum. What is left is two breadths. 12 minus 2 equals 10.
Halve it to get the breadth. 10 divided by 2 equals 5.
The length is 2 centimetres more than the breadth. 5 plus 2 equals 7.
Check that 7 plus 5 equals 12. Now multiply the length by the breadth to get the area. 7 times 5 equals 35.
The area is 35 square centimetres.

Q_CH20_012_V01.q: Each side of a square is 9 centimetres long. What is the perimeter of the square?
hints: This asks for perimeter, the distance all the way round the square. All four sides are the same length.
A square has 4 equal sides. So you need 4 lots of 9 centimetres.
Here is a similar one: a square with side 7 centimetres. Perimeter equals 4 times 7, which is 28 centimetres.
steps: A square has 4 equal sides, so the perimeter is 4 times side.
4 times 9 means 4 groups of 9. Add them up. 9 plus 9 plus 9 plus 9 equals 36.
So the perimeter is 36 centimetres. 4 times 9 equals 36.

Q_CH20_013.q: Which of the following has the least perimeter?
options: An equilateral triangle of side 6 centimetres
A rectangle with dimensions 5 centimetres and 3 centimetres
hints: Perimeter is the distance around a shape. Find the perimeter of each of the four shapes, then compare them.
Count the sides of each shape. A square and a rhombus each have 4 equal sides, an equilateral triangle has 3 equal sides, and a rectangle has two lengths and two breadths.

Similar example: compare an equilateral triangle of side 9 centimetres with a square of side 7 centimetres. The triangle's perimeter is 3 times 9, which is 27 centimetres and the square's is 4 times 7, which is 28 centimetres. The triangle has the smaller perimeter, even though its side is longer.
steps: The square has 4 sides of 5.5 centimetres, so its perimeter is 22 centimetres.
The equilateral triangle has 3 sides of 6 centimetres, so its perimeter is 18 centimetres.
The rectangle has two sides of 5 centimetres and two sides of 3 centimetres, so its perimeter is 16 centimetres. 2 times, 5 plus 3, equals 16.
The rhombus has 4 sides of 5 centimetres, so its perimeter is 20 centimetres.
Compare 22, 18, 16 and 20. The smallest is 16 centimetres, so the least perimeter belongs to a rectangle with dimensions 5 centimetres and 3 centimetres.

Q_CH20_014.q: The perimeter of an equilateral triangle is equal to that of a square of side 6 centimetres. What is the side of the triangle?
hints: Square perimeter equals 4 times 6, which is 24 centimetres. The triangle perimeter is the same, 24 centimetres.
Equilateral triangle: P equals 3 times side. So 3 times side equals 24.
Side equals 24 divided by 3, which is 8 centimetres.
steps: Square P equals 4 times 6, which is 24 centimetres
Triangle P equals 3 s, which is 24
S equals 24 divided by 3, which is 8 centimetres

Q_CH20_014_V05.q: Each side of a square is 19 centimetres long. What is the area of the square?
hints: This asks for the area of a square, the space inside it. All the sides of a square are equal.
For a square, area is side times side. Set up 19 times 19.
Here is a similar one: a square with side 7 centimetres. Area equals 7 times 7, which is 49 square centimetres.
steps: The area of a square is side times side.
Split 19 into 10 and 9. Multiply 19 by 10. 19 times 10 equals 190.
Now multiply 19 by 9. 19 times 9 equals 171.
Add the two parts. So the area is 361 square centimetres. 190 plus 171 equals 361.

Q_CH20_015.q: The area of a square is equal to the area of a rectangle whose length and breadth are 16 centimetres and 4 centimetres. Find the perimeter of the square.
hints: There are three stages here: the area of the rectangle, then the side of the square with the same area, then the perimeter of that square.
Multiply 16 by 4 to get the rectangle's area. Then look for a number that, multiplied by itself, gives that area.

Similar example: a square has the same area as a rectangle 9 centimetres by 4 centimetres. The area is 9 times 4, which is 36 square centimetres. Since 6 times 6 equals 36, the square's side is 6 centimetres, and its perimeter is 4 times 6, which is 24 centimetres.
steps: Find the area of the rectangle. 16 times 4 equals 64.
The square has the same area, 64 square centimetres. Since 8 times 8 equals 64, the side of the square is 8 centimetres.
The perimeter of a square is 4 times its side. 4 times 8 equals 32.
The perimeter of the square is 32 centimetres.

Q_CH20_016.q: The perimeter of a square equals the perimeter of a rectangle with length 16 centimetres and breadth 4 centimetres. Find the area of the square.
hints: There are three stages here: the perimeter of the rectangle, then the side of the square with the same perimeter, then the area of that square.
Find the rectangle's perimeter by adding 16 and 4 and doubling. Then share that perimeter equally among the 4 sides of the square.

Similar example: a square has the same perimeter as a rectangle 9 centimetres by 3 centimetres. The rectangle's perimeter is 2 times, 9 plus 3, which is 24 centimetres. The square's side is 24 divided by 4, which is 6 centimetres, so its area is 6 times 6, which is 36 square centimetres.
steps: Find the perimeter of the rectangle. 2 times, 16 plus 4, equals 40.
The square has the same perimeter. Share 40 centimetres among its 4 equal sides. 40 divided by 4 equals 10.
The area of a square is side times side. 10 times 10 equals 100.
The area of the square is 100 square centimetres.

Q_CH20_016_V04.q: A rectangle is 12 centimetres long and 11 centimetres wide. What is its perimeter?
hints: This asks for perimeter, the distance all the way round the rectangle. Remember that a rectangle has two lengths and two widths.
Add the length and the width first: 12 plus 11. Then think about how many of each side there are.
Here is a similar one: a rectangle 15 centimetres long and 10 centimetres wide. 15 plus 10 equals 25. Double it: 25 times 2 equals 50 centimetres.
steps: Perimeter is the distance all the way round. Start by adding the length and the width. 12 plus 11 equals 23.
There are two lengths and two widths, so double it. The perimeter is 46 centimetres. 23 times 2 equals 46.

Q_CH20_016_V08.q: A rectangle is 25 centimetres long and 16 centimetres wide. What is its area?
hints: This asks for area, the space inside the rectangle. Think about how the length and the width work together to cover it.
The area of a rectangle is length times width. Set up 25 times 16 and work it out.
Here is a similar one: a rectangle 11 centimetres long and 7 centimetres wide. Area equals 11 times 7, which is 77 square centimetres.
steps: The area of a rectangle is length times width.
Split 16 into 10 and 6. Multiply 25 by 10. 25 times 10 equals 250.
Now multiply 25 by 6. 25 times 6 equals 150.
Add the two parts. So the area is 400 square centimetres. 250 plus 150 equals 400.

Q_CH20_017.q: In a parallelogram, opposite sides are:
hints: Think about what a parallelogram looks like: a rectangle that has been pushed over to one side. Look at each pair of sides that face each other.
The name of the shape gives a clue about one property of its opposite sides. Then think about whether the two sides facing each other are the same length.

Similar example: in a trapezium, one pair of opposite sides is parallel, but those two sides are not the same length, and the other pair is not parallel at all. Ask the same two questions about a parallelogram: are the opposite sides parallel, and are they equal? Drawing one will help.
steps: The word parallelogram comes from the word parallel. Both pairs of opposite sides are parallel, which means they run in the same direction and never meet.
Measure the sides of any parallelogram and you find that each side is the same length as the side facing it.
So in a parallelogram, opposite sides are parallel and equal.

Q_CH20_018.q: In a rhombus, the axes of symmetry are:
options: There are no axes of symmetry
hints: A rhombus has 2 axes of symmetry. What are they?
If you fold a rhombus along either diagonal, both halves match perfectly.
The diagonals are the axes of symmetry.
steps: A rhombus has 2 axes of symmetry.
These axes are its two diagonals.

Q_CH20_019.q: Which of the following statements is true?
hints: Each statement says that every shape of one kind is also a shape of another kind. To test one, ask whether the first shape always has everything the second shape needs.

Write down what each shape needs. A rectangle needs four right angles. A square needs four right angles and four equal sides. A rhombus needs four equal sides. A parallelogram needs two pairs of parallel sides.

Similar example: is every square a rhombus? A rhombus needs four equal sides. Every square has four equal sides, so every square is a rhombus. Test each statement in the same way, by checking what the second shape needs.
steps: A rectangle is a four-sided shape with four right angles. A square has four right angles and also four equal sides.
Every square has four right angles, so every square has all that a rectangle needs.

The other statements can each be shown untrue with one drawing: a slanted rhombus has no right angles, a slanted parallelogram has no right angles, and a long rectangle does not have four equal sides.
The true statement is: Every square is a rectangle.

Q_CH20_019_V09.q: A rectangle is 26 centimetres long and 24 centimetres wide. What is its area?
hints: This asks for area, the space inside the rectangle. Think about how the length and the width work together to cover it.
The area of a rectangle is length times width. Set up 26 times 24 and work it out.
Here is a similar one: a rectangle 12 centimetres long and 5 centimetres wide. Area equals 12 times 5, which is 60 square centimetres.
steps: The area of a rectangle is length times width.
Split 24 into 20 and 4. Multiply 26 by 20. 26 times 20 equals 520.
Now multiply 26 by 4. 26 times 4 equals 104.
Add the two parts. So the area is 624 square centimetres. 520 plus 104 equals 624.

Q_CH20_020.q: A quadrilateral with exactly one pair of parallel sides is called a:
hints: Different quadrilaterals have different numbers of pairs of parallel sides. Go through the shapes you know and count the parallel pairs in each.
A parallelogram and a rhombus each have two pairs of parallel sides. Look for the shape that has just one pair.

Similar example: which quadrilateral has two pairs of parallel sides and four right angles, but not always four equal sides? Checking the shapes one by one, the rectangle fits. Check the shapes for parallel pairs in the same way.
steps: Count the pairs of parallel sides in each shape. A parallelogram has two pairs, and a rhombus also has two pairs.
A kite has two pairs of equal sides, but usually no parallel sides at all.
A trapezium has one pair of parallel sides, and its other two sides are not parallel.
So a quadrilateral with exactly one pair of parallel sides is called a trapezium.

Q_CH20_021.q: A kite has how many axes of symmetry?
hints: An axis of symmetry is a fold line that makes the two halves match exactly. Picture a kite, with two shorter sides at the top and two longer sides at the bottom.
Try folding the kite along each of its two corner-to-corner lines. Count only the folds where one half lands exactly on the other.

Similar example: a rhombus has four equal sides. Folding it along either of its corner-to-corner lines makes the halves match, so a rhombus has 2 axes of symmetry. The sides of a kite are not all equal, so test each of its folds with care.
steps: A kite has two pairs of equal sides that are next to each other: two shorter sides and two longer sides.
Fold along the line that joins the corner where the short sides meet to the corner where the long sides meet. One half lands exactly on the other, so this is an axis of symmetry.
Fold along the other corner-to-corner line. A short side would land on a long side, so the halves do not match.
A kite has 1 axis of symmetry.

Q_CH20_022.q: Three angles of a quadrilateral are 90 degrees, 85 degrees, and 110 degrees. What is the fourth angle?
hints: The four angles of any quadrilateral always add up to the same total. If you know three of them, the fourth is what is left.
The four angles add up to 360 degrees. Start by adding the three angles you know: 90 degrees, 85 degrees and 110 degrees.
Similar example: three angles of a quadrilateral are 80 degrees, 100 degrees and 120 degrees. They add to 300 degrees. The fourth angle is 360 degrees minus 300 degrees, which is 60 degrees.
steps: The four angles of a quadrilateral add up to 360 degrees.
Add the three angles you know. 90 degrees plus 85 degrees plus 110 degrees, which is 285 degrees.
Take that from 360 degrees to find the fourth angle. 360 degrees minus 285 degrees, which is 75 degrees.
The fourth angle is 75 degrees.

Q_CH20_023.q: The area of a square is 144 square centimetres. What is its side?
hints: The area of a square is its side multiplied by itself. Here you work backwards from the area to the side.
Look for a number that gives 144 when it is multiplied by itself. Try numbers a little bigger than 10, since 10 times 10 equals 100.

Similar example: a square has an area of 169 square centimetres. 10 times 10 equals 100, which is too small and 15 times 15 equals 225, which is too big. Trying 13 gives 13 times 13, which is 169, so the side is 13 centimetres.
steps: The area of a square is side times side, so find a number that multiplied by itself gives 144.
10 times 10 equals 100, which is too small, and 11 times 11 equals 121, which is still too small.
The next number to try is 12, and it gives exactly the area. 12 times 12 equals 144.
The side of the square is 12 centimetres.

Q_CH20_023_V04.q: A rectangle is 23 centimetres long and 7 centimetres wide. What is its area?
hints: This asks for area, the space inside the rectangle. Think about how the length and the width work together to cover it.
The area of a rectangle is length times width. Set up 23 times 7 and work it out.
Here is a similar one: a rectangle 11 centimetres long and 7 centimetres wide. Area equals 11 times 7, which is 77 square centimetres.
steps: The area of a rectangle is length times width.
Split 23 into 20 and 3. Multiply the 20 by 7. 7 times 20 equals 140.
Now multiply the 3 by 7. 7 times 3 equals 21.
Add the two parts. So the area is 161 square centimetres. 140 plus 21 equals 161.

Q_CH20_024.q: A rectangle has area 96 square centimetres and length 12 centimetres. What is its breadth?
hints: The area of a rectangle is length times breadth. Here the area and the length are known, so you work backwards with the opposite operation.
Ask yourself: 12 times what number gives 96? You can find it by dividing the area by the length.
Similar example: a rectangle has an area of 70 square centimetres and a length of 14 centimetres. The breadth is 70 divided by 14, which is 5 centimetres, because 14 times 5 equals 70.
steps: Length times breadth gives the area, so 12 times the breadth is 96.
Divide the area by the length. 96 divided by 12 equals 8.
Check: 12 times 8 equals 96. The breadth is 8 centimetres.

options: Are unequal but bisect at right angles
Are equal and bisect each other at right angles
Are unequal and do not bisect each other
Are equal but do not bisect at right angles
hints: A square is both a rectangle and a rhombus. Rectangle diagonals are equal. Rhombus diagonals bisect at 90 degrees.
So square diagonals are both equal and bisect at right angles.
This is the strongest diagonal property, only a square has both!
steps: From rectangle: diagonals are equal.
From rhombus: diagonals bisect at 90 degrees.
Square has both properties.

Q_CH20_025_V03.q: A rectangle is 28 centimetres long and 26 centimetres wide. What is its perimeter?
hints: This asks for perimeter, the distance all the way round the rectangle. Remember that a rectangle has two lengths and two widths.
Add the length and the width first: 28 plus 26. Then think about how many of each side there are.
Here is a similar one: a rectangle 9 centimetres long and 5 centimetres wide. 9 plus 5 equals 14. Double it: 14 times 2 equals 28 centimetres.
steps: Perimeter is the distance all the way round. Start by adding the length and the width. 28 plus 26 equals 54.
There are two lengths and two widths, so double it. The perimeter is 108 centimetres. 54 times 2 equals 108.

Q_CH20_025_V10.q: Each side of a square is 19 centimetres long. What is the perimeter of the square?
hints: This asks for perimeter, the distance all the way round the square. All four sides are the same length.
A square has 4 equal sides. So you need 4 lots of 19 centimetres.
Here is a similar one: a square with side 11 centimetres. Perimeter equals 4 times 11, which is 44 centimetres.
steps: A square has 4 equal sides, so the perimeter is 4 times side.
Split 19 into 10 and 9. Multiply the 10 by 4. 4 times 10 equals 40.
Now multiply the 9 by 4. 4 times 9 equals 36.
Add the two parts. So the perimeter is 76 centimetres. 40 plus 36 equals 76.

Q_CH21_001.q: A circle is a set of all points that are equidistant from a fixed point called the:
hints: All points on a circle are the same distance from one special point.
This fixed point in the middle is called the centre.
The centre is not on the circle, it's inside it!
steps: A circle is defined by its centre and radius.
The fixed point is the centre.

Q_CH21_003.q: If the radius of a circle is 9.5 centimetres, what is its diameter?
hints: This question is about two parts of a circle. The radius goes from the centre to the edge, and the diameter goes all the way across through the centre.
The diameter is made of two radii laid end to end. So the diameter is 2 times the radius. Work out 2 times 9.5.
A similar example: if the radius of a circle is 6.5 centimetres, the diameter is 2 times 6.5, which is 13 centimetres.
steps: The diameter goes right across the circle through the centre, so it is as long as two radii.
Multiply the radius by 2. 2 times 9.5 equals 19.
The diameter is 19 centimetres.

Q_CH21_004.q: The longest chord of a circle is called the:
hints: This question is about the names of the parts of a circle. A chord is a straight line that joins two points on the circle.
Picture a chord sliding across the circle. It gets longer as it moves towards the middle. Think about where it is longest, and what that line is called.

A similar example: a straight line from the centre of a circle to its edge is called the radius. It reaches only halfway across. Now think of the name for the straight line that goes all the way across, through the centre.
steps: A chord is a straight line joining two points on a circle.
A chord gets longer as it moves closer to the centre. It is longest when it passes right through the centre.
A chord that passes through the centre is called the diameter. So the longest chord of a circle is the diameter.

Q_CH21_005.q: How many axes of symmetry does a circle have?
hints: This question is about symmetry. An axis of symmetry is a fold line that makes the two halves of a shape match exactly.
Think about folding a paper circle in half. Any fold through the centre works. Now think about how many different folds through the centre you could make.

A similar example: a square can be folded exactly in half in 4 ways, two through the middles of opposite sides and two through opposite corners. So a square has 4 axes of symmetry. A circle is different, because it looks the same whichever way you turn it.
steps: An axis of symmetry is a line that cuts a shape into two matching halves.
Every line through the centre of a circle, which is every diameter, cuts it into two matching halves.
You can draw a diameter in any direction, and there is no end to the directions. So the number of axes of symmetry of a circle is infinite.

Q_CH21_006.q: Find the circumference of a circle with radius 21 centimetres. Use pi as 22 over 7.
hints: This question is about the circumference, the distance all the way round a circle. It is found from the diameter and pi.
The circumference is pi times the diameter. The radius is 21 centimetres, so first double it to get the diameter.

A similar example: a circle has radius 14 centimetres. The diameter is 2 times 14, which is 28 centimetres. The circumference is 22 over 7 times 28. Since 28 divided by 7 equals 4, this is 22 times 4, which is 88 centimetres.
steps: The circumference is pi times the diameter. First find the diameter by doubling the radius. 2 times 21 equals 42.
Now multiply the diameter by 22 over 7. Divide 42 by 7 first, which gives 6.
Then multiply 22 by 6. 22 times 6 equals 132.
The circumference is 132 centimetres. 22 over 7 times 42 equals 132.

Q_CH21_006_V01.q: A circle has a radius of 28 centimetres. What is its area? Use pi as 22 over 7.
hints: This asks for the area of a circle, the space inside it. The rule uses pi and the radius.
Area equals pi times radius times radius. Put 28 in for the radius and 22 over 7 for pi. Try dividing 28 by 7 first.

A similar example: a circle with radius 21 centimetres. Area equals 22 over 7 times 21 times 21. First 21 divided by 7 equals 3. Then 22 times 3 times 21 equals 1386. The area is 1386 square centimetres.
steps: The area of a circle is pi times radius times radius. The radius is 28 centimetres.
Divide 28 by 7 first to make the sum easy. 28 divided by 7 equals 4.
Now multiply 22 by 4, then by 28. 22 times 4 times 28 equals 2464.
The area is 2464 square centimetres. 22 over 7 times 28 times 28 equals 2464.

Q_CH21_006_V05.q: A circle has a radius of 14 centimetres. What is its circumference? Use pi as 22 over 7.
hints: This asks for the circumference, the distance all the way around the circle. The rule uses pi and the radius.
Circumference equals 2 times pi times radius. Put 14 in for the radius and 22 over 7 for pi. Try dividing 14 by 7 first.

A similar example: a circle with radius 21 centimetres. Circumference equals 2 times 22 over 7 times 21. First 21 divided by 7 equals 3. Then 2 times 22 times 3 equals 132. The circumference is 132 centimetres.
steps: The circumference of a circle is 2 times pi times radius. The radius is 14 centimetres.
Divide 14 by 7 first to make the sum easy. 14 divided by 7 equals 2.
Now multiply 2 by 22, then by 2. 2 times 22 times 2 equals 88.
The circumference is 88 centimetres. 2 times 22 over 7 times 14 equals 88.

Q_CH21_006_V07.q: A circle has a radius of 28 centimetres. What is its circumference? Use pi as 22 over 7.
hints: This asks for the circumference, the distance all the way around the circle. The rule uses pi and the radius.
Circumference equals 2 times pi times radius. Put 28 in for the radius and 22 over 7 for pi. Try dividing 28 by 7 first.

A similar example: a circle with radius 21 centimetres. Circumference equals 2 times 22 over 7 times 21. First 21 divided by 7 equals 3. Then 2 times 22 times 3 equals 132. The circumference is 132 centimetres.
steps: The circumference of a circle is 2 times pi times radius. The radius is 28 centimetres.
Divide 28 by 7 first to make the sum easy. 28 divided by 7 equals 4.
Now multiply 2 by 22, then by 4. 2 times 22 times 4 equals 176.
The circumference is 176 centimetres. 2 times 22 over 7 times 28 equals 176.

Q_CH21_006_V09.q: A circle has a radius of 7 centimetres. What is its circumference? Use pi as 22 over 7.
hints: This asks for the circumference, the distance all the way around the circle. The rule uses pi and the radius.
Circumference equals 2 times pi times radius. Put 7 in for the radius and 22 over 7 for pi. Try dividing 7 by 7 first.

A similar example: a circle with radius 21 centimetres. Circumference equals 2 times 22 over 7 times 21. First 21 divided by 7 equals 3. Then 2 times 22 times 3 equals 132. The circumference is 132 centimetres.
steps: The circumference of a circle is 2 times pi times radius. The radius is 7 centimetres.
Divide 7 by 7 first to make the sum easy. 7 divided by 7 equals 1.
Now multiply 2 by 22, then by 1. 2 times 22 times 1 equals 44.
The circumference is 44 centimetres. 2 times 22 over 7 times 7 equals 44.

Q_CH21_007.q: Find the circumference of a circle with diameter 14 centimetres. Use pi as 22 over 7.
hints: This question is about the circumference, the distance all the way round a circle. It is found from the diameter and pi.
The circumference is pi times the diameter, and here you are given the diameter. Multiply 14 by 22 over 7, dividing by 7 first to keep the numbers small.
A similar example: a circle has diameter 21 centimetres. The circumference is 22 over 7 times 21. Since 21 divided by 7 equals 3, this is 22 times 3, which is 66 centimetres.
steps: The circumference is pi times the diameter, so we need 22 over 7 times 14.
Divide 14 by 7 first, which gives 2.
Then multiply 22 by 2. The circumference is 44 centimetres.

Q_CH21_007_V01.q: A circle has a radius of 35 centimetres. What is its area? Use pi as 22 over 7.
hints: This asks for the area of a circle, the space inside it. The rule uses pi and the radius.
Area equals pi times radius times radius. Put 35 in for the radius and 22 over 7 for pi. Try dividing 35 by 7 first.

A similar example: a circle with radius 21 centimetres. Area equals 22 over 7 times 21 times 21. First 21 divided by 7 equals 3. Then 22 times 3 times 21 equals 1386. The area is 1386 square centimetres.
steps: The area of a circle is pi times radius times radius. The radius is 35 centimetres.
Divide 35 by 7 first to make the sum easy. 35 divided by 7 equals 5.
Now multiply 22 by 5, then by 35. 22 times 5 times 35 equals 3850.
The area is 3850 square centimetres. 22 over 7 times 35 times 35 equals 3850.

Q_CH21_007_V05.q: A circle has a radius of 14 centimetres. What is its area? Use pi as 22 over 7.
hints: This asks for the area of a circle, the space inside it. The rule uses pi and the radius.
Area equals pi times radius times radius. Put 14 in for the radius and 22 over 7 for pi. Try dividing 14 by 7 first.

A similar example: a circle with radius 21 centimetres. Area equals 22 over 7 times 21 times 21. First 21 divided by 7 equals 3. Then 22 times 3 times 21 equals 1386. The area is 1386 square centimetres.
steps: The area of a circle is pi times radius times radius. The radius is 14 centimetres.
Divide 14 by 7 first to make the sum easy. 14 divided by 7 equals 2.
Now multiply 22 by 2, then by 14. 22 times 2 times 14 equals 616.
The area is 616 square centimetres. 22 over 7 times 14 times 14 equals 616.

Q_CH21_008.q: The circumference of a circle is 440 metres. Find its radius. Use pi as 22 over 7.
hints: This question works backwards. You know the distance round the circle and must find the radius. Think about how the circumference is made from the diameter.
The circumference is 22 over 7 times the diameter. So for every 22 metres round the circle there are 7 metres across it. Start by dividing 440 by 22.

A similar example: the circumference of a circle is 88 metres. Dividing, 88 divided by 22 equals 4, so the diameter is 4 times 7, which is 28 metres. The radius is half of the diameter, so it is 28 divided by 2, which is 14 metres.
steps: The circumference is 22 over 7 times the diameter. So the circumference is 22 equal parts when the diameter is 7 of the same parts.
Find one part by dividing the circumference by 22. 440 divided by 22 equals 20.
The diameter is 7 parts, which is 140 metres. 7 times 20 equals 140.
Be careful here, because 140 metres is the diameter and the question asks for the radius. Halve it. The radius is 70 metres. 140 divided by 2 equals 70.

Q_CH21_009.q: The circumference of a circular park is 176 metres. Find its diameter. Use pi as 22 over 7.
hints: This question works backwards. You know the distance round the park and must find the distance straight across it.
The circumference is 22 over 7 times the diameter. So for every 22 metres round the circle there are 7 metres across it. Start by dividing 176 by 22.
A similar example: the circumference of a circular pond is 132 metres. Dividing, 132 divided by 22 equals 6. The diameter is 6 times 7, which is 42 metres.
steps: The circumference is 22 over 7 times the diameter. So the circumference is 22 equal parts when the diameter is 7 of the same parts.
Find one part by dividing the circumference by 22. 176 divided by 22 equals 8.
The diameter is 7 of these parts. 7 times 8 equals 56.
The diameter of the park is 56 metres.

Q_CH21_010.q: Find the area of a circle with radius 7 centimetres. Use pi as 22 over 7.
hints: This question is about the area of a circle, the space inside it. The area is found from the radius and pi.
The area of a circle is pi times the radius times the radius. Start by working out 7 times 7.

A similar example: a circle has radius 14 centimetres. First 14 times 14 equals 196. The area is 22 over 7 times 196. Since 196 divided by 7 equals 28, this is 22 times 28, which is 616 square centimetres.
steps: The area of a circle is pi times the radius times the radius. First multiply the radius by itself. 7 times 7 equals 49.
Now multiply 49 by 22 over 7. Divide 49 by 7 first, which gives 7.
Then multiply 22 by 7. The area is 154 square centimetres.

Q_CH21_011.q: Find the area of a circle with diameter 14 centimetres. Use pi as 22 over 7.
hints: This question is about the area of a circle. The area is found from the radius, so look carefully at which length you have been given.
You are given the diameter, 14 centimetres. Halve it to find the radius first. Then the area is pi times the radius times the radius.

A similar example: a circle has diameter 42 centimetres. The radius is 42 divided by 2, which is 21 centimetres. Then 21 times 21 equals 441. The area is 22 over 7 times 441. Since 441 divided by 7 equals 63, this is 22 times 63, which is 1386 square centimetres.
steps: The area uses the radius, and we are given the diameter. Halve the diameter to find the radius. 14 divided by 2 equals 7.
Multiply the radius by itself. 7 times 7 equals 49.
Now multiply 49 by 22 over 7. Since 49 divided by 7 equals 7, this is 22 times 7. 22 times 7 equals 154.
The area is 154 square centimetres.

Q_CH21_012.q: A circular track has radius 35 metres. How far does a runner go in 3 laps? Use pi as 22 over 7.
hints: This is a two-part question. One lap of a circular track is the circumference of the circle, and the runner goes round more than once.
Find one lap first. The circumference is pi times the diameter, and the diameter is 2 times 35, which is 70 metres. After that, remember there are 3 laps.

A similar example: a circular track has radius 14 metres and a runner does 2 laps. The diameter is 28 metres, so one lap is 22 over 7 times 28, which is 88 metres. Two laps are 2 times 88, which is 176 metres.
steps: One lap is the circumference. First double the radius to get the diameter. 2 times 35 equals 70.
The circumference is 22 over 7 times the diameter. Since 70 divided by 7 equals 10, one lap is 22 times 10, which is 220 metres.
The runner does 3 laps, so multiply by 3. The runner goes 660 metres. 3 times 220 equals 660.

Q_CH21_012_V02.q: A circle has a radius of 7 centimetres. What is its area? Use pi as 22 over 7.
hints: This asks for the area of a circle, the space inside it. The rule uses pi and the radius.
Area equals pi times radius times radius. Put 7 in for the radius and 22 over 7 for pi. Try dividing 7 by 7 first.

A similar example: a circle with radius 21 centimetres. Area equals 22 over 7 times 21 times 21. First 21 divided by 7 equals 3. Then 22 times 3 times 21 equals 1386. The area is 1386 square centimetres.
steps: The area of a circle is pi times radius times radius. The radius is 7 centimetres.
Divide 7 by 7 first to make the sum easy. 7 divided by 7 equals 1.
Now multiply 22 by 1, then by 7. 22 times 1 times 7 equals 154.
The area is 154 square centimetres. 22 over 7 times 7 times 7 equals 154.

Q_CH21_013.q: 5 points are marked on a circle. How many chords can be drawn by joining these points?
hints: This is a counting question about joining points in pairs. Every chord joins two of the points, so you need to count the pairs without counting any chord twice.
Name the points A, B, C, D and E. Start at A and count the chords it makes with the other points. Then move to B and count only the chords that are new.

A similar example: 4 points P, Q, R and S are marked on a circle. P joins to Q, R and S, which is 3 chords. Q joins to R and S, which is 2 new chords. R joins to S, which is 1 new chord. That makes 3 plus 2 plus 1, which is 6 chords.
steps: Name the points A, B, C, D and E. From A we can draw chords to B, C, D and E. That is 4 chords.
From B the chord to A is already drawn, so only the chords to C, D and E are new. That is 3 more.
From C there are 2 new chords, to D and E. From D there is 1 new chord, to E. From E every chord is already drawn.
Add them up. So 10 chords can be drawn. 4 plus 3 plus 2 plus 1 equals 10.

Q_CH21_014.q: A diameter divides a circle into two equal parts. Each part is called a:
hints: This question is about the names of the parts of a circle. Think about what fraction of the circle each part is.
A diameter passes through the centre and cuts the circle into two equal parts, so each part is half of the circle. Think of the word that means half a circle.

A similar example: two diameters that cross at right angles cut a circle into four equal parts. Each part is a quarter of the circle, so it is called a quarter circle. One diameter makes only two parts, so here each part is a half.
steps: A diameter passes through the centre of the circle, so the two parts it makes are equal.
Each part is exactly half of the circle. The word semi means half.
So each of the two equal parts is called a semicircle.

Q_CH21_015.q: A wheel has diameter 28 centimetres. How many complete rotations will it make to cover 440 centimetres? Use pi as 22 over 7.
hints: 1 rotation equals 1 circumference, which is pi d, which is 22 over 7 times 28.
28 divided by 7 equals 4. C equals 22 times 4, which is 88 centimetres per rotation.
Rotations equals 440 divided by 88, which is 5.
steps: C equals pi d, which is 22 over 7 times 28, which is 88 centimetres
Rotations equals 440 divided by 88, which is 5
5 complete rotations

Q_CH21_016.q: Circles that have the same centre but different radii are called:
hints: This question is about a special name for a set of circles. Look closely at what the circles share and what is different about them.
Picture the rings on a target board, or the ripples when a stone drops into a pond. The rings all have the same middle point but different sizes. Think of the word that means sharing a centre.

A similar example: circles that have the same radius are exactly the same size, so they are called equal or congruent circles. Here it is the other way round, because the sizes are different and the centre is the same.
steps: These circles have different radii, so they are different sizes. They cannot be equal or congruent.
They all share one centre, like the rings on a target board.
Circles with the same centre but different radii are called concentric circles.

Q_CH21_017.q: The area of a circle is 616 square centimetres. Find its radius. Use pi as 22 over 7.
hints: This question works backwards. You know the area of the circle and must find the radius. Think about how the area is made from the radius.
The area is 22 over 7 times the radius times the radius. Undo the 22 over 7 first by dividing 616 by 22 and then multiplying by 7. That gives the radius times itself.

A similar example: the area of a circle is 1386 square centimetres. Dividing, 1386 divided by 22 equals 63, and 63 times 7 equals 441. So the radius times itself is 441. Since 21 times 21 equals 441, the radius is 21 centimetres.
steps: The area is 22 over 7 times the radius times the radius. Undo the 22 over 7 by dividing by 22 and then multiplying by 7.
Divide the area by 22. 616 divided by 22 equals 28.
Multiply by 7. This is the radius times itself. 28 times 7 equals 196.
Do not stop at 196. We need the number that gives 196 when it is multiplied by itself. It is between 10 and 20, because 10 times 10 equals 100 and 20 times 20 equals 400.
Trying 14 gives 14 times 14, which is 196. The radius is 14 centimetres.

Q_CH21_018.q: For a circle with radius 7 centimetres, which is larger numerically: the circumference or the area?
hints: This question asks you to find two measurements of the same circle and compare the numbers. One is the distance round it and the other is the space inside it.
Work out both. The circumference is pi times the diameter, and the diameter is 14 centimetres. The area is pi times the radius times the radius. Then see which number is bigger.

A similar example: for a circle with radius 14 centimetres, the circumference is 22 over 7 times 28, which is 88 and the area is 22 over 7 times 14 times 14, which is 616. As numbers, 616 is larger than 88, so the area is the larger number.
steps: The diameter is 2 times 7, which is 14 centimetres. The circumference is 22 over 7 times the diameter, which is 44. 22 over 7 times 14 equals 44.
The area is 22 over 7 times the radius times the radius, which is 154. 22 over 7 times 7 times 7 equals 154.
Looking only at the numbers, 154 is greater than 44. So the area is larger, since 154 is greater than 44.

Q_CH21_019.q: How many radii and diameters can a circle have?
hints: This question is about counting the lines you could draw in a circle. A radius joins the centre to a point on the circle, and a diameter goes right across through the centre.
Think about how many points there are on the circle that a radius could reach. Then think about how many directions a line through the centre could take.

A similar example: how many points are there on a circle? Between any two points on the curve you can always mark another one, so the count never ends. We say a circle has infinite points. Use the same idea for the lines drawn from the centre and through the centre.
steps: A radius joins the centre to a point on the circle. There is no end to the points on a circle, so there is no end to the radii.
A diameter is a straight line through the centre. It can point in any direction, and there is no end to the directions, so there is no end to the diameters.
So a circle can have infinite radii, infinite diameters.

Q_CH21_020.q: Find the perimeter of a semicircle with diameter 14 centimetres. Use pi as 22 over 7.
hints: This question is about the perimeter of a semicircle, the distance all the way round its edge. Look at the shape carefully, because the edge has more than one part.
A semicircle has a curved edge and a straight edge. Start with the curved edge, which is half of the circumference of the whole circle. Then think about the straight edge.

A similar example: a semicircle has diameter 42 centimetres. The whole circumference would be 22 over 7 times 42, which is 132 centimetres, so the curved edge is 132 divided by 2, which is 66 centimetres. The straight edge is the diameter, 42 centimetres. The perimeter is 66 plus 42, which is 108 centimetres.
steps: The circumference of the whole circle is 22 over 7 times the diameter. 22 over 7 times 14 equals 44.
The curved edge of the semicircle is half of this. 44 divided by 2 equals 22.
The perimeter goes all the way round, so it also includes the straight edge. The straight edge is the diameter, 14 centimetres.
Add the curved edge and the straight edge. The perimeter is 36 centimetres. 22 plus 14 equals 36.

Q_CH21_020_V02.q: Each side of a square is 12 centimetres long. What is the area of the square?
hints: This asks for the area of a square, the space inside it. All the sides of a square are equal.
For a square, area is side times side. Set up 12 times 12.
Here is a similar one: a square with side 5 centimetres. Area equals 5 times 5, which is 25 square centimetres.
steps: The area of a square is side times side.
Split 12 into 10 and 2. Multiply 12 by 10. 12 times 10 equals 120.
Now multiply 12 by 2. 12 times 2 equals 24.
Add the two parts. So the area is 144 square centimetres. 120 plus 24 equals 144.

Q_CH21_020_V05.q: A rectangle is 21 centimetres long and 16 centimetres wide. What is its area?
hints: This asks for area, the space inside the rectangle. Think about how the length and the width work together to cover it.
The area of a rectangle is length times width. Set up 21 times 16 and work it out.
Here is a similar one: a rectangle 9 centimetres long and 4 centimetres wide. Area equals 9 times 4, which is 36 square centimetres.
steps: The area of a rectangle is length times width.
Split 16 into 10 and 6. Multiply 21 by 10. 21 times 10 equals 210.
Now multiply 21 by 6. 21 times 6 equals 126.
Add the two parts. So the area is 336 square centimetres. 210 plus 126 equals 336.

Q_CH21_020_V07.q: A rectangle is 29 centimetres long and 20 centimetres wide. What is its perimeter?
hints: This asks for perimeter, the distance all the way round the rectangle. Remember that a rectangle has two lengths and two widths.
Add the length and the width first: 29 plus 20. Then think about how many of each side there are.
Here is a similar one: a rectangle 9 centimetres long and 5 centimetres wide. 9 plus 5 equals 14. Double it: 14 times 2 equals 28 centimetres.
steps: Perimeter is the distance all the way round. Start by adding the length and the width. 29 plus 20 equals 49.
There are two lengths and two widths, so double it. The perimeter is 98 centimetres. 49 times 2 equals 98.

Q_DH_001.q: In a pictograph, one apple picture stands for 5 apples. If Monday shows three apple pictures, how many apples were sold?
hints: This is a pictograph question. Each picture stands for more than one thing, so look at the key first.
Count how many apple pictures Monday shows. Each one stands for 5 apples.
A similar example: one star picture stands for 4 books and Tuesday shows 6 stars. 6 times 4 equals 24 books.
steps: The key says each picture stands for 5 apples.
Monday shows 3 pictures, so multiply. 3 times 5 equals 15.
15 apples were sold.

Q_DH_002.q: In a bar graph, the tallest bar represents:
hints: This question is about reading a bar graph. Think about what the height of a bar tells you.
Imagine a bar graph of marks. A child with more marks gets a taller bar. So what does the tallest bar show?
A similar example: in a bar graph of rainfall, the shortest bar belongs to the month with the least rain. The height of a bar always matches the size of its value.
steps: In a bar graph, the height of each bar shows how big its value is.
A bigger value gets a taller bar.
So the tallest bar represents the largest value.

hints: This asks for the mean, which is another word for average. It is the fair share if the total were split equally.
First add all five numbers together. Then think about how many numbers there are.
A similar example: the mean of 4, 6, 8, 10 and 12. Add them: 4 plus 6 plus 8 plus 10 plus 12 equals 40. There are 5 numbers, so 40 divided by 5 equals 8. The mean is 8.
steps: Add all the numbers. 12 plus 15 plus 18 plus 21 plus 24 equals 90.
There are 5 numbers, so divide the total by 5. 90 divided by 5 equals 18.
The mean is 18.

hints: This asks for the mode. The mode is the number that appears most often in a list.
Go through the list and count how many times each number appears. A tally can help.
A similar example: in 4, 8, 6, 8, 1, 8, 6 the number 8 appears three times and 6 appears twice. Nothing appears more often than 8, so the mode is 8.
steps: Count how many times each number appears in 3, 5, 7, 5, 9, 5, 2.
5 appears 3 times. Every other number appears only once.
The mode is 5.

hints: This asks for the range. The range tells you how far apart the biggest and smallest numbers are.
Find the biggest number and the smallest number in the list. You will need both.
A similar example: the range of 6, 19, 11, 3 and 15. The biggest is 19 and the smallest is 3. 19 minus 3 equals 16, so the range is 16.
steps: The biggest number is 22 and the smallest is 5.
Subtract the smallest from the biggest. 22 minus 5 equals 17.
The range is 17.

Q_DH_007.q: In a pictograph, one smiley face stands for 10 students. Two smiley faces and a half represents:
hints: This is a pictograph question with a half picture. A half picture stands for half of what a full one stands for.
Count the full pictures first and work out what they stand for. Then find what half a picture is worth.
A similar example: one picture stands for 8 toys, and a row shows 3 full pictures and a half. 3 times 8 equals 24, and half of 8 is 4. 24 plus 4 equals 28 toys.
steps: Each full picture stands for 10 students. There are 2 full pictures. 2 times 10 equals 20.
The half picture stands for half of 10. 10 divided by 2 equals 5.
Add the two parts. 20 plus 5 equals 25.
The row represents 25 students.

Q_DH_008.q: Bar A shows 45, Bar B shows 30. The difference is:
hints: This asks for the difference between two bars. Difference means how much more one is than the other.
To find a difference, take the smaller value away from the bigger one.
A similar example: one bar shows 62 and another shows 40. 62 minus 40 equals 22, so the difference is 22.
steps: Difference means subtract the smaller value from the bigger one.
Bar A is 45 and Bar B is 30. 45 minus 30 equals 15.
The difference is 15.

Q_DH_009.q: If you toss a coin, getting a head is:
hints: This is about chance. Think about all the things that can happen when you toss a coin.
A coin has two sides, heads and tails. Is one side more likely to land face up than the other?
A similar example: a bag has 5 red balls and 5 blue balls. Each colour has the same number of balls, so picking red has the same chance as picking blue.
steps: A coin has two sides: heads and tails.
Both sides have the same chance of landing face up.
So getting a head is equally likely as tails.

Q_DH_010.q: A table shows: Monday 12, Tuesday 15, Wednesday 18, Thursday 10, Friday 20. Total:
hints: This asks for a total from a table. Total means add all the values together.
Add the numbers a few at a time. Look for pairs that make easy tens, like 12 and 18.
A similar example: Monday 11, Tuesday 14, Wednesday 9, Thursday 16. Pair them up: 11 plus 9 equals 20 and 14 plus 16 equals 30. Then 20 plus 30 equals 50 in total.
steps: Pair numbers that make tens. 12 plus 18 equals 30.
Add the other easy pair. 10 plus 20 equals 30.
Now add everything. 30 plus 30 plus 15 equals 75.
The total is 75.

Q_DH_011.q: Average of 5 numbers is 20. Four numbers are 15, 22, 18, 25. Find the 5th.
hints: This is an average problem worked backwards. If you know the average and how many numbers there are, you can find their total.
First find the total of all five numbers. Multiply the average by how many numbers there are.

A similar example: the average of 4 numbers is 10, and three of them are 8, 12 and 9. The total must be 4 times 10 equals 40. The three known numbers add up to 29. 40 minus 29 equals 11, so the fourth number is 11.
steps: The total of all 5 numbers is the average times 5. 5 times 20 equals 100.
Add the four numbers you know. 15 plus 22 plus 18 plus 25 equals 80.
The fifth number is what is left. 100 minus 80 equals 20.
The fifth number is 20.

Q_DH_012.q: An event that will definitely happen is called:
hints: This is about the words we use for chance. Each word tells how sure we are that something will happen.
Think of something that must happen, like the sun rising tomorrow. Which word says there is no doubt at all?
A similar example: picking a green ball from a bag that has only red balls can never happen. An event that can never happen is called impossible.
steps: Some events may or may not happen. Others can never happen.
An event that will definitely happen has no doubt about it.
Such an event is called certain.

Q_DH_013.q: In a pie chart, if 'Cricket' takes up one quarter of the circle, the angle is:
hints: This is about a pie chart. A full circle has 360 degrees at its centre, and each slice takes a share of that.
The slice is one quarter of the circle. So you need one quarter of the full turn of 360 degrees.
A similar example: a slice that takes up 1 over 6 of the circle. 360 divided by 6 equals 60, so its angle is 60 degrees.
steps: A full circle is 360 degrees.
One quarter means divide by 4. 360 divided by 4 equals 90.
The angle is 90 degrees.

hints: This asks for the median. The median is the middle number once the list is in order.
First write the numbers from smallest to biggest. Do not pick the middle one until they are in order.
A similar example: the median of 8, 2, 6, 12 and 4. In order they are 2, 4, 6, 8, 12. The middle one is 6, so the median is 6.
steps: Put the numbers in order: 3, 5, 7, 9, 11.
There are 5 numbers, so the middle one is the third.
The median is 7.

Q_DH_015.q: 36 books need to be shown. If each symbol equals 6 books, how many symbols?
